Sports.title: Brown reveals Djokovic advice that will help McLaren after 'underperformance'
Sports.content:
McLaren chief executive Zak Brown says he is using advice from Novak Djokovic to aid his team's attempt to bounce back after losing both of their Formula 1 titles to Mercedes this season.

Lando Norris was replaced as world champion by Kimi Antonelli at the Mexico City Grand Prix earlier this month before Mercedes sealed a dominant Constructors' Championship triumph a week later in Brazil.

McLaren won their first constructors' title in 26 years in 2024 before repeating the feat the following year, but a major change in the sport's regulations reset the pecking order ahead of the 2026 season.

Asked during a special episode of Sky Sports' The F1 Show about watching Mercedes celebrate on the podium after Norris had claimed something of a consolation victory for McLaren at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, Brown jokingly replied: "I just want to push them off and get our team back up there!

"I mean, first of all, congratulations to Mercedes and Kimi. Now I have an appreciation for how hard this is.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes party on the podium after sealing their ninth Constructors' Championship title

"And the sport is so competitive and the top four teams, I mean, to beat a Red Bull, beat a Mercedes, beat a Ferrari, you've got to be damn good.

"It just makes me want it more. We won 14 races last year. I don't think anyone's ever won 14, two in a row.

"We've won three this year. Madrid, coulda, shoulda, woulda. So it's been a year that I feel like we've underperformed on the whole, but that's a learning. It makes us stronger.

"I think Brazil was awesome. That was McLaren at its best. The upgrades were great, the strategy, the drivers.

Brown then explained how tennis icon Djokovic, who has won a record 24 men's Grand Slam singles titles, previously gave him some advice that he and McLaren team principal Andrea Stella have taken on board as they prepare for the 2027 season.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look as Novak Djokovic and Alexander Zverev served up an unbelievable rally during their clash at the China Open

"It's sport, and the big thing is, Novak Djokovic is a good friend of ours, and he's quite inspiring," Brown said. "When people say things to me, they stick with me, certain things.

"And he said, 'you can't control your emotions, how you feel is how you feel, but you can control how you react to them.'

"So, the emotions of not winning, as Andrea says, no poison biscuits, but you kind of sit back, take a deep breath, and you go, you know what, 'that's what happened, now let's go push forward and win.' And it makes winning feel so good."

'A lot of changes' to be made to 2027 McLaren

McLaren's relative struggles this season, during which Norris has still managed three wins with two races to go, were contributed to by the team pushing until the end of 2025 while others switched more focus to working on their 2026 cars.

There ended up being fundamental issues with the MCL40, such as a shorter wheelbase than some of their rivals, that made it difficult for them to consistently compete for wins.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on the Sky Sports F1 Show podcast, Zak Brown explains why McLaren struggled to challenge for the 2026 title, despite Lando Norris attempting to defend his championship

Asked whether this was something that will be addressed on next year's challenger, Brown said: "Yeah, always addressing the race car.

"Weight was a big issue this year for a lot of cars, obviously a shorter wheelbase (results in a) lighter car.

"So yeah, I think there's things that, slow speed corners weren't great for us.

"We've learned a lot about the power unit this year, and deployment, and all the stuff that, we're all still learning.

"So yeah, I think this season, there's a lot of takeaways and changes we're going to make going into 2027."

'I've never seen Lando drive better'

Norris' superb victory at Interlagos saw the Brit continue his dominance over his team-mate Oscar Piastri this season.

After the pair were extremely closely matched last season as Norris edged out Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Piastri for the title, there has been a clear gap between them in 2026.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lando Norris wins the Sao Paulo GP ahead of Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar

Norris is 94 points ahead of Piastri in the drivers' standings, has all three of McLaren's grand prix victories this season, and six podiums to Piastri's two.

There have been similarly surprising shifts in performance from last year to this year at other teams, with Antonelli outpacing George Russell at Mercedes and Lewis Hamilton proving far more competitive against his Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc in the new cars.

Brown reflected: "I think we've seen it mix up a little bit of the grid, right? Charles last year got the better of Lewis. Lewis is getting the better of him. George got the better of Kimi, so I think it's mixed up the grid a little bit.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on the Sky Sports F1 Show podcast, Zak Brown explains why Lando Norris outperformed Oscar Piastri in the 2026 car

"I think if you look at Oscar's strengths, there were kind of big, brave corners. Now all of a sudden these new big, brave corners, it's like, 'hey lift, conserve, preserve.' So, I think there's a small element of him having to adapt to a new car.

"And then let's not take any credit away from Lando. I've never seen him drive better.

"So, I think you have a combination of Lando who's driving the best I've ever seen him drive. Oscar who's just not yet clicked with it. There's your gap, but it's not a big gap."

Sports.title: 'I didn't know' - Price's controversial 145 checkout at Grand Slam explained
Sports.content:
Gerwyn Price produced a controversial 145 checkout en route to a routine Grand Slam of Darts victory over Sebastian Bialecki on Monday night in Wolverhampton.

Price, the three-time champion in Wolverhampton, came through 5-2 against Poland's Bialecki to book his place in the knockout stage.

However, there was controversy during the final Group E match as Price hit a 145 finish when he had 135 remaining in the fourth leg of the match.

What happened?

Image: Price defeated Bialecki to reach the last 16 in Wolverhampton

'The Iceman' needed 135 to hold his throw, and he thought he had taken it out.

After hitting T19 he asked referee Charlie Corstophine what he had left and was told 88.

However, he actually needed 78.

With 88 in mind, Price incorrectly hit T16 and D20 to finish off the leg and was given the hold.

Of course, Price believed he had gone the correct route for what he needed and went on to set up a last-16 date with Ryan Searle.

What did Price say?

"I didn't know until I just walked in [to the press conference]," said Price. "I hit the first treble and I asked what I'd got left and he said 88.

"So I went treble 16 double top and he said, 'game shot'."

The Welshman admitted he was glad he didn't know or it would have weighed on his mind.

He added: "I didn't even know until I came back here. I'm glad I didn't know because it probably would have played on my mind."

What does the PDC rulebook say?

6.4.6 Errors in arithmetic shall stand as detailed on the scoreboard unless corrected prior to the next throw of the player whose score is in error. Any error in the score can be corrected by the Referee at any time until Game Shot is called in that leg.

6.4.7 If the incorrect score resulted in a leg win the result will stand unless corrected prior to the start of the next leg.

Price on new format

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Price thrashed Peter Wright 16-8 to triumph at the Grand Slam of Darts in 2021

Both players went into the contest with one win each after beating Joe Hunt, which made it a straight shoot-out with only the group winners reaching the knockout stage this year.

Price had opened his week with a 5-3 win over Hunt on Saturday, racing into a 4-0 lead before Hunt won three legs in a row. Bialecki needed a deciding leg to beat Hunt 5-4 on Sunday.

The new format has already seen Ross Smith, Jonny Clayton and Luke Woodhouse suffer shock exits and Price said: "I prefer the old one [format], obviously. I've had some good memories here. You can slip up once, but in this one you can't.

"As you can see, a couple of good boys have gone, and they probably thought they'd have a second chance. But once you lose a game, that's it; you're gone."

Sports.title: British doubles No 1 criticises ATP bosses at trophy presentation absence
Sports.content:
British doubles No 1 Henry Patten has taken a swipe at ATP bosses for their absence from a trophy presentation in Turin on Monday.

Upon receiving the year-end doubles No 1 trophy from chief tour officer Andre Silva, alongside his Finnish partner Harri Heliovaara, Patten called out the ATP chairman Andrea Gaudenzi and CEO Eno Polo.

"For us, it's a really big deal. It's a real shame that the ATP chairman and CEO don't think the same." Patten said.

"It would have been nice to have them on court with us today, but here we are by ourselves."

Sky Sports News has contacted the ATP Tour for comment.

Patten and Heliovaara enjoyed a sensational season, winning Wimbledon for the second time in their careers and lifting trophies in Adelaide, Doha, Dubai, and Madrid.

The duo have repeatedly criticised the ATP's approach to doubles, including their proposals that would include smaller draws and reduce prize money for the 2028 season.

Patten and Dutch player Sem Verbeek spearheaded an open letter, signed by over a hundred other players - including former champions Bob and Mike Bryan - calling for the reform project to be scrapped.

Speaking to Sky Sports Tennis, Tim Henman said: "He [Patten] made his thoughts pretty clear about the lack of representation from the chair and the CEO on the tour.

"There is the conversation around massive reform in the doubles world, potentially cutting the doubles draw in half and that would save prize money that could go into the singles, so those doubles players are feeling like their jobs are in jeopardy.

"This is a great platform as the doubles is getting incredible support."

What the open letter opposes

Halving draw sizes. ATP Masters 1000 doubles draws would be cut in half to 16 teams, while smaller ATP 500 and 250 tournaments would drop to just eight teams



Cutting prize money. The share of tournament prize money allocated to doubles would drop from 20% to 10%, shifting roughly $20 million (£15 million) away from doubles specialists to fund early-round singles payouts



Heliovaara also addressed the crowd, thanking Patten and their team, saying: "I'm going to say that Henry is the best partner in the world for doubles. I've been lucky enough to play with him for two and a half years.

"We shared a lot of wins, a lot of losses, but most of all, a lot of time everywhere in the world, really. On the court, off court, it's been a very nice, amazing trip together. But it's not just the two of us, I think it's also our team there in the box, in the spotlight today.

"I would like that we also give a big hand to every one of them. It's a lot of sacrifices from us, from the team, and obviously our families at home. Everybody who has helped us to achieve something like this. And to have a trophy like that at home, we will be very proud for a very long time."

Patten and Heliovaara will now turn their attention to the task at hand in Turin, where they are 1-0 in round-robin play. They defeated Orlando Luz and Rafael Matos in a match tie-break on Sunday.

Sports.title: Fifa accused of climate ‘record of failure’ due to Aramco deal and tournament expansion
Sports.content:
The United Nations has been asked to review Fifa’s status as a signatory to a key environmental initiative, with complainants arguing football’s governing body has a “record of failure” on climate action.

Fifa is a signatory to the UN’s Sports for Climate Action Framework, a coalition which seeks to persuade sporting organisations to “work together to achieve a climate-resilient future”. Under the framework, signatories agree to cut their greenhouse gas emissions by 50% by 2030 and to “partner with key stakeholders to deliver joint climate action”. They can have their status as a signatory removed, however, if “sincerity in participation or ability to participate is a cause for concern”.

According to five organisations that have submitted a joint complaint to the UN, Fifa’s actions are inconsistent with its words. In a letter to executives at the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, they argue “being a signatory of the Framework means making a commitment to both organisational climate progress and climate leadership. On the basis of the facts laid out below, we assert that Fifa has a record of failure on each of these key commitments.”

The letter claims Fifa has undermined its commitments by expanding the size of its tournaments, with the men’s World Cup increasing from 64 matches in 2022 to 104 matches in 16 cities across three countries this past summer, making it what the complainants say is “the most polluting World Cup ever”. In 2030, by which time Fifa’s emissions should have been halved, the World Cup is due to be held in six countries across three different continents, with potentially 64 teams and even more matches.

The complainants acknowledge Fifa launched a climate strategy in 2021, committing it to halving emissions by 2030 and reaching net zero by 2040. “However,” the letter says, “that strategy is not clear on how exactly these targets will be achieved. The evidence indicates that Fifa has expanded, rather than reduced, its emissions in the years since, principally by choosing to expand the footprint of its major tournaments.”

A second part of the complaint argues Fifa has failed in its responsibility to “champion transformative climate action” by agreeing a multi-year commercial arrangement with the Saudi Arabian energy giant Aramco as a “major worldwide partner”.

The letter argues that Aramco is not only the world’s largest oil company but its “largest historic corporate polluter”. It says that at next year’s women’s World Cup, Aramco’s advertising “will be inescapable for the fans watching worldwide. We argue that Aramco is using Fifa … to ‘leverage the influential platform of sports to engage communities, fans and global audiences …’ to obstruct rather than further climate action.”

The organisations behind the letter are the New Weather Institute, the New Weather Institute Sweden, Fossil Free Football, Scientists for Global Responsibility and FairSquare. They have submitted the complaint while the UN’s climate summit, Cop31, is taking place in Turkey, and where athletes have shared with delegates the impact of the climate crisis on their sport.

The complainants say they “fully support the Framework’s Objectives and Principles” but warn that those “could be hindered if an organisation is able to claim signatory status while being seen to directly contradict its commitments”.

Fifa and the UNFCCC have been approached for comment. Aramco declined to comment.

Sports.title: Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta
Sports.content:
Thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February, but he couldn’t wait that long. Having received a reported £8m payoff from Spurs, he kept an extremely low profile in the first few months after an experience at the club that sources close to the 53‑year‑old have described as “traumatic”.

Frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association. It said he would cover the World Cup for the BBC (thereby going head-to-head with Ange Postecoglou, his predecessor at Spurs, who worked for ITV) before “experiencing the Tour de France”, a lifelong passion. Frank usually preferred to run to Brentford’s training ground and home matches from his home in East Sheen during a nine‑year spell as assistant and then manager, but he occasionally cycled because it helped to clear his head.

By the time the statement was released the Crystal Palace chair, Steve Parish, is understood to have sounded out Frank out over his willingness to take over from Oliver Glasner. But it confirmed his intention to keep his promise and not rush back into management. “When the time is right, I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication,” he said.

With Palace facing the prospect of ending a 14-season stay in the Premier League – the eighth‑longest in the division – after a dreadful start under Pierre Sage, that time has arrived. Frank left Tottenham with a win ratio of 34.2% – the worst of any permanent manager in the club’s history – but has the chance to redeem himself at a club he is said to have admired from afar.

According to the biography Thomas Frank: The Premier League Diaries, by the Danish author Kasper Steenbach, published last year, Frank attended the 2025 FA Cup final victory against Manchester City with a childhood friend from Denmark who supports Palace after arranging tickets for him. Frank is said to have been impressed by the atmosphere for which Selhurst Park has become renowned. That said, the absence of the influential supporters’ group the Holmesdale Fanatics since it disbanded at the start of the season has made it less intimidating for visiting teams.

Nonetheless, Frank is said to be itching to return to the dugout after failing at Spurs, where he inherited a squad that had just won the Europa League under Postecoglou but struggled to impose himself at a club with higher expectations. Frank’s preference to play on the counterattack with a more direct style looks a better fit at Palace, although his critics will question whether his success at Brentford was really down to the system put in place by the club’s owner, Matthew Benham, that has allowed Keith Andrews to thrive since the former set-piece coach stepped into Frank’s shoes.

There is no such framework in place at Palace, with their longevity in the Premier League mainly down to a series of shrewd managerial appointments at the right time by Parish which have ensured they have not finished lower than 15th since being promoted in 2013. Frank, who is also understood to have attracted interest from Denmark in the summer and Newcastle and Fulham in recent weeks after difficult starts for Matthias Jaissle and Álvaro Arbeloa respectively, will be expected to make an immediate impression.

For now he must make do with a squad seriously lacking in leaders after the sales of Marc Guéhi, Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Muñoz this year. Frank’s first task must be to instil some defensive discipline in a side who have conceded 24 goals in 10 league games.

His Brentford side were renowned for their organisation and prowess from set pieces, an area Palace have struggled with for several seasons. He will have to tread carefully if he intends to impose the “no dickheads” policy he borrowed from the All Blacks during his time as Brentford manager.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Sage’s attempts to impose himself on the squad by dropping the defenders Jaydee Canvot and Axel Disasi for poor performances and indiscipline respectively backfired because his team kept losing, not to mention that it angered Parish. Frank, who is believed to have been offered assurances that Palace will bring in defensive reinforcements in January, faces a delicate balancing act with a squad desperately low on morale.

The futures of Ismaïla Sarr and Jean‑Philippe Mateta could be key to Palace’s prospects of avoiding the drop. Sarr was the club’s player of the year when they won the Conference League last season but he played only 107 minutes in the Premier League under Sage owing to a groin injury. The Senegal forward’s head was turned by interest from Liverpool in the summer and Frank will have to rely on his best motivational skills to get the best out of him and Mateta, who is suspended for crucial games against Coventry and Hull after his red card against Tottenham.

The France striker tried to annul the final year of his contract after a move to Milan was scuppered by a failed medical in January and he is likely to push for a move again. But he remains popular in the dressing room and could be the talisman for Palace’s survival push if Frank can persuade him that the grass may not be greener.

Sports.title: ‘He wants to change lives’: the story behind Bukayo Saka’s Sócrates award
Sports.content:
Valerie Fiesser will never forget her surprise when Bukayo Saka contacted her out of the blue, asking whether he could help support a project in Nigeria in 2022. “I remember thinking: ‘Is this really Bukayo writing us an email?’” says the president of BigShoe, a non-profit organisation based in Frankfurt that has helped more than 10,000 children worldwide. “But that’s how he is. He’s always asking what more we can do.”

Four years on from that unexpected email, Fiesser was given the secret task of reaching out for a letter for Saka to read from the podium when he was presented with the Sócrates award at last month’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in London for his humanitarian work. She got the words from Byiringiro, a 14-year-old from Rwanda who had his eyesight restored after having surgery thanks to BigShoe’s initiative.

View image in fullscreen Bukayo Saka has teamed up with the charity BigShoe to cover 120 life-changing operations for children in Nigeria. Photograph: BigShoe

“They told me he was going to receive the award, but he didn’t know, so they asked whether I could get a letter from one of the children we had helped,” Fiesser says. “I was really proud of Bukayo, I think the way he did it was really special. He stood there so strongly for all these children around the world that nobody sees and nobody hears. He gave them a voice. He took the attention away from himself and put it into action. That’s how I know Bukayo. It’s never about him, it’s always about the people we help. He’s incredible.”

Saka, who donated more than 1,000 school uniforms to children in his home borough of Ealing in west London last year to help with the cost of living crisis, is understood to have heard about BigShoe from Antonio Rüdiger after the Real Madrid and Germany defender told him about some of the work he had done with the organisation in Africa. It has also worked with Philipp Lahm and Mesut Özil in the past. Fiesser says Saka and his family have taken a particularly close interest in which projects he supports.

View image in fullscreen Valerie Fiesser (left), the president of BigShoe, Saka and BigShoe’s chief executive, Florian Goll. Photograph: BigShoe

“When we had 150 life-changing surgeries taking place in Nigeria, he would message me asking to see pictures. He wanted to know what was happening and whether everybody was safe. He always asks whether the team has returned safely. I don’t know how he manages to find the time, but he does. His family are very similar. They genuinely want to make a big impact and provide meaningful help. I wouldn’t describe Bukayo as simply a donor to BigShoe. He’s more like a member of the BigShoe team. I know that he stands behind us.”

BigShoe was established by four friends in 2006 after the World Cup. As part of its latest projects in Rwanda and Nigeria, about 3,000 people had eye examinations and were provided with glasses if required. “Giving a child a pair of glasses can change their life,” Fiesser says. “We also help entire families. If a father can’t see properly, he might not be able to work or read. That affects the whole family.”

View image in fullscreen Children and community members in Kano, Nigeria, holding a sign for Saka after he partnered with the charity BigShoe. Photograph: BigShoe

BigShoe recently renovated a school in Rwanda and provided clean drinking water through a water filtration system. It has also built a library and provided private changing facilities for girls. “Once a month, some girls miss school because they don’t have suitable facilities or somewhere private to change,” says Fiesser. “We built facilities so they can continue attending school and have a quiet, private area.”

Saka’s hectic playing schedule means he has yet to make a visit but his family have been on the ground in Rwanda and he was heavily involved in funding earthquake relief projects in Morocco and Turkey. “We provided container homes for people affected by the earthquakes,” says Fiesser. “I knew I could count on him. It’s always important to Bukayo that we make a big impact. He doesn’t want money to be wasted. When I present a project to him, he wants to understand it properly. He needs to know exactly what we’re doing before he makes a decision. He’s a 100% person. Whatever he does, he gives it everything.”
