View image in fullscreen Saka giving his acceptance speech from the podium after winning the Sócrates award, which recognises humanitarian and social work. Photograph: Franck Fife/AFP/Getty Images

Saka’s mother, Adenike, is believed to be a driving force behind her son’s charitable work, with Fiesser describing her as “one of the most amazing women I’ve met”. Plans are being made for the next projects, which include providing health insurance to families in Nigeria and food packages for children in Rwanda over Christmas.

“He doesn’t just want to give someone food,” Fiesser says. “Of course, food is important, and we’re providing that too, but he wants to change lives. You can help someone, but if the help doesn’t last, then it hasn’t achieved what you really wanted. If we all work together, it doesn’t matter which team we’re supporting or which country we’re helping. We’re all part of one world.”

Sports.title: Echoes of Azteca but not like Argentina: fearless England start afresh in Madrid
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2. The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before.

The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards.

Against Mexico, the defender was sent off for a late tackle in the 54th minute with England 2-1 up. Against Spain, he contributed to Elliot Anderson being sent off in the 63rd minute with England 3-0 up. Quansah had his pocket picked by Lamine Yamal and Anderson’s attempt to chase back and rectify the situation ended with him fouling the winger.

It was not only a red card but a penalty; the prompt for Spain to launch a furious and hitherto unadvertised fightback. It had the stand that housed the press box shaking. Structural integrity was very much a theme.

As in Mexico, Tuchel made defensive changes. This time, it was Myles Lewis-Skelly for Harry Kane; Djed Spence for Anthony Gordon. Tuchel also withdrew Jude Bellingham, who went off shaking his head. It was easy to understand his frustration. He was excellent. Tuchel had removed his two prime attackers. He also put Dan Burn on towards the end, albeit this time not as part of a back five. England stayed in a 4-4-1 formation, with Quansah moving from central defence to right-back. As in Mexico, the 10-man low block resisted.

As much as Tuchel disagreed, this felt like Argentina reloaded as well. “No, not at all,” he said, when the World Cup semi-final defeat was raised. “Because of one man down. We would not have been in this situation if it was 11 against 11.”

The parallels, nevertheless, were there. Tuchel made defensive substitutions at 1-0 up against Argentina; it was a back five on that occasion. As against Spain, his team could not get out and they faced a flurry of chances. There were other factors in play at the World Cup, chief among them the high levels of fatigue within the squad. England could not hold out, conceding two late goals to exit and bring down a wave of criticism on Tuchel.

View image in fullscreen James Trafford’s double save, the second from Aymeric Laporte, preserved England’s lead late on. Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/Reuters

The score is the ultimate takeaway. It can skew analysis. Had Trafford not got back up after parrying a shot from the Spain substitute Fermín López to brilliantly repel Aymeric Laporte’s follow‑up, England would have gone from enjoying a fabulous result to stewing over an opportunity missed. The stakes were nowhere near as high as at the World Cup, but they would have gone from finishing top of their Nations League group to advancing into the quarter-finals as an unseeded second-place team.

In terms of Tuchel’s approach to the closing stages of a big game, what changed?

The truth for England lay in the opening 63 minutes. This was where the evidence of a decisive shift could be found, the reasons for the swell of optimism. England have never played better under Tuchel – and this was against the team to beat; the world and European champions. On their turf.

Spain were without the injured Rodri and Dani Olmo, and Luis de la Fuente strangely decided to use Pedri only as a substitute, but their lineup still shimmered with menace; Lamine Yamal was frightening. Yet before their penalty, converted by Mikel Oyarzabal, they did not have a shot on target. Or a real chance.

What stood out from the first whistle was England’s front‑foot intent; the bravery on the ball. They believed they would win and there was a fearlessness about them. They made forward moves on the half turn. There was a slickness about their combinations.

Spain have never suffered like this under De la Fuente and it was everything Tuchel had dreamed of when he started to plot a new version of his team after the World Cup; a more fluid game model, a response to the Argentina defeat.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Tuchel loved England’s buildup play, which included some of Trafford’s passing. He loved the high press; the aggression in the duels; the threat on set pieces. He said he loved the low-block defending too. Ben White was excellent at right-back and there was a coming-of-age performance from Lewis Hall at left-back, but it felt wrong to single out individuals.

“We didn’t stop and I think we are ready to go [like this] for 90 minutes,” Tuchel said. “It was a complete performance and we will not look back now. Go forward and stay hungry. We will not go back on this way of playing that we find ourselves since the World Cup.”

View image in fullscreen Lewis Hall, who did not go to the World Cup, put in a coming-of-age display against Spain. Photograph: David Ramos/Uefa/Getty Images

Ezri Konsa, who headed in the second goal from a Declan Rice corner, said England “would have scored two more” if they had kept 11 men on the pitch. “You saw until the red card how much quality we had,” he said.

“We dominated the game. The instruction was to keep going at them. Don’t stop. To keep our foot on the pedal. Argentina was different; different circumstances.”

Tuchel was asked about the journey from the heartbreak of Argentina to this point; the end of a stirring Nations League group campaign, including the 7-0 win against Croatia in Rijeka. It has not all been super exciting; the 2-1 Wembley win against Croatia last Thursday, for example, was a grind. Was he always confident of a successful reboot?

“It took me a while to digest [the World Cup] and see the way forward,” he said. “How we can help and adjust and improve? We had reviews and so on but the clarity came in the first Nations League camp [in September and October] with the players.

“The first week was not so easy. Some players were still upset from the World Cup. Some were new in the team. Some had digested it, some had not. But it was important to have this process together and everyone committed to wanting to improve in certain aspects of the game.

“We had the energy right to take the next steps and from there we went. Full credit to the players, how they buy in. It’s amazing that it came together like this now.”

Sports.title: Switzerland roll over sorry Scotland to increase the pressure on Pocognoli
Sports.content:
A match that should have been about 103 was instead about four. Andy Robertson is due acclaim for becoming the most capped player in Scotland’s history but how the full-back will wish the moment had arrived in different circumstances.

A second-string Switzerland team pulled Scotland apart, raising further and significant questions about the suitability of Sébastien Pocognoli to carry out the job his paymasters boldly entrusted him with. Scottish FA giddiness about Pocognoli as the successor to Steve Clarke, a hugely successful leader of the national team, is looking increasingly ridiculous. “I don’t think you’ve got time in international football,” said Robertson as dust settled here. Ouch.

This was a horrible night for Pocognoli, who is under serious pressure just three months into his tenure. Scotland’s players looked a disillusioned and disorganised lot. Pocognoli has never previously managed in international football, which renders it reasonable to ask his qualifications to improve this grim scenario. Scotland have finished a distant third in a favourable Nations League section. Ramifications exist for the Euro 2028 qualifying draw in December. Pocognoli is taking a pounding in the court of public opinion.

“The score is painful,” said Pocognoli. “I see a lot of good things in the way that we try to play. The result is heavy but the players gave everything. They enjoy playing like this.” An eye test suggests otherwise. Scotland are overly generous in defence, lame in midfield and powder-puff in attack. It is quite the mix.

Pocognoli’s demeanour during pre-match media duties suggested he was irritated by the early questioning of his approach. The Belgian is unwilling to deviate from the deployment of three centre-backs whether Scotland are at home to North Macedonia or away to Switzerland. While the prospect of facing a highly impressive Swiss team would ordinarily make Scots gulp, there was cause for hope in St Gallen. Not only had Switzerland already won Group B1 but they were in makeshift form.

Switzerland’s lack of cohesion was apparent during an opening spell where the visitors looked decent. A flurry of set pieces and a John McGinn half volley that dipped over Yvon Mvogo’s crossbar emphasised Scottish attacking intent. On a difficult pitch, Switzerland’s first 20 minutes lacked purpose. As good as things were to get for Scotland, alas.

View image in fullscreen Andy Robertson’s record-breaking match was a game to forget for Scotland. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

There appeared no real danger as Zachary Athekame fired in a hopeful cross from the Swiss right. Scotland had an abundance of cover inside their own penalty area. The problem was that one of those charged with clearing lines, Lewis Ferguson, instead poked the ball past Angus Gunn. No own goals are pretty; this one was especially ugly. Ferguson had needlessly panicked.

Scotland attempted an immediate response as Aaron Hickey headed wide. The Brentford man had to be withdrawn before the interval, apparently damaging his left hamstring when making a defensive intervention.

Hickey, whose career has been seriously disrupted by injury, was understandably distraught. Although Switzerland were by now in control, McGinn spurned a glorious opportunity five minutes before the interval when heading straight at Mvogo. Adrian Bajrami spared McGinn’s blushes with an even worse miss at the opposite end before the teams headed for their orange wedges. The half had been humdrum in nature.

Ferguson shanking the ball out for a Switzerland corner set the tone for a spell where the game was put firmly out of Scotland’s reach. Samuel Ballet burst forward from midfield before playing a one-two with Remo Freuler and slamming towards the Scotland net. The ball was heading in before Winsley Boteli made certain, with the video assistant referee dismissing Scotland’s appeals for offside. The ease with which Ballet evaded those in navy blue was as striking as the space Freuler found himself in. Scotland’s structure, once a staple, was nonexistent. Five defenders and two deep lying midfielders were being gleefully ignored by the rampaging Swiss.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Alvyn Sanches fires home Switzerland’s third goal of the night. Photograph: Michael Schmid/Keystone/AP

Number three was another Scotland horror show. Nathan Patterson was dispossessed by Boteli. The forward found Alvyn Sanches, who angled a shot across Gunn. So, so easy. Gunn’s positioning was questionable.

Scott McTominay, again peripheral, slammed over when it looked easier to notch a Scotland consolation. Scottish fans jeered after one sideways pass too many in defence. Many headed for the exit as Zeki Amdouni’s shot deflected off Luke Graham and beyond Gunn.

A year ago, Scotland were celebrating World Cup qualification on the most epic of Hampden Park nights as Denmark were vanquished. It is so difficult to square that occasion with 90 minutes in St Gallen. Scotland look a team in ghastly regression.

Sports.title: Nations League: Wirtz doubles up as Germany rout Netherlands to top group
Sports.content:
Florian Wirtz scored twice as Germany delivered a 5-0 rout of the Netherlands in Berlin on Monday, reaching the Nations League quarter-finals as group winners.

Brajan Gruda contributed a goal and two assists, with Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck also on the scoresheet as the hosts delivered their most impressive display so far under Jürgen Klopp’s leadership.

It was Germany’s biggest win over their neighbours since a 7-0 victory in 1959, and the Netherlands’ first defeat since Xavi Hernández took over as coach in August. The Dutch have still advanced to the last eight by finishing second, with Germany’s fifth goal taking Klopp’s side into top spot.

The visitors had the first good chance when Jurriën Timber found Crysencio Summerville unmarked on the penalty spot, but the winger lost his footing before getting a shot away. Germany then went close as the Berlin native Scherhant hit a post after connecting with a cross from his Freiburg teammate Philipp Treu.

Nine minutes later, Scherhant had another chance from the same spot and this time curled a lovely effort across the face of goal and inside the far post. Germany pushed for more goals after the break, and Wirtz delivered with a superb solo effort on the hour, lifting a shot in off the left post from the edge of the penalty area.

Schlotterbeck headed in from Gruda’s free-kick with 65 minutes gone, and the RB Leipzig winger laid on another goal six minutes later when he tore down the right and found Wirtz, who hammered home from close range. Gruda then added one of his own, tapping in a Scherhant shot which rebounded off a post.

Wirtz said: “We don’t mind who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly … We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we’ve taken some great steps in our development as a team.”

View image in fullscreen The Netherlands keeper Bart Verbruggen cannot keep out Brajan Gruda’s effort as Germany score their fifth goal. Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Reuters

“Everyone will go home with a smile on their face – and for at least the next three or four months, no-one will be questioning the German national team,” Klopp said afterwards. “Instead, they’ll be thinking: ‘This could really turn into something.’ We have wonderful footballers, great characters … the lads are even surprising themselves.”

Greece had to settle for third place in Group A2 despite a 1-0 home win over Serbia. Giorgos Masouras scored the second-half winner in Volos, but the hosts missed out on a quarter-final place on head-to-head goal difference, their 7-0 defeat by the Netherlands on Friday proving costly. As group winners, Germany will be seeded in Friday’s draw and will avoid England, France and the winners of Group A4 – probably Portugal – in the last eight.

Switzerland completed a dominant campaign in Group B1 by thrashing Scotland 4-0 in St Gallen. Slovenia finished second in the group, claiming a promotion/relegation playoff place, as Danijel Sturm’s double helped them secure a 3-0 win over North Macedonia.

Quick Guide Dowman becomes England U21s' youngest scorer Show Max Dowman (pictured) became England Under-21s’ youngest-ever goalscorer by grabbing the late winner in a 3-2 friendly victory over France at Ashton Gate. Lee Carsley’s side made a lightning start as Tottenham's Mikey Moore gave England an early lead on his first under-21s start. Divin Mubama doubled their lead with a header as Ethan Nwaneri set up both of the hosts' first-half goals. The Young Lions looked comfortable but Tommy Setford allowed France to pull a goal back after he let Giovani Versini’s cross slip through his fingers. The French winger equalised in style moments later, scoring with a shot from distance. Carsley had handed a first start to promising Arsenal youngster Dowman and he proved to be the hero, tapping in from Harrison Armstrong's pass to give England the win at only 16 years old. Press Association Photograph: Michael Steele/The FA Collection Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

In League C, the Faroe Islands beat Moldova 1-0 to complete an unbeaten campaign and earn a playoff place. Slovakia, already guaranteed Group C3 top spot, earned a 2-2 draw with Kazakhstan thanks to Adrian Kapralik’s last-gasp leveller.

Iceland finished Group C4 unbeaten with a 3-0 home victory against Luxembourg securing first place. Second-placed Estonia beat Bulgaria 2-1 to book a playoff spot.

In League D, Gibraltar earned a 1-1 home draw with Malta thanks to Carlos Richards’s late equaliser, while Lithuania defeated Liechtenstein 2-1 in Kaunas.

Sports.title: Pochettino: I’d tell Guardiola to ‘take it’ if he’s offered US coaching job
Sports.content:
Outgoing US head coach Mauricio Pochettino and former Manchester City head coach Pep Guardiola have a long, storied past. The two faced each other as players, when Guardiola was at Barcelona and Pochettino was making his name across town at Espanyol. They faced each other 22 times as managers in the Premier League and the two share a mutual respect – and intensity – when it comes to their approach to playing and coaching alike.

So when Guardiola visited Yankee Stadium in September to serve as New York City FC’s pre-match hype man before their rivalry match with Red Bull New York, Pochettino – in town anyways to scout the match – made it a point to sit with him during the game. He brought along his assistant coach and confidant Jesús Pérez, and US Soccer CEO and secretary general JT Batson.

“You know what I noticed?” Pochettino asked, smiling as he recounted the story during a meeting with reporters on Monday. “[Guardiola had a] good relationship with JT.”

Back then, Pochettino didn’t seem to be going anywhere. Only a month earlier, he’d signed a four-year contract to guide the US through the 2030 World Cup. Guardiola was, and still is, in the middle of a year-long sabbatical from coaching. He remains the federation’s white whale, often mentioned in the same breath as the US job over the past decade-plus but just as quickly dismissed as a pipe dream.

Just three months after taking in that game at Yankee Stadium, Pochettino is on his way to Manchester United and Guardiola has once again found himself at the center of the rumor mill, with reports suggesting that he and US Soccer are set for exploratory talks.

On Monday, Pochettino was asked what he’d tell the Barcelona and Manchester City legend if he was asked for his opinion on the US job.

“Take it,” Pochettino said, flatly. “Why? Because it’s a perfect moment to arrive at the federation. Everything is on the right path, in the right direction. Of course, take it. Of course, you are going to find really good players, good people – the players can fit his style.”

Guardiola was one of many topics the Argentinian manager covered during the roundtable, which lasted about an hour. At times defiant, at times emotional and cycling through Spanish and English, Pochettino spoke of his potential legacy at US Soccer, what lies ahead for him at United and how he views soccer in America as a whole.

Quotes have been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.

View image in fullscreen Alex Freeman has been a breakout star for the US under Pochettino’s watch. Photograph: JC Ruiz/Getty Images

On assessing players regardless of league level

However you assess his results, one of the inarguable successes of the Pochettino era are the relatively unheralded players whose status has risen over his tenure. The Argentine cited defender Alex Freeman and midfielder Sebastian Berhalter as two such examples, both of whom were playing in MLS when making their national team debuts under Pochettino and both now playing in Europe. Asked how he assesses players to add to the national team, and how he compares players across different leagues and playing styles, Pochettino insisted that the level of competition matters less than individual form.

“You need to project the individual player,” Pochettino said. “Because he’s playing well, the level is no issue. That player can be good, like Freeman, like Sebastian. That is the example, and I think that is so important. There is talent everywhere … This one is one of the things that we learn – all [of us], we were young and then we start to be a coach, no? That we cannot make a mistake [and] measure the level of the player because of the level of the league.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

On managing a club v managing a national team

With the US being his first international job, there were some doubts going in about how Pochettino would adapt to coaching without daily contact with his players and staff.

“I am ready [to return]. This is what I miss a little bit. I miss to be, every day, with something here,” Pochettino said. “Guardiola asked me when I was at the game, he said, ‘Oh, you don’t want to come back to the Premier League?’ I said, ‘No, I’m happy here.’ [He said] ‘Yeah, but you don’t miss, every day, to…’ I say, ‘A little bit, yes, because you think now today, and then we have December camp against Jamaica for the MLS [players in the pool]. But after, you need to wait [until] March. What do you do? You need to watch games, you need to travel – administrative things. That is nice, it’s good. But every day, to be involved: press conference, training, everything … this type of possibility, like with United, you say yes. I want that. I want to prove myself again.”

But what did Pochettino think of his maiden international job?

“I like and not like,” he said. “I like because it provides you the possibility to manage your time, to be busy, but at the same time, be free and to have some time with your family. Now, I have a grandchild, and [number] two is coming. You can share the life with your people. But now, ciao, because now is [gestures] tra-tra-tra-tra-tra. It’s impossible to spend time with the people you want.”

View image in fullscreen Pep Guardiola was in attendance with Mauricio Pochettino at the Hudson River Derby earlier this year. Photograph: Jordan Bank/Getty Images

On the perceived status of the US coaching gig

In the grand scheme of international football, the US national team coaching job has never been close to the top of the list of most desirable destinations. Pochettino’s hire was seen as a possible sign that could be changing. Now, after nearly two years in the position, Pochettino believes it has.

“The vision from Europe, I promise it is completely different after the World Cup,” Pochettino said. “Now, being head coach of the USA is more prestigious. If Manchester United, or Real Madrid, or Barcelona is coming for the US coach, if you start to think about that, if you are another coach – maybe [Antonio] Conte, someone else, you say ‘oh, this is a great opportunity.’ [In my case], ‘Oh, Pochettino, from Chelsea he goes to the US? And now to Manchester United.’

On one thing he’d change about soccer in the United States

Pochettino has coached some of the most famous players and clubs in the world, giving him a unique perspective on how soccer has developed in the US. Pochettino stopped short of prescribing neat solutions to improve the sport, though.

“I think that business [and] the sport, is [done] in a holistic way. Everything is important, and you cannot pick one. You cannot change one [thing], and that can change everything,” he said. “I think it’s a little bit of everything that you need to change. If you adjust this, you need to adjust this. The balance of the thing changes if you touch here, that will force you to touch all the areas in soccer here, or in the world To find the good balance, no? A process of little by little, is all that we made in these last two years. I think it’s the beginning of [a process]. If that has continuity, it’s the beginning of the new soccer in the USA that can be.

“I think that is, for me, the beginning of the change for the future: that idea that the American player can be very good, can be very competitive. The talent is here; it’s so powerful in this country. I think that is why I feel proud. Maybe that was our job, because I don’t believe in coincidence. That has happened because something needed to happen. Now the tough job is done. Maybe now [the United job] is my reward because of this tough job.”

Sports.title: Swansea braced to lose Vítor Matos as Strasbourg seek to replace Hugo Oliveira
Sports.content:
Swansea City are increasingly resigned to their head coach, Vítor Matos, joining Strasbourg after he indicated a desire to join Chelsea’s sister club. The Ligue 1 club have approached Swansea with a view to Matos succeeding Hugo Oliveira.

Strasbourg, acquired by Chelsea’s parent company BlueCo in 2023, have identified Matos as a replacement for Oliveira, who has won three of 10 league matches since succeeding Gary O’Neil in July. The French club are hovering two points above the relegation zone.

Matos is under contract until 2030 and Swansea would be due significant compensation for the 38-year-old, a former Liverpool academy and development team coach.

Matos has won admirers since taking charge of Swansea last November and, despite one win in their past five games, has the south Wales club in the Championship playoff spots. Swansea finished last season in 11th and backed Matos in the transfer market this summer in the hope of pushing on.

Swansea’s next match is at home to West Brom on Saturday, before a trip to Middlesbrough and a south Wales derby against Cardiff in the Welsh capital.

Matos, who is due to celebrate a year in charge at Swansea this month, joined the club from Marítimo, a Portuguese second-division club. His 12-game spell in charge of Maritimo represented his first senior management job.

Strasbourg and Chelsea share a close relationship and have traded players, with Emmanuel Emegha and Valentín Barco joining the English club in recent months.

In the most notable move between the clubs, however, Liam Rosenior left his role as Strasbourg head coach to take charge of Chelsea in January, but the former Hull manager was sacked in April. O’Neil succeeded Rosenior but joined Ipswich in June.

Sports.title: Boxer Lee Reeves dies, aged 31, after three months in a coma - having been knocked out in the ring
Sports.content:
Boxer Lee Reeves dies, aged 31, after three months in a coma - having been knocked out in the ring

Boxer Lee Reeves has died at the age of 31 after spending three months in a coma following his final fight in August.

The Irish southpaw had been carried out of the ring on a stretcher following his defeat to his countryman Gary Cully and immediately taken to hospital.

There, his promoters Queensberry announced that the fighter was in a 'critical but stable' condition before he underwent surgery.

Reeves was then placed in a medically induced coma, and passed away on Monday surrounded by his family.

The tragic news was announced by his friend and coach Jonathan O'Brien, who paid tribute to Reeves' unerring fight in a poignant statement on social media.

'Goodbye son, sleep tight, you fought so hard till the end,' O'Brien wrote. 'We love you so much, rest in peace with your mam and brother waiting at the heavenly gates.

Limerick fighter Lee Reeves has died after spending three months in a coma, his friends and family have shared (Source: Instagram/Lee Reeves)

Reeves' August clash with final opponent Gary Cully saw the 31-year-old knocked down twice in the 10th round

'Look over your sisters and your father, give them the strength to get through this. We love you Lee.'

Reeves, who was nicknamed 'El Champo', had won 16 of his 18 professional bouts since turning professional in 2018, and had been challenging Cully for the vacant BUI Celtic light-welterweight title.

He had been knocked down twice in the 10th round against Cully before being taken out of the ring, and in his tribute message for his opponent, Cully admitted that he was still in shock at how their match had ended.

'I still remember the stadium days when I used to watch Lee in the nationals, the weight above me, and (I would) always be impressed by his fights and his flashy gear,' Cully wrote.

'What a character and a gent. It's never been nothing but love between us champ, can't really believe I'm writing this but RIP brother.'

Limerick-born Reeves spent time away from the ring as a competitor on BBC reality show Survivor in 2023, and served as an ambassador for Limerick Treaty Suicide Prevention group.

The fighter, the oldest of four siblings, lost his mother Cathy to suicide in 2015.

'Limerick is a very dark place tonight with the loss of Lee Reeves. Lee was not just a boxer that excelled in his career - he was a mental health advocate who highlighted mental health and how it can affect young people,' Limerick City councillor and Reeves' family friend Catherine Slattery said in her tribute.

'Lee was a very proud Limerick man, he loved Limerick and its people and any chance he got to promote Limerick, he took it.

'Lee loved his family. He was very proud of his dad, Tony, and he adored his sisters and his nieces and nephews and they, in return, adored him.

'Lee had great faith in God and the only (consolation) is that Lee's mam and brother are embracing him in their arms in heaven.

'The loss of Lee will be felt in Limerick for a long time to come and I am heartbroken for Lee that he lost his fight.

'Rest in peace El Champ - you will be missed by us all.'

Queensberry also shared a statement after news broke, writing: 'Everyone at Queensberry is devastated to learn of the passing of Lee Reeves.

'Lee was an immensely talented boxer, as well as a true role model and inspiration to his community.

'Our deepest condolences go to Lee's family, friends and all those who loved him. We ask that their privacy be respected at this incredibly difficult time.

'Rest in peace, Lee.'

Sports.title: Melbourne Cup horse's body dumped in rubbish bin at Sydney tip just two weeks after race - as devastated trainer seeks answers
Sports.content:
The body of Melbourne Cup runner So You Are has been found in a public rubbish bin at a Sydney tip, leaving his devastated trainer searching for answers and sparking outrage online.

Racing NSW stewards are investigating how the horse came to be dumped among general waste at Cleanaway's Lucas Heights facility.

The five-year-old gelding died on Monday after suffering severe colic while enjoying a spell following a spring campaign that included four victories.

He was rushed to REC Equine Specialists at Randwick for emergency surgery but could not be saved and was euthanised.

Trainer Bjorn Baker and the horse's connections later learned footage had emerged of So You Are in a skip bin at the waste facility.

'Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains,' Baker said in a statement on Tuesday.

Racing NSW stewards are investigating whether a horse found in a skip bin at Lucas Heights was So You Are

Trainer Bjorn Baker described So You Are as a 'kind, beautiful horse' who quickly became a stable favourite

Mr Baker said he was 'deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains'

'He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death.

'I understand the specialist hospital facility REC Equine Specialists are investigating the circumstances, and I expect a full explanation of what occurred.

'My thoughts remain with the Ramsey family, and with all my staff, for whom this has compounded an already devastating loss.'

Builder Gregg Jowett raised the alarm after discovering the horse's body on Monday and posting a video to Facebook.

'I'm at the tip. They've tipped a horse in the f***ing bin,' he said in the footage.

'You're f***ing kidding me. That can't be normal. Does anyone know if that's legal? I'm disgusted by that.'

Mr Jowett said he was concerned about the body being left in a bin accessible to people dropping off everyday rubbish.

'I get it, they do dispose of horses at tips. However, I can't see how they can just tip them into the bins that are open to the public for general mixed rubbish,' he said.

So You Are underwent emergency treatment at a specialist equine hospital but could not be saved

'One would assume they would head straight to the tip edge.'

Mr Jowett claimed staff told him 'this is normal' before asking his followers: 'Am I wrong? Felt disturbing to be honest but I am a city slicker.'

The discovery has compounded the grief of Mr Baker and the horse's connections, who had been celebrating a successful spring campaign only weeks earlier.

Mr Baker initially told the Sydney Morning Herald hat So You Are had quickly become a favourite among his staff.

'He was a kind, beautiful horse. We only had him for a short time and he became a stable favourite,' he said.

The Herald reported that unnamed sources familiar with the situation believed a brand visible in the footage matched So You Are.

Racing NSW stewards are making inquiries into the discovery and the footage has prompted distressed responses from viewers, including people who said they had spent years caring for horses.

'That's disgraceful. What is wrong with people,' a social media user said.

Builder Gregg Jowett posted footage of the discovery, questioning why the body was in a bin accessible to the public

'That's very hard to see from someone that's looked after them for most of my life,' another said.

Others asked whether the discovery had been reported to the RSPCA, while Animals First Australia requested the location of the tip.

According to the Herald, normal practice involves a contractor taking a deceased horse for burial at a licensed landfill. Its sources said euthanised horses require appropriate disposal because of the drugs remaining in their bodies.

The circumstances surrounding how So You Are's remains came to be in the bin, including who was responsible for its transport and handling, have not been established.

So You Are was trained at Warwick Farm and owned by prominent breeder Stuart Ramsey and his wife Trish.

He won four races during the spring, including three Group 3 events at Rosehill, Randwick and Bendigo, before lining up in Australia's biggest race.

After winning the Bendigo Cup a week before Flemington, he started the Melbourne Cup as a $12 chance under jockey Rachel King.

With about 600m remaining, he was running second and chasing leader Royal Supremacy before eventually finishing eighth behind Point of Law.

Thirteen days later, the stable announced his death.

'He had been enjoying a well-earned spell when he was found showing signs of colic this morning,' its initial statement said.

'He was rushed to a specialist equine hospital for emergency veterinary treatment, but sadly could not be saved.'

The Daily Mail has contacted REC Equine Specialists, Cleanaway and Turangga Farm for comment.

Sports.title: Man United's first woman on their backroom team, the fitness enforcer Jesus, a scorpion-kicking goalkeeper coach... and his son! Meet Mauricio Pochettino's team of experts flying in to whip United's flops into shape
Sports.content:
Man United's first woman on their backroom team, the fitness enforcer Jesus, a scorpion-kicking goalkeeper coach... and his son! Meet Mauricio Pochettino's team of experts flying in to whip United's flops into shape

Mauricio Pochettino will have little time to waste when he takes to Manchester United's training ground for the first time on Wednesday, just days ahead of the free-falling giants' crunch clash with bitter rivals Liverpool at Anfield.

The Argentine, however, will not be doing it alone. With him, Pochettino brings to Old Trafford an experienced and familiar cast of trusted colleagues, who will be tasked with supporting the manager in his mission to turn things around in Manchester.

From a first-team coach who has known Pochettino since 1992 to the boss' own son, Daily Mail Sport takes a look at the backroom staff accompanying the Argentine as he takes over at Manchester United.

JESUS PEREZ, ASSISTANT

The Manchester United reporters at Carrington will notice how when they turn up for press conferences, one seat, usually in the front row and to the far left, will have a reserved sign on it. It will be for Perez, who is Pochettino’s eyes and ears. Those same correspondents could clock how Perez may give them a follow on social media so he can stay in the loop of what is being written.

Wherever Pochettino goes, so too does his shadow in Perez. You have probably already heard about the time Pochettino met his idol Sir Alex Ferguson for lunch in London back in 2016. What you may not know is that Perez was there, too. He and Pochettino have been joined at the hip ever since they met in Barcelona when one was an analyst and the other was managing Espanyol.

Mauricio Pochettino (right) arrives at Manchester United with a trusted team of backroom staff

Jesus Perez, pictured with Pochettino at Spurs in 2019, has long been his right hand man

That was in 2010. Perez had studied sports science at university and completed his coaching qualifications but was considering quitting football. Pochettino convinced him otherwise, and they soon learned they shared the same principles, including the importance of creating the correct culture of togetherness inside of a club in order to succeed.

In 2013, it was Perez’s turn to convince Pochettino. The Argentinian was unsure about moving to England to manage Southampton, but the Spaniard had spent a month on these shores studying how Premier League sides train and play. He told Pochettino that the intensity of his sessions and style would fit perfectly and that he could not turn down the chance to take on the Premier League.

They now consider each other family, and Perez’s story itself is a nice one. By his own admission, he will tell you that he failed at becoming a professional player, but he believes the way in which he worked his way in as a coach can inspire others who dream of finding their own place in football. He loves the game, so much so that he would use days off to travel from London to Manchester to visit the National Football Museum. Now he will be living much closer to his favourite hotspot.

As well as being the glue which connects various club departments together, Perez is a fitness and conditioning specialist, and a normal working day might involve arriving at the training ground at 7.30am. After meeting with Pochettino over breakfast, he will then hold a 9am medical meeting where plans for each player are discussed and decided. Programmes tend to be tailored to individuals rather than set as a blanket for the whole squad. Perez was credited with helping to establish Southampton and Tottenham Hotspur as among the fittest teams in the Premier League, and he will take personal circumstances into account as well as physical condition.

Where Pochettino is larger than life, Perez is unassuming, and has never sought to step into management for himself as he prefers to work in the shadows.

When we talk about Pochettino’s man-management prowess, the same extends to Perez.

For example, when Chelsea beat Leicester City 4-2 in an FA Cup quarter-final when they were in charge in 2023-24, Raheem Sterling had a stinker. He missed a penalty, spurned a one-on-one opportunity, and skied a free-kick. Chelsea’s fans booed him, and chanted ‘you don’t know what you’re doing’ at Pochettino when he substituted Mykhailo Mudryk rather than Sterling after 78 minutes at 2-2. Perez was the first to go straight to Sterling to put an arm around him that day.

Another example is how when Cole Palmer was becoming a household name in Pochettino’s one and only season at Chelsea, Perez was among those who tried to privately help the Englishman understand the perils of the distractions of his new-found fame.

When they departed Chelsea, Pochettino and Perez were men of their word, and honoured their commitment to managing the World XI in the Soccer Aid charity match a few weeks later. That was despite it being a little awkward that the game was being held at Stamford Bridge. They lost 6-3 to Frank Lampard’s England XI.

MIGUEL D’AGOSTINO, FIRST-TEAM COACH

To give an idea of how long Pochettino has known ‘Miki’, around 1992, Pochettino purchased his first car while a player for Newell’s Old Boys. He gave his team-mate a lift home. When D’Agostino went to get out of the car, the wind caught it hard, and broke Pochettino’s door. He never paid the bill to have it fixed – something Pochettino occasionally likes to remind D’Agostino about.

Miguel D'Agostino, known as 'Miki', has heaps of experience as a former analyst and scout

The first-team coach has known Pochettino since 1992 (both pictured at Tottenham in 2019)

Pochettino clearly forgave his fellow Argentinian defender who played under Marcelo Bielsa.

D’Agostino was an analyst at Espanyol, with it understood he was initially attached to the scouting department before assuming responsibility for filming training sessions and overseeing player analysis. From there, he followed Pochettino wherever he went, from Southampton to Tottenham to Paris Saint-Germain to Chelsea to the United States national team.

While with the USA, D’Agostino would watch games in the MLS, going to Real Salt Lake or wherever there were players for scouting. In training, he is hands-on, sometimes with a stopwatch in hand or notepad containing that day’s drills.

When Pochettino tested positive for Covid-19 in January 2021, D’Agostino and Perez took temporary charge of his PSG side. They beat Angers 1-0 away from home in Ligue 1.

All of Pochettino’s confidantes have a good grasp of English.

SILVIA TUYA, STRENGTH AND CONDITIONING COACH

The newest member of Pochettino’s inner circle, having joined his USA national set-up in October 2024.

With a PhD in sports science, Tunya had worked with FC Levante Badalona in Liga F, Spain’s top tier for women’s football, while she also served as a lecturer at the National Institute of Physical Education of Catalonia at the University of Barcelona.

Since teaming up with Pochettino, she was seen on the training pitch and in the gym with the players.

Tuya will become Manchester United's first ever female coach connected with the men's team.

Silvia Tuya is the newest member of Pochettino’s team, having joined his USA set-up in 2024

Tuya is set to become Manchester United's first ever female coach in the men's team

TONI JIMENEZ, GOALKEEPING COACH

After winning gold for Spain at the Barcelona Olympics in 1992, Jimenez met Pochettino in 1994 when they became team-mates for Espanyol, but it is worth recalling the 2000 Copa del Rey final when they found themselves on opposing sides.

The goalkeeper represented Atletico Madrid, and Pochettino was in defence for Espanyol, who won 2-1. After full-time, Pochettino delayed his celebrations to go console his friend, who had already endured a challenging year with his father having passed away.

Jimenez has never forgotten that kindness from Pochettino, and like the others, the two have worked together whether the latter has managed, from Espanyol to Southampton to Tottenham to PSG to Chelsea to the USA. They have shared a fair few of their favourite mate teas in their time, and now for United, where Jimenez will work with Senne Lammens and Co.

They say training is rarely boring when Jimenez is involved. He was happy to prove to Tottenham’s players during one tour of Malaysia that he could copy Rene Higuita’s scorpion kick save, for example, and is pretty good when testing his goalkeepers in free-kick practice. Lammens should beware he is liable to do a little dance if he scores past you, however.

Hugo Lloris, the former Spurs goalkeeper who won the 2018 World Cup with France, frequently credited the charismatic Jimenez for adding new areas into his game. Pochettino previously hailed him for how he keeps the second- and third-choice goalkeepers motivated when not playing.

Hugo Lloris frequently credited Toni Jimenez (above) for adding new areas into his game

Sebastiano Pochettino first worked with his father at Tottenham (pictured celebrating at PSG)

SEBASTIANO POCHETTINO, SPORTS SCIENTIST AND FITNESS COACH

The son of the manager. A graduate of Southampton Solent University, Sebastiano first worked with his father at Tottenham. It was said at the time that he had become the Premier League’s youngest sports scientist at the age of 22 when hired.

He soon became a regular sight in training sessions and on match days, seen putting the players through their paces and with the substitutes as they warmed up.

Sebastiano became a fitness coach and joined his old man at PSG and Chelsea and with the USA. One of his specialties is in injury prevention and strength and conditions sessions, and that includes in monitoring the players’ sleep and mood.

Trust being important to Pochettino in his inner circle, he can rely on family. Pochettino also has another son called Maurizio, a professional player for Andorran club Inter Club d’Escaldes.

Sports.title: Florian Wirtz scores twice (including a stunner) as Germany thump Netherlands 5-0 in UEFA Nations League... as Liverpool misfit receives a hug from Jurgen Klopp after impressing
Sports.content:
Liverpool midfielder Florian Wirtz scored a stunning brace for Germany as Jurgen Klopp's side thumped the Netherlands in the Nations League.

The 23-year-old has had a tough time of it at Anfield since his £116million move to the club last summer, but has never really struggled on the international stage.

And he continued that trend on Monday evening with two goals for his side to help them top their Nations League group.

His first was the pick of the bunch. Wirtz moved along the forward line as a Dutch side without Virgil van Dijk struggled to contain him. He picked up the ball around 25 yards out, cut inside onto his weaker left foot, and curled a pearling effort into the far corner off the post.

That goal, which came on the hour mark, put his side 2-0 up after Freiburg's Derry Scherhant had scored the opener, and Wirtz wasn't done there.

Centre back Nico Schlotterbeck made it 3-0 before the Liverpool man picked up his second of the night after drifting into the penalty box unmarked and finishing high after good work from Brajan Gruda.

Cette version de Wirtz avec le maillot de la Mannschaft c’est celle qu’on aimerait voir chaque semaine en PL.



Quel missile pour faire le break !



Meilleur buteur allemand sur cette édition de l’UNL. 🇩🇪🔥 pic.twitter.com/m0DqaOungS — 𝐑𝐮𝐢 𝐏𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐨¹¹⁵🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 (@Saiid_At_Tijani) November 16, 2026

Florian Wirtz scored a brace for Germany as they thumped the Netherlands 5-0 in Nations League action

Liverpool midfielder Wirtz received a big hug from a smiling Jurgen Klopp at full time

Gruda himself, who is on loan at RB Leipzig from Brighton, wrapped up the five-star win on a night that arguably saw Klopp announce himself as Germany boss.

After full-time, the ex-Liverpool manager gave Wirtz a huge hug as the duo beamed with big smiles on their faces.

While it was a night to remember for Germany, a Netherlands team that included the likes of Micky van de Ven, Jurrien Timber and Wirtz's Liverpool team-mate Cody Gakpo were left exasperated.

Van Dijk had pulled out of the squad with a knock after playing with a knock in recent weeks.

His side will still, though, compete in the Nations League quarter-finals after finishing second in the group, finishing ahead of Greece on goal difference.

As for Wirtz, he will hope his performance will help continue what has been an uphill climb so far this season.

He also found the net for Germany in their first match of the international break – a 3-1 win over Serbia – and picked up a goal and assist in Liverpool's 3-1 win over Crystal Palace before the international break.

In total, he has two goals and five assists in 15 games for Liverpool this season – though the Reds will hope those numbers increase as the season goes on.

His second goal came as he drifted into the penalty area and finished high into the net

Last month, meanwhile, Reds manager Andoni Iraola insisted he has full faith in his midfielder.

'I think he has had a little bit of everything this season,' he said. 'He has had good games, probably the other day was not his best game, especially offensively. We trust Florian.

'Florian is a very good player. He was coming from good performances in the international break, I think. I think it is a matter of everyone to find his moment.'

Klopp hailed him 'exceptional', meanwhile, during the last international break.

Sports.title: Push it to the Max! Dowman, 16, becomes England U21s youngest-ever goalscorer - as Arsenal starlet scores 89th-minute winner against France
Sports.content:
Max Dowman broke another record as the 16-year-old became the youngest-ever goalscorer for England's Under-21 side on Monday night.

The Arsenal teenager has already broken a plethora of records at club level, and is now taking that to the international stage too, breaking a record set by senior team star Jude Bellingham, who scored aged 17 years and 67 days in 2020.

Dowman was called into the U21 squad for the first time this international break, and made his debut off the bench in the 1-0 defeat by Portugal on Friday.

On Monday, meanwhile, he was given a start by manager Lee Carsley, and rewarded his manager's faith with an 89th-minute winner to break the record and earn his side a 3-2 win.

It's a record he can add to his already-extensive collection, which includes being the youngest Champions League player, the youngest Premier League goalscorer, and the youngest Premier League winner.

Manager Lee Carsley said after the game: 'He played really well - he was one of four or five outstanding performances. Mikey Moore, Max, Ethan (Nwaneri), they were very good.

Max Dowman became England Under-21s' youngest-ever goal scorer when he scored against France on Monday

'We see how good on the ball he is but he was outstanding off the ball. You have to keep reminding yourself about his age. There's a lot of expectation around him and he seems to handle that so well.

'It's important we keep supporting him and he develops at his own pace. It's so important he enjoys his football.

'Obviously all the players in the squad are under pressure from their clubs and the expectation that surrounds them, so as much as we can we have to make that as easy as we can.'

Despite bursting onto the scene last season, Dowman has just 19 minutes to his name in the top flight this campaign as Arsenal look to defend their title.

He has played a number of games for the Gunners' U21 side, while he was sent off against League Two side Fleetwood Town in the Carabao Cup.

Arteta scolded his player at the time, but said: 'I haven't seen the reaction to my reaction. Whether that's positive or negative. You need to understand the context, the relationship I have with him and what we discussed before we went out.

'If you see the reaction from my mother and father with me sometimes, you'd say "you don't like that reaction", but for me it was the best reaction ever as it enabled me to be who I am.

The Arsenal teenager, 16, broke the record held by Jude Bellingham with his late winner

'But you want to see the best and most beautiful reaction. You want to see the reaction of his team-mates when they have to play with 10 men.

'What do you expect? That's the level and that's the reaction. Whether it's right or wrong, that's the reaction. And the reaction when I don't win, I'm f****d off, big time.

'This is the environment and the reality. We are not in Disneyland, we are in the Premier League. We look after him so much but we are also demanding as he needs to earn the right to play otherwise what are the rest of the boys going to tell me?'

Sports.title: Declan Rice agrees new five-year Arsenal contract: Star to join Bukayo Saka as Gunners' highest-paid player at over £350,000-per-week - days after midfielder declared himself 'extremely lucky' to play for Gunners
Sports.content:
Declan Rice has agreed a new five-year deal at Arsenal that will run until the summer of 2031.

The England midfielder is expected to sign the new contract soon, which is set to put him alongside Bukayo Saka as Arsenal's top earner. Saka is on a deal worth over £350,000 a week.

Rice joined Arsenal in 2023 for £105million from West Ham and has established himself as the fulcrum of their midfield, helping steer them to the Premier League title last season.

The 27-year-old played 55 games in all competitions last season as the Gunners reached their first Champions League final since 2006, but lost out to Paris Saint-Germain.

His contract talks have been ongoing from at least March and are now finalised.

Previously, Rice's deal was expiring in 2028.

Declan Rice has agreed a new-five year deal at Arsenal that will run until the summer of 2031

The deal will put Rice alongside Bukayo Saka as Arsenal's top earner at over £350,000 a week

The Arsenal star had confirmed a new deal was close over the weekend when speaking on international duty with England.

'I've been extremely lucky that I've managed to play at such a consistent level throughout my career.

'I've always been stable in the clubs I've been at.

'A new contract is hopefully on the horizon soon.

'I'm extremely lucky that I'm at a club like Arsenal, where my manager [Mikel Arteta] and my team-mates put so much energy in me.

'I'm extremely lucky I don't have to think about that stuff.'

Sports.title: Switzerland 4-0 Scotland: Swiss stroll leaves serious question marks over Sebastien Pocognoli as Scots round off miserable campaign with defeat on captain Andrew Robertson's record-breaking night
Sports.content:
Despite re-establishing Scotland’s credentials as a credible football nation, by common consent, Steve Clarke’s time in charge of the side was up in the summer.

With qualification for a major tournament no longer satisfying the desires of the Tartan Army, a seven-year itch led to a parting of the ways.

In order to take that elusive step into a knock-out round, the theory went that employing a bolder coach who’d get more out of the players was all that was required. So much for that.

While few would dispute that a change at the helm was required, it was legitimate to question the wisdom in the SFA making one which was quite so radical. Those concerns have only been amplified by what’s been witnessed so far under Sebastien Pocognoli.

The Belgian is young, smart and intense. He won a title in Belgium with Union Saint-Gilloise and will have taken much from his brief, ill-fated spell at Monaco. He wants to play the kind of football supporters long to see.

But this Nations League campaign has been nothing short of dismal. Two wins from six matches, both of those coming against a poor North Macedonia side, and three nights to forget against the Swiss and Slovenia, is a lamentable record.

Andy Robertson endured a miserable night on the occasion of his record-breaking 103rd cap

Notwithstanding the fact that there were always likely to be teething problems, it’s fallen miles short of modest expectations.

Talk of it taking up to 18 months to all come up roses is all very well. But to believe that’s going to be the case, you need to see more green shoots at this point.

Having finished third in the section, Scotland are bound for pot three when the draw for Euro 2028 is made in Belfast next month.

Unless there’s a radical improvement come the qualifiers in March, it’s hard to see how Pocognoli’s side will get there by any means other than the back door.

This was another tough watch for the travelling supporters, one which will only lead to growing concerns about where all this is heading.

For half of a half, Scotland actually looked like they were getting somewhere under their new manager.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli faces some serious questions over a miserable campaign

From the minute Lewis Ferguson scored a horrible own goal, though, they became a rabble. Not nearly enough punch on the front foot. And far too easy to play through.

They shipped two goals inside five minutes early in the second half and looked like they’d have taken the final whistle there and then.

Individual mistakes from players are troubling Pocognoli in the same way they pockmarked the later days of Clarke’s reign.

Having witnessed Grant Hanley, Scott McKenna and Andy Robertson err in the World Cup, the Tartan Army had already seen Jack Hendry sent off against the Swiss at Hampden before Ferguson joined the growing list of sinners here.

Arriving midway through the first half, his unfathomable moment came when there wasn’t a red shirt in close proximity. It was a kick in the teeth for Pocognoli after a reasonable start.

While it would have been stretching matters to suggest that his team were vulnerable, Murat Yakin was without four of his big hitters in Manuel Akanji, Johan Manzambi, Dan Ndoye and Granit Xhaka.

There was a smattering of starters with five or six caps to their name. Two of the front three, Samuel Ballet and Winsley Boteli, were just 20.

Lewis Ferguson can't believe his misfortune after slicing the ball into his own net for the opener

It was a night when Scottish football history was made with Robertson winning his 103rd cap to finally rise above his great friend, Sir Kenny Dalglish.

Pocognoli stuck by the back-three – Ryan Porteous, Luke Graham and Kieran Tierney – who acquitted themselves well against North Macedonia.

There was no great shock that the more defensive-minded Aaron Hickey replaced Ben Gannon-Doak on the right. Without a goal in 21 matches before a ball was kicked, Oli McBurnie’s selection ahead of Che Adams was intriguing.

The infuriating thing from Pocognoli’s perspective was that his side began with the right attitude.

Aside from an Isaac Schmidt shot which was fielded by Angus Gunn, they looked comfortable.

John McGinn’s pass into McBurnie saw the Hull forward flick the ball into space for Hickey to chase. Just when it looked like he might get a shot away, he was caught.

The positive early approach was typified by Porteous flying into a tackle 30 yards from the Swiss goal and winning the ball.

Winsley Boteli enjoys the moment after putting the stylish Swiss two goals ahead on the night

Had it not been for Hickey hesitating to pick out Scott McTominay’s run, the Napoli man would have been in on goal.

To put it mildly, the Swiss didn’t need an invitation to go down. The appropriately named Samuel Ballet was especially fond of the theatrics.

For a brief spell, Scotland had their opponents hemmed in. Pocognoli was miffed that two quick corners didn’t amount to anything.

Billy Gilmour probed and McTominay made key interceptions and sprayed passes. McGinn fired over.

At the midway point in the first half, there was much to admire. Then disaster struck.

The Swiss did well to advance down the right. Zachary Athekame simply launched a cross into the box and hoped for the best.

Aaron Hickey endured a painful injury blow and could now face another spell on the sidelines

With Ferguson running back towards goal and Porteous waiting to boot the ball to safety, there was no obvious danger.

For reasons only he could explain, the Bologna man stretched out a leg and watched on in horror as the ball sailed past Gunn. All that hard work undone in one desperate moment.

Hickey passed up a chance to immediately level when he headed Robertson’s cross wide. It was to be the Brentford man’s last meaningful involvement before he felt his hamstring tighten. Nathan Patterson replaced him.

A gift of a goal gave the Swiss a boost. Boteli launched himself at Alvyn Sanches’ cross. Gunn was untroubled.

Patterson did well to head Robertson’s deep cross back into the danger zone. McGinn’s header was straight into the arms of Yvon Mvogo.

For all Scotland were entitled to feel a little sore at being one down at the break, it could have been worse. The defence were completely static as Adrian Bajrami launched himself at a header. It was a good thing, from Gunn’s point of view, that the defender missed the target.

Alvyn Sanches drills home Switzerland's third goal in what was an entirely one-sided contest

Ferguson truly had a night to forget here. Within two minutes of the restart, he needlessly invited pressure when he launched a ball straight out of play.

Within seconds, with Porteous advanced, the Swiss broke down the left. Ballet fed Remo Freuler who returned the favour. Ballet rolled the ball towards goal from 12 yards with Boteli claiming the final touch. The visitors’ hopes of a VAR reprieve for offside were dashed.

And with that, the roof caved in. Patterson was dispossessed and Boteli worked the ball into the feet of Sanches. You could only admire the finish, but Scotland were an absolute mess in the build-up. It was threatening to get ugly.

With Tierney, Scotland’s best player on the night, lying on the deck, Ballet was only denied by Gunn. The Tartan Army looked at the clock and wished it was over.

With a minute remaining, a bad night got worse when Zeki Amdouni’s deflected shot beat Gunn.

Mercifully, this tortuous Nations League campaign can now be consigned to history. It’s been the most chastening experience for all concerned.

Sports.title: 1966 World Cup hero Sir Geoff Hurst backs Mail's dementia carers appeal after six of his England team-mates developed the disease
Sports.content:
World Cup hero Sir Geoff Hurst has thrown his support behind the Daily Mail’s dementia carers appeal. Sir Geoff, who saw six of his England team-mates suffer from dementia before they died, is now the sole survivor of Sir Alf Ramsey’s 1966 trophy-winning team. Manchester United legend Sir Bobby Charlton and his elder brother Jack Charlton of Leeds United lived with the condition in their later years. So did Martin Peters, who scored a goal alongside Sir Geoff’s famous hat-trick to beat West Germany 4-2 in the 1966 World Cup final at Wembley Stadium. Dementia also hit Ray Wilson, of Everton, Sir Geoff’s strike partner Roger Hunt, of Liverpool, and Manchester United midfielder Nobby Stiles. Six out of the 11 England players who started in the World Cup final 60 years ago developing the disease is a startling ratio, and has driven home research linking heading the ball to degenerative brain conditions in later life. World Cup hero Sir Geoff Hurst has thrown his support behind the Daily Mail’s dementia carers appeal

Your browser does not support iframes.

Sir Geoff has become a staunch advocate of Alzheimer’s Society and vowed to back the Mail’s appeal, delivered in partnership with Alzheimer’s Society and the Mail Force charity, to raise millions towards a nationwide support network for millions of people across Britain caring for friends and family members with dementia. He said: ‘As always, I am supporting Alzheimer’s Society in this endeavour. Several of my colleagues suffered and are still suffering in some cases this disease and the more we can do to research it, for better things will be in the long run hopefully. ‘So, let’s get behind this Alzheimer’s campaign to help the families of those are suffering and do as much good as possible.’ The Mail’s new Dementia Carers Together appeal passed its first target of raising £100,000 in just a week, enough to pay for nearly 3,000 places on new classes to give carers vital support and information about their rights and the services available to them. The six-week courses will allow attendees to meet others in a similar situation and help to address the loneliness, exhaustion and overwhelming responsibilities many face following a loved one’s diagnosis. The appeal has already won the backing of every major political party leader, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying: ‘Just a little bit of help can make something feel bearable or doable that without it, would all of a sudden just overwhelm somebody.’ The family of Ray Wilson, England’s left back in 1966, are also supporting the Mail’s campaign. Wilson died in 2018 at the age of 83 after years with Alzheimer’s disease, during most of which time he was cared for by his devoted wife Pat and their family. His daughter-in-law, Linda Wilson, said: ‘It’s really good campaign. It would be nice to have a six-week programme available to everybody regardless of where they are in the country and not reliant upon some sort of postcode lottery. ‘Pat was always lucky because Ray would go to a Help the Aged day centre in Slaithwaite twice a week and it gave her some respite. Dementia Carers Together Dementia Carers Together is raising money to fund new courses across the UK to give tens of thousands of struggling unpaid dementia carers vital emotional and practical support. For further information, visit dailymail.com/dementia How you can donate Online: Visit justgiving.com/campaign/mailforce By Text: To donate £10, text CARER to 70115. To donate £20, text LOVE to 70115. To donate £30, text HEART to 70115. Texts will cost your donation amount plus your network charge. By phone: Call 0300 1234577. Standard charges may apply. By cheque: Send cheques made payable to Mail Force Charity to: Dementia Carers Together, 42 Phoenix Court, Hawkins Road, Colchester CO2 8JY ‘Having support and knowing where to go and look for it is important. You feel shellshocked when you get the diagnosis. You feel quite alone and wondering what’s going to happen and how fast. ‘So much of the care is patient centred but the people supporting the patient need support as well.’ Wilson’s widow Pat died last year, and the family are on a fundraising mission of their own, selling the drawings done by Ray after his diagnosis with proceeds set to be donated to the Alzheimer’s Society. He had never shown any inclination to draw but one day at the breakfast table picked up a biro and started to sketch on the inside of a cereal box, and hardly ever stopped, producing hundreds of drawings which Pat kept after he died. A small number bear Wilson’s signature, some refer to his footballing past at Huddersfield and Everton. Sky Sports presenter Hayley McQueen’s father Gordon McQueen, the former Leeds, Manchester United and Scotland centre half, died in 2023 at the age of 70 after a long struggle with vascular dementia. She is also throwing her support behind the Dementia Carers Together appeal to make a difference for the families of those suffering from the disease. She said: ‘I’m backing this campaign with the Alzheimer’s Society who’ve been incredibly helpful with my family throughout the battle that we had with my dad and also going through unfortunately another Alzheimer’s situation close to home. ‘I lost both my grandparents so I understand the burden of trying to care for loved ones and family members not knowing where you’re going to get help. So, please get behind this campaign and please note that you’re not going through this alone.’

Sports.title: Boxer Lee Reeves dies aged 31 after brutal knockout in Dublin
Sports.content:
Boxer Lee Reeves dies aged 31 after brutal knockout in Dublin

Lee Reeves was in a coma for three months having suffered a serious brain injury during a fight in Dublin in October

View 2 Images Lee Reeves (right) fighting Gary Culley (Image: Damien Eagers/PA Wire)

Boxer Lee Reeves has died at the age of 31, three months after suffering a brutal KO defeat.

‌



Irishman Reeves was rushed to hospital after being knocked out by compatriot Gary Cully during their fight in Dublin in August. The pair were fighting for the BUI Celtic super-lightweight title on the undercard of Mark Chamberlain's win over Pierce O'Leary.

Reeves, who was the underdog, appeared to be on top heading into the closing stages but in the tenth, with both fighters tiring, he walked onto a heavy left hand from Cully and was immediately knocked unconscious. He received medical attention in the ring and was taken straight directly to a local Dublin hospital.

He later underwent surgery and was placed in an induced coma but passed away over the weekend. Reeves' sister Jessie led the tributes, saying: "I'll see you on the other side my brother. I've no words for this. I love you endlessly El Champo." His final opponent Cully said: “We shared the ring back in August but we been going back for years. I still remember the stadium days when I used to watch Lee in the nationals the weight above me and always be impressed by his fights and his flashy gear.

View 2 Images Lee Reeves has tragically died months after suffering a serious brain injury (Image: Mandatory Credit ©INPHO/Nick Elliott)

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources

“Myself and Luke Thomas used to plague him to spit us out an MC when we were staying in Dublin on training camp and they’d always be fire. What a character and a gent. It’s never been nothing love between us champ can’t really believe I’m writing this but RIP brother.”

A statement from his promoter Queensberry read: "Everyone at Queensberry is devastated to learn of the passing of Lee Reeves. Lee was an immensely talented boxer, as well as a true role model and inspiration to his community. ur deepest condolences go to Lee’s family, friends and all those who loved him. We ask that their privacy be respected at this incredibly difficult time. Rest in peace, Lee."

And Reeves' coach Dee Walsh, added: "I was the last person to ever speak with you. 'Dig deep, one more round, you've done us all proud'. A million things have went through my head on what I should have or could have said to have changed the outcome You did do us proud. The fight you put up in the ring and out of the ring. Five years I had the pleasure of being your coach. I cannot believe you're gone."

Reeves had won 16 of his 17 fights before taking on Cully this summer. He had knocked out five of his previous six opponents and was unbeaten since suffering his first professional defeat in his sixth fight in 2020.

Sports.title: Crystal Palace appoint Thomas Frank as ex-Tottenham boss takes major pay cut
Sports.content:
Crystal Palace appoint Thomas Frank as ex-Tottenham boss takes major pay cut

Crystal Palace sacked Pierre Sage after just 16 games in charge and have tasked ex-Tottenham boss Thomas Frank with steering them away from the bottom of the Premier League table

View Image Thomas Frank is back in management (Image: Justin Setterfield/Getty Images)

Rock-bottom Crystal Palace have confirmed the appointment of Thomas Frank as their new manager on a two-and-a-half-year contract. Frank, 53, arrives with Palace propping up the Premier League table, having won just two of their opening 10 fixtures.

‌



‌



The Eagles gave Pierre Sage the boot last week after only 16 games in charge and have now turned to Frank, who's been out of work since he was sacked by Tottenham in February. Palace hope that the Dane can replicate his brilliant work at Brentford which earned him a lucrative move to Spurs.

‌



Frank was given an £8million per year contract by Tottenham before he was axed eight months into the job. It's understood that the ex-Brondby and Denmark under-19 boss has taken a significant pay cut in order to get back into management with Palace.

‌



After putting pen to paper on a deal that runs until June 2029, Frank commented: "It's an honour to sit here and be in charge of this fantastic Football Club. I'm really, really looking forward to it.

Meanwhile, Palace chairman Steve Parish said: "I'm delighted to be able to welcome Thomas to Crystal Palace. He has a proven track record of both creating winning teams and improving players, making him the perfect fit for our club.

‌



"I'm confident Thomas' extensive experience in the Premier League will help us achieve our goals for the rest of the season."

Is Thomas Frank the right man for Crystal Palace? Have your say in the comments section.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Domestic football isn't the only thing on Frank's agenda. Palace are embarking on their first campaign in the Europa League, having won the Conference League under former manager Oliver Glasner last season.

‌



The Eagles are 20th in the 36-team table after four games. They host Spanish side Real Sociedad next Thursday, a fixture sandwiched by two vital Premier League games against Coventry and Hull, who are two and four points above Palace respectively.

Palace are also still in the Carabao Cup. Frank's side will host Sunderland in a quarter-final clash on Wednesday, December 16.

Sports.title: Inside England’s World Cup recovery including squad overhaul and Thomas Tuchel change
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel says England’s glorious night in Madrid shows they have finally moved on from the World Cup.

England enjoyed one of their greatest victories on foreign soil as they beat world champions Spain and ended their 43 game unbeaten run.

It has put Tuchel back on course to achieve the dream of ending England’s wait for silverware after the heartbreak of losing to Argentina in the summer.

Just 123 days on from that painful night in Atlanta, England showed they have learned their lesson with a “statement win” against Spain.

‌



But it took a player summit, rebuilding belief and confidence together with fresh ideas and Tuchel used a now tried and trusted football line by insisting they had to go through a “process” to get there.

Thomas Tuchel questions Elliot Anderson red card after 10-man England hold off Spain READ MORE :

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Harry Kane took centre stage at a players’ meeting at the start of the first England camp back in September as the squad had their say over what went wrong at the World Cup.

England famously surrendered their 1-0 lead against Argentina, they sat deeper and Tuchel made a string of defensive substitutions - and ultimately paid a heavy price.

‌



Tuchel took on board the players’ views while also ushering in a raft of new players and, by the time the England boss named his squad for this camp, only half of the 22 outfield players in the United States survived the cull.

It has been branded Tuchel 2.0 and the former Chelsea and Paris Saint Germain boss said it was needed “to improve, you need to bring in new players for competition, young players, new energy, fresh energy.”

View 4 Images England have bounced back from their World Cup heartbreak in Atlanta

You could see from the way England approached and started the win against Spain - as they were fast out of the blocks, pressed high and attacked - that this was a strong mindset and back to what Tuchel does best.

‌



If England lost their nerve in the summer then they were back to throwing caution to the wind and proving they belong among the world elite.

Tuchel said: “We took the next steps after the World Cup, and I'm very proud of the performance. It's a real statement victory. The way we won is not only just winning, but the way we won and the way we played the third phase is very impressive.

“Full credit to the players. You could see the steps that we take between every single match, and that's why I'm very, very happy. It's a full package. It's a full package of belief, of courage, of commitment, of togetherness, of relying on each other and stepping up on in this moment.

“And then you need also quality, and we showed the quality today in all aspects of the game, big in defending, or in the high press, or in the low block, in the build-up game or in the set pieces, or in the goal, in the duels.

‌



“It was a complete performance that makes me very proud, and we will not look back now. Go forward and stay hungry.”

View 4 Images Thomas Tuchel wants his England side to keep pushing forward

The Football Association always have a review after each tournament and it is done in a very corporate way as it featured a former civil servant and a former British Army officer.

If that was a box-ticking exercise, then it was the players who really put their views across to allow England to move on from the hangover in the summer to a much better positive place.

‌



The foundations for the Spain win were built in Croatia last month when the handbrake was released with a 7-0 win and then you had the pace, energy and high press from the off in Madrid. Spain could not live with England.

If England sank deep against Spain then it was more about the brave defending from the Mexico win when they had been reduced to ten men rather than Argentina when they just retreated. Tuchel accepts the players had real input and ideas in their meetings.

Tuchel added: “It took me a while to digest and see the way forward, how we can help and adjust and improve, and how we can do this together. Clarity came then in the first camp.

View 4 Images England defended for their lives to get over the line (Image: Thomas COEX / AFP via Getty Images)

‌



“We had of course reviews and so on, but clarity came then together with the players. And straight away we had the energy right to take the next steps and from there we went.

“So once camp started, the ideas became more clear for me. Even if it was not so easy the first week, like to overcome and arrive with different emotions. Some were still upset from the World Cup. Some were new in the team.

“Some had digested it, some had not digested it. But it was important to have this kind of process together to again overcome and everyone committed that we want to improve in certain aspects of the game.

“Full credit then to the players how they buy into it like from meetings and training and you straight away see it's amazing that it came together like this now.”

‌
