Alt Bank Deepens Financial Inclusion with Six New Alt Boxes

Kuni Tyessi in Abuja

Alt Bank has launched six AltBoxes across Agege Local Government Area(LGA) of Lagos State, in partnership with the local government, marking a major step towards establishing a presence in each of the LGA’s seven wards.

With AltBoxes already established in communities across the country, Alt Bank is extending its reach to where people live and do business, making access to financial services more convenient, supporting local economic activity and creating employment opportunities.

Delivering the address on behalf of the bank, Group Head, Institutional Banking Core North, Abimbola Ojo, emphasised the collaborative vision behind the initiative and its lasting value for local residents at an event attended by representatives of the bank and Agege Local Government, community stakeholders and residents

The six AltBoxes in Agege form part of a wider plan to place an AltBox in each of the LGA’s seven wards, extending the bank’s community-based presence across Agege and bringing banking within closer reach of more residents and businesses.

Speaking at the event, Ojo explained the thinking behind the initiative. “At Alt Bank, we see banking as more than the provision of financial services. It is about enabling people and businesses to realise their potential, participate more fully in the economy and build lasting prosperity.

This requires us to develop solutions that are built around how people live, work and do business. Our approach is anchored in a simple belief: wealth creation should be ethical, meaningful, inclusive and within reach of more people,” she said.

The partnership with Agege Local Government reflects the role of collaboration in expanding access to financial services and supporting local economic participation. For alt bank, it forms part of a wider approach to financial inclusion built on practical, community-based solutions that connect individuals and businesses to the formal financial system.

As the AltBox network grows, alt bank will continue to pursue initiatives that bring more individuals, businesses and communities into the formal financial system, and welcomes conversations with other local and state governments that share that goal. It is an approach rooted in the bank’s purpose of creating wealth.

The AltBox initiative is designed to bring banking services closer to residents, traders, individuals and small business owners through dedicated community-based locations.

World.title: Ogun 2027: PDP’ll Win 18 of 20 LGAs, Says Wale Adedayo
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

James Sowole in Abeokuta

Spokesperson for the 2027 Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) Governorship Campaign Council in Ogun State, Wale Adedayo, has declared that his party would win the forthcoming governorship election in the state by a wide margin.

He specifically noted that the PDP would win 18 of the 20 local government areas in the state, adding that ‘federal might’ would not save the ruling party.

Adedayo, a journalist and former Ijebu East Local Government Area chairman, in the administration of Governor Dapo Abiodun, stated that on an Arise Television programme monitored last Sunday.

He said most of those around Senator Solomon Adeola, the All Progressives Congress (APC) candidate, also known as Yayi, would eventually vote for the PDP governorship candidate, Ladi Adebutu.

According to the PDP spokesman, “Real indigenes of Ogun State would not want to sell their birthrights by voting for a stranger.”

Adedayo predicted victory for Adebutu in 18 out of the 20 local government areas of the state.

He alleged that the PDP actually won in 2023, but that the poll was manipulated.

“I can assure you that the PDP will clear between 18 and 19 local government areas in Ogun State. Adebutu will win Ogun East, and other six LGAs of Ogun Central and a minimum of two in Ogun West.

“It is not the noise that makes things happen. When it comes to the real show, those who are following them know the party they will vote for,” he noted.

He added that the hardship across the country had been rejected by all, saying most of those being paid to attend APC campaigns would eventually cast their ballots for Adebutu.

The campaign spokesperson downplayed the influence of federal might in the forthcoming poll, saying the APC’s federal might would be defeated hands down in Ogun State, the same way it happened in Osun State.

“The federal might was there in 2023; it didn’t work. Federal might was there in Osun State, and it didn’t work, and it won’t work again this time,” he declared.

Adedayo hailed the judiciary for allowing democracy to thrive by returning Adebutu to INEC’s list of candidates.

He said the APC was jittery and already realising the landslide defeat it would suffer in the poll next year, which was why the party was plotting to edge out Adebutu in the contest.

Faulting Adebutu’s initial removal from the list, he said: “You can’t mention PDP in Ogun State without talking about Ladi Adebutu. The electoral umpire made itself a laughing stock by coming out to say his name was not on the list. INEC brought a hard copy to court while the list of names submitted was in soft copy.

“The PDP submitted the register and not INEC. It is the party that can prove who is a member and who is not a member. It is not INEC. The judgment of the court was very sound. INEC should have written to the party that submitted the list rather than removing his name from the list.

“INEC monitored the primary that the same Ladi Adebutu won, and INEC updated Adebutu’s name as the winner of the primary.”

He said the removal of Adebutu’s name did not stop the campaign activities of the party, as Adebutu and his running mate, Hajia Lateefat Sowunmi-Kolapo, continued to tour villages and towns, canvassing for votes and selling their manifesto.

“Those who orchestrated the issue wanted to demoralise members, but Ladi Adebutu continued with his campaign, and that is how he has been going round all villages and towns in Ogun State, meeting with the people.

“It didn’t stop our programme; we have been moving around. Seeing the leaders coming out to campaign boosted the morale of PDP members and supporters. There won’t be any battle in Ogun State,” he said.

On the ancestry issue raised against Yayi, Adedayo said that the people of the state were still expecting the APC candidate to clear himself and tell the people his real identity and origin.

“Facts state that his real name is Sulaiman Ogunleye. It was later that his spokespersons acknowledged it, and he (Yayi) also acknowledged it,” he said.

World.title: Report: INEC’s Data Secrecy Risks Public Trust ahead 2027 Elections
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

. Laments umpire’s multiple websites, opaque data protection arrangements

James Emejo in Abuja

A new report has indicted the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) over inadequate transparency and disclosure in its handling and protection of sensitive voter data ahead of the 2027 general election.

Unveiled yesterday by the Digital Rights Lawyers Initiative (DRLI), the “Voter Privacy and Umpires’ Transparency: An Empirical Assessment of Electoral Bodies’ Compliance with the Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) 2023,” identified significant gaps in INEC’s compliance with the Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) 2023, raising questions about the security and accountability of the digital infrastructure underpinning the country’s electoral process.

Presenting the findings at a roundtable on voter privacy and data transparency in Nigeria’s electioneering process in Abuja, Co-founder of DRLI, Dr. Olumide Babalola, said the election umpire had failed to provide Nigerians with critical information about how their personal data were handled, the identity of technology vendors engaged to manage electoral platforms and the safeguards against unauthorised access to sensitive voter records.

Babalola said the findings exposed a troubling disconnect between the enormous volumes of sensitive information collected by electoral bodies and the limited information available to citizens about how such data were processed, stored, shared and protected.

He said the investigation found that INEC operated about three or four websites, some of which were incomplete, without clearly identifying which platform constituted its official information channel.

He noted that the situation undermined the commission’s statutory obligation to provide accessible privacy notices and other disclosures required under the data protection law.

According to him, only about two state independent electoral commissions examined in the research had their own websites, while others relied on platforms belonging to state government agencies, raising further concerns about their institutional independence and transparency.

Babalola said the absence of functional and independent websites made it difficult for citizens to access privacy policies explaining how their information was handled and the rights available to them as data subjects.

He listed the information electoral bodies were expected to disclose to include their identities, data protection officers, technology vendors, organisations with which they shared information, security arrangements and the rights of individuals whose data they collected.

The lawyer also questioned the opacity surrounding the technology companies and service providers responsible for INEC’s major digital platforms, including the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) and the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV).

He said Nigerians were entitled to know who operated the systems, where voter information was stored, who had access to their backend infrastructure and whether adequate safeguards existed to prevent conflicts of interest or manipulation.

Babalola maintained that the concerns went beyond the credibility of election results to the integrity of the information infrastructure through which elections were administered.

He disclosed that DRLI had previously approached the court over alleged transparency violations by INEC, but the commission had yet to respond to the suit.

He also said the organisation submitted a Freedom of Information request to the Nigerian Data Protection Commission (NDPC) to establish INEC’s compliance record.

According to him, the response indicated that INEC had been compliant for only one year in the period examined but was not compliant in the current year.

Babalola, however, stressed that the report focused specifically on transparency obligations and did not constitute a comprehensive assessment of every aspect of INEC’s data protection compliance.

He said the commission’s failure to adequately explain its handling of recent controversies involving allegedly exposed voter registration information and AI-generated voter details had further weakened public confidence.

He cited the reported incident involving the voter registration information of actor Emeka Ike, which was allegedly accessed by a serving government official, as well as controversies surrounding fabricated or AI-generated voter records.

According to him, the commission’s responsibility should not end with announcing that officials linked to such incidents had been arrested.

Nigerians, he said, deserved to know the outcome of investigations, whether those involved had been charged and what measures had been introduced to prevent a recurrence.

Babalola said, “Trust has to be built before the elections. If you are not transparent, there is no way you can build trust.”

He urged INEC to publish comprehensive privacy notices, clearly identify its official websites, disclose the vendors managing its digital infrastructure and explain the procedures for accessing, securing and processing voter information.

He also called for greater disclosure of the individuals authorised to access the backend of electoral platforms, warning that digital systems could potentially allow alterations to electoral information without the visible traces associated with the physical manipulation of ballot papers.

According to him, transparency was not an administrative convenience but a legal obligation and a necessary condition for citizens to trust the electoral process.

Also speaking, Principal at Luminate, Mr. Adebayo Adegoke, warned that the increasing digitisation of the country’s electoral process had expanded the risks associated with the collection, storage and use of voter information.

He said the deployment of technology across different stages of elections, from voter registration to the actual conduct of polls, had made data governance an increasingly important democratic issue.

According to him, the enormous volumes of sensitive information held by INEC could become instruments of electoral manipulation if adequate safeguards were not established.

Adegoke said the emergence of artificial intelligence had made the threat more complicated, as malicious actors could exploit available data to generate fabricated information, manipulate existing records or compromise the integrity of electoral information.

He noted that data corruption could occur not only during collection but also after information had been gathered, particularly where storage systems and digital infrastructure were inadequately protected.

He expressed concern over recent controversies involving AI-generated materials relating to voter registration, arguing that such incidents demonstrated how existing electoral records could be manipulated through technology.

He said the issue was no longer limited to protecting information against external interference but also ensuring that institutions entrusted with citizens’ data had effective governance structures and accountability mechanisms.

Adegoke stressed that electoral data were particularly consequential because they ultimately informed decisions about who became president, governor, senator and other elected officeholders.

He said anyone with unauthorised access to such information could potentially exploit it to influence the electoral process.

The Luminate principal therefore called for stronger institutional accountability, stressing that the management of voter information was inseparable from the fairness and integrity of elections.

Also, in an interview with THISDAY, Executive Director, Digital Africa Research and Safety Lab, Rosemary Ajayi, said Nigerians could not afford to remain passive about the security and integrity of the electoral process ahead of 2027.

While expressing reservations about making definitive judgments on INEC’s preparedness, Ajayi said citizens were increasingly exploring technological tools to monitor elections and protect their votes.

She identified drones, body cameras and other monitoring technologies as some of the instruments citizens were considering deploying to document electoral activities.

According to her, regardless of INEC’s level of preparedness, Nigerians were already demonstrating their determination to safeguard the electoral process.

Ajayi also drew attention to the potential threat posed by insiders within electoral institutions, warning that discussions about electoral interference often focused excessively on external actors while overlooking individuals with authorised access to sensitive systems.

Referring to the reported incident involving the voter registration information of actor Emeka Ike, she said the circumstances surrounding the alleged disclosure had yet to be adequately explained by INEC.

She also raised concerns over reports of ghost voters, adding that such developments reinforced the need for stronger scrutiny of how electoral information was generated, accessed and maintained.

Ajayi said the protection of voter information required more than technological deployment, insisting that institutional accountability and public vigilance were equally important.

The roundtable, organised by DRLI with support from Luminate, to examine the relationship between voter privacy, institutional transparency and electoral credibility under Nigeria’s evolving digital election environment.

Gwarzo Joined in Suit Seeking to Stop NDC from Fielding Guber Candidate in Kano

Ahmad Sorondinki in Kano

The legal battle over the National Democratic Congress (NDC) governorship ticket in Kano State took a new turn as the party’s candidate, Aminu Gwarzo, has now been joined as a party to the suit instituted to stop his candidacy.

The suit, filed by three members of the NDC in the state, seeks an order to restrain the party from forwarding the name of its governorship candidate to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

Gwarzo, who clinched the NDC governorship ticket, is contesting the election alongside his running mate, Mustapha Rabiu Kwankwaso.

However, INEC did not include Gwarzo and his running mate in its published list of governorship candidates for Kano State, attributing the omission to a court order.

The plaintiffs in the suit, Garba Umar Isa, Yau Abubakar, and another NDC member, are asking the court to bar INEC from publishing Gwarzo’s name as the NDC governorship standard bearer for the 2026 election, citing the Supreme Court judgment in the Zenith Labour Party case.

At yesterday’s proceedings in Kano, counsel to the plaintiffs, Moses Ademola Falana, first objected to the joinder application filed by Gwarzo’s lawyer, Sagir Gezawa (SAN), seeking to make Gwarzo a necessary party in the case, but later withdrew his counter-affidavit.

On their part, INEC’s counsel, Hassan Aminu, and NDC’s counsel, Dahiru Ibrahim, did not object to the application.

In his ruling, Justice Amobeda granted the application and formally joined Gwarzo as the third defendant.

He further directed all parties to file their processes reflecting Gwarzo’s inclusion as the third defendant, and adjourned the matter to November 23 for hearing of all pending preliminary applications.

World.title: From the Asaba Declaration to a Future-Ready Civil Service in Nigeria
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

By Tunji Olaopa

Whether we know it or not, at the core of the forthcoming 2027 election is the key issue of the capability readiness of the civil service system to backstop the Renewed Hope Agenda of the Tinubu administration. Every administration that hopes to transform the well-being of its citizens through the efficient implementation of good governance must necessarily need a functional bureaucratic system that will anchor the effective delivery of public goods. This is exactly the issue that was at the center table of critical deliberation at the just concluded 45th National Council and 2026 Annual Conference of the Civil Service Commissions of the Federation, held at Asaba, Delta State. The question on the agenda is very significant: “Towards a Future-Ready Civil Service: The Role of Institutional Re-engineering, Reputation Management and Culture Change at the Civil Service Commissions in Nigeria.”

This theme is apposite and auspicious for many reasons. The first is that this 45th National Council built systematically on the two previous ones. The 43rd conference which held in Katsina in 2024 was committed to a programme of institutional reengineering to transform all the Commissions, federal and state, into game changing agents that will be committed to a renewed governance partnership with the governments at all levels. This commitment galvanises ongoing initiatives that has kept alive the understanding of the civil service commissions and its constitutional gatekeeping mandate to restore the civil service as a professionalised, meritocratic, and efficient value-adding institution in Nigeria. On its own, the 44th annual conference in Umuahia in 2025 thoroughly interrogated the 5-year Strategic Plan (2026-2030) of the Federal Civil Service Commission (FCSC) whose fundamental essence was the commitment to restore the lost glory of the CSCs in Nigeria. This is indeed the first step toward institutionalizing the reform vision for a capable, citizen-centred and accountable civil service. And again, most fortunately, this commitment is unravelling in the form of operationalized frameworks—founded on the core values of integrity, professionalism, innovation and accountability (I-PIA)—that are meant to promote a merit-based, fair and ethical workforce.

We arrived at the 45th conference with lots of reform remnants. One of the most fundamental is the fact that we are reforming mostly within the old and traditional Weberian bureaucratic model and all its administrative limitations and debilitations, especially within the African administrative context. This injects one of the first fundamental relevance of the founding mandate of the CSCs as the custodian of the merit principle. This mandate will only make some significant sense if its HRM practices are sufficiently strong to capacitate the civil service in order to make the Nigerian state truly developmental. This then imposes a high pressure on the CSCs and its gatekeeping mandate to put in place procedures that make it easy to not only recruit the brightest and the best in terms of human capital that will be able to man the civil service system, but to also facilitate a performance-oriented promotion regime that enables talent management and career progression for civil servants. The Asaba conference was therefore expected to move that conversation forward: to take stock of progress, confront the unfinished business of reform and identify practical steps that Federal and State Commissions can take together.

The 45th conference is therefore confronted with the task of reflecting on the significance of a modernized, high-performing civil service of the future that could serve as the operational backbone the Tinubu administration requires to transform into reality its vision of Nigeria as a $1trn economy by 2030. This means that the CSCs must sit up to the need for a paradigmatic shift that turns public administration practice in Nigeria from a slow and patronage-driven bureaucracy into a development-oriented administrative engine. We are therefore talking of a triple task for the CSCs, involving reputation management, institutional reengineering and culture change. This is a task that requires rewiring the bureaucracy and upgrading its institutional intelligence to get things done—to achieve the capability readiness to execute infrastructural projects, trade, digital, and agricultural roadmaps.

Professor Dele Olowu, the keynote speaker for the 45th conference captures the soul of the task ahead aptly: “Technology alone will not give us a civil service fit for the future. Institutions will: institutions that keep finding and attracting talent, protect merit, build competence, reward good work, defend integrity and, in the end, earn the trust of the public.” And his five questions for any civil service prospecting the future are: “Whom do we recruit? Whom do we develop? Whom do we reward? Whom do we hold to account? And does each of those decisions actually serve the country’s long-term development?” If all this speaks to the mandate of the 10th Commission, how do we articulate its three-year scorecard in this regard? And then how does the FCSC and its state CSCs’ partners hope to extend the reach of these reform aspirations in the next two years remaining for the tenure of the 10th Commission to end?

First the scorecard for the three years of getting the FCSC to run on its mandate. The most outstanding to note is the two-fold signature successes of the FCSC. On the one hand, and for the very first time since its establishment, the FCSC introduced a new online mode of recruitment that deploys the computer-based testing (CBT) as a procedure for achieving merit-based selection of civil servants, and facilitates a more convenient, cost effective, friendly and safer recruitment. On the other hand, it has also established a strictly controlled and transparent service-wide and directorate-level promotion system that also utilizes online accreditation and the CBT in ways that undermine undue influence and promotion racketeering. Given the fact that the civil service is dealing with a reputation-reality asymmetry, the Commission is thus confronted with the urgency of implementing series of extensive changes that close that gap in the fight against bureaucratic corruption. This has led to the need to make crucial adjustments in internal capabilities, processes and systems especially in terms of human resource management processes concerning staff appointment, promotion, discipline and appeals. This enables the FCSC to achieve a minimum tolerable integrity threshold that draws the Commission closer to its desired reputation

The Commission has also opened up its visibility in terms of more strategic communication of its policies and activities. This has, on the one hand strengthened a robust relationship with stakeholders from the Office of the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation to the National Salaries, Wages and Incomes Commission, among others, to drum up critical support for its mandates. And on the other hand, it has strengthened the Commission’s capacity to resuscitate its critical presence in inter-institutional bodies, and most critically its membership of the Association of African Public Service Commissions.

How far does the 10th Commission expect that it would have gone (beyond its acclaimed accomplishments for the first three years) by the end of its tenure in 2028? The answer to this lies within the FCSC Strategic Plan (2026-2030). It possesses four domains of change management for achieving sustained performance of a highly-performing civil service. One, it prospects the restoration of the Commission preeminent status as gatekeeper of a valued profession in game-changing Nigeria’s national transformation. Two, is the digital transformation with deepened and consolidated e-recruitment, CBT promotion exercise and digitalized Commission backend. Three, the professionalization of the Commission’s Secretariat. And four, evidence-based scientific best practice methodology in strategy implementation, change management, and in Commission’s internal administrative operations and bureaucratic efficiency.

What the 45th conference and the Asaba Declaration have achieved is to establish a clearer common agenda by which the Strategic Plan of the 10th Commission could be achieved through critical issues that could determine the engagement between the FCSC and its strategic state CSCs’ partners. First, there is the need to develop practical guidelines that frame the relationship between the merit principle and competence on the one hand, and the requirement for national spread in human resource management decisions alias federal character principle. Second, there is the urgent need for the CSCs across the federation to harmonize clear and dependable guidelines on appointment, promotion and discipline (APD) through technical support to states CSCs that are lagging behind. Third, there is the need not just to commence but to work out quality working relationships with the Office of the Head of Service and other relevant stakeholders in ways that positively affect the governance and career management of civil servants.

Fourth, emphasis was laid on the cogency of aligning and operationalizing the performance management system that articulate a credible framework for a fair performance evaluation and promotion. Fifth, the declaration demands the prioritization of digital modernization that affects recruitment procedures, personnel record and other administrative processes to be able to facilitate the restoration of public trust in the system through transparency and accountability. This is meant to ultimately address and undermine, through prompt disclaimers, periodic reports, active websites and stern disciplinary actions, the incidents of scams, frauds and racketeering that damage the reputation of the civil service. Lastly, the Council resolves on the need to collectively strengthen implementation, communication and peer learning across the CSCs. This is achievable through, for example, participation in inter-institutional bodies, such as the Association of African Public Service Commissions (AAPSCOMS).

While the sterling successes and cogent conditions for a robust future for the civil service are outstanding, the 45th Conference is also not unaware of the binding constraints that could water down the significant prospects for the future of the civil service system that the Asaba Declaration announced. The first challenge to watch out for comes from a lack of structured communication, sustained engagement and mutual working collaboration between federal and state commissioners, as well as other stakeholders. Such a crucial disconnect will nullify the intent, principles and workings of true federalism. Fleshing out the shape of the civil service of the future cannot be done outside of the solid partnership between the federal and state commissions. The next challenge will arise from the overlaps, conflicts and misalignment that will surface between the offices of the heads of service and the civil service commissions. Even though this is to be expected, yet its virulence can be mitigated through practical guidelines for collaboration.

The civil service is already facing the challenge that arises from the changing dynamics of work, the workforce and the workplace. It becomes imperative therefore for the CSCs to immediately prepare the civil service on the peculiar sociology of the work culture that incorporates the millennials, Gen Z and the Gen Alpha. Last, but not least, there is the frustrating challenge of confronting the digital technologies and the disruptive force of artificial intelligence. The imperative of digitalization of administrative procedures and processes implies harnessing the potentials of AI. This demands that the CSCs and the civil services across the federation need to confront the need for flexible employment policies and practices given that the new generation of civil servants are increasingly challenging existing frameworks of lifetime careers, 60/35 years retirement options, 8am to 5pm daily routine, etc.

The Asaba Conference has already succeeded in setting a serious common agenda in harmonizing the gains of the previous council meetings, and in outlining cogent imperatives that will guide reform planning among the CSCs in the next one year. This is the essence of collaborative framework that must define the CSCs not just in the next one year before the next National Council meeting, but also for the remainder of the tenure of the 10th Commission.

*Prof. Tunji Olaopa is the Chairman of the Federal Civil Service Commission, Abuja

World.title: As Senate Probes Alleged N210trn Financial Discrepancies in NNPCL…
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

With the erstwhile Group Chief Executive Officer of Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited, Mele Kyari, insisting that the controversial figures linked to the company represent book keeping issues rather than missing funds, the Senate faces a bigger challenge: translating its investigation into concrete sanctions, recoveries and institutional accountability. Sunday Aborisade reports.

The appearance of former Group Chief Executive Officer of the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPCL), Mele Kyari, before the Senate Public Accounts Committee (SPAC) over the controversial N210 trillion financial discrepancy in the company’s audited accounts has reopened an important national conversation about accountability in Nigeria’s petroleum industry.

Beyond the explanations offered by the former oil industry’s chief executive, however, the investigation raises a more fundamental question: Will the Senate’s painstaking examination produce tangible consequences, or will it eventually become another parliamentary exercise whose resolutions generate headlines without compelling the relevant anti-corruption agencies to act?

The question is significant because the Senate Public Accounts Committee is principally an oversight and investigative body. Although it possesses constitutional powers to summon witnesses, demand documents, examine public accounts and make recommendations, its findings do not automatically translate into criminal prosecution, financial recovery or administrative sanctions.

Consequently, the ultimate success of the investigation will depend substantially on whether institutions such as the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) and Nigeria Police Force can act on any credible evidence of wrongdoing established by the committee.

For a country struggling with public confidence in the management of its petroleum resources, the stakes are considerably higher than the accounting explanations currently dominating the proceedings.

The controversy originated from the examination of NNPCL’s audited financial statements and related records covering several financial years, particularly between 2017 and 2023.

During the earlier stages of the investigation, the committee identified two major entries requiring clarification: approximately N103 trillion recorded as accrued expenses in the company’s 2022 financial statements and another N107 trillion reflected as sundry receivables as of December 2023.

The committee, initially chaired by Senator Aliyu Wadada, questioned the explanations provided by the company’s management concerning the composition of the accrued expenses and the identities of institutions and entities allegedly responsible for the outstanding receivables.

The lawmakers also raised questions about certain production-related expenses, alleged duplication of subsidy deductions amounting to approximately N3.8 trillion and the expenditure associated with the incorporation of NNPCL Limited following the enactment of the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA).

However, describing the combined figures as N210 trillion missing from the company’s accounts requires an important accounting qualification.

The N103 trillion and N107 trillion represent entries on different sides of the balance sheet. Adding them together does not, in itself, establish that N210 trillion was stolen, misappropriated or physically removed from the company’s accounts.

Determining whether an actual financial loss occurred requires examining the underlying transactions, supporting documents, accounting treatments and identities of the relevant creditors and debtors.

This distinction is central to the investigation and underscores the need for professional accounting scrutiny rather than political interpretations of the figures.

Appearing before the committee chaired by Senator Ibrahim Dankwambo, last week Kyari categorically rejected suggestions that the disputed amounts represented missing funds.

He maintained that the discrepancies arose from accounting entries and bookkeeping issues rather than financial losses under his leadership.

He submitted a written response to the committee’s queries, accompanied by his lawyer, Professor Sam Erugo, and other members of his legal team.

Kyari also defended his administration’s record, arguing that he introduced transparency and accountability measures that opened the company’s financial records to public scrutiny for the first time in its 43-year history.

He said his administration inherited an NNPC that recorded a loss of $803 million in 2018 but subsequently introduced measures that returned the organisation to profitability.

The former GCEO also explained the controversial payment of approximately N2.99 billion associated with the incorporation and registration of NNPCL Limited.

According to him, the payment was made to relevant government institutions, including the former Federal Inland Revenue Service and the Corporate Affairs Commission, to fulfil statutory requirements arising from the Petroleum Industry Act.

He argued that the Federation, rather than the company, was ultimately responsible for the incorporation expenses under the applicable provisions of the legislation.

Kyari equally dismissed suggestions that billions of naira were spent merely to name the company, insisting that its name had already been established by the National Assembly through the PIA.

Although these explanations provide important information, they do not automatically settle the questions raised by the audit findings. The critical issue is whether they can be independently verified through documentary evidence and professional examination.

Neither an individual’s assurance that financial records were transparent nor the appearance of unusually large accounting entries should substitute for independently established facts.

Perhaps the most important dimension of the investigation concerns the constitutional powers of the Senate Public Accounts Committee and whether its eventual findings can compel accountability.

Section 85(5) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, provides for the consideration of the Auditor-General’s reports by the appropriate National Assembly committee responsible for public accounts.

Similarly, Section 89 empowers the Senate and its committees to obtain evidence, examine witnesses under oath, summon individuals and require the production of documents relevant to their investigations.

These are substantial powers designed to enable the legislature to scrutinise public expenditure and ensure accountability in government institutions.

However, the committee is not a criminal court. It cannot convict an individual of fraud, impose a prison sentence or independently exercise prosecutorial powers.

Its principal responsibility is to investigate, establish facts, identify financial and administrative irregularities, make recommendations and refer matters requiring further investigation to appropriate authorities.

This distinction creates a potential weakness in the accountability process.

Even if the committee eventually establishes serious financial irregularities, its recommendations do not automatically translate into sanctions against those implicated.

A recommendation asking the EFCC to investigate a former public officer does not, by itself, compel the commission to institute criminal proceedings. Similarly, a recommendation to the ICPC does not constitute a prosecutorial order.

The agencies retain their statutory responsibilities to examine the evidence, determine whether offences have been committed and decide whether the legal requirements for prosecution have been satisfied.

In effect, the Senate can expose suspected wrongdoing and recommend action, but the actual investigation and prosecution of criminal offences must be undertaken by the appropriate institutions.

This is where the effectiveness of the current investigation will ultimately be tested.

Nigeria’s experience with legislative investigations has frequently exposed a gap between parliamentary pronouncements and the implementation of recommendations.

Committees of the National Assembly have, over the years, investigated public expenditure, procurement irregularities, revenue remittances and alleged financial misconduct.

While some investigations have generated considerable public attention, the more difficult question has often been what happened after their reports were submitted.

Were recommendations implemented? Were public funds recovered? Were officials found culpable sanctioned? Were criminal investigations concluded and prosecutions initiated?

These questions are particularly relevant to the NNPCL investigation because of the enormous financial implications of the disputed transactions.

The EFCC and ICPC possess statutory powers to investigate offences within their respective jurisdictions, while the police also have responsibilities concerning criminal investigations.

However, the agencies operate under different legal mandates. The Senate cannot simply transfer its conclusions to them and assume that prosecution or financial recovery will automatically follow.

They must independently assess the evidence, establish the relevant offences and determine whether prosecution is legally justified.

Nevertheless, this limitation must not become an excuse for institutional inaction.

If the Senate uncovers credible evidence of fraudulent transactions, diversion of public funds, abuse of office or other criminal conduct, its committee should make specific referrals supported by documentary evidence.

It should identify the agencies expected to act, the issues requiring investigation and the appropriate follow-up mechanisms.

A general recommendation asking government agencies to investigate alleged financial irregularities would be inadequate for a matter of this magnitude.

Dankwambo’s decision to consult the Office of the Auditor-General of the Federation before determining the committee’s next line of action is therefore important.

The controversy is fundamentally rooted in financial statements and audit observations. Professional examination is necessary to establish whether the disputed figures represent legitimate accounting treatments, inadequately documented transactions, recoverable debts, unsupported liabilities or possible financial misconduct.

The committee must also examine whether the external auditors responsible for the financial statements exercised appropriate professional diligence.

If Kyari’s explanations are satisfactory, the committee should establish how the figures were derived and why they appeared in the accounts in that manner.

If they are unsatisfactory, the unresolved discrepancies must be clearly identified and appropriate corrective measures recommended.

The public deserves a technically sound explanation rather than a mere announcement that the matter has been resolved.

Dankwambo disclosed that the committee had identified 23 issues requiring examination, although only a limited number required specific explanations from Kyari.

He explained that the written submissions of former NNPCL officials would be circulated among members for detailed examination before the committee determined its next steps.

His distinction between the N103 trillion and N107 trillion figures was particularly revealing. He observed that while the amounts could be politically presented as N210 trillion, their accounting implications required reconciliation.

The committee’s decision not to immediately discharge Kyari pending examination of his submissions also suggests that lawmakers are not prepared to accept his explanations without further scrutiny.

However, the investigation must not become an endless cycle of invitations, submissions, clarifications and adjournments. Nigerians expect a definite conclusion.

Ultimately, the most damaging outcome would be for the Senate to conclude its investigation, issue a detailed report and leave its recommendations without meaningful implementation.

Such an outcome would reinforce public cynicism about legislative oversight and deepen concerns that high-profile investigations rarely produce consequences for influential individuals.

The NNPCL is not an ordinary commercial enterprise. Its operations are connected to Nigeria’s major revenue-generating sector, crude oil production, petroleum supply, gas development and the country’s broader fiscal stability.

The committee must therefore examine whether the financial management weaknesses identified during the investigation have been corrected under the company’s present management.

Accountability should not be restricted to determining what happened under previous administrations. It must also establish whether institutional weaknesses have been addressed to prevent their recurrence.

Furthermore, where public funds are established to have been improperly spent or withheld, the appropriate authorities should pursue recovery through lawful procedures. Where criminal liability is established, prosecution should follow due process, irrespective of the individuals involved or their former positions.

The Senate also needs to establish a mechanism for monitoring the implementation of its recommendations and demanding periodic progress reports from the relevant institutions.

Although it cannot dictate the outcome of criminal investigations or compel prosecutors to secure convictions, it can ensure that credible findings are formally referred and that Nigerians are informed about subsequent institutional responses.

For now, the N210 trillion controversy remains an unresolved question of financial accountability rather than an established case of missing or stolen money.

But that distinction must not become a convenient escape route for anyone found responsible for financial misconduct.

The real measure of the Senate’s success will not be how many former NNPCL officials appear before its committee, how many questions are asked or how many pages its final report contains.

It will be whether Nigerians eventually know what happened to the disputed financial entries, whether wrongdoing is established, whether public funds are recovered where necessary and whether those found culpable face appropriate consequences.

Otherwise, the Senate risks producing another elaborate investigative report whose recommendations will be filed away while the central questions of accountability remain unanswered.

World.title: State Police: Governors Barred from Unlawful Arrests as 36 States Back Bill
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

• Proposes independent commissions, two-thirds approval for removal of CPs

•Seeks presidential intervention in cases of abuse, breakdown of law and order

•National Assembly completes verification, set to transmit bill to Tinubu

•It’s all clear for establishment of state police services

Sunday Aborisade in Abuja





The proposed constitutional amendment seeking to establish State Police Services across the country has introduced far-reaching safeguards against political interference, arbitrary arrests and abuse of police powers, THISDAY learnt yesterday.

Specifically, the bill has expressly prohibited governors from issuing any unlawful directive compelling police officers to arrest, detain, investigate or deploy force against any named individual, political party, association or group, except in accordance with the law.

The development came as all the 36 State Houses of Assembly have approved the proposed constitutional amendment to establish state police services, clearing a major constitutional hurdle towards the decentralisation of policing in Nigeria.

Clerk to the National Assembly, Kamoru Ogunlana, disclosed the unanimous endorsement by all the state legislatures, in a statement issued in Abuja yesterday.

Similarly, the bill seen by THISDAY has provided for independent police commissions to oversee recruitment, promotion, discipline and accountability at the state level.

The proposed Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026, published in the National Assembly Journal No. 11, dated June 22, 2026, seeks to replace the existing constitutional provision establishing a single Nigeria Police Force with a two-tier policing structure comprising the Federal Police Service and State Police Services.

However, despite the restrictions, governors would be empowered to issue lawful written directions of general policy to their respective Commissioners of Police on matters relating to public safety and public order.

The proposed law also prohibits the use of police institutions to suppress lawful political activities, violate fundamental human rights, discriminate against individuals or groups, or enforce the law for partisan, ethnic, religious, sectional or personal purposes.

The proposed piece of legislation further provides that the Inspector-General of Police (IGP) and state Commissioners of Police cannot be arbitrarily removed from office.

Under the arrangement, a state Commissioner of Police would be appointed by the governor on the recommendation of the National Police Council (NPC), subject to confirmation by the State House of Assembly.

The commissioner would, however, be removable only for stated cause, following a fair hearing, a recommendation by the national police council and approval through a resolution supported by at least two-thirds of the members of the State House of Assembly.

Similarly, the IGP would be appointed by the president on the advice of the National Police Council and subject to Senate confirmation. The IGP’s removal would require stated cause, fair hearing, a recommendation by the national police council and approval by a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the Senate.

The bill, therefore, seeks to establish institutional safeguards intended to protect police leadership from arbitrary political interference at both federal and state levels.

Under the proposed constitutional arrangement, there would be a Federal Police Service responsible for policing the federation, while each state would have the constitutional authority to establish its own police service through legislation passed by its House of Assembly.

However, the establishment of State Police would not automatically translate into the commencement of operational policing.

The bill stipulates that no state police service shall commence operations until it has been established by a law of the relevant State House of Assembly and certified as meeting national minimum standards prescribed under an Act of the National Assembly.

Until such certification and commencement, the Federal Police Service would continue to perform policing functions in the affected state, the bill stated.

Even after state police become operational, the Federal Police Service would retain responsibility for federal policing functions, including the enforcement of federal laws, protection of federal institutions and assets, and policing matters involving terrorism, cybercrime, organised crime, arms trafficking, border security and other national security concerns.

State Police, on the other hand, would be responsible for enforcing state laws, maintaining public safety and order, preventing and detecting offences within their jurisdiction, and protecting lives and property.

The proposed amendment also establishes an important mechanism for federal intervention in state policing.

It empowers the Federal Police Service to temporarily intervene in the internal security affairs of a state where there is an actual or imminent breakdown of public order, the state police authority is unable or unwilling to contain the situation, or the governor requests federal assistance.

Other grounds include: Serious administrative, financial or operational incapacity, substantial evidence of systematic human rights violations, partisan or electoral intimidation, ethnic or religious persecution, and threats to national security or the sovereignty of the federation.

Such intervention, however, must be temporary, necessary, proportionate and restricted to the territory, functions and period required to address the situation.

According to the bill, the President must authorise the intervention in writing, stating its grounds, scope and duration.

In the same vein, the governor, Speaker of the State House of Assembly, national police council and National Assembly must receive notification within 48 hours. Any intervention extending beyond the period prescribed by an Act of the National Assembly would require Senate approval.

The legality, scope, duration and conduct of such intervention would also remain subject to judicial review.

Another major feature of the proposed legislation is the establishment of State Police Service Commissions as independent constitutional institutions.

The commissions would recommend qualified candidates for appointment as state commissioners of police, appoint other officers, oversee promotions, transfers, dismissals and disciplinary matters, and perform oversight, complaints and accountability functions.

The bill also provides that funds standing to the credit of a state police service commission would be paid directly to the commission, a provision designed to strengthen its financial independence.

To ensure uniformity and professionalism, the National Assembly would prescribe minimum standards covering recruitment, background checks, training, certification, appointments, promotions, discipline, firearms, use of force, custody of suspects, complaints management, criminal information systems and public accountability.

Individual state assemblies could prescribe additional or higher standards but would not be permitted to fall below the national minimum requirements.

Importantly, the proposed amendment expressly prohibits federal authorities from exercising routine command, deployment, appointment, promotion, transfer or disciplinary control over personnel of state police services, except where constitutionally authorised federal intervention becomes necessary.

The bill also provides for cooperation and information-sharing between federal and state police authorities, including the development of criminal information systems and coordinated security arrangements.

It further stipulates that police officers may carry only arms, ammunition and equipment authorised by an Act of the National Assembly, while every use of force must be lawful, necessary, proportionate and accountable.

The proposed amendment is designed to create a constitutional framework for decentralised policing without dismantling the federal policing structure.

Its explanatory memorandum states that the detailed organisation, operational procedures, certification, complaints mechanisms, grants and implementation arrangements would be provided for in subsequent federal legislation and, where applicable, laws enacted by state assemblies.

The legislation, therefore, seeks to combine state-level policing autonomy with national standards, independent oversight and constitutional safeguards against the abuse of police powers.

All 36 State Assemblies Approve Bill, Await Tinubu’s Assent

Meanwhile, all 36 State Houses of Assembly in Nigeria have approved the proposed constitutional amendment to establish state police services, clearing a major constitutional hurdle towards the decentralisation of policing in Nigeria.

The Clerk to the National Assembly, Ogunlana, disclosed this in a statement issued yesterday, confirming that the proposed legislation had received unanimous endorsement from all the state legislatures.

The development represents 100 per cent approval by the state assemblies, far exceeding the constitutional requirement of at least 24 states under Section 9(2) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended.

With the endorsement of all 36 state legislatures, the proposed constitutional amendment is now set for transmission to President Bola Tinubu for assent, following the completion of the verification process by the Office of the Clerk to the National Assembly.

Ogunlana explained that although the bill had earlier satisfied all constitutional and administrative requirements for transmission, the leadership of the National Assembly deliberately delayed the process to allow for broader national consensus and engagement with all the states.

He said the decision was aimed at ensuring wider participation and securing the support of all federating units before advancing the proposed amendment to the next constitutional stage.

According to the Clerk, the unanimous endorsement represents an unprecedented demonstration of cooperation between the National Assembly and the State Houses of Assembly, as well as constructive collaboration between the executive arms of government at the federal and state levels.

“Following the completion of the verification process by my Office, the Bill is set for transmission to the President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, for His Excellency’s assent,” Ogunlana stated.

He said the successful approval of the state police amendment had also provided a foundation for the National Assembly to advance other proposed constitutional alterations.

The Clerk disclosed that the National Assembly would, as soon as possible, transmit the remaining Sixth Constitution Alteration Bills to the state legislatures for consideration.

The establishment of state police has remained a major issue in Nigeria’s security and constitutional reform debate, with proponents arguing that decentralising police administration would enable states to respond more effectively to security threats within their jurisdictions.

The proposed amendment, however, must complete the remaining constitutional processes before the framework can become operational.

Ogunlana commended the 36 state governors, speakers and members of the various state legislatures, as well as other stakeholders, for their cooperation and commitment to the proposed reform.

He said their collective support had contributed to the successful completion of the state-level approval process.

World.title: Could Rassie Erasmus be in hot water with World Rugby again?
World.content:
Springbok boss Rassie Erasmus could be in trouble with World Rugby once again. Image: Charmaine Visser

Springbok boss Rassie Erasmus has made headlines around the rugby world after an explosive press conference on Monday in which he highlighted several contradictions and questions that had left him mystified after the loss against France.

In particular, Erasmus pointed out more than 15 ‘leg drop’ tackles that were missed or overlooked by officials, despite this illegal technique having been identified by World Rugby as something where there would be zero tolerance.

However, what could land Erasmus in hot water is the fact he intimated that some of the absent interventions could be perceived as ‘match fixing’.



“There’s 17 knee-drop tackles and the TMO doesn’t come in once,” Rassie Erasmus commented.

“I’m not saying he’s wrong, I’m saying if he didn’t see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing? Is that not interfering with the outcome of a game if you see this injury that happened there, a knee-drop tackle happened there, and it’s been decided that knee drop tackles are out.”

According to Sky Sports, the statements from Erasmus will be reviewed “in the context of the match official abuse sanction framework that was introduced earlier this year”.



This framework will see an independent three-person panel assess the comments to determine if they were made to undermine confidence in officials. Outcomes range from “no further action” to a guidance letter, formal warning, or automatic sanction under the framework.

Erasmus of course does have a chequered history with World Rugby, having received a two-month suspension from all rugby activities at the end of 2021, while a year later he had to serve a two-match ban for comments on social media that were seen to be critical of officials.

Clear protocols in place

Earlier this year, in line with the provisions of the Match Official Abuse Sanction Process, World Rugby handed an automatic two-match suspension to Italy coach Gonzalo Quesada for comments regarding match officiating.



“The Match Official Abuse Sanction Process is targeted at reducing comments which often are the basis of the unacceptable increase in abuse and threats towards match officials,” World Rugby stated.



“Under the process, an independent panel comprising the independent judicial panel chair and two experienced judicial panel members consider whether any conduct or comments made by team personnel includes among other things, allegations that a match official acted with bias, prejudice, improper motive, external influence, or deliberate intent to affect an outcome and/or conduct which, viewed objectively, they knew or ought to know would undermine public confidence in match officials.

“Assessment of comments takes account of a full range of factors including the nature and reach of the comments, the timing, the role of the speaker and any aggravating factors, such as whether the conduct led directly to an increase in personal abuse against a match official.”

The process runs in parallel with existing misconduct provisions under Regulation 18 and recognises World Rugby’s leading social media protection programme for match officials and players which has shown, since 2023, that a large proportion of social media abuse begins with inaccurate comments on refereeing performance from those in positions of authority.

World.title: Sandton bomb scare: SAPS issues stern warning
World.content:
Police and emergency services responded to a bomb threat in Sandton on Monday, forcing authorities to close several roads. Image: X

One phone call brought parts of Johannesburg’s financial district to a standstill on Monday, forcing about 300 employees to abandon their offices.

A day after the Sandton bomb scare, police have warned that those responsible for hoax calls could face legal consequences.

SANDTON BOMB SCARE: NO ARRESTS

Gauteng police spokesperson Lieutenant-Colonel Isaac Mudau confirmed that investigations were continuing following the security operation.



Police reportedly found no explosives during a search of the building.

Authorities declared the premises safe.

However, police have yet to announce an arrest.

ONE PHONE CALL SPARKS EVACUATION

Mudau said Bramley police received a complaint from a woman on Monday, 16 November, after an unidentified man allegedly phoned her at around midday.

He claimed he had planted a bomb inside the office park.

The building’s safety officer activated the alarm, prompting staff to evacuate.



Police explosives experts and the K9 unit subsequently searched the premises.

POLICE WARN AGAINST HOAX CALLS

The South African Police Service (SAPS) has urged the public to refrain from making false reports or abusing emergency numbers.

Meanwhile, the Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department (JMPD) reopened Sandton Drive and Alice Lane on Monday afternoon following the all-clear.

World.title: Is the Cameron Waldeck-Cooks murder investigation still ongoing?
World.content:
The murder investigation into the death of 17-year-old Cameron Waldeck-Cooks remains ongoing more than three months after she was found dead. Image via X/Canva

The murder investigation into the death of 17-year-old Cameron Waldeck-Cooks remains ongoing, with her family still seeking answers more than three months after she was found dead at a holiday property in Sabie in Mpumalanga.

The South African has reached out to Mpumalanga police spokesperson Colonel Mavela Masondo for the latest information.

The latest publicly reported developments raised serious questions about the handling of potential evidence, particularly the cellphones belonging to Cameron and 19-year-old Ethan Coetzee, who was found dead alongside her.



No arrest or criminal charge in connection with Cameron’s murder has been publicly confirmed.

Waldeck-Cooks and Coetzee were discovered at the Waterval Self-Catering Holiday Home near Sabie on 3 August 2026.

Police initially opened inquest dockets before preliminary post-mortem findings prompted a murder investigation into Waldeck-Cooks’s death.



Why is Cameron Waldeck-Cooks’ death being investigated as murder?

The investigation was upgraded after preliminary post-mortem findings indicated that Waldeck-Cooks may have died from strangulation.

Mpumalanga police spokesperson Colonel Mavela Masondo confirmed to The South African in August that a murder case had been added to the original inquest investigation.

Coetzee’s death was being investigated separately as a suspected suicide.



Waldeck-Cooks’s parents, Derrick Cooks and Claire Waldeck-Cooks, also appointed an independent forensic pathologist.

They subsequently said the preliminary findings from that examination were consistent with strangulation and suffocation.

These findings prompted the murder investigation but do not, on their own, establish who was responsible for Waldeck-Cooks’s death.



More than 22 000 WhatsApp messages found on Cameron’s cellphone

One of the most significant developments emerged in a report published on 30 October.

The family’s attorney, Daniel Witz, confirmed that more than 22 000 WhatsApp messages from Coetzee had reportedly been found on Waldeck-Cooks’s cellphone.

Witz said he had seen screenshots of some of the messages but had not yet studied their full contents.



According to the attorney, the messages were sent during February, when the teenagers were still in a relationship.

The family has questioned why police allegedly returned both teenagers’ cellphones to their respective parents at the scene without first securing the devices and downloading their contents for forensic examination.

Waldeck-Cooks’s phone reportedly remains with her parents.



It is not clear whether investigators have since taken possession of the devices or completed a forensic examination.

The messages have also prompted renewed questions about the nature of the teenagers’ relationship before their deaths. Waldeck-Cooks’s family has raised concerns about possible controlling behaviour and gender-based violence.

Family questions whether police secured other evidence

The cellphones are not the only potential evidence the family wants investigators to account for.



Earlier reports also raised questions about whether police secured available CCTV footage from the accommodation and relevant records from its Wi-Fi router.

The family wants clarity on what evidence was collected, what forensic examinations have taken place and whether all relevant material has been included in the investigation.

There has been no public confirmation that CCTV footage or Wi-Fi records were lost or deliberately overlooked.



The family’s concerns relate to whether these potential sources of evidence were properly secured and examined.

Cameron’s parents reportedly received little feedback

The family’s attorney has also expressed frustration about communication with investigators.

In the 30 October report, Witz said that, almost 88 days after the teenagers’ deaths, Waldeck-Cooks’s parents had received little feedback from police.



He said the investigating officer had contacted him to request the parents’ contact details, but that neither parent had been asked to provide a statement or affidavit at that stage.

Colonel Mavela Masondo declined to discuss the details of the investigation, saying police would not comment until it had been finalised.

Family wants answers through an inquest

Waldeck-Cooks’s family has called for the circumstances surrounding the deaths to be properly examined through an inquest.



The family naturally wants clarity about the forensic findings, the handling of the teenagers’ cellphones and whether investigators followed every relevant line of inquiry.

An inquest is a judicial process that examines the circumstances surrounding an unnatural death. It can help establish how and when someone died and whether another person may have been responsible.

The family believes the process is important in obtaining answers and achieving some measure of closure.



What happened to Cameron Waldeck-Cooks?

Cameron was a Grade 11 pupil at St Stithians Girls’ College and had been part of the school community since Grade R.

She travelled to the Sabie area for a hiking trip connected to her efforts to achieve the Gold level of The President’s Award for Youth Empowerment.

Coetzee, 19, was a former St Stithians Boys’ College pupil who matriculated in 2025.



The teenagers were reportedly in a relationship before their deaths, although questions about that relationship have since become part of the wider public discussion surrounding the case.

The Coetzee family has previously called for restraint while the investigation and related processes continue.

Are you confident that an outcome will ever be reached in this case?

World.title: SABC to televise AFCON qualifier clash between Kenya and Bafana Bafana
World.content:
The SABC has confirmed that it will televise the crucial AFCON qualifier between Kenya and Bafana Bafana on Tuesday evening.

The two teams meet again just four days after their previous encounter at the Orlando Amstel Arena on Friday.

That match ended in a 2-2 draw, with both sides sharing the points. Pitso Mosimane’s men controlled large parts of the contest but failed to finish off the Harambee Stars.



With just over 10 minutes remaining, Relebohile Mofokeng appeared to have scored the winner for Bafana. However, Kenya struck an equaliser in the dying minutes to silence the Orlando crowd.

How can fans watch Bafana Bafana vs Kenya?

The match will be broadcast live on SABC 2, with television coverage starting at 17:30 on Tuesday.

Kick-off in Nairobi is scheduled for 18:00 South African time.



Bafana will be targeting all three points as they look to return to the top of Group C.

A victory would strengthen their position in the qualification race, while dropped points could leave them under pressure as the battle for AFCON qualification continues.

Kenya have already qualified for next year’s AFCON as hosts, but Tuesday’s match will test their readiness against a very strong Bafana team.



For South Africa, this is a must-win match as they face a risk of failing to qualify for next year’s competition should they lose in Nairobi. Guinea are now top of the group and will play Bafana next year which could be the ultimate match which decide the fate of the group.

Will Bafana qualify for AFCON?

World.title: Extreme heat alert: Five mistakes that could put your health at risk
World.content:
A man pours water over his head to cool down. Image: Pexels

South Africans in parts of the Western and Northern Cape should prepare for very hot to extremely hot conditions from Tuesday, 17 November.

The South African Weather Service (SAWS) warns that daytime temperatures could reach the high 30s and low 40s.

The advisory remains valid from 08:00 on Tuesday until 18:00 on Thursday, 19 November.



SAWS expects the heat to affect the interior of Namakwa, the West Coast, the City of Cape Town and northern Cape Winelands on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Conditions will spread to the rest of the Cape Winelands, the interior of the Overberg, the Central and Little Karoo, and the Hessequa municipality from Wednesday to Thursday.

Five mistakes to avoid as SAWS issues an extreme heat aleRT

Waiting until you feel thirsty to drink water



Do not wait until thirst sets in before drinking water.

Your body loses fluids through sweating, and extreme heat can increase the risk of dehydration.

Spending too much time in direct sunlight

Prolonged exposure to direct sunlight can place additional strain on your body, particularly during the hottest part of the day.



Exercising or doing strenuous work during the hottest hours

Strenuous activity makes your body produce more heat.

Combining physical exertion with very hot weather can increase the risk of heat-related illness.



Wearing heavy clothing and ignoring ways to cool down

Tight, heavy clothing can make it harder for your body to lose heat.

Choose loose-fitting, lightweight clothing, preferably in light colours.



Ignoring warning signs and leaving vulnerable people unattended

Do not dismiss symptoms such as dizziness, weakness, headaches or fainting during extreme heat.

Pay particular attention to babies, older people and anyone who may struggle to cope with high temperatures.



Check on relatives, neighbours and people who live alone.

Take the heat advisory seriously

The advisory warns that extreme heat can have serious health effects.

Taking simple precautions can help reduce the risk as temperatures rise across parts of the Western and Northern Cape.

World.title: It’s true: Survey finds dogs bring more joy than social media
World.content:
South African dog owners are far more likely to find reasons to smile through their pets than through social media, according to a new survey. Image: Supplied

South African dog owners are far more likely to find reasons to smile through their pets than through social media, according to a new survey.

The findings show that 85.6% of dog owners surveyed smile or laugh daily because of their dogs, compared with just 49.4% who say social media has the same effect.

The Feed the Joy survey, conducted by Bobtail in October 2026, collected 2 029 responses from South Africans, including 1 801 current dog owners.



The results highlight the role dogs play in their owners’ everyday lives, from lifting their spirits after a difficult day to providing companionship and encouraging families to spend less time on screens.

Dogs offer more than companionship

For many owners, the simple experience of arriving home to an excited dog is enough to improve their mood.

A significant 93.9% of dog owners surveyed said their dog’s greeting was something likely to lift their spirits after a difficult day.



Companionship was also cited almost twice as often as security as a reason for having a dog. Some 68.9% identified companionship as a reason, compared with 34.7% who pointed to security.

The survey also revealed just how much owners talk to their pets.

Two-thirds of respondents said they speak to their dogs throughout the day. Meanwhile, 48.3% share what has been happening in their lives with their pets, while 46.8% even discuss what is being prepared for supper.



South Africa’s multilingual nature is reflected in the findings, with 44.4% of respondents saying they speak to their dogs in more than one language.

Children would choose dogs over screens

The survey also explored the relationship between pets, children and screen time.

Among adults living with children aged 16 or younger, 77.5% believed their children would choose playing with dogs over spending time on electronic devices.



Even more strikingly, 94.1% said they would prefer their children to choose time with their four-legged companions over screen time.

Bobtail assistant brand manager Savashnee Naidoo said the findings highlighted the difference between capturing people’s attention and creating meaningful connections.

“Screens compete for our attention, but the findings suggest that attention isn’t the same as connection,” she said.



Naidoo added that dogs offer a genuine relationship that can lift people’s moods and bring them into the moment.

Dog owners prioritise time with their pets

The affection owners have for their dogs also extends to gifts and special occasions.

Some 74% of dog owners surveyed said they give their pets birthday presents or other gifts. Women were more likely than men to do so, at 77.5% compared with 66.4%.



A further 19.6% said they did not currently give their dogs gifts but believed they deserved them.

When asked how they would spend extra money in December, 80.4% of dog owners said they would choose simple experiences with their dogs at home rather than a holiday or getaway for themselves.

What brings you more joy on a daily basis: Pets or social media?

World.title: Bafana Bafana expected starting XI against Kenya
World.content:
Bafana Bafana are expected to make several changes to their starting XI when they face Kenya on Tuesday evening.

Pitso Mosimane’s men take on the Harambee Stars in Nairobi in their fourth AFCON qualifier, looking to return to winning ways after being held to a 2-2 draw at home on Friday. The draw was a setback for Bafana, who were hoping to get a step further in their qualifying campaign.

Changes are expected in several areas, particularly in defence, midfield and attack.



Mbokazi set to return to Bafana lineup AGAINST Kenya

Mbekezeli Mbokazi is expected to return to the starting lineup after missing Friday’s encounter against Kenya. The 21-year-old could replace Olwethu Makhabane in central defence.

In midfield, Thalente Mbatha is another player who could come into the starting XI as Mosimane looks to freshen up his team.

Upfront, Lyle Foster could replace Iqraam Rayners as Bafana look for more firepower in attack.



Relebohile Mofokeng and Oswin Appollis are expected to retain their places as they look to provide creativity and attacking threat. If Bafana are to beat Kenya, both of these attackers need to be on form and clinical in front of goals.

Meanwhile, Tshepang Moremi could make way for another winger, with Tashreeq Matthews among the possible options following Moremi’s wasteful display in the previous encounter.

Bafana Bafana predicted starting XI vs Kenya

Ronwen Williams, Thabang Matuludi, Ime Okon, Mbekezeli Mbokazi, Samkelo Kabini, Thalente Mbatha, Sphephelo Sithole, Relebohile Mofokeng, Oswin Appollis, Tashreeq Matthews and Lyle Foster.



Can Bafana get a win?

World.title: Kruger National Park introduces new digital system for day visitors
World.content:
The Kruger National Park is testing a new digital system that could make entry easier for day visitors at one of its busiest gates. Image: Travel Buddies Lifestyle Blog

The Kruger National Park is testing a new digital system that could make entry easier for day visitors, with SANParks introducing electronic indemnity forms at one of its busiest southern gates.

The pilot programme runs from Monday, 16 November, to Friday, 20 November 2026, at Crocodile Bridge Gate.

Day visitors using the gate are encouraged to complete the electronic indemnity form by scanning a designated QR code before or upon arrival.



The QR code is available through the SANParks website and its social media platforms.

READ | South Africa’s cheapest national parks for a summer getaway

Paperless entry process being tested

SANParks said the initiative forms part of its broader digital transformation efforts and aims to improve convenience for visitors while reducing processing times at the entrance gate.

The electronic form is intended to streamline the registration process without compromising the legal and safety requirements associated with visitor entry.

The pilot will allow SANParks to assess how the system works in practice and identify any improvements needed before expanding it.

More Kruger National Park gates could follow

Following the assessment of the Crocodile Bridge pilot, SANParks plans to introduce the next phase at another busy gate in the southern section of the park.



The system could then be progressively rolled out to additional entrance gates.

SANParks has encouraged visitors participating in the pilot to provide feedback to help improve the process.

For now, the trial is limited to day visitors entering through Crocodile Bridge Gate during the five-day pilot period.

World.title: What issues do leaders face at the APEC summit?
World.content:
BEIJING - From nuclear weapons to artificial intelligence, world leaders will tackle a range of issues when they gather in China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week.

With all eyes on a crowning trilateral meeting between US, Chinese and Russian leaders on Thursday, AFP takes a look at the topics that may be discussed:

- Trade -
