It sends a clear message: If Huang can be forced out, any leader can.

It took a public scandal

Huang appeared untouchable.

He very well may have been – up until this week, before his infidelity spilled out into public view and could no longer be ignored by the board.

Nvidia and Huang had been synonymous for decades. He maintained an extraordinarily flat organization, with 60 direct reports and no clear succession plan. He boasted that the company was structured such that he was uniquely qualified to run it.

Huang’s genius was the stuff of legend. He correctly predicted in 2013 – a decade before ChatGPT – that the company’s graphics processors would serve as the foundation for AI. He was right, and his company became the first ever to be worth $5 trillion on the stock market.

The Nvidia Groq 3 LPU chip. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg/Getty Images

So the board failed to challenge Huang, despite numerous missteps and bad bets along the way. It was apparently unfazed by reports dating back more than a year about Nvidia’s odd relationship with Megaspeed – the major Nvidia customer run by Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese agent with whom Jensen Huang had a relationship. The board failed to investigate Huang when the New York Times reported last month that US intelligence feared Alice Huang may be a spy, or when photos of its CEO and Alice Huang were plastered all over the internet.

It took the scandal becoming an unavoidable topic of public conversation this week for the board to hire an outside counsel to investigate. It took another revelation – by The New York Times that Huang had an alleged affair with an executive who reports to him – to ultimately force him to resign.

That made the board negligent in its duties, said Nell Minow, chair of corporate governance advisory firm ValueEdge Advisors.

“The single biggest failure of corporate boards is succession planning, and there’s no evidence that was done here,” said Minow. “We love to think about superstar CEOs and founders, but they’re never as special as they think they are.”

Huang’s aura of invincibility stems from one of his favorite boasts: Nvidia’s humble 1993 founding during a meeting held at a Denny’s – and how its shaky beginnings forced him to repeatedly save the company from near extinction. He made the company’s motto: “Our company is 30 days from going out of business.”

Jensen Huang holds up a wafer lined with chips at the company headquarters on January 17, 2002. Julie Jacobson/AP

But the board misjudged that past success as evidence of Huang’s unique talents, Minow said.

The biggest risk for the life of a company, she argued, is not failure – because when a company is on the verge of destruction, everyone is working together and problem solving. Instead, the biggest risk is when the company is doing spectacularly well: No one can sustain that hockey stick-like growth, and the board starts attributing success to intangible things like its uniquely talented leaders.

“That puts a lot of pressure on the snowflake genius from Denny’s,” Minow said. “It’s like a baseball team with a winning streak no one can explain. The whole team starts wearing lucky socks. Nvidia’s board thought it had its lucky CEO.”

The myth of the invincible tech CEO

Huang may have wielded incredible power at Nvidia, but more recent tech founders have worked to place a buffer around themselves even more durable than Huang’s.

Huang is an outlier among his tech CEO peers: He controls just 3.6 percent of his company’s shares. Many founders, including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and soon-to-be public Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei all have dual class stock arrangements that give them significantly more voting power over common shareholders – and effectively unilateral power over their corporations’ governance.

Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX; and Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta, walk to a press briefing with President Donald Trump on September 29, 2026. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Even those stronger insulators are permeable. Shareholders aren’t powerless against dual class stock structures or seemingly untouchable CEOs: They can bombard companies with lawsuits – which have already started against Nvidia.

And it’s not clear that even a CEO as wealthy and powerful as Musk could survive a scandal like Huang’s. Musk’s friendly, hand-picked Tesla board began a CEO replacement search and successfully pressured him to return his focus to the company after spending much of 2024 and 2025 engaged almost exclusively in the political spotlight, damaging Tesla’s global brand in the process.

“There’s a lot of myth-making in tech that there’s one person who is uniquely qualified to run the company,” said Sonnenfeld. “That’s not true: They have human frailties, they’re imperfect, and they’re replaceable.”

Nvidia board’s decision here was cut and dry: Anyone else at Nvidia would have been let go if they had engaged in Huang’s alleged conduct. Huang may have put his company’s trade secrets at risk of theft by a foreign competitor. He lost trust with Nvidia’s customers and demonstrated a lack of candor with his board. Huang lost the legitimacy to lead.

So that means the CEO – even the visionary leader of the chipmaking bedrock of AI – can be held responsible, just like any other employee who may have violated the company’s code of conduct.

And, on Thursday, he was kicked out of the company he built.

World.title: Beyond the GERD: Ethiopia’s shifting regional balance
World.content:
The dispute between Egypt and Ethiopia is no longer a mere quarrel over a completed dam, deadlocked negotiations, or traded diplomatic barbs.

Crucially, Addis Ababa now views the Nile’s waters as a cornerstone of a grander ambition to reshape its regional standing—an agenda that links hydropolitics with demands for Red Sea access to tilt the balance of power across the Horn of Africa.

The recent launch of the “Nile and Red Sea Strategic Forum” in Addis Ababa underscores this shift.

While legally registered as a civil society organization rather than a state body or formal negotiating party, its mandate extends well beyond traditional civic work.

The forum is designed to mobilize scholars, policy experts, and legal specialists to shape public discourse, draft policy, and bolster Ethiopian diplomacy on both the Nile dispute and maritime access—all while forging external partnerships to advance state strategy.

What matters here is not the forum’s immediate size or clout, but the trajectory it signals.

Moving past reactive rhetoric during moments of crisis, Ethiopia is building a permanent apparatus—spanning research, law, and media—to continuously manufacture arguments and lend intellectual and legal legitimacy to its positions both at home and abroad.

Even more telling is the deliberate fusion of the Nile and Red Sea dossiers. Through this framing, water is elevated beyond merely just technical management, and maritime access is elevated beyond a commercial bid to lower shipping costs.

Both are cast as existential matters of national security and inherent historical and geopolitical “rights” designed to rally both the Ethiopian public and international institutions.

Egypt must read this message clearly: Addis Ababa is actively widening the arena of contention. It aims to pivot the debate away from the technical operating rules of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) toward a wholesale renegotiation of the regional order.

The core questions are now far broader: Who holds the authority to manage shared resources? Who dictates the rules of engagement? And what place does Ethiopia claim in the strategic equation of the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea?

Remarks made two days ago by Ethiopian Minister of Water and Energy Habtamu Itefa reinforce this reality.

Declaring that the GERD’s completion proved his country’s resilience against external pressure, he noted that the expertise gained will streamline future water projects.

Though he named no specific initiatives, his message is unmistakable: Addis Ababa views the GERD as an opening chapter, not a final destination.

Even without hard evidence of signed contracts or secured financing for new dams, waiting until excavators break ground before responding would be a grave strategic miscalculation.

As Ethiopia builds the institutional machinery to craft and export its narrative, Egypt can no longer afford a reactive posture, perpetually responding to facts on the ground set by others.

Egypt must urgently evolve its own strategic toolkit—the pressing question now is how.

World.title: Liberia: From Monrovia to Sinoe – Koon’s Political Move Reignites Debate Over Constituency Hopping
World.content:
MONROVIA – Romeo Quioh did not mince words.

Speaking on a Monrovia radio station on Monday, the lawmaker who represents District #1 of Sinoe County, a coastal stretch of Liberia’s rural southeast, said he would beat the most powerful man in the House of Representatives “face down.”

By Rodney D. Sieh



“Speaker Koon will be a former lawmaker after 2029,” Quioh declared, describing himself as a true son of the county.

The target of his warning, House Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon, does not currently represent Sinoe at all. Since 2017, he has represented Electoral District #11 in Montserrado, the crowded county that is home to the capital, Monrovia. He was reelected there in 2023 and elevated to the speakership the following year. But Koon was born in Sinoe, and he has signaled that when Liberians next go to the polls in 2029, he wants to represent his home county instead.

It is a move that would have been almost unthinkable a generation ago. Today, it is becoming something of a pattern.

The Man Who Wrote the Playbook

The road Koon appears ready to travel was first paved by Edwin Melvin Snowe Jr., himself a former Speaker.

Snowe was first elected in Montserrado in 2005 and later represented the capital’s District #6. Ahead of the 2017 elections, while still sitting in the Legislature for that Monrovia district, he registered as a voter in Senjeh, in Bomi County, about an hour’s drive north-west of the capital, and announced he would run for Bomi’s District #1 seat. At the time, it was described as the first move of its kind in Liberia’s modern democratic history.

Bomi’s political establishment fought back. The county’s senator, Sando Johnson, and the district’s sitting representative, Samuel Gayah Karmo, argued that a lawmaker serving Montserrado could not simply change his home mid-term to chase a seat elsewhere. An elections hearing officer agreed and blocked Snowe, before the National Elections Commission’s board reversed that decision.

The fight ended at the Supreme Court. In September 2017, the justices ruled that no law forbids a sitting representative from changing his domicile to another county while still serving the one that elected him. They went further, acknowledging that neither the Constitution nor the election law says whether a lawmaker must keep living in the district he represents, and declining to fill that silence themselves.

Snowe went on to win the Bomi seat. Three years later, in a December 2020 special election, he won a seat in the Senate representing the whole county. For ambitious politicians watching from Monrovia, the lesson was plain: it could be done.

Others Follow, With Mixed Results

In the years since, others have tested the same path.

Thomas P. Fallah, a long-serving representative for Montserrado’s District #5, said an emotional goodbye to his Monrovia constituents in August 2023 and headed for Lofa County in the far north, where he contested and won District #1. He is now Deputy Speaker of the House.

That same year, Nathaniel McGill, a former Minister of State for Presidential Affairs and one of the most powerful figures in the previous government, sought a Senate seat in Margibi County, next door to the capital. Citizens petitioned the elections commission, accusing him of falsely swearing that he lived in Margibi while his home was in Monrovia, and rival candidates branded him a “stranger” to the county. The Supreme Court upheld his eligibility, and Margibi voters elected him.

Not every attempt has succeeded. Hanson Kiazolu, then representing Montserrado’s District #17, ran for the Senate in Grand Cape Mount County in 2023, arguing that his home county had been held back by poor leadership. He lost to Dabah Varpilah of the Unity Party, while some of his own Monrovia constituents openly complained that he was walking away from them.

And at least one lawmaker thought better of it. George Beyan Samah, of Montserrado’s District #12, publicly explored a Senate run in Lofa in 2020 before stepping back, saying that spending his resources campaigning elsewhere would betray the people who had trusted him with their votes.

The common thread is hard to miss. Most of these journeys run in the same direction, out of the capital and into the rural counties that many Monrovia politicians call home, carrying name recognition, money and influence built up over years in the city.

A Thin Legal Line

Liberia’s rules on this are remarkably light.

Article 30(b) of the 1986 Constitution requires anyone seeking a seat in the Legislature to have been domiciled in the county or district they want to represent for at least one year before the election, and to be a taxpayer. That is it. The Constitution says nothing about whether a lawmaker must keep living in the district through his term, nothing about whether he may campaign or channel resources elsewhere while still drawing a salary to represent his current voters, and the courts have made clear they will not add such conditions on their own.

In practice, a candidate aiming for 2029 needs only to establish a home in his chosen district by around October 2028. He can remain the sitting representative of somewhere else the entire time.

Some citizens think the bar is too low. During consultations on electoral reform, residents of Grand Cape Mount called for the residency requirement to be doubled to two years.

What It Means for Voters

For the people at the heart of all this, the voters, the trend raises uncomfortable questions.

The first concerns the district left behind. The voters of Montserrado’s District #11 elected Koon in 2023 to a six-year term that runs until 2029. If his attention, energy and political capital shift to Sinoe in the final stretch, those voters are left with a representative in name only. And they lose the one tool every democracy gives citizens to judge their lawmaker: they will never get to vote him in or out again, because he will not be on their ballot.

The second concerns the blurred line between office and campaign. In July, Koon traveled to Greenville, Sinoe’s capital, and pledged to mobilize legislative support to restore the nursing program at Sinoe Community College, adding that the Legislature intends to increase its support for the county.

Few would argue that Sinoe does not need the help. But when the Speaker of the House makes promises in a county where he hopes to run, voters are entitled to wonder whether they are hearing a commitment from the Legislature, or the opening pitch of a campaign.

The third is about what “home” really means. Almost every lawmaker who has switched counties has framed the move as a homecoming. Yet representation is meant to be about the people who live in a place, its roads, its clinics, its schools, rather than where a candidate happened to be born. A politician who has spent two decades building a career in Monrovia may be a son of the soil on paper, while the local representative is the one who has lived with the district’s daily struggles.

The fourth is about power and money. Montserrado’s districts are crowded and fiercely contested. Rural districts are far smaller: Sinoe District #1 had roughly 20,800 registered voters in 2023. A well-funded outsider with a national profile can make a big splash there. Critics worry that rural counties are quietly becoming safety nets for Monrovia’s political elite, places to retreat to when the city turns against them or when a smoother path to power beckons.

Some political observers have argued that these cross-county ambitions are driven largely by deep pockets and self-promotion.

Finally, there is the question of who gets squeezed out. When a Speaker or a former minister parachutes into a county race, local aspirants who have spent years building support at the grassroots can find themselves overshadowed.

Quiah’s fiery response suggests how threatened sitting rural lawmakers feel. If the trend continues, the next generation of county-based leaders may find the doors to the Capitol closed to them.

The Case for Freedom to Move

There is, of course, another side to the argument.

Liberians are free to live and vote where they choose. When Snowe’s candidacy was challenged in 2017, his lawyer, former Attorney General Benedict Sannoh, argued that no law restricts a citizen from voting wherever he wants.

Snowe’s bid also came with the backing of at least 27 chiefs and elders in Bomi. Supporters of these moves argue that experienced lawmakers bring clout, connections and resources to counties that have long been neglected, and that the decision on whether an outsider deserves a chance should rest with voters, not with courts or rival politicians.

The record also suggests that voters are not easily swept off their feet. Kiazolu’s defeat in Grand Cape Mount is a reminder that a seat in Monrovia does not automatically travel with its holder. A familiar name may open doors, but it does not guarantee victory.

The Road to 2029

With the Speaker of the House now part of the story, a debate that once lived on the margins of Liberian politics has moved to the center, and it deserves an open public discussion before the 2029 campaign gets fully under way.

There are practical questions for lawmakers and the elections commission to consider. Should a sitting lawmaker who intends to run elsewhere be required to declare it early, or even step down? Should the residency requirement be extended? Should there be clearer rules separating a lawmaker’s official pledges and spending from his campaign ambitions in another county?

There is a certain irony in the fact that the person best placed to put those questions before the House is Speaker Koon himself.

For voters in Sinoe’s District #1, the choice in 2029 may come down to a local incumbent who says he never left and a powerful native son who says he is coming home.

For voters in Montserrado’s District #11, the more urgent question is simpler: who is speaking for them right now?

World.title: Liberia: After Reshuffle, Female Representation in Boakai’s Cabinet Stays Steady, but Advocates Say the Proof Will Be in Outcomes
World.content:
President Joseph Boakai and Vice President Jeremiah Koung (front row, in hat) pose with cabinet members at the Executive Mansion on Capitol Hill in Monrovia in March 2025. Photo: Spoon FM

Summary

President Joseph Boakai appointed a woman to lead the Justice Ministry in September but removed two others from defense and commerce a day later, leaving women in charge of seven of the government’s 19 ministries, or 37 percent.

Women’s representation in Boakai’s Cabinet had reached a record 42 percent before the reshuffle, higher than at the start of previous administrations.

Women’s rights advocates say the real test for the new justice minister will be access to justice for victims of sexual violence after a FrontPage Africa/New Narratives revelation that just two perpetrators of sexual violence have been convicted in six years.

By Joyclyn Wea, gender reporter with New Narratives

President Joseph Boakai’s Cabinet reshuffle in September raised concerns among women’s rights advocates about whether gains in women’s representation in government would be sustained.



In September, Boakai appointed former Solicitor General Betty M. Lamin-Blamo as acting minister of justice and attorney general. Blamo was the fourth woman to serve in the role, and women’s advocates applauded the appointment, which came after FrontPage Africa/New Narratives reported that the justice system has failed ordinary Liberian victims at every turn. In one case, bribes had stopped human trafficking cases from getting to court.

And in an astounding revelation, a prosecutor conceded that just two people accused of sexual violence had been convicted in six years. More than 300 cases are on the docket, with many accused in pretrial detention for years.

After Lamin-Blamo’s appointment, Boakai’s cabinet had near gender parity for the first time in Liberia’s history. But just 24 hours later, Boakai removed Geraldine J. George, Liberia’s first female defense minister, and Commerce and Industry Minister Magdalene E. Dagoseh, from their posts. Two men were named in their places. The number of women in Cabinet fell back to seven of the 19 positions, or 37 percent.

The changes have renewed questions about whether women’s growing presence in government is translating into lasting decision-making power and influence. Women’s advocates say Boakai still needs to prove his commitment to give women the authority and resources to improve public services, including security and justice for survivors of sexual and gender-based violence.

Boakai has made a strong push for women’s representation in international forums, where he knows European donors prioritize it. Ten days after the reshuffle, Boakai made women’s participation in decision-making a centerpiece of his speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York. A 2026 to 2031 plan aims to expand women’s participation in leadership and peacebuilding.

“Liberia does not intend to advocate for women’s participation in peacebuilding around the world while failing to create space for women at home,” Boakai said. “Now, we must ensure they have the opportunity, authority and institutional support to lead.”

When Boakai took office in 2024, six of his Cabinet ministers were women. By January 2025, that number had risen to seven of 19 ministers. The later appointment of Cornelia Wonkerleh Kruah as youth and sports minister raised that number to eight, or 42 percent. That represented a big increase compared with the start of previous administrations. Women held five of 23 Cabinet positions, or 22 percent, when Ellen Johnson Sirleaf began her first term in 2006. The number increased to six of 23, or 26 percent, at the start of her second term in 2012. When George Weah took office in 2018, four of his 19 ministers were women, or 21 percent.

Boakai also broke ground by appointing Geraldine Janet George, a retired brigadier general, the first female defense minister, at the start of his administration with a mandate to increase female representation in the armed forces. Women made up just 7.4 percent of the Armed Forces of Liberia.

In February, the Ministry of National Defense and UN Women launched a US$663,000 project, paid for by the Elsie Initiative Fund, an international effort to get more uniformed women into UN peacekeeping missions. Its stated aim is for women to make up 15 percent of the force within two years.

“When we have more intelligent, qualified, and talented women in decision-making positions, it creates benefits for everyone in the military, including our male personnel,” George said at the time.

From mid-2026, ministry and AFL teams ran an awareness and recruitment campaign under the slogan “Women in Uniform, Peace in Action” to counties across the west, centre and southeast, holding radio programs, school and university visits and community meetings. There is no public data yet on how many women have actually enlisted.

With George out, women’s advocates are wary.

“I think progress should be measured by the impact on the people,” said Frances Greaves, a longtime women’s rights advocate and former head of the National Civil Society Council of Liberia. “What are the policies that are in place, and how impactful are they in the community?”

Lamin-Blamo is Liberia’s fourth female justice minister. Gloria Musu-Scott became the first in 1996, followed by Frances Johnson-Morris, who served from 2006 to 2007, and Christiana Tah, who held the position from 2009 to 2014.

But advocates say Lamin-Blamo’s appointment creates an important opportunity to address longstanding failures in the justice system, particularly in cases involving sexual and gender-based violence.

“I believe it is significant to have a woman leading the Ministry of Justice at a time when survivors of rape and other forms of sexual violence continue to face serious barriers to justice,” said Evangeline Sirleaf, executive director of Her Voice Liberia, which provides legal assistance to survivors of sexual and gender-based violence.

Sirleaf urged Lamin-Blamo to focus on the handling of sexual violence cases, access to legal aid and enforcement of laws protecting women and children. Success in those areas will be the measure of her leadership.

Frances Greaves said achieving those improvements would require police to conduct thorough investigations and properly preserve evidence before cases reach the courts. She said prosecutors must then use evidence to build stronger cases, while the courts must handle them effectively, and that the Ministry of Justice cannot improve outcomes for survivors unless these parts of the justice and law enforcement system work together.

“The system has to work,” Greaves said. “It’s not one person. The system should work for everybody.”

For now, Liberia’s women advocates will be watching closely.

This story was produced in collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by a private donor. The donor had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Ex-President Sirleaf Warns Leaders Against Threatening Liberia’s Peace
World.content:
Monrovia — Former Liberian President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf has issued a strong warning to those in positions of power, urging them to prioritize national unity, political inclusion and equal opportunities as essential safeguards against a return to conflict.

By Patience Jones

Sirleaf cautioned that Liberia’s hard-earned peace must not be taken for granted, emphasizing that maintaining stability requires deliberate efforts from political leaders and every Liberian.



“My message is to those in power: Beware. You need inclusion. You need equal opportunity. You need true unity,” Sirleaf declared while delivering a goodwill message at the 2026 West African Women Peacebuilding Convening in Monrovia.

The conference, held at the Ministerial Complex Conference Hall under the theme, “Honoring the Past, Strengthening the Present, and Co-Designing the Future of Women’s Leadership for Peace,” brought together women leaders and peace advocates to reflect on women’s contributions to peacebuilding and discuss strategies for sustaining peace across the West African region.

The GBOWEE Peace Foundation Africa hosted the gathering, with LUMA serving as co-host.

Reflecting on Liberia’s turbulent history, Sirleaf reminded participants that the country’s peace before the April 12, 1980, coup was not built on genuine national unity, inclusion, or equal opportunities.

She explained that the absence of these fundamental values eventually undermined the country’s stability, leading to decades of conflict, destruction of infrastructure, weakened institutions and widespread hopelessness.

According to her, Liberia’s experience demonstrates that peace cannot survive on the mere absence of war; it must be supported by justice, national cohesion, equal participation, and opportunities for all citizens.

Sirleaf also acknowledged the critical role Liberian women played in the country’s peace process, particularly during the negotiations in Accra, Ghana, where women peace advocates remained engaged despite difficult circumstances and uncertainty surrounding the outcome of the talks.

She credited the women who participated in the peace negotiations and continued advocating for an end to the conflict, noting that their determination helped create the conditions for Liberia to begin rebuilding.

“When the peace talks were going on in Accra and there were difficulties, and we didn’t know whether the war leaders would ever give up on Liberia, you and your group of women sat for days and nights,” she recalled.

The former president stressed that rebuilding Liberia after the war required more than restoring damaged infrastructure and institutions. It also demanded a new approach to leadership, with women taking an active role in restoring hope and rebuilding the nation.

Sirleaf, who became Africa’s first elected female head of state in 2006, said the country’s continued peace should be celebrated but must also serve as a reminder of the collective responsibility to protect it.

She noted that Liberia has enjoyed 23 consecutive years of peace, urging citizens not to become complacent about the progress made since the end of the civil conflict.

“Peace is not enough. That peace must be accompanied by unity, by inclusion, by equal opportunity. It is through unity that it will last,” she emphasized.

Beyond those occupying the highest political offices, Sirleaf challenged every Liberian entrusted with responsibility to recognize their role in protecting the country’s stability.

She argued that the responsibility for sustaining peace does not rest solely with the president or other national leaders but extends to every citizen, regardless of position or influence.

“It’s not just the head that carries the banner. It’s not just the head that has the responsibility. It’s the responsibility for each and every Liberian to know that peace is what we need, but peace is what we have to earn,” she said.

Sirleaf further urged participants to leave the convening with renewed commitments to patriotism, gender equality, inclusion, and national development.

She also acknowledged the difficult period Liberia is navigating, calling on citizens to work collectively toward addressing the country’s challenges and restoring the aspirations that inspired voters during the 2005 elections.

Her message places renewed attention on the responsibility of political leadership to preserve Liberia’s post-war stability, particularly through inclusive governance and equal participation in national decision-making.

As women leaders from across West Africa gathered to reflect on their contributions to peacebuilding, Sirleaf’s warning served as a reminder that the preservation of peace requires more than political declarations. It demands responsible leadership, genuine inclusion, equal opportunities, and the commitment of every citizen.

World.title: Liberia: With Her Mother Battling Kidney Disease, Raquel Hage Turns Her Family’s Estate Battle Into Music
World.content:
MONROVIA – For Raquel Hage, the road to her new record runs through two cities on two continents: a courtroom in Monrovia and a dialysis clinic in New Delhi, India.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Her mother, Oumou Hage, has been treated in India for severe kidney problems, along with hypertension and other health conditions that the family blames on the stress she has lived under since her husband’s death. To pay for that care, Raquel says, the family must go back to a Liberian court and ask permission to use money from the estate of her late father, Milad Hage – money the family believes already belongs to them.



“According to the will, my mother is entitled to healthcare, but we have to beg the courts for money from our estate to help with her treatment,” she said.

Now the Liberian singer is taking that fight out of the courtroom and into people’s headphones. Justice, a five-track EP released on November 13, runs just 12 minutes. But in that short space, Raquel says what years of legal filings have not let her say.

“This album is a beef album,” she said. “For years we wanted peace, but the system refuses to give us peace. There comes a time when you say enough is enough. Now I feel I can express myself through music.”

A FAMILY FIGHT IN A SLOW COURT

The songs grow out of a long and bitter dispute over the estate of Milad Hage. In Liberia, as in many countries, when a person dies their property passes through probate – a court-supervised process meant to protect the estate until it is properly distributed. For the Hage family, Raquel says, that protection has become a wall.

In recent weeks the family has pressed the probate court to release funds held in escrow from the estate, including money for Mrs. Hage’s medical care.

The probate judge has refused.

Milad Hage died in 2010 after a medical procedure that, the family says, still leaves questions unanswered. Sixteen years later, his estate remains under the court’s control, and his widow and children are still asking it for money.

For a family watching a mother’s health decline, the delays are not abstract. Every request to the court, Raquel says, feels like begging for something that is already theirs.

FIVE SONGS, NO MORE PEACE

Justice, released independently under Raquel Hage Music and filed under Afrobeats, does not hide who it is talking to.

On “Shame on You,” she turns on the government and the justice system. The executive branch, she says, will not step in because the judiciary is a separate branch of government, leaving the family’s fate in the hands of the courts and, ultimately, the Supreme Court.

“This is addressed in the song ‘Shame on You,’ where I take aim at the system for what it has done to our family,” she said.

She has not given up. “We are still hopeful to expose the thieves, because 99 days for rogue, one day for the master,” she said, quoting a Liberian proverb that means a thief’s luck always runs out in the end.

On “Fraudster,” she goes after a relative whom, Raquel says, a jury unanimously found liable for fraud. The case, she says, turned on paperwork: Ecobank has held the original documents since 2007, when Mr. Hage took out a loan with the bank.

“Julie” is about Edith Smith, a former girlfriend of Raquel’s late father and, she says, one of the people on the other side of the estate battle. Raquel describes her as a gambler whose habit left her bankrupt.

On “Winner,” the mood turns from anger to faith. Raquel says she always wins in the end, because God is on her side and the truth always comes out.

The EP closes with “Satan Move,” built on one of Liberia’s oldest nursery rhymes: the old man’s car has no brakes, so get off the road. In Raquel’s version, she is the old man, and the people she blames for her family’s suffering had better clear the road before her brakeless car arrives.

MUSIC AS A LAST RESORT

Turning private pain into public song is an old tradition in West Africa. Nigeria’s Fela Kuti built a career aiming his music at those in power, and generations of African artists have since used the dance floor to air grievances that courts and governments ignored.

For Raquel, the choice was less about tradition than exhaustion. The family, she says, tried for years to settle things quietly. Justice is what happened when that stopped working.

The record is sharp, personal and, by her own description, a “beef album.” But underneath the jabs is a simpler story: a daughter trying to keep her mother alive while waiting for a court to say yes.

For now, Mrs. Hage’s treatment continues. So does the case. And Raquel Hage has found the one place where no judge can tell her to wait.

Justice is available on Apple Music and other streaming platforms.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Launches 285 Yellow Machines Operations To Improve Rural Roads, Calls For Maintenance Amid Public Criticisms
World.content:
PAYNESVILLE, Montserrado County — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has officially launched the nationwide deployment of 285 heavy-duty earth-moving machines intended to improve rural road connectivity across Liberia’s 15 counties, warning that poor maintenance and management could undermine the government’s investment.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Speaking Monday at the state-owned Liberia Broadcasting System (LBS) in Paynesville, President Boakai described the initiative as a major infrastructure intervention aimed at rehabilitating feeder roads, connecting farming communities to markets, and improving access to essential services.



However, amid persistent criticisms over the procurement process, the cost of the equipment, and its long-term sustainability, the President stressed that the success of the initiative would depend on professional management, technical training, accountability, and regular maintenance.

The first consignment of the machines began arriving in February 2026, with the final batch delivered in May, bringing the total to 285. The equipment will operate through 19 strategic hubs serving all 15 counties.

Transforming Rural Roads

President Boakai said the deployment would help address longstanding transportation challenges that have isolated rural communities, increased the cost of moving agricultural products, and restricted access to healthcare and education.

“We are launching the national deployment of 285 pieces of heavy earth-moving equipment, organized through 19 operational hubs serving all 15 counties of Liberia,” he announced.

According to him, the equipment represents more than an investment in machinery, describing it as an investment in farmers, communities, and Liberia’s future.

He recalled that poor road conditions, particularly during the rainy season, have made it difficult for farmers to transport their produce to markets, resulting in agricultural losses and higher food prices.

“Sometimes we say people are lazy, but sometimes we need to create an enabling environment, something the people cannot do for themselves. Yet many farmers struggle to bring their harvest to market because of deplorable road conditions,” the President said.

He added that the initiative would support the rehabilitation and maintenance of feeder roads, farm-to-market roads, and other routes across the country.

Maintenance and Accountability

While celebrating the deployment, President Boakai cautioned that acquiring the equipment was only the first step, emphasizing that maintaining the machines would determine whether the initiative delivers lasting results.

“The acquisition of this heavy equipment is only the first step. The real challenge is to ensure that these machines remain operational, productive, safe, and properly maintained over many years,” he warned.

He called for regular inspections, preventive maintenance, adequate resources, and technical training for operators and mechanics.

“Heavy equipment is expensive. It is technically demanding and requires professional management. Without proper maintenance, even the best machine will eventually break down. My call is: maintenance, maintenance, maintenance,” he emphasized.

Using a local example to illustrate what he described as a culture of neglect, the President said public assets must be handled differently.

“Here in Liberia, we sometimes watch a car deteriorate—we wait for the wiper to fall off, then we wait for the bumper to fall off, then we kick it and say the car is still good. These machines must be maintained differently,” he stated.

President Boakai said technicians must be trained, resources provided, and mechanical problems addressed before they develop into major failures.

He tasked the Special Presidential Coordinating Committee (SPCC), working with relevant government institutions, with ensuring that professional operating procedures, maintenance schedules, technical support systems, and performance-monitoring mechanisms are established.

The President also announced that counties would be periodically assessed based on their management and utilization of the equipment, with consideration given to rewarding those demonstrating strong performance.

He called on the Ministry of Public Works, the Yellow Machines Board, the SPCC, and other responsible institutions to uphold transparency, efficiency, and operational discipline.

Roads and Economic Opportunities

Beyond improving transportation, President Boakai said the initiative was intended to strengthen agricultural production, expand economic opportunities, and improve food security.

He maintained that better feeder roads would allow farmers to transport their produce more efficiently, reduce post-harvest losses, and connect previously isolated communities to economic activities.

“A road is not merely a path between two places. It is a connection between people and opportunity. Every connected community can become more active in the national economy,” he said.

The President stressed that the initiative’s success should be measured by the condition of Liberia’s roads and the economic opportunities created years after the launch, rather than the ceremony itself.

“The true measure of success will not be this ceremony. It will be the condition of our roads five years from now, the number of roads built, and the agricultural opportunities created,” he added.

He expressed appreciation to Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung, the late Minister of State for Presidential Affairs Sylvester Grigsby, the Ministry of Public Works, the Armed Forces of Liberia, the General Services Agency, and the SPCC team for their contributions to the initiative.

He also charged operators, mechanics, and managers to handle the equipment responsibly, describing the machines as national assets intended to benefit all Liberians.

Following his remarks, the President called out the counties as the machines were symbolically started, marking the formal launch of their nationwide operations.

Procurement and Cost Controversies

Despite the government’s celebration of the initiative, the Yellow Machines program has faced sustained criticism from lawmakers, opposition politicians, and civil society organizations since its announcement in 2024.

Concerns have centered on the procurement process, financing arrangements, the total cost of the equipment, and whether the government complied with constitutional and public procurement requirements.

Initially presented as a Special Presidential Project, the arrangement was subsequently described by the government as a “gentleman’s agreement.”

Critics questioned compliance with Article 34(d) of the Liberian Constitution, which grants the Legislature authority over public borrowing, and demanded clarity about the suppliers and financing terms.

In April 2025, Public Procurement and Concessions Commission (PPCC) Executive Director Bodger Scott Johnson told The Liberian Investigator that the commission had no record of involvement in the arrangement.

“My office has no record to show that PPCC was involved in any part of the deal,” Johnson was quoted as saying.

Lawmakers also demanded accountability. Representative Moima Briggs-Mensah of Bong County District #6 called for a full accounting of the initial batch of machines unveiled in 2024, while Representative Gizzie K. Kollince of Lofa County questioned whether a transaction of such magnitude could be negotiated without legislative concurrence.

The advocacy group Solidarity and Trust for a New Day (STAND), headed by Mulbah K. Morlu, also warned that the acquisition must comply with procurement laws and constitutional requirements, arguing that bypassing competitive bidding or necessary legislative approval could expose responsible officials to legal liability.

Meanwhile, Cllr. Moriah Yeakula of the opposition Alternative National Congress described the machines in February 2026 as “metaphors for empty spectacle,” arguing that development must produce tangible results beyond public displays.

Anderson Miamen, Executive Director of the Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL), also questioned the need for additional management structures, including the SPCC and the Yellow Machines Board of Authority.

He warned that establishing new structures could impose additional financial burdens on the government and divert resources from critical sectors such as education, healthcare, and agriculture.

Sustainability and Government Response

Financial concerns have further intensified the debate. Initial estimates placed the cost of the 285 machines between US$79 million and US$85 million. The government later announced that it had renegotiated the arrangement to approximately US$22 million under a three-year payment structure.

However, a technical white paper by the Engineering Society of Liberia, presented by its President, David D. Wounuah, estimated that the initiative’s lifecycle costs could reach approximately US$238 million, with annual operating expenses projected at US$21.6 million, including fuel costs across the 19 operational hubs.

The report warned that without effective monitoring and expenditure controls, recurring operational costs could place considerable pressure on public finances and threaten the program’s sustainability.

The government, for its part, has maintained that no public funds were disbursed under the initial arrangement. Officials have also said that the first batch of 35 machines, which arrived in 2024, was returned as part of a restructuring of the original arrangement, after which the procurement was renegotiated.

The government has further maintained that the revised arrangement was aligned with national laws and procedures.

With all 285 machines now formally launched for nationwide deployment, the Boakai administration faces the challenge of translating its infrastructure promises into measurable improvements in rural connectivity.

Ultimately, the initiative’s success will depend not only on the number of roads rehabilitated but also on transparent management, effective maintenance, and whether rural communities experience lasting economic and social benefits.

Editorial note: The article is approximately 1,000 words. Before publication, verify the financial figures, the Engineering Society’s projections, and the government’s claims about procurement compliance against the original documents.

World.title: Liberia: Ambassador Kenneth, Qatar Labour Minister Al Marri Compare Notes on Strengthening Bilateral Labour Cooperation and Advancing Implementation of 2014 Labour Agreement
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberia’s Ambassador to the State of Qatar, Mohammed B.O.S. Kenneth, on Sunday, November 15 held a productive forty-five-minute meeting with Dr. Ali bin Saeed bin Samikh Al Marri, Minister of Labour of the State of Qatar and they discussed strengthening bilateral labour cooperation and advancing the implementation of the 2014 Labour Agreement signed during the State Visit of former President Madam Ellen Johnson- Sirleaf to Doha.

By Augustus D. R Bortue-augustusd.rbortue@frontpageafricaonline. com

Ambassador Kenneth informed his host that Liberia has qualified and skilled workers capable of contributing to Qatar’s workforce and expressed appreciation for the Minister’s willingness to strengthen labour cooperation.



Minister Al Marri reaffirmed the strong bilateral relations between the two countries and welcomed the initiative to advance the agreement’s implementation.

He emphasized his commitment to expanding employment opportunities for African nationals, noting that there are approximately 33 million migrant workers presently employed in the Middle East, with fewer than four million originating from Africa, according to figures he cited.

He also highlighted previous labour forums held in Doha and Tanzania, which Liberia did not attend.

He then used the occasion to encouraged Liberia to participate in future initiatives on Labour matters.

As a major point during the meeting, the Qatari Minister confirmed his intention to invite Liberia’s Minister of Labour for an official working visit to Doha between December 2026 and January 2027 to advance the implementation of the 2014 Labour Agreement.

He further assured the Liberian Ambassador that following such a visit, he would initiate the process of signing recruitment contracts for qualified Liberian security guards with additional employment opportunities in other sectors expected to follow.

Additionally, the Qatari Labour Minister requested Ambassador Kenneth to convey Qatar’s appeal for Liberia’s support for its candidate, the former Minister of Public Health of Qatar, in an upcoming World Health organization election scheduled for May 2027.

The Ambassador took note of the request for onward transmission to the Government of Liberia through appropriate diplomatic channels.

The Sunday meeting concluded on a positive note, with both sides expressing their commitment to strengthening bilateral labour relations and creating meaningful employment opportunities for Liberian nationals.

The Ambassador expressed its sincere appreciation to the Qatari Minister for his warm reception, constructive discussions and the invitation and said he will coordinate with Liberia’s Ministries of Foreign Affairs and Labour to facilitate the necessary follow-up arrangements.

World.title: Liberia: Thompson Urges Tumutu Student Leaders to Prioritize Integrity over Positions
World.content:
TUMUTU – William Telebo Thompson, a native of District Six, Bong County has urged newly inducted student leaders of Tumutu Vocational Training Institute to place integrity and service above the titles they have just received. He warned that positions are temporary, but the reputation a leader builds can follow them for life.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Thompson delivered the keynote address under the theme “Character Before Position.” His audience included the institute’s administration, members of the faculty, invited guests, parents and guardians, outgoing student leaders, the newly inducted leadership and the wider student body.



He opened by calling the occasion more than a point on the academic calendar. It was not simply a ceremony to distribute titles, recognize individuals or celebrate the assumption of new offices, he said. “Today is a moment of responsibility. Today is a moment of reflection. Today is a moment of commitment,” he told the gathering.

After congratulating the incoming officers, Thompson cautioned them against celebrating too quickly. He said society often applauds people for the offices they hold, the vehicles they drive, the clothes they wear and the influence they command, while forgetting to ask a more important question: “What kind of person is occupying that position?”

He pressed the point with a series of questions to the students. What is the value of a leader who has authority but lacks integrity? What is the value of a student leader who demands respect but cannot respect others? What is the value of a president who cannot accept criticism, a secretary who cannot be trusted, or a representative who remembers the people only when elections approach?

“Leadership is much deeper than a title,” Mr. Thompson said. A person can occupy an office without becoming a leader, wear a leadership badge without possessing leadership qualities, and command people without earning their respect. “That is why character must always come before position,” he said.

Speaking directly to the new officers, he stressed that their tenures would end. “Today, you may be a student president. Tomorrow, you will graduate,” he said, noting that the offices of secretary, treasurer, minister and class representative would soon belong to others. The lasting question, he said, is what people will remember about them. He asked whether they would be remembered as accessible, honest, compassionate and committed, or as people who became arrogant the moment they received a title. He also asked whether colleagues would remember that they stood up for them, or that they abandoned them once they gained authority.

Thompson said leadership should not be measured by how many people answer when a leader calls their names. “It is measured by how many people can confidently speak about your integrity when you are not present,” he said. He urged the students never to become so attached to their positions that they forget the people who gave them the opportunity to hold them.

Challenging what he called one of the greatest misconceptions about leadership, he said that becoming a leader does not make a person superior to anyone else. Leadership does not make someone more intelligent than colleagues, make their opinions automatically correct, or give them the right to intimidate, humiliate or disrespect others. If anything, he said, it demands more patience, understanding and accountability, and a greater willingness to listen.

He offered the students two contrasts. A true leader does not ask how many people he can control, but how many he can positively influence. A true leader does not ask what he can gain from a position, but what he can contribute through it. “If the only reason you wanted to become a student leader was to enjoy the privileges associated with the office, then you have misunderstood leadership,” he said. “Leadership is service.”

According to Thompson, service sometimes means sacrificing personal comfort for the collective good, accepting criticism even when it hurts, and standing alone for what is right when everyone else is choosing what is convenient. It also means doing the right thing when nobody is watching, he said, and that, in his words, is “putting character before your position.”

Drawing a distinction between popularity and principle, Mr. Thompson said, “Popularity makes people applaud you. Character makes people trust you.” He added that he would rather be a leader trusted by ten people than one applauded by a thousand but trusted by none.

He then gave the incoming leaders a set of direct charges. They should not compromise their integrity to impress friends, join in wrongdoing simply because the majority supports it, or misuse authority to settle personal scores. They should not turn student leadership into an opportunity for discrimination, favoritism or personal advancement. They should make every reasonable effort to keep their promises, have the courage to acknowledge mistakes, and apologize when they are wrong. They should listen when colleagues disagree with them, and do good without waiting for recognition. “Your integrity is your most valuable leadership currency,” he said. “Once you lose it, no title, position, or public recognition can fully replace it.”

Turning to the national picture, Thompson said Liberia has experienced decades of difficulty and has seen the consequences of poor leadership, corruption, dishonesty, division and the abuse of public trust. But he said he refuses to believe that the country’s history must permanently determine its future, that the next generation must inherit every mistake of the last, or that young Liberians cannot build a different society.

That change, he cautioned, will not come through slogans or through complaints about those who came before. It will come “when we become the change we continuously demand from others.” He tied national ideals to everyday campus behavior: students who condemn corruption should demonstrate honesty in their classrooms, those who demand accountability from political leaders should practice it in student government, and those who want respect from society should respect their fellow students. “If you want responsible national leadership, begin by becoming responsible student leaders,” he said.

Thompson noted that the leadership habits students form at the institute may follow them into their careers, communities and businesses, and eventually into the highest levels of national service. “Do not underestimate the importance of this moment,” he told them.

In a personal challenge to the new officers, he said leadership is not about making people feel small so that one can feel important, but about helping others discover their own importance. He urged them not to become inaccessible or arrogant, and not to let the excitement of office disconnect them from the realities of the students they represent. He asked them to remember the student who cannot afford certain academic materials, the colleague who is struggling academically, those too afraid to speak because they believe their opinions do not matter, and those who lack the confidence or resources to compete for leadership positions.

“A great leader does not build a legacy by making everyone dependent on them,” he said. “A great leader builds a legacy by empowering others to become better than they were before.” He added that the true test of leadership will not be behavior when everyone is celebrating, but “how you behave when nobody is applauding you.”

In his concluding remarks, titled “When the Title Is Gone, Let Your Character Remain,” Thompson asked the leaders to imagine a future in which their tenure has ended, another student holds their office, their badges have been returned, and the applause has stopped. “What will remain?” he asked. Titles will disappear and authority will end, he said, but the memories created, the lives touched and the integrity maintained “will continue to speak for you.” Character, he said, “does not need a microphone to be heard,” a title to be respected, or an office to make an impact.

He also reminded every student in the auditorium, whether inducted or not, that leadership does not begin when someone gives them a title. It begins when they take responsibility for their actions. “You do not have to be a student president to demonstrate honesty,” he said. “You do not have to be a class representative to help someone in need.” Every student, he said, can begin to be an agent of positive change “today, exactly where you are.”

World.title: Liberia: Chief of Staff to VP Koung   Donates 200 Bags of Cement to St. Mary Catholic Parish
World.content:
SANNIQUELLIE CITY, Nimba County– The Chief of Staff to the Vice President of Liberia, Jeremiah Kpan Koung, Prince Menkalo Gbieu, has donated 200 bags of cement to St. Mary Catholic Parish in Sanniquellie City, Nimba County, to support the church’s ongoing compound development project.

By Franklin Doloquee

The donation represents an initial contribution toward the parish’s efforts to improve the security and general condition of its premises.



The project is intended to provide a safer and more suitable environment for worship, fellowship and other parish activities.

Gbieu made the contribution after honoring an invitation from the parish, joining members of the congregation in worship and expressing support for the church’s development plans.

His visit brought together his commitment to his Christian Faith and his personal connection to Sanniquellie, where he once lived and received part of his education.

Speaking during the occasion, Gbieu described the donation as an opportunity to contribute to the work of God through practical support. He said assisting religious institutions and initiatives that strengthen Christian values was a responsibility he deeply appreciated.

Gbieu, a Christian and an elder of the United Liberia Inland Church, noted that his ties to Sanniquellie gave the contribution special personal significance.

He reflected on the city’s place in his upbringing and education, linking his support for the parish to a desire to give back to a community that helped shape his life.

The cement is expected to support construction work associated with improvements to the parish compound. These improvements are intended to strengthen the security of the premises while making the surroundings more conducive to the church’s religious and communal activities.

For the parish, the contribution provides building materials toward an ongoing project whose benefits are expected to extend beyond regular worship services.

A better-maintained compound can also provide a more welcoming setting for fellowship and other church gatherings.

The donation illustrates how individual assistance can complement a congregation’s efforts to develop and maintain its facilities. Contributions of construction materials offer a direct way of supporting such work, helping translate development plans into physical improvements.

Gbieu presented his support as an expression of faith and gratitude to a community with which he maintains a personal connection.

His contribution adds to the resources available for the parish’s continuing efforts to improve its compound and sustain a suitable environment for its members.

World.title: LAZ Ready To Go To Court To Defend Presidential Term Limits
World.content:
The Law Association of Zambia (LAZ) has restated its long-standing support for presidential term limits and warned that it may take legal action to protect Article 106(3) of the Constitution, as petitions seeking to remove the two-term limit sit before the National Assembly.

In a statement dated 16 November 2026, the Association welcomed an assurance by Minister of Justice Mr Jack Mwiimbu, SC, that the Executive will not interfere with the consideration of the petitions and that Parliament will handle the matter in accordance with the law. LAZ described the assurance as an important affirmation of institutional independence and the rule of law.

The Association traced term limits back through three constitutional review commissions. It said the Chona Commission of 1972, the Mvunga Constitution Review Commission of 1990 and the Mwanakatwe Constitutional Review Commission of 1996 all recommended limiting presidential tenure to two five-year terms. In its view, this shows the limits were never the arrangement of any single administration or political grouping.

LAZ urged Parliament to look beyond immediate political circumstances and to weigh the long-term implications for constitutional governance and institutional stability. It said it would continue to monitor the petitions and reserved the right to make representations to constitutional institutions and to pursue legal action where necessary.

The full statement follows.

PRESS STATEMENT

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

LAZ REAFFIRMS ITS LONG-STANDING POSITION ON PRESIDENTIAL TERM LIMITS

The Law Association of Zambia (LAZ) welcomes the remarks made by the Minister of Justice, Hon. Jack Mwiimbu, SC, MP, during a press briefing held on Friday, 13th November 2026, concerning the petitions submitted to the National Assembly seeking the removal of the presidential term limit provision under Article 106(3) of the Constitution of Zambia.

The Association particularly welcomes the Minister’s assurance that the Executive will not interfere with the consideration of the petitions by the National Assembly and that the matter will be dealt with by Parliament in accordance with the law. The Association further welcomes the Government’s recognition of the constitutional right of citizens to petition the National Assembly on matters of national interest.

The doctrine of separation of powers requires that each arm of Government operates within its constitutionally prescribed mandate, free from improper interference or undue influence by another. LAZ, therefore, considers the Minister’s assurance an important affirmation of the need to respect institutional independence and the rule of law.

The Association considers it necessary to set out the historical and constitutional context of the debate on presidential term limits and to restate its long-standing position on the matter.

THE HISTORICAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL BASIS FOR PRESIDENTIAL TERM LIMITS

Presidential term limits in Zambia are not a recent constitutional innovation. They are the product of a long-standing national discussion on constitutional governance, democratic accountability and the need to guard against the concentration of political power. Successive constitutional review processes have consistently recommended that presidential tenure be limited.

In 1972, the National Commission on the Establishment of a One-Party Participatory Democracy, commonly referred to as the Chona Commission, recommended that the tenure of the President be restricted to two terms of five years each. This position was subsequently reaffirmed by the 1990 Mvunga Constitution Review Commission, which recommended that presidential tenure be limited to two five-year terms. The recommendation was adopted and incorporated into Article 35 of the 1991 Constitution, which ushered in the restoration of multiparty democracy in Zambia.

The question was revisited by the 1996 Mwanakatwe Constitutional Review Commission, which reaffirmed the continued desire of the Zambian people to limit presidential tenure to two five-year terms. The subsequent constitutional amendment expressly provided that a person who had twice been elected President would not be eligible for re-election to that office.

This history shows that the introduction of presidential term limits was not the arrangement of a particular administration or political grouping. They emerged from successive national constitutional review processes and reflect a considered national position on the limits of presidential power.

LAZ’S HISTORICAL POSITION ON PRESIDENTIAL TERM LIMITS

The Law Association of Zambia’s position on presidential term limits is equally long-standing and is a matter of historical record. On 1st July 2001, the Association entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Council of Churches in Zambia, the Evangelical Fellowship of Zambia, the Zambia Episcopal Conference and the Non-Governmental Organisations’ Coordinating Council.

The MoU, subsequently revised on 22nd December 2005, established a common platform for promoting constitutionalism, the rule of law, democratic governance and the protection of the Constitution.

In the said MoU, the participating organisations (the “Forum”) recalled the recommendations of the Chona, Mvunga and Mwanakatwe Commissions and reaffirmed the importance of limiting presidential tenure to two terms of five years each. The Forum also called upon the then incumbent President to uphold, protect and defend the Constitution. It also called upon the people’s representatives in the National Assembly to uphold and respect the will of the Zambian people in relation to the limitation of presidential tenure.

The MoU also called upon the Executive and all other organs of the State to remain resolute and committed to their respective constitutional responsibilities of upholding, protecting and defending the Constitution. It further identified the promotion of a culture of constitutionalism and the doctrine and practice of separation of powers as central objectives of the Forum.

LAZ recalls this history to demonstrate that its commitment to constitutionalism and to presidential term limits is long-standing, institutional and principled, and does not depend on any individual office holders, political parties or administrations.

THE IMPORTANCE OF PRESIDENTIAL TERM LIMITS

Presidential term limits are a safeguard in a constitutional democracy. They promote regular leadership renewal, strengthen democratic accountability, limit concentration of executive power and affirm the principle that public office is held in trust for the people and not as a personal entitlement. They also reinforce the principle that no individual is above the constitutional limits governing the exercise of public power.

The current Article 106(3) of the Constitution provides that a person who has twice held office as President is not eligible for election as President. This provision is a deliberate constitutional safeguard and should be understood in the broader context of Zambia’s democratic evolution and constitutional history.

The Association maintains its position on presidential term limits and reiterates that the Constitution is the supreme law of the Republic, and that its protection must be given priority in any constitutional reform process.

THE ROLE OF PARLIAMENT AND THE RESPONSIBILITY OF THE NATION

In considering any proposal affecting presidential term limits, Parliament must look beyond the immediate political circumstances and consider the long-term implications for constitutional governance, democratic accountability and the institutional stability of Zambia.

The Association further calls upon all political actors, public institutions and citizens to approach this debate with restraint and with due regard for the constitutional principles at stake. Constitutional reform must be informed by the national interest and the collective aspirations of the Zambian people, and not by the interests of particular individuals or political formations.

THE ROLE OF THE LAW ASSOCIATION OF ZAMBIA IN SAFEGUARDING THE CONSTITUTION

The Law Association of Zambia reiterates its long-standing commitment to the preservation of the constitutional safeguard of presidential term limits as provided for under Article 106(3) of the Constitution.

The Association will continue to monitor developments surrounding the proposed amendment to Article 106(3) of the Constitution and any processes undertaken in furtherance of the petitions before the National Assembly. In this regard, the Association reserves the right to take such measures as may be lawfully available to it, including making appropriate representations to relevant constitutional institutions and pursuing legal action where necessary, to safeguard the Constitution and protect the current constitutional order.

This Press Statement is issued pursuant to Section 4 of the Law Association Act, Chapter 31 of the Laws of Zambia.

World.title: Grow Zambia Agenda needs united action
World.content:
The Grow Zambia Agenda (GZA), introduced by the New Dawn Administration, is a welcome and long-overdue strategy for the development of our country. In my view, it should be embraced as a long-term national development programme and sustained for at least 25 years, irrespective of changes in political leadership.

Such continuity would provide the consistency, stability and strategic direction necessary to transform Zambia into an economically prosperous and socially developed nation. It has always been the aspiration of well-meaning Zambians to see our country transformed and developed for the common good.

There is no doubt that we all want to see a Zambia that is prosperous and peaceful, where every citizen has an opportunity to enjoy a better quality of life. However, this aspiration cannot be realised without a sufficiently developed economy, modern infrastructure and productive industries capable of creating employment, generating wealth and improving living standards.

It is both sad and deeply disappointing that, more than six decades after attaining independence, Zambia continues to grapple with widespread poverty and underdevelopment, despite being generously endowed with natural resources that are the envy of many developed nations. Our country possesses vast mineral wealth, abundant water resources, fertile agricultural land, favourable climatic conditions and a youthful, energetic population.

Yet, regrettably, a large proportion of our people continue to live in poverty, with many communities struggling to access basic social and economic opportunities. Our continued dependence on external assistance, in spite of our enormous resource potential, should challenge our collective conscience.

This situation is unacceptable and calls for a fundamental change in our approach to national development. Zambia has the potential to do much better, and we must no longer allow our natural wealth to coexist with widespread poverty and economic deprivation.

It is undeniable that our country needs transformation and development. However, transformation and development cannot be achieved merely by wishing, talking or praying for them. They require deliberate, purposeful and sustained action, supported by commitment, discipline and hard work at both individual and national levels.

We must make a conscious effort to move from where we are today to where we aspire to be as a nation. I genuinely believe that it is against this background that the New Dawn Administration, under the leadership of President Hakainde Hichilema, conceived the Grow Zambia Agenda: to provide our country with a clear sense of direction and a practical framework for achieving economic growth, national transformation and shared prosperity.

What is particularly commendable about the initiative is that it is not merely an expression of good intentions. It has been translated into a programme with clearly articulated priorities, objectives and measurable targets. This provides citizens, the private sector, investors and cooperating partners with a better understanding of the country’s development aspirations and the contribution expected from each stakeholder.

The agenda identifies key areas of intervention, including economic decentralisation, energy and power, agriculture and livestock, tourism and infrastructure, innovative financing, and digital inclusion. These sectors are critical to accelerating economic expansion, creating employment, increasing productivity and improving the general welfare of our people.

To accelerate economic growth and job creation, the agenda sets out ambitious production and development targets, including:

· 10 million tonnes of maize production;

· 10,000 megawatts of electricity generation;

· 5 million international tourist arrivals annually;

· 3 million tonnes of copper production;

· 3 million tonnes of soybean production;

· 1 million tonnes of wheat production;

· 1 million tonnes of sugar production; and

· The development of a US$1 billion annual beef export industry.

These are undoubtedly ambitious targets. But the important question we should all be asking ourselves is: are these targets achievable? My answer is an emphatic yes! They are achievable, provided we collectively commit ourselves to their implementation.

Indeed, with proper planning, investment, innovation, efficient resource utilisation and effective coordination, Zambia could potentially achieve even more. What is required is a decisive and collective commitment to the national development agenda. Every Zambian has a role to play, regardless of political affiliation, tribal identity, regional origin or religious belief.

National development should never be held hostage by our political and social differences. We must recognise that, beyond our individual affiliations and differences, we share one country and one common destiny.

Our leaders have provided a development framework and articulated the direction in which the country should move. The responsibility now extends to all of us to translate that vision into reality through practical action. As I have already observed, Zambia will not develop simply because we wish or pray for development.

Prayer and hope have their place, but they must be accompanied by purposeful action. We must each identify clear goals and targets, both at national and individual levels, and take responsibility for contributing to their achievement.

Government must continue to provide policy direction, create an enabling environment, invest in strategic infrastructure and ensure that public resources are used efficiently and accountably. The private sector must respond through investment, innovation, production and job creation. Farmers must increase productivity and embrace modern agricultural practices.

Professionals must apply their knowledge and expertise towards solving national challenges. Young people must be encouraged to become productive, innovative and entrepreneurial. Above all, every citizen must recognise that national development is a shared responsibility.

It is therefore utterly disappointing to see sections of our educated elite, who should be at the forefront of providing ideas, expertise and constructive solutions, instead devoting their energies to discrediting government policies and development initiatives.

Constructive criticism is necessary in every democracy, and no government programme should be beyond question. However, criticism should be informed, objective and accompanied, wherever possible, by practical alternatives and solutions.

We should not allow political differences to overshadow the greater national interest. Our collective responsibility should be to make good policies and development programmes work for the benefit of the country.

My appeal to all well-meaning Zambians is therefore simple: let us become active participants in the Grow Zambia Agenda. Let us support its objectives, contribute our ideas, invest our energies and play our respective roles in ensuring its success.

Zambia belongs to all of us. We must build it not only for ourselves but also for future generations. The responsibility to transform our country cannot be left to government alone. It requires a united national effort, driven by patriotism, hard work, integrity and a shared determination to succeed.

Let us rally behind the national development vision with the same determination and unity demonstrated by the Israelites when they embarked on their journey out of Egypt towards the Promised Land. Just as they had to undertake a journey of faith, perseverance and collective responsibility, we too must be prepared to undertake the difficult but necessary journey from poverty to prosperity.

We must abandon the tendency to merely wish for a better Zambia and instead commit ourselves to building one. Let us stop talking about the Zambia we want and start working towards creating it.

No amount of rhetoric will develop our country. No development vision, however well-conceived, will achieve its objectives without commitment and implementation. It is our collective actions, sustained over time, that will ultimately determine whether Zambia fulfils its enormous potential.

Let us therefore turn our aspirations into action, our natural resources into wealth, our potential into productivity, and our collective determination into national prosperity. Let us make the Grow Zambia Agenda a national commitment, not merely a government programme.

Let us migrate from poverty to prosperity through honest work, enterprise, innovation and national unity. Let us make Zambia grow!

The author is former Special Assistant to the President for Policy and Project Implementation and Monitoring.

By Jack Kalala

Source: Times of Zambia
