World.title: FRA Says 70 Per Cent Of Farmers Paid, Promises Rest Within 10 Days
World.content:
The Food Reserve Agency (FRA) has paid 70 per cent of the farmers who supplied it with Grade A non-genetically modified white maize and paddy rice during the 2025/2026 Crop Marketing Season, and says the rest will be paid within 10 days.

FRA Executive Director Mr Justin Chuunka said the latest payout to farmers came to about K300 million. The money followed the release of funds to the agency by the Treasury on Friday last week.

Mr Chuunka said the timeline was set at the highest level. He assured all farmers that they would receive what was due to them within 10 days, in line with a Presidential Directive.

The agency says it is working around the clock to meet that deadline.

“The Agency is working 24 hours in collaboration with the banks to ensure that the process is quickened and it’s done in a timely manner,” Mr Chuunka said.

He expressed confidence that the target is within reach. Based on the current pace of payments, he said, the agency expects to clear all farmers inside the window set by the President.

“The Executive Order that was given to the Agency was that every farmer should be paid within 10 days, and when we did our permutations, with the rate at which we are paying, we are equal to the task that the 10 days will be attained,” Mr Chuunka said.

Technology has helped speed things up. Mr Chuunka said the agency’s digital payment platform had eased the process because farmers’ details were already in the database. Priority, he said, is being given to farmers who supplied their crops to the agency early.

The payments come alongside a strong national food position. Mr Chuunka said Zambia would be food secure for at least three years, even with the El Niño weather pattern on the horizon, because the country holds maize stocks of close to four million tonnes.

Those stocks come from two sources. Mr Chuunka said the reserve is made up of 1.3 million tonnes of carry-over stock from the previous season and a record 2.6 million tonnes bought during the 2025/2026 Crop Marketing exercise.

He set those figures against national demand. With annual consumption at about 1.2 million tonnes, he said, the stocks on hand could cover the country for roughly three years.

“In terms of food availability, the Agency has, as at now, close to four million metric tonnes, and given our annual consumption of about 1.2 million tonnes, you can actually do the permutations that the country is secure, maybe for the next three years,” Mr Chuunka said.

For the 30 per cent of farmers still waiting, the clock is now running on the 10-day directive. The agency says payments are going out daily through its partner banks, with early suppliers first in line.

World.title: Invest In Refugee-Hosting Areas, Mutale-Nalumango Tells Private Sector
World.content:
Vice-President Calls For Private Investment To Turn Refugee Areas Into Economic Hubs

Vice-President Mrs W.K. Mutale-Nalumango has called on the private sector to invest in refugee-hosting areas, saying they offer major economic opportunities that can promote shared prosperity, self-reliance and national development.

Mrs Mutale-Nalumango said investment in agriculture, value chains, financial services, enterprise development and job creation would benefit both refugees and the communities that host them. It would also, she said, support Zambia’s broader economic growth.

Her remarks were delivered in a speech read on her behalf by Home Affairs and Internal Security Minister Dr Clement Andeleki at the official opening of the Private Sector Forum on Refugees and Host Communities in Lusaka.

The Vice-President placed the call within a long national record. She said that for more than six decades, Zambia had shown an unwavering commitment to providing protection and asylum to people fleeing conflict and persecution.

The numbers remain substantial. Mrs Mutale-Nalumango said Zambia currently hosts more than 100,000 asylum seekers, refugees and former refugees in urban areas and refugee settlements, a reflection of the country’s longstanding values of peace, solidarity and humanity.

This year carries a particular milestone. With Zambia marking 60 years of refugee hosting in Mayukwayukwa, she said the Government remained committed not only to protecting refugees but also to empowering them to become self-reliant and active contributors to national development.

That approach, she said, is guided by the National Refugee Policy, which seeks to promote refugee inclusion while strengthening host communities.

“Our vision is to transform refugee-hosting areas into productive economic hubs that contribute to local and national development,” Mrs Mutale-Nalumango said.

She pointed to work already under way. The Vice-President cited the One Meheba Local Area Plan and the wider Mayukwayukwa Local Area Plan as examples of the Government’s efforts to integrate refugee-hosting areas into national development priorities and economic corridors.

The United Nations backed the call. United Nations Resident Coordinator Dr James Wakiaga urged the private sector to invest in refugee-hosting areas, saying such investment could drive economic growth, create jobs and promote shared prosperity among refugees and host communities.

Dr Wakiaga said these areas should be seen differently. In his view, refugee-hosting areas should be viewed not merely as humanitarian spaces but as productive economic centres capable of contributing to Zambia’s socio-economic development.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) made the same point. Mr Zephania Amuiri, UNHCR representative for the Multi-Country Office covering Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe, said the private sector had an important role in moving beyond humanitarian assistance towards sustainable economic inclusion.

The UNHCR has also set out where the openings lie. In a factsheet, the agency urged private investors, agribusinesses and financial service providers to explore commercial opportunities in settlements such as Maheba and Mayukwayukwa, which it described as offering scalable business opportunities for the domestic private sector.

Maheba stands out in that assessment. The factsheet said the settlement offered openings in structured agricultural aggregation, institutional supply, agro-processing and corridor logistics, pointing to contract farming and bulk aggregation of soya beans, legumes, rice, poultry and horticulture produce to serve institutional buyers and mining supply chains across Kalumbila and Solwezi.

The settlement already has a commercial base. The factsheet said Maheba has nine designated commercial areas, led by Block D, Road 36, as a hub for retail trade, hospitality, financial services and value addition, supported by three major rice mills processing local harvests. Grid extension completed in partnership with the Rural Electrification Authority (REA) now powers Maheba A, B and Kananga, enabling grain milling, cold storage and enterprise growth.

Location adds to the case. The UNHCR said Maheba sits directly beside North-Western Province’s major copper-mining hubs and is linked to the emerging Lobito Trade Corridor, creating strong demand for food, transport, agro-processing and commercial services.

The Lusaka forum now puts the Government’s plan in front of the investors it is meant to attract, with the One Meheba and Mayukwayukwa local area plans as the framework for that investment.

World.title: Court Orders Esther Lungu Theft Trial To Resume December 16, No More Adjournments
World.content:
The Lusaka Magistrate’s Court has set December 16, 2026, for the resumption of the theft trial of former First Lady Mrs Esther Lungu and four others, and ruled that there will be no further mentions or adjournments in the matter.

Lusaka Resident Magistrate Ms Mbuyanwa Sinvula fixed the date in chambers. She said the case had gone for more than a year without the trial continuing and must now move forward.

The order brings to an end a long stretch in which the case only came up for mention. That pattern began in June 2025, after former President Mr Edgar Lungu fell ill and later died in South Africa. Mrs Lungu has been out of the country since her husband’s death, and Mr Lungu has not yet been buried.

Mrs Lungu stands trial alongside four co-accused. They are police officers Mr James Phiri and Mr Lee Chisulo, Mr Kapambwe Lungu, and Ms Catherine Banda, a niece of the late former President.

The five face four counts of theft. The charges involve three motor vehicles and a certificate of title to a property in the Water Works area of Libala.

The prosecution’s case covers a period of just over a year. It is alleged that between August 9, 2021, and September 30, 2022, the five stole a Mitsubishi Canter valued at K320,000, a Toyota RunX valued at K110,000 and a Toyota Alex valued at K110,000. The vehicles belonged to Ms Elizabeth Phiri and Ms Furhana Patel.

The property count is the largest by value. The accused are alleged to have stolen the certificate of title for Stand No. S/Lusaka/0003/2977 in Libala, valued at K1,050,000 and belonging to Ms Phiri.

The road to the new trial date ran through two sittings. Ms Sinvula mentioned the case on October 4, 2026, and adjourned it for another mention and the fixing of trial dates. When the matter returned in chambers, she settled on December 16.

Her directive leaves little room for further delay. With no further mentions or adjournments allowed, the trial is now expected to proceed on the set date.

The December 16 sitting will be the first time in more than a year that the trial itself continues. The question of Mrs Lungu’s presence remains open, as she has been outside Zambia since her husband died.

World.title: UPND Hits Back At Khama Over Term Limits As 63,000 Youths Plan Parliament March
World.content:
The ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) has rejected claims by former Botswana President Mr Ian Khama that President Hakainde Hichilema is trying to remove presidential term limits Zambia, saying the question belongs to all Zambians and not to one man.

UPND Media Director Mr Mark Simuuwe said the matter should not be personalised around the Head of State. He said President Hichilema had issued no statement suggesting he wanted term limits removed, and that Mr Khama had misread what was being proposed regarding presidential term limits Zambia.

The distinction, in Mr Simuuwe’s view, lies between scrapping limits altogether and stretching them. He said the proposal under discussion was about removing term limits, not extending presidential tenure from two terms to three, including the context of presidential term limits Zambia.

“There is a difference between a third term and term limit. Khama’s posting is purely off. What we are talking about is removing the term limit, not transitioning from two terms to three, no,” Mr Simuuwe said.

He went further on what removal would mean in practice. Mr Simuuwe said lifting the limits would give citizens the power to decide through elections how long a president should remain in office. The proposal, he said, had nothing to do with a perpetual presidency or with undermining multiparty democracy.

The party also confronted the videos now circulating on social media. In those clips, Mr Hichilema, while in opposition, spoke against a constitutional provision that would have allowed a sitting president to seek a third term. Mr Simuuwe defended the current discussion against criticism drawn from that footage, saying laws should evolve in response to changing societal circumstances.

Opponents, he said, have a proper route open to them. Mr Simuuwe said those against the proposal, including the Tonse Alliance, were free to challenge it through legal and democratic channels rather than through protests. Any constitutional amendment, he added, should be handled through established institutions, particularly Parliament.

Support for the proposal is set to take to the streets next week. More than 63,000 youths are expected to march to Parliament Buildings on November 25, 2026, in support of proposals to remove presidential term limits.

The march has been organised by the Zambia Youth Organisation Consortium, which says it has confirmed the participation of 63,151 young people from all 10 provinces. Consortium Vice-Chairperson Mr Boas Kanyama announced the figures in Lusaka after formally notifying the Zambia Police Service of the organisation’s intention to hold the procession.

The route has already been set. Mr Kanyama said marchers would gather at Northmead Bus Station and proceed to Parliament Buildings.

The organisers are keen to keep party colours out of it. Mr Kanyama said the march was not being organised on behalf of any political party and that the consortium had no affiliation with partisan politics.

“We believe that presidential term limits should not prevent citizens from exercising their democratic rights,” Mr Kanyama said.

With police formally notified, the consortium’s next step is the procession itself on November 25. On the governing party’s side, the position is now on record: the matter is for citizens and Parliament to settle, and the President has made no statement seeking to remove the limits.

World.title: High Court Reserves Two Rulings In Mundubile, Makebi Bail Fight
World.content:
The Lusaka High Court has reserved rulings in two separate bail applications involving opposition politicians Mr Brian Mundubile and Mr Makebi Zulu, leaving the pair and 16 co-accused in detention until at least Friday on one matter and November 24 on the other.

The first ruling turns on jurisdiction. A panel of three judges led by Judge Geoffrey Mulenga will decide on Friday whether the court can hear a bail application by Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu, who face two counts of seditious practices. The second ruling, set for November 24, 2026, will determine whether Mr Mundubile and 17 others charged with treason and terrorism-related offences should be granted constitutional bail.

The sedition charges stem from the period after the general election. The two are accused of attempting to influence the announcement of the presidential results through a Parallel Vote Tabulation (PVT) and of announcing on Facebook that Mr Mundubile would address the nation. Both contested the polls on the ticket of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP).

Attorney General Mr Mulilo Kabesha asked the court to dismiss the sedition bail application outright. He questioned whether the High Court in Lusaka had jurisdiction to hear a bail application filed directly before it while the substantive case remained before the Solwezi High Court.

The defence pushed back on that objection. Mr Sakwiba Sikota, representing the two politicians, told the court that his clients could not have applied for bail in Solwezi because that court lacked jurisdiction to hear the substantive matter in the first place. The preliminary issue, he said, should therefore fail.

The treason matter is heavier and involves more people. A separate panel of Judge Derrick Mulenga, Judge Davies Chibwili and Judge Ireen Wishimanga reserved its ruling after hearing submissions from both sides on the constitutional bail petition brought by the 18 detainees.

In that petition, the applicants allege that their constitutional rights have been violated in several ways. They cite prolonged detention without being taken to court, falsified remand warrants, detention in unauthorised sections of prison and delays in accessing medication.

The State resisted the application on several grounds. Represented by Mr Kabesha and Director of Public Prosecutions Mr Gilbert Phiri, it told the court that the offences were serious and complex and had required extensive forensic and financial investigations.

The prosecution also raised concerns about release. The State said the applicants posed a flight risk, could interfere with witnesses and needed to remain in detention in the interests of public safety and national security.

Defence lawyers stood firm on the rights question. Mr Bonaventure Mutale, Mr Chifumu Banda and Mr Sikota maintained that their clients’ constitutional rights had been violated through prolonged detention, and that the court should grant relief on that basis.

The two rulings now set the immediate path for the opposition figures. If the court finds it has jurisdiction on Friday, the sedition bail application can proceed to a hearing on its merits. The constitutional bail decision on November 24 will determine whether Mr Mundubile, Mr Zulu and the 16 others leave custody while the treason case moves forward.

For now, all 18 remain in detention. The next court date in the sedition matter is Friday, when the Judge Geoffrey Mulenga panel delivers its ruling on jurisdiction.

World.title: Minister orders ZIMDEF to deliver results, not just collect money
World.content:
Local News

Valentine Maya · November 12, 2026

HIGHER and Tertiary Education minister Frederick Shava has reminded the Zimbabwe Manpower Development Fund (ZIMDEF) that its success will be measured by the skills it imparts on students and the jobs it supports, not by the money it collects or disburses.

Officially opening the 2026 ZIMDEF strategic planning workshop in Mutare this Thursday, Shava said, “ZIMDEF must remain focused on interventions that deliver tangible value to the economy, within its statutory mandate and the Ministry’s policy priorities.”

Shava said the retreat must produce a comprehensive assessment of 2026 performance against the strategic plan; clearly defined corrective measures for outstanding commitments and implementation challenges; and a realistic, costed and prioritised 2027 annual work programme and budget aligned with the government’s long-term plans.

He also said the workshop’s outcomes must be an evidence-based assessment that demonstrates what has been achieved, what remains outstanding and what must be done differently to improve delivery.

“Last year, ZIMDEF developed its 2026–2030 strategic plan, aligned with the Second National Development Strategy (NDS2). Our task today is to take stock of implementation during 2026, identify areas requiring improvement and agree on strategic priorities for 2027,” he said.

He urged delegates to approach the exercise with openness, objectivity and a clear focus on results.

The Minister of Higher and Tertiary Education, Innovation, Science and Technology Development, ambassador Frederick Shava, receives a token of appreciation from ZIMDEF vice chairperson colonel Siwinile Tauya at the ZIMDEF 2026 Strategic Planning Review Workshop in Mutare.

Pictures: MHTEISTD Communications and Advocacy Officer Kudakwashe Hunda

On the 2027 budget, Shava said resource allocation must be guided by strategic priorities, available resources, demonstrated needs and the readiness of proposed projects for implementation.

“Particular attention must be given to completing ongoing projects and ensuring that previous investments generate their intended benefits,” he said.

Shava also called for tighter revenue collection.

“I wish to emphasise the importance of strengthening revenue mobilisation and compliance and ZIMDEF must sustain engagement with contributing employers, improve the efficiency of collections and pursue outstanding obligations consistently and professionally, within the applicable legal framework,” he said.

The minister also tied the fund’s work to the ministry’s heritage-based education 5.0 philosophy.

“Within this framework, ZIMDEF has a critical responsibility to support the development of a skilled, competent and productive workforce that responds to the needs of our economy,” he said.

He acknowledged the ZIMDEF board and management’s continued commitment to strengthening the fund’s contribution to skills development and human capital formation in Zimbabwe.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 17, 2026
World.content:
South Africa Investigates Shootings That Left 17 Dead

South African police are investigating two separate mass shootings that left 17 people dead in KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng. Eight men were found shot dead inside a minibus outside Pietermaritzburg. In a separate shooting, six men and three women were killed inside a shack in the Jeffsville informal settlement in Atteridgeville, west of Pretoria. Community members initially mistook the gunshots for thunder and lightning. Police have said the incidents are unrelated. They have launched manhunts for the suspects. The motives remain unknown amid growing concerns over gun violence and organised crime in the country. In September, 28 people were killed in two separate cases.

Five EU Countries Plan Rwanda Migrant Deportation Hub



Five European Union countries, Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, plan to establish a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda in 2027 as part of efforts to increase the removal of people who have exhausted their legal right to remain in their countries. Under the proposed arrangement, deportees will be able to settle in Rwanda or return to their countries of origin. The initial phase is expected to focus on single men, with the centre potentially accommodating about 100 people. However, the plan has been criticized by human rights groups over safety concerns for migrants and Rwanda's human rights record. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has also criticised the proposal, questioning its humanity and effectiveness. The five countries maintain that the scheme will comply with EU and international law.

Guinea Arrests Over 1,200 in Illegal Gold Mining Crackdown

Guinea has banned illegal gold mining in its northeastern Siguiri region. At least 1,263 suspected miners were arrested, including nationals from Burkina Faso, Mali, Togo, Nigeria, Ivory Coast and Ghana. Authorities said that the crackdown aims to protect the environment from mining activities that damage soil, vegetation and water sources, as well as improve regulation of the sector. However, the operation has sparked criticism over alleged human rights abuses, mistreatment and deportations of foreign miners. The crackdown comes as Guinea begins operations at its first gold refinery in Conakry, with the government seeking to process more of its gold locally. Officials said the ban applies to all illegal miners, not only foreign nationals. Neighbouring Burkina Faso and Mali have raised concerns over the treatment of their citizens caught up in the operation.

Declining Aid Exposes Refugee Children to Exploitation, UN Warns

The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and Oxford University have warned that declining humanitarian funding is leaving refugees in Bangladesh and Ethiopia increasingly vulnerable to trafficking, child labour and exploitation. Since 2024, more than 170,000 Rohingya refugees have fled to Bangladesh, where conditions have worsened because of deteriorating shelter conditions and reduced access to clean water. Ethiopia's child protection programs, family reunification services and schools for refugee children have been hit by funding shortfalls. Children, especially those separated from their families and unaccompanied minors, are at greater risk of sexual violence, forced labor and early marriage, the organizations warned. In Ethiopia, planned child protection needs were only 18% funded in 2025, leaving thousands of vulnerable children without adequate support. The studies call for predictable humanitarian funding to strengthen protection services and prevent further exploitation.

DR Congo Ebola Outbreak Remains Out of Control - Africa CDC

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has warned that the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo remains out of control, six months after it was declared, with more than 11,200 infections and 5,500 deaths reported. Director-General Jean Kaseya cited insecurity, attacks on health workers, unpaid medical staff and shortages of resources as major obstacles to containing the outbreak, which has spread to eight provinces. He also warned of further regional transmission, particularly to the Central African Republic and South Sudan. Vaccine and treatment trials are underway. The absence of an effective vaccine targeting the Bundibugyo strain remains a major challenge. Kaseya is urging international donors to release billions of dollars in pledged funding to strengthen the response.

Close 

Harare Halts Housing Demolitions Until Further Notice

Harare City Council has suspended all housing demolition operations with immediate effect until further notice. Acting Town Clerk Warren Chiwawa issued a memorandum instructing all council departments and operational teams to stop demolition activities unless authorised by his office. The directive requires strict compliance across the municipality, with no further demolitions permitted until a new instruction is issued. Chiwawa warned that all departments must ensure the suspension is communicated to their staff and operational teams.

World.title: South Africa: Two Arrested in Tembisa Hospital Fraud Probe - South African News Briefs - November 17, 2026
World.content:
press review

Two More Arrested in Tembisa Hospital Corruption Scandal

Two more people have been arrested in connection with the R635 million Tembisa Hospital corruption scandal after handing themselves over to police at the Tembisa police station, reports EWN. The suspects are allegedly linked to tender fraud involving the manipulation of the hospital's procurement system. Officials and service providers are accused of splitting transactions to keep them below the R500,000 threshold. A 37-year-old suspect was previously arrested in August as part of the investigation.

Court Hears Arguments Over Detention of Asylum Seekers



The Johannesburg High Court is set to continue hearing arguments over the detention of undocumented foreign nationals seeking asylum, following a Constitutional Court ruling that declared parts of the Refugee Act unconstitutional, reports SABC News. Lawyers representing the asylum seekers argue that their continued detention is unlawful and that they should be released and have their applications processed within 48 hours. However, the Home Affairs Department has said that this timeframe is impractical due to an overwhelming backlog of applications and has proposed a minimum 14-day period, assessed on a case-by-case basis.

Protest Disrupts Traffic Along Johannesburg's Heidelberg Road

Motorists in Johannesburg have been urged to avoid Heidelberg Road in City Deep following renewed protest action linked to suspected service delivery grievances, reports EWN . Burning tyres and debris have been reported between Impex Avenue and Mpumelelo Road, disrupting traffic. The Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department said the demonstrations initially began over power outages. Road users have been advised to use alternative routes until the protest subsides and the road is cleared.

World.title: Africa: The End of a Cancer Is in Sight for the First Time in Public Health History
World.content:
guest column

To mark Tuesday’s World Cervical Cancer Elimination Day, global health leaders highlight the progress achieved and prospects of consigning cervical cancer to the annals of history.

For the first time in public health history, the end of a cancer is in sight. We already have the tools to make this possible. With HPV (human papilloma virus) vaccination, screening and timely treatment, cervical cancer could become the first cancer ever eliminated.

Each year more than 600,000 women are diagnosed with cervical cancer and about 280,000 lose their lives. Behind every number is a woman whose life, family and future matters. When a mother dies, her children will be left to grow up without her love, protection and support. These maternal orphans are among the often-invisible victims of cervical cancer, their loss echoing across families, communities and generations.

Women in the world’s poorest places are the most affected.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The disease burden is profoundly unequal. Cervical cancer disproportionately affects women and families in the world's poorest communities, and 19 of the 20 countries with the highest burden are in the World Health Organization (WHO) African Region. Beyond the physical suffering caused by advanced disease, too many women face stigma, silence and formidable barriers to lifesaving care.

That’s why WHO made a forceful call to action in 2018. Countries have been rising to the challenge. In 2020, even in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic, WHO Member States adopted a ‘Global Strategy to Accelerate the Elimination of Cervical Cancer’. The strategy set ambitious but achievable targets: 90% HPV vaccination coverage for girls, 70% screening coverage for women, and 90% access to treatment for those with precancerous lesions or cancer.

Science, solidarity and commitment are delivering results.

At a time when the world often seems overwhelmed by intractable problems, cervical cancer elimination offers a different story: one of science, solidarity and sustained commitment delivering results.

Progress is accelerating. Australia and Sweden are approaching the historic milestone of eliminating cervical cancer as a public health problem, while Rwanda is demonstrating that similar progress is possible in Africa, with several districts already meeting key WHO elimination targets.

Six years after the strategy's launch, the landscape has changed dramatically. Vaccine supply constraints that once threatened progress have largely been overcome, and there are now more HPV vaccines on the market. Today, 166 countries have introduced HPV vaccination into their national immunization programmes, including Burundi, Papua New Guinea and Ukraine in the past year alone. India recently rolled out one of the world's largest HPV vaccination campaigns, reaching more than 11 million girls.

Meanwhile, scientific advances have enabled a simplified single-dose schedule for most girls, making vaccination easier and more affordable to deliver at scale. Ninety-six countries already report implementing a one-dose schedule. Global HPV vaccination coverage has now reached 33%.

Screening and treatment are advancing alongside prevention provided by vaccination.

Screening and treatment have advanced too. More countries are adopting HPV testing, which is more effective at identifying women who need preventive treatment than the traditional Pap test or visual inspection performed with vinegar in low-resource settings. Today’s HPV tests even allow a woman to collect her own sample, offering more options for privacy and convenience, while portable thermal ablation devices are enabling nurses to treat precancerous lesions in minutes, even in remote communities. Science is opening new frontiers too: artificial intelligence-assisted screening could soon improve early detection and further accelerate progress toward elimination.

Behind these advances stands something just as powerful: a growing global movement.

The heroes of this global movement are survivors, advocates, health workers and community leaders who are turning the promise of elimination into a reality.

In Kenya, nurse Martha Wanjiru travels in a mobile clinic across the highlands of Kiambu County, bringing screening services directly to women in urban settlements and rural communities while educating them about their health. Kenya is now advancing a national elimination action plan, transitioning to single-dose vaccination and expanding integrated screening services.

In Sierra Leone, healthcare worker Sallay Carew takes her bullhorn into Freetown’s crowded marketplaces, loudly breaking down stigma as she encourages women to be screened. Today, screening services are available across all 16 districts. Through a training partnership with Zambian colleagues, Sierra Leone’s gynecologists are now performing life-saving cervical cancer surgery, with treatment provided free of charge. Women who once had to travel abroad for care can now receive it in their own country.

Bravest of all are the survivors driving change. In Zambia, Karen Nakawala used her radio show to broadcast her battle with cervical cancer to the whole country. Organizing HPV vaccination drives and screening campaigns to push toward the WHO targets, Karen’s “Teal Sisters” network is now over 100,000 strong. The sisters even accompany one another through treatment and survivorship. In Malaysia, Selina Yeop is building a grassroots network of survivors. With teal-colored fashion shows, peer support groups, and heads held high, they are changing how their country talks about cervical cancer. Across borders and continents, survivors are connecting, organizing and leading.

Their efforts are being matched by political commitment. Last year, governments meeting at the World Health Assembly reaffirmed their determination to eliminate cervical cancer and established 17 November as World Cervical Cancer Elimination Day.

These achievements deserve applause. But progress is not permission to slow down. Too many women are still being left behind.

Governments must sustain investment in vaccination, screening and treatment, until every woman and girl can access the services she needs, regardless of where she lives. Women living with HIV deserve particular attention. They face a six-fold higher risk of developing cervical cancer. While the HIV/AIDS movement delivered extraordinary results in the last four decades, on this count, we are falling short. A complete package of care must include the services that women need too: that means cervical cancer screening and treatment. As countries adapt to a changing global health financing landscape, it is more sustainable to invest in cervical cancer prevention than to face the consequences of the disease.

Industry also has a critical role. Vaccines, tests and treatment technologies must be available at prices that enable all countries, especially low- and middle-income countries, to continue scaling up access. Elimination will only be possible if innovation is matched by affordability.

Close 

Be part of making history on this World Cervical Cancer Elimination Day

Our message is simple: history is waiting to be made, so choose to be part of it.

The tools exists. The strategy is clear. The momentum is real.

Now we need every government, every health worker, every community leader, every parent and every advocate to help carry this movement forward. Vaccinate your children. Get screened. Support someone you love to access care. Advocate for services in your community. Put on a teal ribbon and start a conversation: tell others that you, too, are standing up for women’s health, for the end of cancer, and for the unifying power of public health.

If we sustain the commitment that countries and communities have already shown, cervical cancer can become the first cancer humanity eliminates as a public health problem. Millions of women and girls will live longer and healthier lives. And future generations will know that when the world had the chance to end this suffering, we chose to finish the job.

Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus is WHO Director-Genera. Dr Princess Nono Simelela is Advisor to the Minister of Healt of South Africa. Prof Groesbeck Parham is Consultant Gynecologic Oncologis at the University of Zambia. Richard Freeman is Executive Officer of WHO. Dr Prebo Barango is WHO Cross-Cutting Specialist for NCDs and Special Initiatives. Claire Kimilu is Consultant, WHO Cervical Cancer Elimination Initiative.

World.title: Sudan: Sudan's State Collapse - Canary in the Coal Mine for International Peace and Security
World.content:
Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs) are community-led volunteer networks made up of Sudanese citizens, many of them young people, that serve as the primary humanitarian lifeline for millions of civilians amid Sudan the ongoing and devastating civil war.

guest column

Sudan's harrowing state implosion since war resumed in 2023 presents a warning for other states in Africa and elsewhere currently heading in that direction as well as stark dilemmas for U.S. foreign policy.

Just as Somalia's state collapse provided an instructive example in the 1990s, Sudan is experiencing a much more consequential slide into a country where multiple international security and peace threats emerge, from chemical weapons to interconnected conflicts throughout a broad regional swathe to the world's most devastating humanitarian crisis. Sudan's state collapse is a canary in the coal mine for similar countries at risk from Libya to Lebanon to Haiti to multiple neighbors, first and foremost South Sudan.

Sudan's collapse is a canary in the coal mine for countries at risk from Libya to Lebanon to Haiti to multiple neighbors.

At a moment when there are more simultaneous conflicts globally since WWII, Sudan's war stands out in its size and scope. The numbers are staggering. It is the world's largest displacement crisis, with 14 million people rendered homeless by the violence. It is the world's largest hunger crisis, with 40% of the country's population facing acute food insecurity. And it is arguably the world's largest sexual violence crisis. The UN's Tom Fletcher concluded, "Sudan is an atrocities laboratory: sieges, denial of food, weaponized sexual violence…"

As the fighting rages on, the crisis only will metastasize, as fertilizer and fuel shortages due to the Iran conflict increase the cost of food, thus driving millions more into extreme hunger.

The funding gaps are gaping, with UNICEF, the World Food Program, and the UN High Commission for Refugees all facing shortfalls between 70 and 85 percent of assessed needs. That directly translates into more starving kids, more virulent epidemics, etc.

The roots of Sudan's collapse share commonalities with other states in extreme distress.

Sudan's case is extreme but not isolated. The roots of its collapse share commonalities with several other states in extreme distress.

First, state capture. For decades, Sudan's rulers and their external collaborators have hijacked state institutions for private gain, creating a classic violent kleptocracy. A coalition of thieves of state ruled the country, and then fell out over its spoils, as thieves do, tearing the country apart in the process. The worst abuser of human rights, the genocidal militia known as the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), was originally a collection of racist militias known as the Janjaweed, subsequently organized by Sudan's long-time dictator Omer al-Bashir to fight an incipient rebellion in Darfur. Unsurprisingly, as those militias grew in power and acquired greater wealth, they turned on their former government benefactors and made a play for raw power, leading to massive civil war, total state collapse, and the possible further partitioning of the country.

Second, resource extraction. Sudan's rich resources, particularly oil and gold, have been pillaged by successive governments, allied militias, rebel groups, and unscrupulous external actors. Parasitic multinational networks have created an assembly line of violently extracted and smuggled raw materials in Sudan and many other failing states, enriching a handful of insiders and outsiders while the communities and countries are ravaged economically and environmentally. The result is war as an economic system fueled by resource extraction, smuggling, checkpoint taxation, and the fleecing of humanitarian aid efforts. In Sudan and other African states such as the Democratic Republic of Congo, South Sudan, and the Central African Republic, the global acceleration in the price of gold has led to ever more violent contestations over control of the mining and trafficking of conflict gold, particularly to the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE imports well over $1 billion worth of illicit gold from Sudan per year.

Third, environmental poisoning. As part of the gold rush in Sudan and many other countries, increased artisanal mining is contributing to public health emergencies resulting from chemicals poisoning the groundwater, soil, and communities surrounding the mines. Agricultural communities near the mines in River Nile state now say that crop production has decreased by up to 80% to 90% due to toxic chemicals used in gold mining.

Fourth, external intervention. The Cold War construct of the United States versus the Soviet Union has been replaced in Sudan by a raging rivalry between the UAE backing the RSF and Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkey, Iran, and Russia backing the rival Sudan Armed Forces. At a recent international donors' conference in Berlin on the Sudan crisis, the UAE and Saudi Arabia tanked the joint communique because the Emirates couldn't even agree to the Saudi insistence on preserving "state institutions." The rise of the so-called Middle Powers has created a more complex chessboard in war-torn states from the Democratic Republic of Congo to Yemen where external actors pour in arms and/or trade in conflict resources such as gold with no consequences, as they pursue conflicting agendas related to influence and resources that make mediation efforts much more challenging.

Fifth, weapons systems. Provided by Iran, Egypt, Türkiye, and especially the UAE to the belligerents, attack drones have become the weapon of choice in Sudan, representative of a trend also seen in conflicts as far afield as Iran, Ukraine, and Mali. The use of these drones has completely changed the nature of warfare. The usual ebb and flow of conflict related to seasonal rains has been rendered moot; attacks on civilian targets can be mounted from further away with deadly accuracy. The cost of a quick and dirty "offensive" can be minimal for the attacker, but devastating for the target, usually civilian. Recently, there has been a surge of drone attacks on food distribution efforts, which ties drone strikes directly to increased starvation. Even more alarmingly for international security, the Sudan Armed Forces were recently found to be using chemical weapons—chlorine gas bombs—in violation of international arms treaties.

UNICEF/Mohammed Jamal A woman searches through the burnt remains of her shelter at a displacement camp in Darfur, Sudan.

Sixth, failed crisis response. In Sudan, international efforts at brokering a semblance of peace, creating accountability for massive war crimes, providing consistent humanitarian assistance, and countering abject state collapse have all failed spectacularly. More broadly, in response to wars around the world, the UN system and various regional entities have proven unable to develop crisis response mechanisms relevant to evolving conflict dynamics.

Seventh, eroding U.S. relevance. The United States still has the most leverage over the external patrons in Sudan, and using that in coordination with a more sophisticated mediation effort would hold the biggest potential for peace in Sudan. But the U.S. has been unwilling to use that leverage in any meaningful way, particularly regarding US allies UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Egypt, who are all pouring gasoline on Sudan's inferno by supporting the armed factions. The US says it is focused on getting both sides to accept a humanitarian truce and to commit to an inclusive political dialogue to lead to a civilian government, but the cold reality is that kind of soft diplomacy can never succeed without changing the conflict's lucrative financial incentives, which in turn requires impacting the calculations of the external backers to the conflict. Sudan and other crisis-torn countries perceived to be less strategically important have been downgraded on the Washington mattering map, leaving in tatters peace processes and the failed elite bargains on which they were built.

Eighth, regional security risks. Sudan's war now risks spreading into a regional war, as several of its neighbors have supported one faction or another. The recent resumption of war in Tigray, northern Ethiopia, is a case in point, as Ethiopia has been supporting the RSF (a claim they reject), and now the Sudan Armed Forces may be supporting the Tigrayan rebels against the Ethiopian government (a claim the SAF deny). Sudan's state collapse and Ethiopia's renewed conflict are now risking a wider regional war, which could engulf other countries including Eritrea, Chad, and others, while also having connections to Yemen. This is already creating significant concerns for U.S. foreign policy in the region, which could escalate.

The playing field in Sudan and other collapsing or failed states has become wildly skewed in favor of elite networks that have captured state institutions for their own gain; in Sudan's case, the contest over these hijacked institutions has led to their utter destruction. At the same time, an assault has unfolded on pro-democracy and anti-corruption human rights advocates, the free press, independent legislatures and judiciaries, women's organizations, and any other independent voice.

A different crisis response paradigm is needed - kleptocratic war machines, including their multinational facilitators, need to be dismantled.

In response to this new, more dangerous era, a different crisis response paradigm is needed. To level the playing field and give peace and democracy a chance, the kleptocratic war machines, including their multinational facilitators, need to be dismantled, or at least more substantially weakened, and the incentives that sustain these war economies need to be disrupted.

This can be achieved if the US, UK, European Union, and other states with influence deployed much more robust sanctions against networks of corrupt officials, weapons suppliers, conflict gold traffickers, and companies they control, as well as anti-money laundering measures. Whole-of-government pressure of this nature is usually reserved for high-level national security issues. It's time to enhance the tools used for Sudan and other developing cases of state collapse.

Additionally, non-governmental organizations can create impact through campaigns aimed at undermining the reputation laundering strategies of some of the key arms-providing countries, like Emirati and Saudi sportswashing efforts using commercial branding deals with leagues, teams and tournaments from multiple sports around the world. More systematic and focused countering of the networks and actors benefiting from chaos and predation is critically needed.

Simultaneously, the constituencies for peace and reform in Africa need far greater support. Without more tangible assistance to the local groups pressing for system change, it's hard to imagine progress.

In Sudan, that means supporting the Emergency Response Rooms, women and youth organizations, unions, local peace committees, and other local institutions that can provide the backbone of social reconstruction, and not trotting out the same tired, failed diplomatic models of power sharing involving only the most heavily armed factions. Sudan is Exhibit A for how that mediation strategy has spectacularly failed.

This is a moment to rethink how the U.S. and the world respond to national implosions and to cobble together … a more effective way forward.

Sudan's complete state collapse and ensuing rising threats to international peace and security - along with a massive border-crossing humanitarian crisis - are a harbinger of things to come for other countries on similar trajectories that begin with predatory state capture.

This is a moment to rethink how the United State and the world respond to such national implosions, and to cobble together the coalition of civil society organizations, multilateral institutions, and concerned governments that can begin to envision a more effective way forward.

Sasha Lezhnev is a Senior Policy Adviser at The Sentry, which John Prendergast co-founded.

World.title: Africa: Facebook Exposure Is Behavioral Intelligence - Not Vanity Metrics
World.content:
guest column

In March 2026, as Nigeria implemented its measles-rubella vaccination campaign, the World Health Organization (WHO) Africa Infodemic Response Alliance was listening to what happened online. It revealed how people were receiving, questioning and interpreting the intervention in real-time.

This demonstrates why public health must take social media seriously as a source of behavioral intelligence to inform interventions. Today, people socialize, trade, network, find love and seek information on social media. Public health must meet people where they already are. As of April 2026, there were an estimated 5.79 billion social media user identities worldwide, equivalent to about 70% of the global population.

To be sure, social media metrics cannot prove behavior change, but that does not make them "vanity metrics." When interpreted carefully, they can provide valuable behavioral intelligence about how people encounter and respond to an intervention.

Facebook is a useful case study of using social media to promote health



With over 3 billion users globally, Facebook offers a useful case study. Its metrics broadly capture exposure and engagement. Impressions and reach tell us how often content was displayed and how many people saw it, while likes, shares and comments show how people engaged with it.

Impressions: How often did people encounter the message?

Imagine a public health program places banners promoting vaccination against HPV (human papillomavirus - the leading cause of cervical cancer worldwide) at strategic locations across Abuja, Nigeria, such as at major intersections, markets, schools, bus stops, pharmacies and health facilities. A mother might pass one while taking her daughter to school, encounter another on her way to the market and see the campaign again at a health facility.

Each encounter creates another opportunity for the message to register. But we cannot assume she read every banner, understood the message or subsequently vaccinated her daughter.

Facebook impressions work similarly. An impression is counted each time content is displayed on a screen, including repeat displays to the same person.

Reach: How many different people saw the message?

Using the same banner example, imagine one mother passes the same banner 20 times while another encounters the campaign only once. Impressions capture those repeated opportunities for exposure. Reach asks how many different people had an opportunity to encounter the campaign?

Facebook reach estimates the number of unique users to whom content was displayed. If an HPV vaccination post reaches 500,000 people, it does not mean they all paid attention, agreed with the message or vaccinated their daughters. But it tells implementers something important about the breadth of the campaign.

Likes: What resonates?

A 'like' is often the easiest metric to dismiss. Someone can like a post about cervical cancer screening without ever getting screened. Someone can 'like' one of my Keep Walking With Dr. Bill videos while remaining sedentary.

But a 'like' is nevertheless a small behavioral signal. Someone encountered something and decided it was interesting, agreeable, useful or emotionally resonant enough to respond.

When certain messages consistently generate stronger reactions, program teams should investigate why. Maybe personal stories resonate more than statistics; messages about protecting one's family perform better than messages emphasizing individual risk; or hopeful messages generate stronger reactions than fear-based ones.

A 'like' does not prove behavior change. But patterns of likes can generate hypotheses that programs can test and use to improve content.

Shares: What are people willing to pass along?

Now imagine a mother who sees one of the HPV vaccination banners around Abuja, takes a photo of it and shares it with her networks on WhatsApp. Her decision to share the message tells us she considered the information relevant or important enough to pass along to others.

A Facebook share is similar. Someone deliberately passes a post within their own networks, becoming an informal messenger for the intervention.

Again, sharing does not prove behavior change. But if certain HPV vaccination messages are shared far more frequently than others, implementers should ask why. Was it the language, messenger, image, practical information or way the content addressed a common concern?

Conversely, people may also spread misinformation and disinformation.

Comments: What are people telling us?

Comments may provide the richest behavioral intelligence of all. They allow people to ask questions, express fears, share experiences, challenge claims and sometimes spread misinformation.

Comments can transform social media communication into conversation.

As Project Director of VITAL, an HPV vaccination initiative in Nigeria, I saw this firsthand. Under one Facebook post, a caregiver asked, "What is the full meaning of HPV?" Another asked, "What is HPV vaccine and can someone about 20 take it?"

These were important questions. The first revealed a basic knowledge gap that could easily be overlooked by implementers accustomed to talking about "HPV." The second showed interest but also uncertainty about eligibility, a potential barrier to taking the next step.

Neither told us whether the individuals ultimately sought vaccination. But both told us what our audience needed from us. We answered their questions immediately and used those questions to improve content.

Close 

Measuring behavior change from social media interventions

To confirm if behavior changed as a result of VITAL, we conducted an end-of-project evaluation comparing caregivers exposed to the social media campaign with a control group.

Girls in areas exposed to the campaign had 48% higher odds of being vaccinated, while exposure was associated with an 8.9 percentage-point increase in the probability of vaccination compared with the control group.

The evaluation also helped us understand how the intervention may have worked. Exposed caregivers reported greater motivation to vaccinate, better knowledge of where to obtain the vaccine and greater perceived ease of getting their daughters vaccinated. Interestingly, the campaign did not significantly improve factual knowledge about HPV vaccination. It appeared to work more through behavioral drivers such as motivation and ability to act than simply by increasing knowledge.

As WHO's listening analysis shows, when public health listens carefully to what people are telling us on social media, reactions stop being vanity metrics and become intelligence for better action.

Dr. Ifeanyi Nsofor is a public health physician, behavioral science researcher, and global health equity advocate. His work focuses on applying behavioral science and digital approaches to improve health outcomes globally. He is Co-Founder of the Africa Behavioral Science Network.

World.title: Uganda: Muhoozi Returns to X With 10-Year Jail Threat for Media Critical of Museveni
World.content:
Nairobi — Uganda's Chief of Defence Forces Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba has returned to X with a fresh warning that media organisations and journalists who criticise or "belittle" his father, President Yoweri Museveni, could face 10 years in prison.

In a series of posts on Tuesday, Muhoozi also threatened to subject foreign media personnel he considers agents of foreign interests to trial by court martial, while announcing plans to introduce a new policy governing foreign media operations in Uganda.

"Any media from wherever insulting or belittling Mzee, Maama, Afande Saleh, or me will be imprisoned for 10 years," he wrote, referring to his father, mother and uncle, Gen Salim Saleh, a former military logistics chief who has repeatedly stepped in to contain diplomatic fallout from Muhoozi's controversial social media remarks and is widely regarded as a moderating influence on his nephew.



"I shall announce a new policy on the operations of ALL foreign media in Uganda soon. Their days of insulting our country are over," he added.

The posts mark his return to the platform after deactivating his account following a series of threats against Vice President Jessica Alupo over alleged links to what he described as a plot involving his former deputy, Lt Gen Peter Elwelu.

Muhoozi also announced that he had restored Elwelu's rank of Lieutenant General, weeks after publicly declaring that he had demoted the former deputy military chief to private.

"I was very, very angry with Elweru some weeks ago. I demoted him to a private. I was ready to do much worse. I now restore his rank as a Lt. General of our great army. He will face the Court Martial with his restored rank," he wrote.

Elwelu was arrested on November 2 over allegations of involvement in activities aimed at destabilising the country.

Muhoozi had previously accused him of treachery and threatened to take action against Vice President Alupo if she was found to have supported him.

Presidential ambitions

The army chief also used his return to X to restate his intention to succeed his father, declaring that he would contest the presidency after Museveni.

"I am going to stand for the Presidency of this country after Mzee. No one will stop me. I place my hope in Almighty God and my fellow countrymen and countrywomen," he posted.

The declaration comes amid growing uncertainty over the succession question within the ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM), which has been in power since 1986.

An AFP report published on November 11 said the party's leadership had failed to agree on a proposal to designate Muhoozi as Museveni's successor, citing five party sources familiar with deliberations.

The report said a meeting of the NRM executive committee on November 10, convened to consider succession, ended without a decision on Muhoozi's candidacy after several members opposed the proposal.

Four members had reportedly voted in favour of his candidacy and three against before the vote was abandoned, with opposition to the proposal drawing loud cheers from some attendees.

One party source told AFP that Muhoozi's combative conduct on social media had created unease within the party.

Another said NRM Vice-Chairman Calvin Echodu had advised Museveni to retire his son from the army and give him a civilian role to prepare him for leadership.

Echodu reportedly also suggested that Museveni should seek another term in 2031, arguing that Muhoozi was not yet ready to take over.

Muhoozi, 52, currently heads Uganda's military and has increasingly become a central figure in the country's political succession debate as his 82-year-old father approaches four decades in power.

Controversial pronouncements

Muhoozi's latest statements add to a series of provocative social media interventions that have drawn domestic and international criticism.

Before deactivating his account, he threatened Vice President Alupo with arrest and dismissal from government over claims that she supported Elwelu's alleged treachery.

Close 

He also invoked previous confrontations with opposition figures, including Kizza Besigye, Kampala Lord Mayor Erias Lukwago and opposition leader Robert Kyagulanyi, popularly known as Bobi Wine, as evidence that his threats should be taken seriously.

In January 2026, Muhoozi threatened to kill Bobi Wine following Uganda's disputed presidential election, claiming that security forces had killed twenty-two "terrorists" belonging to the opposition National Unity Platform and expressing hope that the opposition leader would be next.

He also threatened to cut military ties with the United States after accusing its ambassador of aiding Kyagulanyi's escape.

The remarks attracted criticism from US Senator Jim Risch, Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, who rejected an apology subsequently issued by Muhoozi and urged Washington to consider tougher measures against Uganda.

Muhoozi has also previously issued directives touching on government administration, including an order requiring ministers to obtain his permission before travelling abroad.

World.title: Kenya: Gachagua Faults Ruto's 'Usawa Ni Sawa' Over 'Tribal' State Appointments
World.content:
Nairobi — DCP leader Rigathi Gachagua has taken a swipe at President William Ruto's "Usawa ni Sawa" campaign, questioning the government's commitment to equal opportunities following a series of appointments involving people from the Kalenjin community.

Gachagua's remarks came shortly after the Teachers Service Commission (TSC) named Cheptumo Ayabei as its new Secretary and Chief Executive Officer.

In a sarcastic post on X, the former Deputy President linked Ayabei's appointment to other recent selections, including Ronoh Kibet as KenGen Managing Director and CEO, and Lydia Sitienei Chelagat's nomination as Data Commissioner, which is awaiting parliamentary approval.

The appointments have revived Gachagua's criticism of what he describes as favouritism in the distribution of senior government jobs, even as Ruto promotes his "Usawa ni Sawa" message of equal opportunities for Kenyans.

Gachagua, who was impeached in October 2024 after facing several charges, including accusations of promoting ethnic divisions, has repeatedly accused his former boss of favouring members of his community in public appointments.

However, government allies have defended the selections, maintaining that the individuals were picked on merit and through competitive recruitment processes.

World.title: Rwanda: What to Know About Migrant Partnership Between Rwanda and Five EU Countries
World.content:
Rwanda's Minister of Interior Vincent Biruta (third right) joined senior officials from the five EU countries at a press conference announcing the new migration partnership.

The government and five European Union member states have announced a partnership to establish a migrant return hub in Rwanda, targeting the first transfers in 2027.

The proposed arrangement would cover people who have no legal right to remain in the participating European countries and are subject to enforceable return or removal decisions.

Announced in Vienna, Austria, on Monday, November 16, the initiative brings together Rwanda, Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands. Negotiations will determine how the proposed hub will operate.

People transferred to Rwanda would have the opportunity to integrate into Rwandan society, voluntarily return to their countries of origin or move to another country where they have the legal right to reside.



ALSO READ: Rwanda, five EU countries announce migration partnership

Here are eight key things to know about the proposed arrangement.

1. It involves five EU member states

Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands are pursuing the initiative with Rwanda as part of a broader partnership covering migration and other areas of common interest.

The participating countries describe the partnership as equal and mutually beneficial.

Austria's Interior Minister Gerhard Karner said the initiative would help curb irregular migration, disrupt people-smuggling networks and ease pressure on receiving countries.

2. Who would be transferred to Rwanda?

The proposed hub would receive migrants who have no legal right to remain in the five participating European countries and are subject to enforceable return or removal decisions.

Those covered must not be in need of international protection or have another legal basis to stay.

The initiative seeks to address difficulties in implementing return decisions, particularly where migrants' countries of origin do not cooperate with repatriation.

ALSO READ: What Rwandans say about UK asylum deal

Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said return hubs could provide an alternative for people without the right to remain in Europe who cannot be returned to their home countries.

3. Migrants would have an opportunity to settle in Rwanda

People transferred under the arrangement would have the opportunity to integrate into Rwandan communities.

Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said Rwanda will work with its partners to develop skills and employment programmes to support those who choose to stay.

"These people who choose to stay in our country, to live in our country, will be integrated into our communities. And of course we work on a development programme to give them skills. They will need to be able to work," he said.

Biruta said the programmes would also benefit Rwandans through wider community development.

4. Returning home or moving elsewhere remain options

Settling in Rwanda would not be the only option.

Migrants would also be able to return voluntarily to their countries of origin or relocate to another country where they have the legal right to reside.

Biruta said the arrangement would offer a second chance to people who no longer have the right to remain in the participating European countries, allowing them to choose among the available legal options.

ALSO READ: What to know as Rwanda-UK migration dispute hearing starts

Support for integration and voluntary return would be developed with international partners.

5. European partners would cover the costs

The five European countries would meet the costs associated with the arrangement, including receiving migrants and supporting their integration in Rwanda.

Biruta said Rwanda's participation was driven by a commitment to finding a sustainable response to migration challenges.

He said partner countries would need to fund the support required by those transferred, including skills development and employment programmes.

6. International organisations are advising on the proposal

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the United Nations refugee agency, UNHCR, are engaging with the countries involved, although their roles differ.

IOM is providing technical input on the return hub process. It has indicated that it could provide care and assistance to migrants at the receiving government's request, provided the necessary safeguards are in place.

UNHCR is advising on compliance with international human rights standards and the protection of asylum systems, including ensuring that people who need international protection continue to receive it.

Their engagement should not be taken to mean that either organisation has agreed to implement the proposed arrangement.

The European Commission has followed the preparatory discussions, with implementation expected to comply with applicable EU and international law.

7. Rwanda's experience in receiving displaced people

Rwanda has cited its experience hosting refugees and asylum seekers as a basis for its participation.

Biruta highlighted the Emergency Transit Mechanism, established in September 2019 through a partnership between Rwanda, the African Union and UNHCR to evacuate vulnerable refugees and asylum seekers from Libya.

Close 

According to the minister, Rwanda has received more than 3,000 people through the mechanism, most of whom have subsequently been resettled in countries including Canada, the United States, Germany and Finland.

He said Rwanda's own history of displacement had shaped its understanding of the challenges facing refugees and asylum seekers.

The Emergency Transit Mechanism and the proposed return hub serve different groups: the former provides protection and assistance to people evacuated from Libya, while the latter would receive people found to have no legal right to remain in the participating European countries.

8. First transfers are targeted for 2027

The countries intend to develop the hub through a phased approach, with the aim of beginning transfers in 2027.

Denmark's Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bødskov described the initiative as a breakthrough in efforts to reform Europe's migration system.

Greece's Migration and Asylum Minister Athanasios Plevris said it was expected to help reduce irregular migration and increase returns.

The Netherlands' Deputy Prime Minister Bart van den Brink said the partnership should strengthen the return system while giving migrants an opportunity to settle in Rwanda.

The announcement sets out the countries' intentions, but further negotiations are required to finalise the operational arrangements.

World.title: Duffy vows to modernize aging air traffic system after nationwide ground stop
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Monday said he plans to modernize America’s aging air traffic control system and build new architecture that is "worthy of America" following a nationwide ground stop on Friday that stranded more than a million passengers.

During an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity," Duffy said he wants to build a modern, resilient telecommunications network.

"Congress did give me $12.5 billion. That’s for radar and radios. I am well on my way to deploying all that money. You can’t buy this off the shelf, so I’ve ordered it. As it is delivered, we pay for it, and we deploy it into the NAS. But what’s really important is the next phase of the investment," he told host Sean Hannity on Monday.

The $12.5 billion in congressional funding is part of a broader effort to modernize the nation's air traffic control system, including communications, surveillance and other infrastructure.

DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE'

"So you saw a telecom issue on Friday. We’re replacing old copper wires with fiber, but this is an old architecture of a network. You’ve seen Newark go down. You’ve seen Dallas go down. You saw all of New York go down just a couple of months ago because of telecom issues. I want to build a brand-new architecture of a resilient telecom network that’s worthy of 2026 and worthy of America," he continued.

Duffy added that the department needs new software.

"The software we use to manage our airplanes in the airspace was built in the 1990s. It works. It works well. But if we’re going to drive more safety and more efficiency, we need brand-new software," he explained.

The secretary also said intelligence agencies found no evidence that a cyberattack forced the ground stop on Friday and that the Federal Aviation Administration was investigating whether a network problem, router issue or installation error caused the system failure.

The FAA is working with contractor L3Harris, which installed the router in question and is assisting with the investigation at its Florida laboratory.

"We had all of our intelligence agencies, at Donald Trump’s direction, talk on Friday night," Duffy said. "No one was seeing any kind of hack into our system. And we’ve now secured the router."

BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We’re doing an analysis in Florida with L3Harris and the FAA. I actually asked the FBI to come in just to make sure, to put people at ease, that this was not a hack. So I think it was a network problem or a router problem or an installation error," he continued.

The roughly five-hour ground stop affected more than 1.5 million passengers whose flights were scheduled to depart on Friday afternoon and evening. More than 12,000 flights were canceled that day, according to the FAA, while delays and cancellations continued through the weekend.

World.title: Chargers, Justin Herbert finally win first game of season after brutal mistake by Ravens star
World.content:
It’s happened, folks. There is no longer a winless team in the 2026 NFL season.

The Los Angeles Chargers have notched their first victory of the season, as Justin Herbert and company took down the Baltimore Ravens on "Monday Night Football," spoiling Jacoby Brissett’s first game with his new team since being traded by the Arizona Cardinals.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The Ravens’ troubles continue, as they dropped their fifth straight game and fell to 4-6 on a season that seems to be slipping away from them.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Meanwhile, head coach Jim Harbaugh and everyone within the Chargers organization can all breathe a sigh of relief knowing they’ve at least avoided some embarrassing NFL history.

It was no easy feat against a desperate Baltimore team trying to right the ship in any way possible, especially at quarterback. The injuries to Lamar Jackson and Tyler "Snoop" Huntley have decimated the team’s offense, leading to a necessary trade with the Cardinals, who had made Brissett their third-string signal caller amid their own struggles.

The Ravens and its fan base hoped Brissett would be the answer to get the ball rolling again, but he was forced into a late fourth-quarter comeback scenario, down 23-20, but with ample time, and timeouts, to work with.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

On second-and-10 from their own 39-yard line, Brissett hit receiver Zay Flowers right between the numbers, and he crossed midfield into Chargers territory. But, instead of trying to get out of bounds or simply taking the first down and heading back to the huddle, Flowers tried fighting through two Chargers defenders.

It was a grave mistake.

Tarheeb Still made a tremendous play, stripping Flowers of the ball and Elijah Molden fell on it for a clutch fumble recovery with 2:11 to play in the game.

All Herbert needed to do was kill the clock with a couple of first downs, and considering he was doing everything in his power to will his team to victory on Monday night, he knew he was just about at the finish line.

Los Angeles did their jobs, with Herbert finding Charlie Kolar for a first down just after the two-minute warning. It was enough to melt the clock down to 18 seconds, and with no timeouts on their end, the Ravens couldn’t muster the miracle Hail Mary to avoid disaster as the pass from Brissett was batted down near the goal line as the clock struck zero.

In the end, the Ravens are not going to win games if Derrick Henry is rushing for only 10 total yards on 10 carries. He had nine rushing yards on 16 carries back in 2023 during his time with the Tennessee Titans, but this performance, or lack thereof, was astonishing to see, especially for a Ravens home game and considering the circumstances heading into Monday night.

No team rushing for a team total of 16 yards can function as an offense, and that’s credit to a hungry Chargers defense that certainly did their part in keeping Brissett uncomfortable in his first start for Baltimore.

Brissett did, however, look better once settled in the second half. He finished 33-of-49 for 340 yards, though he was unable to notch his first touchdown pass while throwing an interception. He seems to like tight end Mark Andrews, who had a team-high eight catches and 82 yards.

Meanwhile, Herbert was 12-of-18 for 129 yards through the air, but it was his legs that played such a vital role in the Chargers getting things done on the road. He was a running threat, rushing for 51 yards on seven carries with the game’s first touchdown under his belt.

Then, Omarion Hampton had the running performance he’s been searching for since the start of the season, racking up 105 yards on 22 carries with his own touchdown run.

While Harbaugh and his Chargers can celebrate and look to build off their first win, head coach Jesse Minter and his staff are back to the drawing board as their playoff hopes hang in the balance after handing their opponent its first win of the year.

World.title: DHS chief tells Americans to 'breathe' amid tech outages, insists homeland is 'secure'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin had a direct message for concerned Americans after the U.S. experienced a slew of technology disruptions that halted flights, email services and online banking platforms across the country.

"Well, breathe. The homeland is secure. Our banking system is secure and when something like this happens, we’re able to react and react fast," he said Monday on "Hannity."

Mullin’s remarks came as customers Monday reported trouble accessing online services of major U.S. banking platforms, including Wells Fargo, Chase, U.S. Bank and Bank of America. United Airlines also faced a widespread system outage on Monday that briefly affected departing flights.

UNITED AIRLINES SAYS TECHNOLOGY ISSUE RESOLVED AFTER ‘WIDESPREAD SYSTEM OUTAGE’

The latest disruptions follow a nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday, which caused widespread flight delays and cancellations, as well as a separate Microsoft outage last week that affected Outlook email services.

Mullin maintained that the incidents were not a result of cyberattacks and described the disruptions as "individually unrelated."

DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK

"I can tell you with 98% certainty we’re not seeing the cyberattack," the DHS secretary said.

"We’re not seeing the footprints going in. We’re not seeing the footprints going out," he continued. "And so, nothing points to it being connected."

FAA SAYS AIR TRAVEL SHOULD BE BACK TO NORMAL SUNDAY AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Four banks reportedly faced outages on Monday, according to Downdetector.com.

JPMorgan Chase said the problems were not related to cybersecurity issues in a statement to FOX Business, adding that customers still have access to their accounts and funds and that the company was working to fix the issue.

Mullin suggested the broader technology disruptions highlight vulnerabilities in aging infrastructure as newer technologies place demands on legacy systems.

"We just have a lot of technology thrown at us and our world runs on technology now," Mullin told host Sean Hannity. "We used to have backup systems and the backup systems are overwhelmed by the new systems now."

TRUMP INTEL CHIEF WARNS AI FIRMS ON HACKS, SAYS NEW DEPARTMENT IS THE 'COP ON THE BEAT'

Mullin also said a prominent technology expert briefed him earlier Monday and suggested to him that "super intelligence" could have contributed to the disruptions. The DHS secretary believed the theory "kind of makes sense."

"He said, because these programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is. And so when they put in a program that’s able to write codes, and it goes in and it self-fixes itself, as it starts self-fixing itself, it’s like doing a change order on a house. When you change one thing in a house, everything else starts changing. That’s a ripple effect," he explained.

"It causes these systems to be overrun that weren’t designed to run as fast as the SI technology is today," he added.

Mullin defended the Trump administration’s response to recent technology disruptions and pledged to deploy federal resources to help companies experiencing technology problems.

"We are very secure, and I feel very comfortable about where we’re at," he said.
