World.title: Ro Khanna pitches $1,700 checks for Americans to offset Iran war costs: 'A chance to deliver'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., on Monday proposed giving every American family a $1,700 refund check to offset higher costs driven by the war in Iran.

Khanna, a frequent critic of President Donald Trump's war in the Middle East, said the checks would be sent to every American family to reimburse them for the higher gas, food and electricity prices sparked by the conflict and resulting disruptions to oil transport routes.

The congressman said Democrats "have a chance to deliver" following their sweeping midterm victories earlier this month, urging the House and Senate to approve the payments in January.

"I want to give every American family a $1,700 check to make them whole for the war in Iran," Khanna said in a video posted to X.

RO KHANNA REJECTS WARNINGS THAT TRUMP ADMIN INVESTIGATIONS COULD DERAIL DEMOCRATS' AFFORDABILITY AGENDA

"This is to cover their higher gas prices, their higher food prices, their higher electricity bills. Now Democrats have a chance to deliver. The first week in January, the House and Senate must pass a $1,700 refund check to Americans. Let’s put it on Donald Trump’s desk," he continued.

Khanna had previously urged Congress to block all funding for the war.

Khanna also introduced legislation in September that would redirect certain unused Pentagon funds to compensate taxpayers and dependents for the economic costs of the war. The bill does not specify a $1,700 payment and has not advanced beyond the committee referral stage.

Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, estimated last month that the conflict in Iran had cost the average American household about $2,000, adding up to $265 billion nationwide. His estimate included higher energy costs, borrowing costs and military expenditures.

VOTERS HAVE A BLUNT MESSAGE FOR TRUMP ABOUT HIS IDEA TO DOLE OUT $5,000 CHECKS

Gas prices soared after the war began in February, with the national average rising above $4 per gallon before declining in recent weeks. The average was $3.81 per gallon as of Monday, about 75 cents more than a year ago, according to AAA. Diesel averaged nearly $6 per gallon, about $2.23 more than a year earlier.

Trump has repeatedly argued that higher prices are worth it to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon, although the president, Vice President JD Vance and other Republican leaders have acknowledged that the party's midterm losses were at least partially due to Americans' frustrations about higher prices.

Before the midterms, the president promised a $5,000 "Trump dividend" check to every adult U.S. citizen if the Republican Party retained control of the House and Senate, but Republicans lost control of both chambers.

TRUMP’S $5K CHECKS COULD JOIN STACK OF PAST UNFULFILLED PROMISES, FORMER CONGRESS BUDGET CHIEF WARNS

Several GOP leaders expressed skepticism about Trump's plan, pointing to concerns over the escalating national debt, potential inflationary pressures and the need for congressional approval.

It remains unclear if Khanna's proposal will receive the same pushback from Democrats.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Trump has previously floated or endorsed other similar payments in his second term that never materialized, including a $5,000 "DOGE dividend" tied to government savings and a $2,000 payment funded by tariff revenue.

The expenses, which were partly covered by contributions from Biden’s presidential inaugural committee and individual donors, primarily went toward staff, consultants and legal fees. Despite this year's fundraising recoveries, some of Biden’s close allies have reportedly criticized Democratic donors for failing to proactively offer support for his library.

Biden has "never been a good fundraiser, even when he was in the Senate," one source said.

JOE BIDEN SAYS CANCER SLOWED HIM DOWN, LIMITING MEMOIR PROMOTION TOUR

OBAMA CENTER ISN'T A TRADITIONAL PRESIDENTIAL LIBRARY. CRITICS SAY IT'S AN ACTIVISM CENTER.

As Biden works to build financial support for the project, the foundation’s fundraising total still pales in comparison with that of President Donald Trump’s presidential library foundation, which has already secured tens of millions of dollars.

World.title: U.S. loses measles-elimination status, erasing decades of progress
World.content:
Endemic measles poses a serious risk to people who are unvaccinated, said Walter Orenstein, former director of the U.S. Immunization Program at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The risk is especially pronounced for infants, who are not typically eligible for the first dose of the vaccine until they turn 1, as well as those who cannot get the shot because they are immunocompromised.

“People can go into a supermarket and get infected,” he said.

At least four of the measles deaths this year were in babies too young to be vaccinated.

Some health departments in outbreak zones are now recommending an early dose for infants as young as 6 months.

Measles is among the most contagious viruses known to humans: One infected person can spread the virus to 9 out of 10 others in close proximity. It can linger in the air for up to two hours. Infections in unvaccinated people can lead to deadly complications like pneumonia or swelling of the brain.

Brewer said the U.S. desperately needs a strategy for tackling measles.

“The lack of action to address the growing outbreak is clear negligence,” he said.

Under past presidential administrations, the CDC has responded to measles outbreaks with media briefings and vaccination campaigns, but the agency has not done so this year.

A spokesperson for the Health and Human Services Department said the CDC has “mounted an aggressive response to measles outbreaks,” including allocating $100 million in additional funding in October and deploying experts to support state responses. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz “continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” the spokesperson said.

“We know where transmission is occurring and we’re working with state and local health departments to reach those communities,” Schwartz said in a separate statement. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.”

Since taking office, Kennedy has questioned the safety and effectiveness of measles vaccines and touted unproven remedies like inhaled steroids. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, falsely suggested in August that the combined measles shot could be “quite lethal,” despite decades of evidence demonstrating its safety.

“We have seen frequent and damaging public comments that have been shaking the confidence of parents about vaccination,” Brewer said.

Since 2019, 82% of counties and jurisdictions across the U.S. have reported declines in measles vaccination rates. Three small, rural counties — Catron County, New Mexico, and Adams and Custer counties in Idaho — have rates for kindergarteners below 50%.

A measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is displayed at Pennsylvania Department of Health measles vaccination clinic in Lancaster County on Oct. 20. Matt Rourke / AP

The pandemic accelerated the downward vaccination trend. Some parents avoided taking their children to the pediatrician, which meant delaying routine shots. An onslaught of misinformation about the Covid vaccines also reignited debunked theories, including the false notion that measles shots are linked to autism.

Even before the pandemic, the World Health Organization warned that vaccine hesitancy was contributing to a global resurgence of measles.

“It’s not just a U.S. problem, and it’s not just this administration,” Brewer said.

Last year, Canada’s status was revoked following an outbreak that led to more than 5,000 cases.

“It wasn’t for a lack of effort in Canada. There was a political commitment at the highest level to sustain measles elimination and to stop that outbreak. That was for me the sad part of the story, because they really did try,” said Jon Andrus, a global health professor at George Washington University and the chair of the PAHO commission that determines measles elimination status.

It could take years, experts say, for the U.S. to reclaim that designation.

World.title: Robert Pattinson named as the newest James Bond
World.content:
Agent 007 has a new face.

Actor Robert Pattinson has been tapped to take on the role of James Bond as Amazon MGM Studios seeks to continue the blockbuster film franchise.

The studio announced the “Twilight” and “The Batman” alum as its choice to pick up the secret agent mantle, making the 40-year-old the latest in a list of leading men who have had the honor of playing the spy.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement, adding, “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”

The news comes after years of speculation over who would take over the role after Daniel Craig announced in 2019 that he was leaving the franchise.

In the last week, rumors over Craig’s successor centered on Pattinson after a report from Puck suggested he was the front-runner.

Denis Villeneuve is directing the new Bond film, which further fueled the speculation given that Pattinson collaborated with Villeneuve on the “Dune” franchise. The third installment of that franchise hits theaters in December.

From starring in A24’s indie film “The Drama” to blockbuster epic “The Odyssey,” Pattinson has had a massive year, joining the handful of Hollywood stars who have dominated the big screen. Most recently, he starred as “Dateline NBC” alum Chris Hansen in “Primetime,” the A24 film that follows the TV personality’s “To Catch a Predator” era.

Pattinson at the Venice Film Festival in September. Tiziana Fabi / AFP via Getty

The script for the new Bond film is being written by Steven Knight, who created the TV series “Peaky Blinders.”

Amazon MGM Studios, the tech giant’s film unit, took over “creative control” of the James Bond series under a new deal with the franchise’s longtime producers, Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli. The deal was announced in February 2025.

Now, “Spider-Man” producer Amy Pascal and “Harry Potter” producer David Heyman will take on the latest installment, producing through Pascal Pictures and Heyday Films.

In a statement, Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, emphasized that Pattinson’s casting is helping to “usher in a new era of Bond.”

“This iconic character has captivated audiences around the world for more than six decades, and there’s no doubt that Robert’s remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice to carry that legacy forward,” he said, praising the “world-class creative team in place” that will be carrying on the franchise’s legacy.

Bond fans have had many thoughts as to who would take on the mantle, with many hoping that Idris Elba would be tapped as the next British super spy. But Elba told People magazine in August that he was never truly in the race to become the next Bond.

In recent months, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner reportedly also tested for the role.

Bond has evolved into one of the most coveted roles for male actors in the United Kingdom. The book-to-screen character written by Ian Fleming has had a unique staying power across generations, beginning with Sean Connery in the 1962 film “Dr. No.” The Scottish actor played Bond across seven films and two decades.

Sean Connery in "Goldfinger." Michael Ochs Archives / Getty

George Lazenby in "On Her Majesty's Secret Service." The Legacy Collection / Shutterstock

George Lazenby, the only Australian to play Bond, starred in 1969’s “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service.” He only played Bond for that film, which some have called one of the most underrated. Among the film’s fans is director Christopher Nolan, who called it his favorite of the franchise.

But it was Roger Moore who was considered to be the one who replaced Connery in the iconic spy franchise. Moore was often criticized in comparison to Connery, but he was chosen to star in seven of the franchise’s movies.

Roger Moore and Jane Seymour in "Live And Let Die." Express / Getty

Timothy Dalton in a publicity still for "The Living Daylights." Keith Hamshere / Getty Images

After Moore’s final Bond film in 1985, actor Timothy Dalton was given a smaller stint as the British agent. Dalton starred in two films, including “Licence to Kill,” in which he chose to portray Bond with a darker, more serious tone than previously seen by fans.

The character took another turn when Pierce Brosnan was given the role. Brosnan said he grew up adoring both Connery and Moore in the role, telling GQ in 2014 that it never felt “real” to him that he held the job.

Pierce Brosnan as James Bond. Getty

Brosnan was told following his final Bond film, “Die Another Day,” that the character was being rethought and negotiations with his agent to continue his role had stopped.

“And that certainly dug into the solar plexus of life, just because it was pretty gut-wrenching and because it had been somewhat heralded that I was coming back,” the Irishman told GQ. “So, it’s just business. And you’re the one caught in the crosshairs.”

Brosnan was replaced by Craig, who was lauded by critics and fans alike after he made his 007 debut in the franchise’s “Casino Royale” installment.

Daniel Craig and Ana de Armas in "No Time to Die." Nicola Dove / MGM

The actor chose to leave the fictional spy life behind after five films, saying on “The Graham Norton Show” in 2021 that he was glad to be leaving on his own terms even though it was an emotional decision.

“I’m grateful to the producers for allowing me to do that,” Craig said. “But I shall miss it. I’ll probably be incredibly bitter when the new person takes over.”

In a statement posted to X, Ian Fleming Publications, which owns and manages the literary rights to James Bond, praised the casting news.

“As Bond himself reflects at the end of Moonraker when facing the fact that the object of his affections is engaged to another man, ‘He must play the role which she expected of him. The tough man of the world. The Secret Agent. The man who was only a silhouette.’ We look forward to Pattinson stepping into that silhouette and making it his own,” the account wrote. “We have no doubt that Ian Fleming would be amazed at the longevity of his creation and the fact that the world is still hungry for tales of the world’s greatest spy.​”

Lazenby also posted a congratulatory video message for Pattinson on X, saying “Robert, welcome to the most exclusive club in the world. But remember to enjoy yourself.”

Online, many diehard Pattinson fans — particularly millennials who identified as “Twihards” — were thrilled by the star’s newest role.

“A great day for us Team Edward girlies,” wrote one X user, referring to Pattinson’s role as brooding, telepathic vampire Edward Cullen.

Several users even posted a scene from the first “Twilight” film, released in 2008, in which Pattinson’s Edward is seen opening the car door for his romantic interest Bella Swan (Kristen Stewart) after one of their peers announces the school dance theme is Monte Carlo.

“Gambling, tuxedos and Bond, James Bond,” one of the characters says, before it cuts to Pattinson and Stewart.

“Twilight literally predicted Robert Pattinson being James Bond btw,” wrote one X user who shared the clip.

Within minutes after the news dropped, many had also already cut thirsty fan edits compiling clips of the actor in his various roles and appearances.

But there were many who blasted the choice. “robert pattinson as bond is such a boring choice man, please for the love of god choose an unknown,” one X user noted.

And others who worried that Pattinson will be too busy with Bond for other roles.

“we’re never getting that second Batman movie…” wrote one X user.

“He’ll do great, I’m sure of it,” wrote another user. “But man am I still disappointed.”

World.title: Vance says there’s ‘no daylight’ between him and Trump on the war in Iran
World.content:
JD Vance on Monday said he and President Donald Trump are totally aligned on the war in Iran after the vice president this month attributed Republicans’ electoral beatdown in the midterm elections to voter frustrations with the conflict.

“There’s no daylight, Laura,” Vance told Fox News host Laura Ingraham in his first TV interview since the midterms. “And I think there’s no daylight between the president or any other senior member of the administration. Now, politically, yes, and I think the president himself has absolutely said this as well, there was a political cost: the higher gas prices, the higher energy prices.”

Vance, a potential 2028 presidential contender, also argued that other factors have also contributed to higher fuel prices, including what he described as a lack of investment in American energy infrastructure in recent decades.

It was part of a broader theme he echoed throughout the interview, doubling down on what he dubbed “economic nationalism,” and calling to re-shore factories as a response to the election results.

“Now we got shellacked, of course we did, and I do think that we have to take messages from that,” Vance said. “But the message that we have to take from that is that the American people want prosperity, they want freedom, they want sovereignty within their own country, and they want us to do more of the good things that we’ve done, and they also want us to recognize that there is some economic pain out there in the United States of America.”

“But the way that you deal with that economic pain, it’s not by opening the border, it’s not by giving up on American sovereignty, and it’s sure as hell not by shipping more American factories and more American jobs overseas,” he continued. “It’s doubling down on economic nationalism and bringing prosperity to the homeland.”

Immediately after Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections — the party’s strongest electoral performance since just after the Watergate scandal — Vance took to X to write: “The reason we lost is the war,” adding that Trump himself had made similar remarks.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he wrote on X, seemingly to Republicans who have more forcefully backed the war. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

Trump later told reporters he thought Vance’s analysis was correct, but added that his vice president “should have made one other statement … If you had it to do again, would you do it again? The answer is yes.”

Those remarks preceded the president last week announcing he was taking Vance off of Iran peace negotiations, asking him to instead redouble his focus on alleged government benefits fraud.

In his Fox News interview, Vance confidently pledged that the administration is “not going to allow” the war to become “even a two-year commitment.” Trump and senior administration officials said at the onset of the conflict, which began Feb. 28, that it would be wrapped up within a matter of weeks.

“But my prediction, Laura, is that whatever the president ultimately decides to do, there are going to be people who demand more, who want the war to go on indefinitely, and what I feel quite confident about the president of the United States, and again, there’s no daylight here, is that whatever he ultimately decides to do, however he ultimately decides to bring the conflict to a close, he is not going to let this become a forever war,” Vance said. “And the people who want it to become a forever war, they can attack me all they want to because we signed up to not do this, we told the American people we would do no more forever wars.”

“Yes, the president felt he had to destroy the nuclear program, and yes, the Iranian nuclear program is a threat to the United States of America,” Vance continued. “But we are not going to allow this to become a 10- or 15-year commitment, or frankly, even a two-year commitment.”

The vice president said he hasn’t made up his mind on running for president in 2028 but said a decision will come “sometime next year.”

“When I make a decision, Laura, I will be all in on whatever that decision is,” he said.

On the scandal that has engulfed former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Vance said the core issue at play isn’t whether he had a relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset — which Vance said the administration was not sure of — but was about reindustrializing the U.S., in this case so that the supply chain of the advanced chips needed to fuel the AI boom is more fully contained domestically.

“The main issue is we need to reindustrialize the country and protect our critical technology and our critical infrastructure,” he said. “And the only way to do that is to build more of it in the United States of America and prevent it from falling into the wrong hands.”

Responding to a question about Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., who Vance frequently clashed with on the campaign trail, the vice president expressed hope the two of them and other newly elected Democrats could work together.

“So, I hope Democrats actually try to govern on what they ran on. Because if you look at what they ran on, what do they talk about? Reindustrializing America, lowering energy costs for Americans,” he said. “They ran on a lot of the themes that Donald Trump ran on in 2024. Let’s work together.”

Ingraham pressed Vance on the Federal Aviation Administration’s nationwide ground stop on Friday that stranded hundreds of thousands of passengers after a router issue derailed air traffic control communications as well as a series of other tech outages in recent days. Vance echoed other administration officials in requesting new funding from Congress to modernize the air traffic control system while seeking to assure viewers that these problems were not building up to some larger crisis.

“Yeah, I’ve had a lot of my friends reach out and say, ‘Should we be preparing to build a bunker or to stock up on food and water?’ And my answer to that is no,” Vance said after Ingraham pointed to European governments recently pushing citizens to ramp up their emergency preparedness. “We do not see some crisis coming down, but you have to be prepared for everything. And what we want to do is make sure that we prevent the worst outcomes, but we’re also prepared for the worst outcomes.”

World.title: Somali Uber driver left with life-threatening injuries as police investigate possible hate crime
World.content:
An Uber driver was “fighting for his life” Monday following an attack that Minnesota police are investigating as a potential hate crime against the Somali American man, authorities said.

The driver was a “victim of a serious assault” on Saturday, leaving him with “life-threatening injuries that investigators believe were inflicted by a passenger in the vehicle,” according to a Hopkins police statement.

Hopkins is a city in Hennepin County, just outside Minneapolis.

“Investigators are examining all available evidence and considering all potential motives, including whether bias played a role in the assault,” Hopkins Police Chief Brent Johnson said.

Police did not immediately identify the driver.

The Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) and the victim’s family identified him as Somali American Mohamed Yusuf.

“A passenger asked his name, told him he didn’t like that name and then he attacked him,” said Suleiman Adan, deputy executive director of CAIR Minnesota.

The attacker tried to strangle the driver and then used the victim’s car to try running over him, according to Jaylani Hussein, executive director of CAIR Minnesota.

“This is one of the most heinous attacks that we have ever seen,” Hussein said.

Uber said it was shocked by the attack. “We banned the rider from the Uber platform and are keeping the driver and his loved ones in our thoughts as we continue to support law enforcement with their investigation,” the company said in a statement.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison reposted a Somali news story identifying the victim with a picture of him in the hospital.

“There will be accountability for this horrific crime,” Ellison added. “My heart breaks for Mohamed, his loved ones, and our Somali and Muslim communities apparently targeted by this assault. Everyone should feel safe and be safe in Minnesota — no exceptions. Hate and violence have no place here.”

Minnesota has become a hub for Somali immigration, and President Donald Trump has told Minnesotans to “fight back” against this community of recently arrived Americans.

The president has repeatedly verbally attacked Somalis, as well as Rep. Ilhan Omar, who was born in Somalia. Federal agents searched the lawmaker’s home last month in an inquiry of possible irregularities in her immigration process. Omar has denied any allegations and said she feels “confident in my truth.”

Trump’s attacks on Somali immigrants in Minnesota come in the wake of reports last year about dozens of people of Somali descent who were convicted of fraud schemes. Since then, Trump has called Somalis “crooks” and referred to Somalia as “filthy, dirty, disgusting, dirty.”

Somali immigrants are living in “fear, hatred, bigotry and demonization” that’s “come from the highest office of the land,” according to Hussein.

“This rhetoric has built an environment that we are living in today, an environment which we believe has created this heinous attack that took place on Saturday night here in Minnesota,” he added.

Hopkins Mayor Patrick Hanlon asked the public for time to allow department investigators to do their work.

“We ask for the community’s patience and understanding as investigators work diligently to determine the full circumstances surrounding this case,” the mayor said. “All of our investigators have been working non-stop to follow up on evidence and determine the facts.”

World.title: California lifeguard recalls braving relentless waves in rescue caught on video
World.content:
SAN DIEGO — Police run toward the sound of gunfire and firefighters climb up burning buildings, but over the weekend, Griffin Houldin demonstrated what lifeguards do best: He swam undeterred toward a man in distress amid powerful surf off the Southern California coast to make the rescue.

Houldin, a 29-year-old San Diego lifeguard, was captured on video swimming toward a struggling man Saturday, taking multiple waves on the head and emerging in whitewater, determined to keep moving.

The lifeguard said he didn’t like what he was seeing when the unidentified man hit the water without swim fins and took an unusual line out to sea, so he dove in behind him immediately.

The surf, Houldin said in an interview Monday, had doubled in size from late morning to early afternoon, and water was moving around the cove chaotically.

“It was heavy,” Houldin said. “It’s a lot of surf, but we train for it, we prepare for it.”

Griffin Houldin recalls Saturday's daring, caught-on-cam rescue. NBC News

The vide shows Houldin displaying impressive athleticism and determination as his red rescue can trails him behind on its tow line. But as he reaches the man, the video captured by visitor Jamie Rea shows, the two did not initially connect.

A second attempt, despite the relentless waves, concluded with a solid grab by the swimmer, who held on to the red can through multiple waves.

“We got pulled back 5 to 10 feet every wave, and they just kept coming,” Houldin said. “All I was trying to do was stay in this current here and fend off the rocks for as long as possible.”

As the swimmer held on to the rescue can, Houldin told him to hold fast.

Houldin raced into the dangerous surf to save a swimmer in distress. NBC News

“If he hadn’t been able to hold on, it would have been a very different outcome,” Houldin said.

The rescue lasted more than 3 minutes, according to multiple videos.

He said the swimmer later told him he misjudged the conditions. Houldin said he would have advised the man not to swim or to at least use swim fins.

It was a big day at the cove as the National Weather Service put the Southern California coastline under high surf advisories scheduled to remain in effect through early Wednesday for some beaches.

Waves driven by a weekend Pacific storm struck the California coast from north of San Francisco to the U.S.-Mexico border, with waves higher than 30 feet recorded at Mavericks, the noted surf spot in Half Moon Bay, according to the weather service and private wave forecaster Surfline.

In Santa Cruz, three surfers were also rescued amid high surf on Saturday, NBC Bay Area reported.

Federal forecasters said San Diego beaches would be treated to 6- to 8-foot waves — with some sets reaching 10 feet and beyond.

La Jolla Cove isn’t normally a surf spot, but it occasionally breaks in winter, drawing a crowd of surfers and body boarders outside the surf line.

San Diego Lifeguard Services, part of the Fire-Rescue Department, completed 175 rescues in the last week, officials said.

“It’s dangerous on a normal day, but on a day like Saturday — we haven’t had surf that big in a couple years,” Houldin said. “You can get stuck in that hole, you can get washed up on the cliff here.”

Houldin credited fellow lifeguard Cortez Ritumalta for rushing in on a jet ski that ultimately pulled him and the wayward swimmer from the impact zone and toward safety. Both said they have been on the job for more than 10 years.

Fellow lifeguard Cortez Ritumalta used a jet ski to pull Houldin and the man to safety. NBC News

Ritumalta credited onlookers atop the bluffs for pointing him to the rescue in progress. Riding the jet ski on liquid hills amid the foamy aftermath of breaking waves made it hard to see the swimmer, he said Monday.

The swimmer was in good hands, though, Ritumalta said, referring to Houldin.

“That swimmer probably got the best lifeguard you can have,” he said.

World.title: Widespread service outages at major U.S. banks appear to be over
World.content:
Customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, U.S. Bank and other major financial institutions reported service outages on Monday, according to Downdetector.com.

Other banks that saw a spike in customer complaints about difficulty accessing their accounts included Capital One, Truist and Wells Fargo, while users also reported problems with the digital payments app Zelle, according to the outage tracker.

However, Downdetector showed that service was back to normal at the banks and Zelle early Tuesday.

CBS News has reached out for comment to Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Capital One.

Chase Bank's services were experiencing a technical bug issue, not a cyber issue, a spokesperson said Monday.

"Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds," a Chase spokesperson said in a statement. "We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible."

Chase also said in a social media post that a software bug in its systems affected other institutions "when we were party to a transaction involving other banks." The issue is not systemic, the bank added.

"Please try back later"

Some Chase customers received a message that said, "Some services aren't available. We're working on them. Please try back later."

Bank customers started reporting problems accessing online services on Monday morning. By the afternoon, reports of outages had surged, according to Downdetector.com. As of 2 p.m. ET, nearly 4,800 users had reported problems with Chase, the most of any bank.

Chase customers reported issues accessing their online accounts, including viewing balances and performing transactions such as bank transfers and wire transfers, according to Downdetector.

Bank of America clients reported problems with ATMs as well as online and mobile banking services, according to the outage tracker. A Bank of America spokesperson told CBS News its "systems have been operating normally today."

U.S. Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app. They also had problems transferring funds, while Wells Fargo customers reported difficulty signing in to their accounts, as well as with getting account balances and conducting transactions.

A Chase Bank customer in Texas told CBS News he tried to deposit a check at a Dallas branch early Monday, but the transaction could not be completed. A bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" without providing additional details, he added, expressing frustration at the lack of clarity about the situation.

A spokesperson for U.S. Bank said its systems were not directly impacted by the cyber outage. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays," the company said in a statement to CBS News.

A Capital One spokesperson said it hasn't been affected by the outage and continues to operate normally.

Zelle told CBS News its service was "operating as it should," but that some users could be experiencing issues related to problems at their financial institutions, which could be delaying Zelle payments.

"Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds," a Zelle spokesperson said. "Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds."

Zelle's network operator, Early Warning Services, is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo.

3 tech crises highlight fragile systems

The banking outages occurred after Microsoft restored services on Saturday following a global outage affecting its Outlook and Teams services, which disrupted users, companies and government operations worldwide. Microsoft said a technical issue caused the outage and that it was not linked to a cyberattack.

The glitches also came only days after overloaded routers forced the Federal Aviation Administration to order a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday, stranding travelers and causing thousands of canceled flights. The FAA said Sunday that airline schedules across the U.S. were returning to normal. (On Monday evening, United Airlines also said it resolved a "widespread system outage" it had been dealing with that afternoon.)

Cybersecurity experts said the root causes of the bank service disruptions, Microsoft outage and FAA system failure, while different on their face, also point to a common problem.

"Our country has seen three very serious technology incidents over the past week," Mike Chapple, an IT, analytics and operations expert at the University of Notre Dame, said in a statement to CBS News. "When we dig into the details, each one has an explanation that makes sense on its own, but they all point to a common theme: the complexity and fragility of the systems that we depend on every day."

He noted that in each case, a technical issue quickly rippled through interconnected systems, causing massive disruptions nationwide.

"We don't yet know much about today's banking system outage, but it appears to stem from a technical issue at Chase that affected other banks through their shared payment networks," Chapple added.

When big companies like JPMorgan Chase experience technical disruptions, their impact often reverberates industrywide, added Karen Panetta, dean of graduate engineering at Tufts University.

"The larger companies have global reach that affords their customers flexibility and seamless integration with other businesses," she told CBS News. "Unfortunately, when one of these backbone providers has disruptions, the downstream effects are magnified. The multiple entities that rely on those services are also affected."

What should bank customers do?

Kayne McGladrey, a security expert and senior member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, said bank customers might have better luck going to their local branch in person, noting that financial services often still work on site when online banking resources go down.

"Try ATMs, cards, phone banking and branches, which often keep working when the app doesn't," she said in a statement to CBS News.

She also advised people to keep records of any attempted or failed transactions.

"Screenshot failed transactions and error messages, since you may need them for reconciliation or fee waivers. Once service is back, ask the bank to reverse any fees the outage caused," McGladrey said.

She also urged consumers to ignore unsolicited emails about the bank outages, which she warned might be phishing scams. Instead, people should rely on their bank's official communication channels for information, McGladrey said.

Craig Timm, senior director of anti-money laundering at ACAMS, an anti-financial-crime organization, told CBS News he expects criminals to exploit consumer anxiety about potentially losing access to their money, and that consumers should "assume they will be targeted." That's in part because AI lets scammers act fast and at scale.

Timm said common tactics to be alert to include criminals exerting pressure on targets "to take urgent action to protect their funds or restore account access."

"These scams may take the form of fake bank alerts, phishing texts or emails, or social media posts that claim to offer help," he said. "Some schemes aim to steal banking login credentials, while others use malicious links to gain access to a victim's computer."

World.title: Protests flare in Philippines over Trump's visit and planned AI hub
World.content:
Manila, Philippines — Protests against President Trump's visit to the Philippines have popped up around the country, as local residents criticize a Trump administration project to build an artificial intelligence and manufacturing hub just north of the country's capital of Manila.

In the opening salvo for Pax Silica, a U.S. State Department-led international initiative to secure non-Chinese supply chains for high-tech manufacturing, a more than 4,000-acre manufacturing hub is planned to be built in the Philippines.

Protesters in Manila on Monday held signs reading "Trump Out," drawings of him as a clown or a devil, and signs calling on the public to reject the Pax Silica initiative.

Critics argue the proposed industrial hub will displace farming communities and the Indigenous Aeta tribe, harm the country's water supply and represent U.S. imperialism over the Philippines.

"They have been grabbing our lands. They have been grabbing our economy. … Pax Silica is just for the U.S. It's not for us," said Maninging Vilog, a teacher and advocate for Aeta communities.

"If you look at the farmers, what do they care about AI? The people selling water … selling cigarettes, the people who drive buses. What do they care about AI?" said Kaiser Cortina, a 20-year-old protester.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., also a subject of the protests this week, supports the hub. He said in October he is "terribly excited" about the project's economic benefits, framing it as a "grand opportunity" for the country to move up the "value chain" by shifting into advanced manufacturing and research, according to PhilStar Global.

Marcos' administration has claimed the project could create 100,000 to 130,000 jobs.

A proposed 4,000-acre artificial intelligence hub north of Manila is drawing opposition ahead of President Trump’s visit to the Philippines.



The project is part of Pax Silica, a U.S.-led initiative aimed at reducing reliance on China for critical technology supply chains.… pic.twitter.com/9BQJFClqL8 — CBS News (@CBSNews) November 16, 2026

Over 25 countries have signed on to the Pax Silica initiative since it was announced by the U.S. State Department in December 2025, including the United Kingdom, Israel, Japan and India. The Philippines joined the initiative in April, leading the U.S. to announce plans for a manufacturing hub.

The U.S. has raised concerns for years about supply chains for the hardware that powers AI, including worries that China could get access to advanced chips. The issue has drawn new attention in recent weeks, amid revelations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset whose company was under investigation for smuggling chips. (The company has denied chip smuggling.)

Pax Silica participants signed a declaration on Sunday that sets out a "common understanding of the sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure that underpin" artificial intelligence supply chains.

U.S. and Filipino officials have said there aren't expected to be any big announcements about Pax Silica this week during Mr. Trump's visit during the ASEAN summit in Manila. The U.S. president is expected to meet with Marcos on Wednesday before flying to China.

CBS News has reached out to the State Department for comment.

Antonio Tinio, a member of the Philippine House of Representatives, said there aren't any specific votes on Pax Silica planned in the country's legislature, and claimed "it's far from certain" that the Pax Silica hub will start construction and be successful.

And he added that the critiques of the Manila hub mirror the anti-AI data center sentiment in the U.S.

"The opposition to AI data centers is global. … That was one of the big issues in your election. It's a big issue. There's a lot of opposition throughout Southeast Asia, including Malaysia and Indonesia, and also in the Philippines," Tinio said.

World.title: 3 killed when minivan crashes into Los Angeles food stand
World.content:
Police say three people are dead after a minivan crashed into a food stand near a North Hollywood bus stop in Los Angeles on Tuesday night.

The collision occurred at around 5:55 p.m. local time near the Metro station at the corner of Lankershim and Chandler boulevards, according to the LA Police Department.

Firefighters said three people were pronounced dead at the scene, while three others were taken to a nearby hospital, two of whom were in critical condition at the time. As of 11 p.m., one of the victims remained in stable condition, while the other was still critical.

On Wednesday, the LA County Medical Examiner identified two of the victims as 57-year-old Teodora Villalobos and 73-year-old Maria Peck. The third victim was identified as 39-year-old Francesca Krystine Esker on Friday.

Witnesses told CBS LA the three women were street vendors in the area, and one had worked there for more than 15 years.

The critically injured individuals are also women between 50 and 55 years old.

Crews extricated one person, the driver, from the wreckage, according to LAFD.

"I'm heartbroken for the families of everyone impacted," Mayor Karen Bass wrote in a statement on X. "We will continue to provide updates as more information becomes available."

The scene of a crash in North Hollywood that left three people dead and several others hospitalized on Nov. 10, 2026. CBS LA

LAPD officers said the driver of the white SUV was in serious condition and was determined to be under the influence of drugs or alcohol at the time of the crash. Police identified him as Ihor Demianenko, a 61-year-old Valley Village resident. He was arrested on suspicion of three counts of murder.

Demianenko is currently being held on more than $6 million bail.

The circumstances surrounding the collision remain under investigation, but LAPD Major Collision Investigation Team and Valley Traffic Division detectives said that Demianenko was attempting to avoid another car that was driving "legally and safely" before the crash. Police said they would continue looking for security camera footage from the Metro bus station and businesses in the surrounding area as their probe continued.

"It'll be a prolonged but a very deliberate investigation to determine what happened here," LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell said. "Our hearts go out to the families of the victims that were struck here tonight."

Aerial footage showed the white SUV stopped on the sidewalk underneath a canopy, where the food stand was set up.

Friends and loved ones remember street vendors killed

Mourners identified two of the women as Teodora, a 57-year-old woman known fondly as Doris, and Maria, 73.

On Tuesday night, some of Doris' family members of one of the three women killed stopped by a growing memorial.

"There are no words to express the absence that she's gonna have over my life," Doris' daughter, Melissa Villalobos, said. "Every goal, everything that I do is gonna be for her. Everything that I achieve will be for her, because of every sacrifice that she has done for me."

She said she hopes that her mother is remembered as a selfless, independent and hardworking woman.

"She never neglected to give someone food, never neglected to give a bottle of water," Melissa Villalobos said. "I am grateful of that time that I had her for."

Los Angeles City Councilman Adrin Nazarian, who represents the area, has partnered with nonprofit organization ICON CDC to create a GoFundMe fundraiser to assist the families of the three victims. It can be found by searching for the keywords: "NoHo Metro Station Street Vendor Support Fund."

"We sat there and talked all day, two days ago," said Laduke Warwick. "Today, she's in heaven. I guarantee they're all in heaven."

He said their relationship began years ago when he was homeless. Though he's now housed, he'll never forget the day that Doris handed him a bacon-wrapped hot dog, a soda, and struck up a conversation with him.

"They're just such amazing people. I can't believe they left like that," Warwick said. "If I could say anything to them, I'd say thank you so much for all the amazing blessings that you have shared with me in a short moment of my life, that I can't even repay with words, money or kindness.

Local street photographer Jeff Wilson snapped some photos of Doris just four months ago, calling her an "anchor" of the community after more than a decade of serving food.

"Pre-COVID to COVID, past COVID to all the ICE crazy stuff, she was here," Wilson said. "She was always doing something, helping people."

The memorial continued to grow at the spot of the crash throughout the day Wednesday, with dozens of community members stopping by to pay their respects. Of the dozens who stopped, many remembered the trio of women who were always there to lend a helping hand to those who needed it the most.

"They're mothers, grandmothers. They're somebody's somebody," said Mike Sandoval, a regular customer. "They were out here every day. I had good days, I had bad days coming through this area, and every time I needed something they were always there."
