World.title: Gunmen Kill Costa Rican Journalist Camilo Rodríguez on Route 32 in Heredia
World.content:
Journalist and writer Camilo Rodríguez Chaverri was shot dead Monday afternoon while driving his red pickup on Route 32 near San Miguel de Santo Domingo in Heredia. The Costa Rican Red Cross said it received the alert at 3:21 p.m. and that rescuers found him without any vital signs inside the vehicle.

According to preliminary reports, men riding a motorcycle pulled alongside the pickup, fired repeatedly and fled. Fuerza Pública officers secured the scene until agents from the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) arrived. The attack took place less than 50 meters (about 165 feet) from where radio journalist Parmenio Medina was shot dead on July 7, 2001. In recent years, Rodríguez had used his social media channels to denounce drug trafficking, corruption and alleged links between judges, lawyers and criminal organizations.

Attorney General Carlo Díaz said Rodríguez had reported threats against his life but declined to join the Public Ministry’s victim and witness protection program. Díaz said one line of inquiry will be the complaints Rodríguez made publicly, including a review of the people he named in his posts.

Díaz described the killing as a strong signal that Costa Rica lacks real freedom of expression. He noted that Rodríguez is the third journalist murdered here, after Medina in 2001 and Ivannia Mora in 2003. The attorney general said prosecutors and the OIJ will carry out an exhaustive investigation to identify both the gunmen and anyone who may have ordered the attack. Deputy prosecutor Tatiana Chaves, who covers the area, is handling the scene. Lawmakers also urged judicial authorities to ensure the crime does not go unpunished.

No arrests had been announced as of early this evening. Authorities had not said how many shots were fired or released a description of the motorcycle or its riders, and investigators have not confirmed a motive.

World.title: US Airline Seats to Costa Rica Fall 14% as Fares Climb
World.content:
Travelers flying from the United States to Costa Rica this winter will find fewer seats and higher fares, with scheduled US airline capacity projected to fall 14% between August 2026 and March 2027.

The steepest cut is at Juan Santamaría International Airport outside San José, where seats from the United States are projected to drop 20%, according to projections from two international consultancies that were shared with tourism sector representatives. Capacity into Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport in Liberia, Guanacaste, is expected to dip only 3%.

Fares have already moved. A study built on Altura and Cirium data, shared by former Tourism Minister William Rodríguez, found that base fares from the United States to Costa Rica rose 22% between January and July, before taxes and airport fees. In June and July alone, the increase reached 36% nationally and 45% on routes into San José.

The same data show US passenger numbers still grew 4% from January through July, with Liberia up 9% and San José up 1%. The trend turned in midyear, however, when US passengers fell 2% nationally in June and July and 9% at San José, while Guanacaste kept growing. The gap between the country’s two main airports widened in October. In the third week of the month, weekly flights fell from 450 a year earlier to 390, a 13.3% drop. Juan Santamaría lost 70 weekly flights, going from 407 to 337, while Liberia rose from 43 to 53.

Four airlines account for 59 of the 60 weekly flights lost. Volaris cut 23 after suspending its routes linking Costa Rica with Central America and Miami in April, amid Pratt & Whitney engine inspections. Avianca cut 17. Spirit, which ceased operations on May 2 following its bankruptcy, accounted for 12, ending its Orlando and Fort Lauderdale service to San José. JetBlue cut seven after suspending its Orlando route on July 8.

Frontier paused its San José flights from August through October, and American Airlines dropped its seasonal Chicago route. Southwest, which announced a San José-Las Vegas route in January for an October start, suspended it before launch because of weak advance ticket sales, the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) confirmed.

The ICT said the cuts reflect individual airlines’ decisions on route profitability and capacity rather than a general decline in the Costa Rican market. Through 2027, the institute plans to expand marketing and public relations in priority markets, working with travel agencies, booking platforms and US airlines to fill more seats and attract visitors who stay longer.

Víctor Umaña, executive director of the Center for Tourism Studies (CET), described a structural shift in which arrivals have stagnated and Liberia has gained ground on San José. He linked the change to a visitor profile centered on luxury, sun and beach travel, with shorter stays and fewer destinations visited.

Umaña said high costs, the strong colón and gaps in infrastructure and security are making the country less accessible and squeezing the sector’s margins. Weaker demand, he said, leads airlines to cut frequencies and seats. The CET estimates that if the gap of 60 weekly flights persists from October through December, Costa Rica could receive between 35,000 and 70,000 fewer tourists, a loss of roughly $65 million to $129 million in foreign exchange.

Martí Jiménez, president of the National Chamber of Tourism (Canatur), said fewer seats do not automatically mean fewer visitors if planes fly fuller. He noted, however, that Costa Rica’s drop in air capacity exceeds the averages for Latin America, at 4%, and Central America, at 9%, which he attributed to a loss of competitiveness specific to the country.

Jiménez added that Juan Santamaría has not grown in passengers in seven years, while Liberia keeps growing where luxury tourism is concentrated. A record number of Costa Ricans traveling abroad is filling some of the remaining seats, he said, which shows foreign arrivals are not growing.

Other markets are moving in the opposite direction. Seats from Canada rose 19.6% from January through July, led by a 28.9% increase into Liberia, while capacity from Europe grew 17%, mostly into San José, helped by new service such as nonstop flights from London Heathrow. Latin American routes shrank, with about 112,400 seats lost over the same period. Some new US service has also arrived, including the first Tampa nonstop in 25 years.

Tourism still brought in a record $5,543.7 million in foreign exchange in 2025, up 2% from 2024, according to Central Bank figures compiled by the ICT. Average spending per tourist rose from $1,601.8 in 2024 to $1,848 in 2025, though the CET cautioned that exchange rate effects may explain much of that increase, with the dollar hitting a record low against the colón last week.

The average stay for foreign tourists has fallen from 12.6 nights in 2019 to 10.3 in 2025. Tourism employment dropped from about 188,000 jobs in the second quarter of 2024 to about 167,000 in the second quarter of 2026, according to the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC).

The squeeze on seats comes just days after a US ground stop disrupted flights to and from Costa Rica. With fewer nonstop options into San José, fares into the capital have risen fastest, while Liberia has continued adding service heading into the busiest months of the year.

World.title: Costa Rica President Says Jailed Gang Members Ordered Her Killing
World.content:
President Laura Fernández said Monday that she has received prison intelligence reports indicating that gang members held in Costa Rica’s prisons have ordered her assassination.

Fernández made the remarks while opening the International Congress Against Synthetic Drugs and Organized Crime at a hotel in San José, an event attended by Attorney General Carlo Díaz, Justice and Peace Minister Gabriel Aguilar and other members of the cabinet. She said the reports describe alleged plots against her originating in several prisons.

The president did not say how many reports she had received, which groups were allegedly involved or what security measures had been taken in response. Neither the Presidency nor the Ministry of Justice and Peace had released further details by Monday afternoon. Fernández told the audience she was speaking as a victim and did not need anyone to describe the threat to her.

She said she has seen relatives, neighbors and friends have their bank accounts emptied, which she tied to criminal groups operating both inside and outside the prison system. She said imprisoned gang leaders use their access to the outside to call their organizations and commission hit men. Fernández pledged to keep purging the police forces and to cut off communication between inmates and criminals on the outside.

The president said the threats had not weakened her resolve, which she credited to her faith, and called for a hard-line approach to transnational organized crime. She also argued that illegal mining should not be treated as a mere environmental offense, describing it as one of the engines that finance organized crime, an issue at the center of the debate over gold mining in Crucitas.

It is not the first reported threat against Fernández, who took office on May 8. In early June, the Ministry of Justice and Peace confirmed it had received a report of an alleged plan to attack the president but declined to comment on security, intelligence or any investigation.

An internal ministry alert dated May 29 said a confidential source had overheard two inmates held under maximum-security conditions allegedly planning the attack. The document did not describe any investigative or judicial steps, and no charges have been reported in connection with it. Local media reported at the time that the alleged plot originated inside La Reforma prison in Alajuela.

Monday’s remarks come as tensions inside the prison system have risen. The government’s new maximum-security prison, the Center for High Containment of Organized Crime (CACCO), has received more than 600 inmates since it began taking transfers, and Fernández has pushed tighter limits on visits to maximum-security prisoners, arguing that gang leaders should not be able to keep directing their organizations from behind bars.

Ombudswoman Angie Cruickshank recently visited CACCO following complaints of mistreatment. She said inmates raised allegations of physical assaults and of inadequate medical care for seriously ill prisoners, and that there was no mechanism for them to file complaints with her office. She said the claims will be investigated and warned prison authorities that retaliation against inmates who provided information is prohibited.

Attorney General Díaz, who joined the inspection, reportedly confirmed that some inmates had been beaten, following prosecutors’ findings of signs of abuse at the facility. The allegations remain under review, and no individual has been charged. Security has been the defining issue of Fernández’s government, which has clashed with the judiciary over the release of detainees and over her proposed judicial overhaul.

A Wall Street Journal report in late August noted that homicides in Costa Rica have risen about 50% since 2020, as drug-trafficking violence has spread across the country.

World.title: San José’s Festival de la Luz Swaps Floats for 10 Giant Balloons This Year
World.content:
San José will welcome the Christmas season with one of Costa Rica’s best-loved holiday traditions when the Festival de la Luz returns to the capital on Saturday, December 12, with giant illuminated balloons, marching bands, and live street performances. The Municipality of San José unveiled the 2026 program on Friday, confirming that this year’s parade will feature 10 balloons, 14 marching bands, and six ground-level shows.

The parade begins at 6 p.m. and will run from Plaza de la Democracia west along Paseo Colón to Torre Mercedes. That is a change from last year’s festival, when the parade looped around La Sabana Park. The biggest difference this year is the absence of floats. The municipality turned to balloons after six public institutions pulled their floats out of the festival in August, a withdrawal Mayor Diego Miranda has attributed to political differences with the central government.

The balloon lineup includes three blimp-style figures that will float above the route and seven illuminated inflatables. Four of the designs were chosen through a consultation with students from Escuela Metálica and Escuela República del Perú, giving local children a say in the celebration.

The six ground shows will bring characters, artistic performances, and moments of interaction with the crowd along the route. Bands in the parade are also scheduled to perform at the Band Fest the same day, and a street procession is planned ahead of the main event. Miranda said the municipality wants to offer a renewed experience that brings families together through music, creativity, and entertainment.

The municipality has not yet released road closures, public transportation arrangements, or security plans for the night. Officials said those details will be published through municipal channels as the date approaches. Last year, streets around the parade area closed from 11 p.m. the night before the festival.

The Festival de la Luz anchors a wider holiday calendar the municipality calls the Mes de la Luz, or Month of Light. On Monday, November 30, the municipality and the National Power and Light Company (CNFL) will switch on the capital’s Christmas lights at Plaza de la Cultura. Ten districts will also host community Christmas festivals between November 14 and December 20, with music, parades, local businesses, food vendors, recreational activities, and artistic performances.

The district festivals open Saturday, November 14, at the Zapote Sports Complex, followed by Catedral on Sunday, November 15. The other participating districts are San Francisco, Pavas, Hospital, San Sebastián, Mata Redonda, Merced, La Uruca, and Carmen. Most of the neighborhood festivals run from noon to 8 p.m., though some keep different hours. The last one is scheduled for December 20 at the Aranjuez Sports Complex in Carmen.

World.title: Flying Between Costa Rica and the US Today? Cancellations Have Dropped Sharply
World.content:
If you’re flying between Costa Rica and the United States today, the worst of the disruption from Friday’s nationwide US ground stop looks to be over. FlightAware reported 144 Monday cancellations and 641 delays as of Sunday afternoon. That’s a fraction of what travelers faced over the weekend. Of the 41,000 flights scheduled Saturday, more than 6,600 were canceled, according to FlightAware. On Sunday, FlightAware reported 2,291 cancellations as of 3 p.m. ET.

US officials say schedules should be close to normal today. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy expects air travel to be “back to normal” by Monday, and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford had said airlines expected to recover by the end of Sunday. Check your flight before you leave for the airport anyway. When a ground stop strands planes and crews in the wrong cities, later flights can be delayed or canceled because crew members can’t get to them, and that knock-on effect can last a day or more.

Two airlines with major Costa Rica routes were among the hardest hit. American had the most cancellations on Sunday with 611, followed by JetBlue with 253. For JetBlue, that was about 27% of its schedule. At Juan Santamaría International Airport, the impact on Friday night was limited. Airport operator Aeris reported 12 departures and 11 arrivals affected, with six departures and four arrivals canceled, while the rest operated overnight and into the early morning. Aeris advised passengers to check flight status directly with their airlines, since schedules may change.

If your trip was affected, you may be able to change it without paying a fee. JetBlue’s fee waiver covers travel from Nov. 13 to 15, American extended its waiver through Nov. 18, and Delta is urging travelers with flexible plans to move their trips to Monday or later. Read your airline’s terms before rebooking, because waivers usually cover only certain dates and fare types.

The FAA has ruled out foul play. Bedford said the ground stop was caused by faulty equipment and that there was “zero evidence of anything nefarious.” Departures nationwide were halted for more than four hours on Friday after an equipment outage cut radar feeds and communication with aircraft, and the agency lifted the stop at 8:15 p.m. ET.

Duffy has given a more detailed account. He said the outage began during work to switch lines from copper to fiber at an FAA site in El Dorado, Arkansas, when turning on a new router there caused a router in Amarillo, Texas, to start flooding the system. The FAA has since disabled the broadcast feature on 69 routers of that type.

It could happen again as Duffy warned that further disruptions are possible until the copper lines are fully replaced at the end of 2028. With the busy holiday travel season about to start, turn on your airline’s app notifications and give yourself extra time on connections through US hubs.

World.title: Busted at the bus stop in nothing but his birthday suit
World.content:
Busted at the bus stop in nothing but his birthday suit

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Akeem Loredo walked out of the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday after receiving a three-month suspended sentence for exposing himself in public at a bus stop in Hattieville.

Police said they found Loredo naked at the Hattieville bus shed on Saturday, November 14. Loredo, a first-time offender who appeared without an attorney, pleaded guilty to a single count of exposing his person in public.

The prosecutor asked for immediate jail time, arguing that Loredo had no fixed address and would be difficult to locate. Loredo told the court he could not afford to pay a fine and asked the magistrate not to send him to prison.

A police officer who said he had dealt with Loredo before raised concerns about his mental health. The magistrate also took into account that there was no psychiatrist available at the prison to assess him.

With these considerations, the magistrate imposed no fine and told Loredo he must remain on good behaviour for the next three months or risk serving the jail term.

World.title: Arthur ‘Uncle’ Williams charged after common-law wife says he hit her in the face with a cellphone; He says she’s not even his woman just ‘roommate’
World.content:
Arthur ‘Uncle’ Williams charged after common-law wife says he hit her in the face with a cellphone; He says she’s not even his woman just ‘roommate’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Arthur Roy Williams, better known as “Uncle,” is out on $1,000 bail after a woman accused him of striking her below the right eye with a cellphone and scratching her neck during an argument in Belize City. Williams, 56, pleaded not guilty to harm and aggravated assault with a dangerous instrument when he appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday.

The 42-year-old woman identified Williams to police as her common-law husband, however, in an interview with Breaking Belize News after posting bail, Williams disputed that account. He said they were just roommates who lived in separate quarters of the same house. He denied assaulting her and called the case a “witch hunt.”

The woman told police she was at home around 9 a.m. on November 10 when a conversation about spending time at a hotel turned into an argument. The police report also refers to a disagreement involving her daughter. The woman alleged that Williams pointed a blue cellphone at her face and pushed it against her, striking her under the right eye. She said he then grabbed and scratched the left side of her neck, leaving a burning sensation. A doctor later examined her and classified her injuries as harm.

Police issued a wanted notice for Williams, who turned himself in at the Gender-Based Violence Unit on Monday morning. He was arraigned that afternoon in Court No. 4. The prosecution did not object to bail, and Williams met the $1,000 bond with one surety in the same amount.

During the arraignment, Williams asked the magistrate for help getting his account on record, saying police had refused to take his report. The prosecutor advised him to make a report at the Professional Standards Branch. Williams told BBN he intended to go there to give his side.

Williams is a retired Belize Defence Force soldier and the brother of former Commissioner of Police Chester Williams. In a separate case, BBN reported in April 2025 that cybercrime-related charges against Williams were withdrawn after the brothers reconciled.

World.title: Police constable Mervin Mendez remanded after allegedly pulling gun on supervisor at Belize Family Court
World.content:
Police constable Mervin Mendez remanded after allegedly pulling gun on supervisor at Belize Family Court

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police Constable Mervin Mendez, 34, was remanded to the Belize Central Prison on Monday after pleading not guilty to an aggravated assault charge. He is accused of pointing his service pistol at his supervisor, Corporal Erick Watson, inside the Belize Family Court in Belize City.

Mendez appeared without an attorney and was denied bail. His next court date is January 11, 2027.

Watson told investigators that Mendez arrived late for guard duty at the court’s cashier area on Friday, November 13, and appeared to be under the influence of alcohol. Watson said he escorted Mendez to the cell block and asked him to hand over his police-issued firearm, but Mendez refused.

According to Watson’s report, the two argued before Mendez allegedly drew his 9 mm Taurus pistol, cocked it and pointed it at Watson as he moved toward him. Watson said he feared for his life and ran through a doorway, slamming the door behind him to take cover.

Police say Mendez later set the pistol down and walked out of the building, where Watson and another officer detained him. Watson recovered the weapon and a magazine containing 15 live rounds. Investigators took witness statements and reviewed the court’s surveillance footage before formally charging Mendez on Saturday.

At Monday’s police briefing, Assistant Superintendent Stacy Smith said Watson had asked for the weapon because he believed Mendez was not fit to carry it. Smith said Mendez eventually relinquished the pistol after removing its magazine and setting the weapon down, allowing police to secure it. She also confirmed that internal disciplinary proceedings are underway.

Breaking Belize News exclusively obtained the surveillance footage and published it on Facebook on Sunday. The video has since drawn nearly 125,000 views.

World.title: Why isn’t Southside calling for Bukele?
World.content:
Why isn’t Southside calling for Bukele?

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

By Nuri Muhammad: Why is it that some of the loudest voices calling for Bukele-style policing in Belize are not coming from the very communities supposedly living at the epicenter of gang violence? Where are the mothers and fathers, the grandmothers, aunties, sisters and brothers demanding that the police descend upon their neighborhoods with overwhelming force, round up hundreds of young men and lock them away?

Could it be that the people who actually live in these communities understand something that those calling for draconian police action do not?

I have spent more than fifty years working with young people and families in Belize, much of that time in the very neighborhoods now being portrayed as war zones. I know the pain that violence has caused. I know mothers who have buried their sons, children who have lost their fathers, and families who have suffered terribly because of the actions of a relatively small number of individuals.

But I also know that the people of Southside Belize City do not live in perpetual fear of every young man standing on a street corner. These young men are their sons, brothers, nephews, cousins and grandchildren. They know who is dangerous and who is not. They know that there are bad seeds or renegades in some neighborhoods who must be dealt with, but they also know that not every neighborhood is under siege and not every young Black man is a gangster.

And there is another uncomfortable question that those advocating the Bukele model should consider. What happens when the people themselves have reason to fear those entrusted with protecting them?

On January 7, 2013, four young Black men were brutally massacred in an apartment building at the corner of Dean and Plues Streets in Belize City. Their bodies were discovered the following morning. The brutality of those killings shocked the nation. There were serious allegations and suspicions involving members of the security services, allegations that the authorities denied. Yet, more than thirteen years later, no one has been brought to justice for those murders.

I am not presenting suspicion as established fact. But how can we ignore the damage that such an unresolved atrocity does to public confidence in law enforcement? How can we demand that communities surrender more of their rights and freedoms without first addressing their concerns about accountability and justice?

Perhaps the people who live in these neighborhoods understand that giving the security forces extraordinary powers, like Bukele’s police, does not automatically translate into greater security for ordinary citizens.

Let us not misunderstand the argument. There are dangerous criminals in Belize who must be apprehended, prosecuted and punished. The people of Southside want protection from violence just as much as anybody else. But wanting protection is not the same as demanding indiscriminate arrests, prolonged detention and the suspension of fundamental rights.

Belize is not El Salvador. We do not have the same gang structures, and culture, the same history or the same social circumstances. We must stop pretending that importing another country’s methods will somehow solve problems we have failed to address for generations.

We have to inject hope into these neighborhoods, not fear.

What would happen if we invested as much energy, money and national determination into education, employment, skills development, entrepreneurship and rebuilding families as we invest in emergency policing operations? What if young people could see a future beyond unemployment, frustration, the streets and prison?

I have long advocated for a comprehensive, multipronged **25-year National Crime Prevention and Community Development Plan**, implemented in five-year cycles, with clear objectives, measurable results and continuity regardless of which political party forms the government.

Such a plan must be administered by a permanent, statutory, quasi-governmental institution, staffed by trained professionals and supported by government, the private sector, civil society and the communities themselves. It cannot be another temporary political project that disappears with the next change of minister or government. We have rolled that stone up the hill many times only to start over and over again

Crime and violence are national problems requiring a national response, not just a police response. We need effective policing, certainly, but also serious investment in the social and economic conditions that shape the lives of our young people. We need a national commitment that rises above party politics and continues for a generation.

After decades of states of emergency, police operations, arrests and promises, surely, we should be asking whether we are prepared to do something fundamentally different.

Before we impose Bukele on Southside, shouldn’t we first ask the people who live there? Or are we afraid they might tell us that Bukele is not the answer?

World.title: Rumors of 72-hour global blackout debunked as U.S. FEMA clarifies November 17 emergency alert test
World.content:
Rumors of 72-hour global blackout debunked as U.S. FEMA clarifies November 17 emergency alert test

By Zoila Palma: Rumors circulating on social media about a supposed 72-hour global blackout that would disrupt electricity, internet access, banking services and artificial intelligence systems between November 16 and 17 have been debunked.

The speculation appears to have been fueled, in part, by a scheduled emergency alert test in the United States, but the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) has clarified that there is no secret emergency or planned shutdown.

FEMA confirmed that it will conduct a routine test of the U.S. Emergency Alert System on November 17 at approximately 2:20 p.m. Eastern Time.

The exercise, required under the IPAWS Modernization Act of 2015, is intended to ensure that public warning systems are functioning properly. The test will be broadcast through television and radio stations only, with regular programming interrupted for approximately one minute. Cell phones will not receive alerts, and the public is not required to take any action.

Meanwhile, claims of a coordinated global blackout, cyberattack or shutdown of technological infrastructure have not been supported by verifiable evidence, Univision reports.

Cybersecurity specialist Juan D. Guevara described the claims as unfounded conspiracy theories, noting that social media algorithms can amplify fear and misinformation.

Recommendations encouraging households to maintain 72-hour emergency supplies have also been misrepresented, as these are general preparedness guidelines rather than warnings of an impending blackout.

Other online claims have referenced an episode of “The Simpsons” allegedly predicting a November 17 blackout, as well as the November 13 nationwide grounding of flights ordered by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration.

However, no evidence has established a connection between these events and the alleged blackout.

World.title: 39 public officers complete Advanced Certificate in Secretarial Studies
World.content:
39 public officers complete Advanced Certificate in Secretarial Studies

By Zoila Palma: Thirty-nine public officers representing 16 government ministries have successfully completed the Advanced Certificate in Secretarial Studies Programme, following a three-month training initiative conducted by the Ministry of the Public Service, Disaster Risk Management and Enterprise, in collaboration with the University of the West Indies (UWI) Global Campus Belize.

The programme ran from July to October 2026 and covered five key areas: protocol and management of meetings, principles of supervision, effective communication, advanced keyboarding and document formatting, and minutes of meetings and report writing.

Delivered through a hybrid approach combining online and in-person instruction, the programme recorded a 97.5 percent success rate.

Two participants were recognized as top performers, with Keily Lisbeth Avila of the Office of the Auditor General placing first in Cohort I, while Alfreda Hemsley of the Ministry of Health and Wellness secured first place in Cohort II.

UWI Global Campus Belize representatives also highlighted the institution’s more than 15 years of partnership with the Ministry in delivering the programme.

Minister of the Public Service, Disaster Risk Management and Enterprise, Henry Charles Usher, emphasized that strong public institutions depend on the knowledge, abilities and commitment of their employees.

World.title: Belize strengthens Climate finance and resilience partnerships at COP31
World.content:
Belize strengthens Climate finance and resilience partnerships at COP31

By Zoila Palma: The Government of Belize, in partnership with the Green Climate Fund (GCF), continues to advance key initiatives aimed at strengthening climate resilience and sustainable development.

The Belize delegation met with representatives of the GCF at COP31 this week.

Priority initiatives include the Belize Climate Investment Platform, Maya-led pathways for climate resilience, strengthening the Belize National Protected Areas System, and advancing National Adaptation Plans.

“These efforts reflect Belize’s commitment to mobilizing climate finance, empowering communities, protecting ecosystems, and building a more climate-resilient future,” the Climate Change Department noted.

World.title: Belize highlights wildlife conservation at COP31 in Türkiye
World.content:
Belize highlights wildlife conservation at COP31 in Türkiye

By Zoila Palma: Belize’s delegation is highlighting the importance of wildlife conservation in strengthening climate resilience at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), being held from November 9-20, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye.

Through its Wildlife for Climate Action initiative, Belize is emphasizing the role of species such as the Baird’s tapir, which supports forest regeneration through seed dispersal, and jaguars, which help maintain ecological balance.

The delegation is also highlighting the Wildlife for Climate Declaration as an opportunity to strengthen the link between biodiversity conservation, ecosystem restoration and climate action.

Belize continues to promote forest conservation, habitat connectivity and community-based conservation, recognizing that protecting wildlife is essential to preserving healthy ecosystems and strengthening the country’s resilience to climate change.

World.title: Haitian trafficking network
World.content:
This file photo shows a group of Haitians who landed at Boston Beach, Portland, in 2023.

HEAD of the Portland police Superintendent Ainsley McCarthy has charged that the frequent arrival of Haitians on the shores of the parish is part of a broader trafficking network across Jamaica.

“We have a Haitian population here in Jamaica. For example, in Montpelier, St James, we have Haitians there. So these Haitians who come in from time to time, some of them are trafficked. They pay to get here, and then there are persons who pick them up to take them to other locations, most times outside of the parish,” McCarthy said during the latest episode of the Jamaica Constabulary’s

Force4good podcast.

McCarthy was supported by head of Police Area Two Assistant Commissioner McArthur Sutherland, who told the podcast that many of the Haitians are being employed by Jamaicans to conduct farming in the hills of Portland.

He said police have done numerous operations targeting that practice and, “We believe some level of coordination is outside of the Portland parish.”

According to Sutherland, last year the police had to intervene after a dispute between two of the immigrants during a party held on one of the farms left one of them dead.

“The matter is still before the court and that [Haitian] is still in custody. From an organised approach, we have sufficient reason to suspect — or I would say believe — that it is organised, to an extent. One of the evidence of that organisation is the fact that we see returnees — persons who were removed [and] returned. The last trip we had one such case, and we are dealing with it,” Sutherland added.

Last month, police apprehended 22 Haitians across Area 2 — which covers Portland, St Mary, and St Ann — within a one-week period, raising concerns about a possible human-smuggling operation along Jamaica’s north-eastern coastline.

In June, 17 Haitians arrived in the Passley Gardens area of Port Antonio. Days later an additional 11 landed on Jamaica’s shores. They were taken to Port Antonio Police Station for health and immigration processing.

According to Sutherland, Jamaica requires “infrastructural support” to successfully tackle the issue as there are multiple uncontrolled ports across the island.

“The maritime coastal domain awareness is critical, [and] Portland is no exception. We have been looking at this from several years back — from the days when we were looking at it as gun-for-drugs [trade]… where they bring down the weapon and in exchange they get the marijuana. We have not seen much of that activity. But the emergence now of, what I’d say, either people smuggling or people seeking refuge, whichever category you look at it from, we definitely need the right infrastructural support as a country to really handle that,” added Sutherland as he argued that an ongoing cross-border collaboration is needed.

That collaboration, he explained, would be “a very solid intelligence network that can identify the triggers and alert us so we can mobilise and respond to these situations as quickly as possible”.

“We know that at times they will get off the boat, out in the water, and swim towards shore in order to avoid detection. So it’s not necessarily that [the] boat [is] coming up on the shore. They have different approaches to getting here,” explained Sutherland.

He underscored that the Haitians do not arrive through a controlled port, making it difficult for law enforcers to conduct risk assessment and, in instances, health risks came to the surface and had to be treated with appropriately.

Meanwhile, McCarthy reported that through the support of the Portland Disaster Risk Management Committee and other agencies, law enforcers are better able to deal with the arrival of immigrants.

“Although it’s considered disaster risk management

— dealing with hurricane, earthquake

— we also come together to deal with the influx of illegal Haitians coming into the island. And we have the Red Cross that provides food, clothing, and meals also on a daily basis to these people while they’re here.

“We have the health department, who I just [need to] pick up my phone and I call Dr [Sharon] Lewis [medical officer of health for the Portland Health Department] and I say, ‘Doc, we have some visitors to the island and she should make special arrangement to get them medically examined.’ Then I will call PICA (Passport, Immigration and Citizenship Agency) and PICA comes in, does the interviews, and we get them out of the island as quickly as possible, in most cases. And where people apply for asylum, the matter goes through the court,” said McCarthy.

World.title: Dumb and dumber!
World.content:
CARNEY... these devices we walk around with in our hands, we become so dependent on these devices to answer questions, tell us what to do, how to think, that we’re thinking less (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

University of Technology (UTech), Jamaica chancellor, Ambassador Lloyd Carney has warned youngsters that increasing dependence on smartphones and other modern communication devices is doing more than wasting their time — it is making them dumber.

Carney issued the warning at all three of the university’s graduation ceremonies at Alfred Sangster Auditorium on the Papine, St Andrew campus over the weekend.

He urged graduates to reduce their social media use, citing studies which, he said, showed that high school students worldwide had experienced two consecutive years of declining thinking and problem-solving abilities.

According to Carney, the reported decline in thinking and problem-solving abilities marked a change from the pattern in previous years when each group of students leaving high school was expected to have stronger thinking skills than the one before.

“It’s the second year now in a row international studies have shown that students graduating high school from all over the globe, they have less cognitive skills, less logical thinking capability than students from two years ago. Two years in a row, our students are leaving high school not as smart as they used to be. Before there was always a progression every year, they’re a little bit smarter than the group before,” he said.

Carney said the findings had been linked to people’s growing reliance on devices, which, he believes, is reducing the amount of independent thought and analysis they exercise.

“These devices we walk around with in our hands, we become so dependent on these devices to answer questions, tell us what to do, how to think, that we’re thinking less. We’re not being as analytical in our way of thinking, and it is actually debilitating to us,” said Carney, who did not identify the studies he was pointing to, or provide details about the countries, number of students and methods used to reach those findings.

However, a study published in the Journal of Adolescence in 2025, which examined the academic performance of more than 1.78 million students aged 15 and 16 across 36 countries, found that results in mathematics, reading, and science had declined in many countries, particularly between 2012 and 2022.

The research, which analysed data from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Programme for International Student Assessment, also found that declines were greater in countries where young people’s access to smartphones and use of electronic devices for leisure during school hours had increased.

At Sunday’s ceremony, Carney delivered the warning in even more blunt terms.

“These smart devices we walk around with, these phones, they are sapping your intellectual capacity because they want to think for you. So it’s to their benefit that you get dumber, and that’s exactly what’s happening,” Carney said.

He pointed to China and Singapore as the only two countries which, according to the studies he referenced, had not experienced decline in young people’s thinking skills over the two-year period.

The chancellor attributed this to restrictions in those countries on young people’s access to social media.

Carney also took aim at the pressure to create an image of wealth and success on social media.

“There are people borrowing money to rent a car to look like they have money so they can show on

Facebook, or whatever, that they have money. They are going into debt to pretend they have money, so that the billionaires in Silicon Valley can make money off of your foolishness. It is time to stop doing that,” he said.

Carney also warned that artificial intelligence (AI) could make it easier for people to misrepresent themselves and urged graduates to be careful about the information they share with such tools.

He said people should also avoid becoming so dependent on AI that they use it for every decision or task, arguing that technology companies had a financial interest in encouraging people to rely heavily on their products.

Drawing on his experience in business and technology, Carney said most everyday tasks in industry and business did not require expensive large language models, such as ChatGPT, Claude or Google’s Gemini.

He estimated that about 90 per cent of the work could be done using cheaper models.

Carney also shared a story of an engineer at one of his companies who left an AI model running for a month and generated a US$200,000 bill.

The chancellor also encouraged parents to lead by example if they wanted their children to spend less time on social media.

“If you want to curtail what your children are doing on social media, when you come home from work, read with them, play a board game, talk to them; imagine that, talk to them. If they see you on social media, spending your time talking to your friends on social media, posting on social media, your children are going to imitate what you are doing,” he said.

World.title: The bet pays off for Shaggy
World.content:
Shaggy (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Ahead of the release of his seventeenth studio album Lottery in May, Shaggy scored Billboard chart entries with two of the album’s singles — Til a Mawnin (featuring Sting) and Boom Body (with Akon and Aidonia).

The project, which bears his Ranch Entertainment and the New York-based independent label VP Records, didn’t crack the major charts, but it didn’t go unnoticed by Grammy voters.

On Monday, Lottery paid off for Shaggy when it was among six albums nominated in the Best Reggae Album category of the 69th annual Grammy Awards.

When the Jamaica Observer caught up with Shaggy moments after the nominations were released, the Boombastic deejay was quite upbeat when asked how he felt about receiving the nomination.

“Amazing! I titled the album Lottery because it’s how I’ve lived my whole career. Nobody hands you a winning ticket. You bet on yourself, put in the work, and see what comes back. Thirty-plus years in, having the Recording Academy recognise this record means the bet paid off again, and I’m incredibly grateful for that,” said Shaggy.

The album contains 13 tracks and features collaborations with Sting, Robin Thicke, Anthony Hamilton, Akon, Jeremih, Beres Hammond, Dexta Daps, Aidonia, 450, Mutabaruka, Vanessa Amorosi, Noah Powa, Olaf Blackwood, and Rayvon. It combines reggae, dancehall, and pop with elements of hip hop, soul, and R&B.

Shaggy shared that Lottery was the result of a combined team effort.

“A lot of work went into this project. I’m hands-on with everything I do — from writing to production. I brought in people I trust from different corners of music, like Sting, Robin Thicke, Akon, and Jeremih, so reggae and dancehall could sit next to R&B and pop and still feel like one; cohesive record. It was a real team effort, and I’m proud of everyone who contributed,” Shaggy disclosed.

This is Shaggy’s eighth nomination in the Best Reggae Album category. He was first nominated in 1996 for his platinum selling album

Boombastic. That album, released via Virgin Records, catapulted him to international success.

Since then he has racked up nominations for 2006’s Clothes Drop, 2009’s Intoxication, 2012’s Summer in Kingston, 2015’s Out of Many, One Music, 44/876, a joint project with Sting, which won the award, and 2023’s Com’ Fly Wid Mi.

Also receiving a nomination in this year’s Best Reggae Album category were Buju Banton (Too Too Bad), Chronixx (Exile), Ziggy Marley (Brightside), Runkus (Supernova) and Protoje (The Art of Acceptance).

This is the first nod for Runkus. He commented about the nomination on his Instagram story.

“Jah is glorious. Supernova Grammy nominated.”

Brightside has given Ziggy Marley his 7th solo nomination in the Best Reggae Album category. He earned nods for Wild and Free in 2012, Rebellion Rises in 2019 and won for Love is My Religion (2007), In Concert (2014), Fly Rasta (2015) and Ziggy Marley (2017).

This is Protoje’s third attempt at winning a Grammy. He was nominated previously for A Matter of Time (2019) and Third Time’s a Charm (2023).

Buju Banton won the Grammy in 2011 for Before the Dawn. He has eight nominations to date including Inna Heights (1999), Friends for Life (2004), Too Bad (2007), Rasta Got Soul (2010), Upside Down 2021 (2020), and Born for Greatness (2024).

Chronixx’s Chronology lost out to Damian “Jr Gong” Marley’s Stony Hill in 2018. This is his second nomination.

World.title: Promoted Tru-Juice play down title aspirations despite claiming JPL summit
World.content:
Tru-Juice FC’s starting line-up against Treasure Beach FC for a Legend Jamaica Premier League football match in October 2026.

Despite Tru-Juice FC’s dream start to their debut Legend Jamaica Premier League (JPL) season, head coach Damion Gordon is refusing to entertain talk of them winning the title.

Tru-Juice extended their lead at the top of the table to four points following a 2-0 win over Racing United on Sunday at Ferdie Neita Park.

The newly promoted club took the spoils in the St Catherine derby, thanks to an own goal from Markovich Brown in the 77th minute and a stoppage time strike from Rodave Murray.

Gordon says he was pleased with the team’s execution throughout the game, despite the goals coming late.

“We have a good framework and the team does actually work along that line,” he said. “The substitutions were spot on today, I think tactically we were very involved and were able to execute what we actually asked from the players. But the starting team created a platform for the substitutes to come and finish the job and we just have to grow as a unit.”

Following their promotion from the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) Championship, known as the Tier Two competition, Tru-Juice were busy during the summer transfer window as they brought in several top talent including national players Alex Marshall, Gadail Irving and Tafari Chambers.

However, Gordon believes there’s no favouritism within the set-up as the entire squad has been proving their worth.

“It’s just the work that we have been putting in and we have to choose the players so irrespective of what the others have been doing,” he said. “If we see it fit where we need to interject a player, I don’t think it really matters the name of the player. It’s just what we want at the moment and I think sticking to that has been playing out for us and we just have to continue on that.”

“Those players have been doing well and we encourage them and I hope they continue to do well. But we as coaches, we have to know when to balance things and when to pull a player and when to make sure, you know, we keep everybody motivated.”

Tru-Juice have lost only once from their 10 games and are currently on a five game winning streak which included their 2-1 win over defending champions Portmore United earlier this month. They move to 23 points, four clear of second place Montego Bay United.

Gordon, though, says he won’t be carried away by any title talk despite their impressive start.

“We’re in the league for the first time. I know we have been doing some wonderful things but we consistently made mention of being humble and [asking] the group to stay humble,” he said.

“For us, it’s just a game at a time, what we can do a game at a time. We cannot look on ‘oh we’re going to win’, nothing like that. It’s a new team, players are learning to play together, we’re actually still in the process of working on the cohesiveness of the group, and once we can get that, we’ll be alright.”

Other winners in Sunday’s action were champions Portmore, last season’s finalists Cavalier, Montego Bay United, Arnett Gardens, and Dunbeholden.

Waterhouse’s clash with Mount Pleasant Football Academy, scheduled for Monday night, was postponed due to the number of players from the clubs called up for international duty.

— Daniel Blake

World.title: BOYZ ON A MISSION
World.content:
Members of Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz squad train at Stadium East on November 13, 2026. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

INSPIRED by their famous victory over Mexico on Saturday, Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz will be looking to complete the job today and book their place in the Concacaf Nations League semi-finals.

Jamaica take on host Mexico at the BBVA Stadium in Monterrey in their second-leg quarter-final starting at 9:30 pm. The national team needs only a draw to advance following their 3-2 first-leg victory at the National Stadium.

However, the Rudolph Speid-led Boyz will be hoping the long journey to Mexico doesn’t take a toll on their performance after spending much of Sunday travelling to Monterrey on commercial flights.

The team left the island early Sunday morning but didn’t arrive in Monterrey until late Sunday evening. Players and technical staff were split in two groups, with one travelling through Miami and the other via Panama.

The team conducted their sole training session at the BBVA Stadium on Monday evening.

Speid will also be one player short after Tottenham Hotspur midfielder Tyrese Hall, who was recently named Premier League 2 Player of the Month, returned to London for personal reasons. The 21-year-old, who only has two caps including his debut last March, was left on the bench in Saturday’s win.

Mexico’s playing conditions are often a concern for visiting teams, although the Boyz will avoid the high-altitude conditions associated with the Azteca.

Speid says he isn’t concerned about the external factors as they seek to topple the hosts.

“We played in Mexico this year so some of the players are used to [the conditions]. I am not one of those coaches that worry about where we play because if you let that weigh heavily on what you do, it [causes] an adverse reaction to how the team performs,” he said.

“It is what it is. Wherever they put us to play, we’ll do the best we can. It’s the same thing when it comes to teams; whoever we get to play, we’re going to try our best. So we’re really not worried, we’re focused on Mexico. They’re a top-ranked team; they didn’t get there by fluke, but that’s where we want to be so we have to prepare for them.”

Barring any late issues, Jamaica could field a similar line-up which led the world number 10 ranked Mexicans 3-0 after 69 minutes.

They could also stick to the same approach that proved successful against Rafa Marquez’s side.

“If we sit back and just watch the Mexico team play, they’ll just take us apart eventually,” he said. “So part of the plan was not to let that happen and we picked our moments, when we press forward. So it wasn’t just a total press, it was always calculated ones; press forward when it was necessary to ensure that we kept them in their half for long periods of time.”

Jamaica have never beaten Mexico on Mexican soil in a senior men’s international match from 10 attempts. However, they did earn a 2-2 draw in their last game back in March 2023 in the Nations League group stage.

Mexico, though, have a slight advantage with the away-goals rule in effect, meaning a 1-0 or 2-1 win would be enough to send them through despite the aggregate score being level.

Head Coach Marquez is currently under immense pressure from the Mexican media having gone winless in his five games since taking over in July.

He’s expecting a strong response from his team who have made the semifinals of every Nations League tournament since its inception in 2019.

“It’s almost the same defensive line that played in the World Cup and they were extraordinary back then,” he said. “While the contexts are obviously different, I believe we must demand more of ourselves to ensure we don’t repeat these kinds of errors.”

“I think we should [also] focus on the positives, the way the team reacted, and how the substitutions really helped spark that reaction,” he said. “Now we need to take advantage of playing at home. Monterrey is a city where the atmosphere and the fan support can really give us a boost and that’s what we’re hoping for in the next match.”

Jamaica’s sole appearance in the Nations League semi-finals was in the 2023/24 season where they went on to finish third.

Jamaica Squad:

Goalkeepers – Jahmali Waite, Amal Knight, Joshua Grant

Defenders: Joel Latibeaudiere (captain), Miguel Freckleton, Richard King, Ronaldo Webster, Kyle Ming, Denzel Hall, Christopher Ainsworth, Damion Lowe, Jeovanni Laing

Midfielders: Courtney Clarke, Karoy Anderson, Dwight Merrick, Ramone Howell

Forwards: Kaheim Dixon, Renaldo Cephas, Javon East, Ricky Jade-Jones, Khori Bennett, Daniel Green, Warner Brown

World.title: Ozempic approved for local distribution
World.content:
Diabetes drug Ozempic. Photo: NBC News

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Ozempic, a prescription medication used to treat Type 2 diabetes and support weight loss, has been approved for distribution on the island as the Government moves to expand treatment options for obesity.

Minister of Health and Wellness, Dr Christopher Tufton, made the disclosure while addressing the launch of the Ministry’s Lifestyle Clinic at the Sandy Bay Health Centre in Hanover on November 12.

Ozempic helps to control blood sugar levels and promote weight loss by reducing appetite and slowing digestion. It is usually administered through a once-weekly injection.

Tufton informed that other branded medications to manage obesity are being considered for approval.

“We hope that by next year, they will be approved, and also the generic equivalent to those,” he said, noting that the medications will be available through pharmacies.

The minister noted that individuals

seeking obesity treatment have been purchasing these medications informally, including from overseas, often at higher prices.

“What used to happen in the past is that it was a black market. People used to buy it in Miami and those places or wherever, and take in and sell it at [higher] costs,” he pointed out.

“So, over the next quarter or so, those drugs should be available, and the generic version would be the cheaper version,” he stated, noting that consideration will be given to facilitating access through the National Health Fund (NHF).

Meanwhile, Tufton said that the Lifestyle Clinic will target people whose health is at risk due to obesity.

Patients will be referred to the clinic by doctors after medical assessment and will get support from specialists, including psychologists, nutritionists, physical activity specialists and social workers, to assist them in making healthier lifestyle choices and reduce their risk of serious illnesses.

He cautioned that medication should not be viewed as a replacement for healthy lifestyle practices, emphasising that managing obesity calls for a broader approach which includes proper nutrition, exercise and medical supervision.

“That’s part of controlling obesity. It’s not the full picture. So, I’m not here prescribing the one solution to the problem,” Tufton said

— JIS

World.title: Science, technology take centre stage at SRC conference
World.content:
Executive director of the Scientific Research Council, Dr Charah Watson speaking at a SRC Science and Technology Conference

The Scientific Research Council’s (SRC) 32nd National Science and Technology Conference kicks off Tuesday, bringing together leading scientists, policymakers, industry leaders, innovators, development partners and young people from Jamaica, the Caribbean and beyond to chart a coordinated path towards science, technology and innovation-driven development.

The three-day conference is expected to provide a platform for collaboration, knowledge-sharing and the exploration of innovative solutions in science and technology to build resilient systems, competitive industries and globally relevant economies across the region.

“The SRC Science and Technology Conference and Exhibition provides an important platform to demonstrate, in very practical and relatable ways, how research, technology and innovation can improve lives, strengthen industries and support national development,” Dr Charah T Watson, Executive Director, SRC, said.

“Science is at work every day in the challenges we face and the solutions we depend on. Whether we are talking about food security, extreme weather, public health, the use of artificial intelligence, waste management, or helping a small business improve a product, science provides the evidence, tools and innovation needed to move from problem to solution. That is what we want Jamaicans to connect with through this year’s theme, ‘Science Solves’,” she added.

The conference is expected to address critical thematic areas including food security and sovereignty, emerging technologies and artificial intelligence, science policy and diplomacy, science communication in times of crisis, and digital transformation, while showcasing practical solutions, partnerships, and pathways to scale.

Among the notable speakers over the three days are Dr Andrew Wheatley, Minister Without Portfolio in the Office of the Prime Minister responsible for Science, Technology and Special Projects; Dr Alejandro Adem President, Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council; Senator Aubyn Hill, Minister of Industry, Investment and Commerce; Floyd Green, Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Mining; Ana Vásquez Herrera Head of National and International Cooperation, National Agency for Research and Innovation (ANII) Uruguay; Dr Dana Morris Dixon, Minister of Education, Skills, Youth and Information; Matthew Stone, President, Jamaica Artificial Intelligence Association; Dr Cliff Riley Director General, Hazardous Substances Regulatory Authority; and Yusuf N Henriques, Founder & CEO of IndyGeneUS AI & IndyGeneUS Institute.

A major highlight of the 2026 staging is Jamaica’s successful bid to host the Global Research Council (GRC) Americas Regional Meeting, which will be held in conjunction with the conference.

“The staging of the Global Research Council Americas Regional Meeting in Jamaica is equally significant. It brings research funding agencies and science leaders from across the Americas into the Caribbean to have important conversations about the future of research, the priorities that deserve investment, and how research systems can respond more effectively to the realities of our countries,” Watson said.

“For Jamaica to host this meeting, and for it to be held in the Caribbean, is an opportunity to ensure that our experiences, challenges and perspectives are part of those discussions rather than being considered from a distance,” the SRC executive director explained.

Watson added that the closing meeting of the IDRC-supported ‘Deepening the Knowledge Ecosystem in the Caribbean’ initiative will form part of the wider GRC dialogue, noting that work provides a timely, evidence-based perspective on the strengths, gaps and opportunities within the Caribbean’s research and knowledge ecosystem.

“Bringing those findings into a forum that includes research funders is particularly important because the discussion can help inform future funding calls, partnerships and capacity-building support that are better aligned with the needs of the region,” Watson said. “Taken together, these activities during Science and Technology Month create an important continuum, from showing the public that science solves everyday problems, to strengthening the institutions and funding systems that allow science to deliver solutions at scale.

“It is about ensuring that Jamaica and the wider Caribbean are not simply consumers of science and technology, but active participants in producing the knowledge, innovation and solutions needed for our own development,” she explained.

World.title: What the EU can learn from Mark Carney on digital sovereignty
World.content:
At Davos earlier this year, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney offered a compelling response to a world increasingly shaped by great-power rivalry. Middle powers need greater strategic autonomy, he argued, but they cannot secure it by retreating behind their borders.

Instead, they need to build their own capabilities while working more closely with like-minded partners. On technology, he reasoned that countries should cooperate so they are not ultimately forced to choose between “hegemons and hyperscalers.”

At the recent EU-Canada Summit, that philosophy began to translate into policy. Canada and the EU launched an “Alliance for the Future” based on closer economic, technological and strategic cooperation. They also concluded negotiations on a Digital Trade Agreement designed to support a “secure, open and trusted digital environment”​ resilient economic relations​,​ and trusted cross-border data flows.

That principle matters not only for Europe’s new relationship with Canada, but for its approach to other trusted partners.

Sovereignty without isolation

Like Canada, Europe has diagnosed its technology problem correctly. It depends too heavily on a handful of providers for the cloud, computing power, digital infrastructure and ​artificial intelligence (​AI​)​ models underpinning its economy and security.

Reducing those dependencies will require Europe to put its money where its mouth is, including by unlocking more diversified private investment. Mario Draghi estimated that the EU needs an additional €750 billion to €800 billion of investment each year until 2030. The European Commission, meanwhile, wants to mobili​z​​​e €200 billion for AI and at least triple Europe’s data cent​er​​​ capacity within five to seven years.

Europe cannot expect investment on an unprecedented scale while narrowing the field of companies able to provide it.

But Europe’s approach risks moving in the opposite direction. ​ ​It could exclude some of the businesses investing most heavily in the continent and building European capabilities, while favo​ring others that remain dependent on non-European technology.

That is the risk confronting policymakers as they shape the Cloud and AI Development Act. The legislation seeks to influence not only how Europe expands and secures its technological capabilities, but also which companies can take part.

Herein lies the core trade-off.​ ​ Europe cannot expect investment on an unprecedented scale while narrowing the field of companies able to provide it. Whether it closes its technology gap will depend partly on its ability to draw on the capital and expertise of experienced, trusted partners.

Look beyond ownership

The debate over digital sovereignty therefore needs to move beyond the simplistic question of ownership or headquarters.

A definition based principally on corporate nationality could exclude trusted companies with decades of investment, infrastructure and employment across Europe. It could also protect nominally European suppliers without necessarily making Europe more secure or resilient.

Effective sovereignty should mean that Europe can keep essential services running during a crisis, protect critical systems and retain a choice of secure, trusted suppliers. Assessments should therefore examine who controls data, encryption, operations, security and continuity.

Corporate nationality is relevant, but it cannot answer these questions on its own. A cloud provider may be EU-owned yet rely on processors, software and security tools developed elsewhere. Another may be headquartered outside the EU but operate European data cent​er​​​s, employ European engineers, place data and encryption keys under European control​,​ and comply with demanding European regulation. Any nationality test alone tells policymakers little about which arrangement provides greater sovereignty.

​​ ​In practice, sovereignty done right depends on who can access critical systems, where operational decisions are taken, whether data and encryption remain protected and, ultimately, whether services continue when normal arrangements fail.

Nationality should carry the greatest weight where a provider is controlled from a country that presents a recognized security threat, or where the relevant jurisdiction has the capacity and record of exploiting technological dependencies. ​​The strictest restrictions are justified where foreign interference could threaten national security, including defense, law enforcement and the most essential public services.

Countries such as Switzerland, Canada​ ​and the UK should not automatically fall into the same category as recognized security threats. Where the security conditions do not apply, nationality-based restrictions risk becoming protectionist rather than protective.

Instead, Europe should apply three tests for trusted partners and domestic firms alike: whether operational control rests in Europe; whether the service can continue during a crisis; and whether the provider makes a substantial, long-term contribution to Europe’s technological capacity.

​​In practice, sovereignty done right depends on who can access critical systems, where operational decisions are taken, whether data and encryption remain protected and, ultimately, whether services continue when normal arrangements fail.

Telecoms is a case in point. Regardless of where they are headquartered, operators must keep essential services running through cyberattacks, power failures and supply-chain disruption while protecting the confidentiality of EU data.

A company’s registered address answers none of those operational questions.

Build with trusted partners

This matters beyond the Cloud and AI Development Act. The approach Europe takes to sovereignty could shape policy toward​ ​telecommunications, satellites, semiconductors and other strategic technologies.

Rules that exclude trusted foreign investors primarily on the basis of nationality risk fragmenting the market and deterring some of the capital and experti​se Europe is trying to attract. They could also encourage reciprocal restrictions on European companies operating abroad.

The better approach is the one Carney has begun to articulate: build domestic capability while deepening cooperation with countries that share your security interests and can contribute technology, infrastructure and investment.

The EU should therefore provide a route for British companies that meet demanding security, control and resilience requirements to receive equivalent treatment as trusted providers.

The EU’s developing relationship with Canada shows that this is possible. Its new Alliance for the Future explicitly combines closer economic integration with technological cooperation, security and resilience, while the Digital Trade Agreement seeks to remove unjustified barriers while maintaining strong safeguards.

If deeper integration with Canada can strengthen European sovereignty, the same principle should apply to other trusted partners that meet equally demanding standards.

The obvious next test is the UK.

Britain sits outside the EU’s institutions but remains closely connected to Europe’s economy, technology sector and security. Infrastructure, investment and supply chains cross the Channel, while the UK and EU face many of the same cyber and geopolitical threats.

​​The EU should therefore provide a route for British companies that meet demanding security, control and resilience requirements to receive equivalent treatment as trusted providers, with reciprocal arrangements for qualifying European companies in the UK.

Strategic autonomy does not require strategic isolation.

The second UK-EU Summit on 20 November provides an opportunity to turn that principle into practice.

Leaders should establish a UK-EU Digital Partnership, covering the mutual recognition of trusted providers, coordinating rules affecting cloud and AI infrastructure, and the removal of unnecessary procurement barriers before they become embedded.

Such a partnership would support both sides’ sovereignty objectives by distinguishing genuine strategic dependencies from relationships that add to their resilience and security.

Europe is right to seek greater control over its technological future. But ​​Carney has identified the crucial distinction:​ ​strategic autonomy does not require strategic isolation.

Canada and the EU have begun to show what trusted partnership can look like. The UK should be next.
