World.title: Bilkis Bano says Supreme Court did not inform or hear her before granting bail to two convicts; vows to fight order
World.content:
Bilkis Bano, who survived gangrape and the murder of her family during the 2002 Gujarat riots, has issued a statement conveying her “pain, shock and disbelief” at the Supreme Court’s decision to grant bail and suspend the life imprisonment of two men convicted of the crimes that changed her life forever.

Ms. Bano, through her counsel senior advocate Shobha Gupta, stated she was neither informed nor heard before the order was passed on October 28.

“I still cannot believe that once again, for the second time, an order has been passed by the Supreme Court without calling me up and without hearing me. I learnt of this through press reports,” her statement read.

A Bench of Justices M.M. Sundresh and Prasanna B. Varale, on October 28, had suspended the life sentences of Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya, who were two of the 11 men convicted of gangraping the then 19-year-old Ms. Bano and murdering 14 members of her family, including her infant daughter, in 2002.

The short order, published recently on the court website, had reasoned that the two men had already undergone more than 17 years in prison and one of them suffered a severe handicap.

The apex court order for the duo’s release on bail came in an appeal filed by them against a 2017 Bombay High Court judgment upholding a CBI court decision of 2008, convicting the men and sentencing them to life terms in prison.

The two convicts had only arraigned the States of Gujarat and Maharashtra, where the trial was transferred to on a Supreme Court order, in their appeal.

“How could the Honourable Supreme Court simply suspend the sentence if the men who did this to me? How could they not even inform me? How could they not even make sure my voice was heard in their courtroom?” Ms. Bano asked.

In 2024, the apex court had quashed the order of en masse remission granted by the State of Gujarat in August 2022 to the 11 men.

The court had then empathised with Ms. Bano, noting how she had been “coerced to live the life of a nomad and an orphan… the gruesome and horrific acts of violence have left an indelible imprint on her mind which will continue to torment and cripple her”.

In her statement on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), Ms. Bano said she had “rebuilt from the rubble of my life… learned to smile”, but the October 28 order has made her scared, once again.

Ms. Bano stated she would fight the October 28 order granting bail to the two convicts.

“I must. I do this for my children, who do not deserve to live haunted by these fears and scars for the rest of their lives… I do this for women everywhere. Because no woman, no survivor, no citizen should have to endure this eternal test of belonging and equality, and fight for justice for the rest of her life,” she said.

World.title: Adults pack Chennai’s quirky gelateria Ciacco for Cerelac in a baby bottle
World.content:
I walk into Ciacco to the sight of adults sipping on Cerelac out of a feeding bottle.

This is a sight that has been taking over my social media account over the last couple of days against my will. It is an odd one, but Ciacco has never been one to shy away from a spectacle.

The Chennai-based gelateria has previously served biryani, rasam, and mango pickle-flavoured ice creams. Its latest offering, a cold bottled Cerelac takes the novelty a little too far. Somewhere between culinary experimentation and viral marketing, the line between the two appears to have blurred.

The idea, Praveen Dante Rajagopal says, was conceived as a limited-edition drop for Children’s Day, in keeping with Ciacco’s penchant for unusual flavour experiments. “We were thinking of ideas for Children’s Day when we came up with Adult Cerelac gelato, and a customer joked about how we’re so crazy that we might even serve it in a baby bottle. So we did,” says the owner, adding that they sell anywhere from 50-100 bottles a day and it will only be available for another week or 10 days.

But while the bottle (they do not reuse, the management adds) makes for an easy talking point, and perhaps a pivotal social media moment, it does little to tell us whether the inside is any good. So, I go in to find out.

The Cerelac drink, made with hazelnut and almond pastes, evaporated milk, Cerelac and full-fat milk, and vanilla bean is pasteurised for over six hours to make it smooth and creamy. Truth be told, the drink is a tad too milky for my liking, with little of the distinct malt-forward taste one might expect from a flavour built around a childhood staple. It is also availabe in gelato form, topped with chocolate and crumb topping: a creamier version of the Cerelac drink.

That said, the drink certainly has its share of takers. Ever since it went viral on social media, the gelateria has been packed with people, who often stand in long lines just for this. While some seem hesitant to drink it out of the bottle, many film themselves doing it (from many angles) as they suck it down.

The cold Cerelac is served in both the feeding bottles and regular cups and customers can choose either. “Some customers prefer the cups, and some have even asked for it to be served warm,” says Praveen, adding that it was only meant to be a small marketing idea that has blown out of proportion. “We did this with the intention of serving nostalgia. There are customers who are enjoying it, but if people are sexualising it, it’s obviously wrong. However, I can’t control what they post,” he says.

But the Cerelac is only one of Ciacco’s many experiments. Over the past year, the gelateria has ventured into increasingly unusual territory with flavours such as biryani, rasam, mango pickle, cereal, ube, charcoal, pandan, and even parmesan. It is an ambitious exercise in reimagining familiar flavours, though the more interesting question is whether these combinations work as gelato or merely make for good conversation and social media content.

Ironically, Ciacco fares considerably better when it plays safe. The counter has a tempting selection of bombolinis, croissants and pain au chocolat, all of which make a rather convincing case for sticking to the classics. Unlike some of its experimental gelatos, these offerings do not need an elaborate backstory to make their appeal.

The savoury offerings are a mixed affair. A breaded and fried halloumi wrap proved rather too overwhelming after a few bites. The arancini, on the other hand, was crisp on the outside, with a satisfying filling.

Perhaps Ciacco’s best ideas are the ones that do not need a gimmick. The pastries are good, the savouries have their moments, and the gelato could do with letting its flavours do the talking.

All that said, there is enough on Ciacco’s menu to make a visit worthwhile without having to suck on a feeding bottle for the experience.

Ciacco is at 532, Anna Salai, Thiru Vi Ka Housing Board, Teynampet. A meal for two costs ₹1,500.

World.title: SIR row: Supreme Court to hear Rahul Gandhi’s application on December 9
World.content:
The Supreme Court has agreed to hear an application filed by the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, and leaders of the INDIA bloc, posing 48 interrogatories to the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC), Election Commissioners, and senior ECI officials regarding the conduct of the Service Information Report (SIR) and the veracity of the claims made in an October 26 affidavit filed by the poll body.

Also Read | ECI should give details of decisions taken and whether they had majority backing: former Election Commissioners

The affidavit asserted that the massive exercise (SIR), in which approximately 13 crore voters were excluded, was a unanimous decision of the ECI.

A Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant posted the case for December 9.

The petitions were originally listed for Tuesday (November 17, 2026). However, while the Bench was rising for lunch break, senior advocate Harish Salve, appearing for the Election Commission of India, enquired whether there would be enough time to hear all of the petitions.

Also Read: SC says ‘will examine’ petitioners’ ‘innocuous’ plea to direct ECI to preserve or file in court ‘complete’ SIR records

Mr. Salve said there was already a Special Bench scheduled later in the afternoon, and suggested an adjournment to a later date.

Mr. Gandhi, on Monday (November 16), told the Supreme Court that the ECI failed to produce any proof to establish its claim that the special intensive revision (SIR) was a “unanimous” decision made by Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi.

The reported friction between Mr. Kumar and the two Election Commissioners over the SIR and the CEC’s allegedly unilateral and authoritarian conduct had triggered widespread protests across India demanding his removal from office.

The ECI’s October 26 affidavit, in response to a petition filed by INDIA bloc leaders led by Mr. Gandhi, denied any differences of opinion between the CEC and the Election Commissioners over the SIR process.

Mr. Gandhi said the court must not accept such “bare assertions” from the ECI. He questioned why the affidavit was filed by the ECI when Mr. Kumar, Mr. Sandhu and Mr. Joshi were separately made respondents.

The Opposition leader, represented by senior advocate A.M. Singhvi and advocate Prasanna S., said the ECI chose not to explain when and where exactly the decision to conduct a nationwide SIR was made.

World.title: SCBA seeks contempt action against lawyer for derogatory remarks about CJI
World.content:
The Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) conveyed to the Supreme Court its intention to seek contempt action against a lawyer who made deprecatory remarks about Chief Justice of India Surya Kant in open court on Monday (November 16, 2026).

SCBA secretary Praghya Baghel and joint secretary Meenesh Dubey made an oral mentioning before the CJI that Attorney General R. Venkataramani had already given the necessary statutory consent to file the contempt petition against the lawyer.

Also Read | Lawyer led out after making derogatory remarks in court against CJI

The office bearers urged the court to tag the petition along with pending contempt pleas against journalist Nikhil Wagle and Rajya Sabha MP Sanjay Raut, who are also facing contempt proceedings for allegedly making derogatory online remarks against the CJI.

The petitions against Mr. Raut and Mr. Wagle is listed for hearing on Tuesday (November 17, 2026).

The SCBA office bearers said they had recordings of the same lawyer making unsavoury remarks against the CJI on previous occasions too.

The CJI agreed to list the petition, if all procedural necessities were completed, on November 18.

Also Read | Supreme Court directs physical appearance of Rajya Sabha MP Sanjay Raut in contempt case

The alleged comments of Mr. Wagle and Mr. Raut on social media was triggered by the Chief Justice of India’s decision to decline a request by the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and Congress party president Mallikarjun Kharge to meet the top judge.

The CJI had refused the leaders’ request for audience on the grounds of judicial propriety and had asked them to file a petition on the judicial side. They had subsequently filed a writ petition seeking an independent probe into allegations of arbitrary use of power by Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

World.title: Our future must be shaped by ‘cooperation, not competition’: PM Modi to ASEAN leaders
World.content:
India and ASEAN together represent nearly a quarter of the world's population, and their common future must be shaped by "cooperation, not competition," Prime Minister Narendra Modi told leaders of the 11-nation grouping on Tuesday (November 17, 2026).

Mr. Modi, speaking at the India-ASEAN summit, said New Delhi's commitment to the grouping's unity and centrality in the partnership "is and will remain steadfast."

ASEAN Summit 2026 | Key highlights of the summit in Manila

"In the past few years, the world has faced a series of crises. What the world needs most today is peace, stability and predictability," said the prime minister. "In this context, our theme this year - 'Navigating Our Future, Together' - holds special significance."

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is a regional intergovernmental bloc that promotes economic growth, political stability, security, and cultural cooperation among its member countries in Southeast Asia.

Founded in 1967, ASEAN has 11 members — Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Timor-Leste and Vietnam. India and several other countries, including the U.S., China, Japan and Australia, are its dialogue partners.

"India and ASEAN together represent nearly a quarter of the world's population. Therefore, it is essential to ensure that our future is determined by cooperation, not competition," the Prime Minister said.

Mr. Modi said India and ASEAN have both the strength and the resolve and together, both sides can make this region a symbol of peace and stability.

"We believe that India's development and ASEAN's prosperity are deeply intertwined. In the coming years, the ASEAN Community Vision 2045 and Developed India 2047 can play a crucial role in realising our shared aspirations.," he said

"I am confident that today's meeting will elevate our Comprehensive Strategic Partnership to new heights and contribute to building a secure, inclusive, and prosperous Indo-Pacific," he added.

World.title: Dengue spurt in Thiruvananthapuram: KU’s Karyavattom campus, Cliff House compound emerge as hotspots
World.content:
The Karyavattom campus of Kerala University (KU) has emerged as a hotspot of dengue in the city, where over 50 cases have been reported since November 9. Health department suspects that this is a gross underestimation, as the transmission is likely to have begun weeks before

Intermittent spells of rain, followed by hot and humid weather, have led to the spike in dengue cases in Thiruvananthapuram, even when the general dengue case trend has been on a slow decline since July across the State.

In the last 10 days, Thiruvananthapuram district has reported 200 probable cases of dengue and 97 confirmed cases.

On Monday, following a meeting called by the Health department, which was joined by the Vice Chancellor, some KU syndicate members as well as public health experts of the School of Public Health under Kerala University of Health Sciences, it was decided to shut the Karyavattom campus and the hostel buildings for three days so that intense vector control measures can be taken up and a break in disease transmission can be achieved.

“District health officials and vector control teams had visited the campus and hostel and we found that solid waste management was a huge issue in the campus. Plastic disposable containers used for food delivery which are disposed of carelessly are emerging as a major contributor to vector breeding in urban areas.. Rain water stagnation in these containers which are strewn around is a major hazard. Indoor plants in hostel rooms, broken manholes and blocked drains leading to rainwater stagnation have all led to intense mosquito breeding inside the vast campus,” a senior Health official said.

The Health department has also decided to serve notice to the KU Registrar under the Kerala Public Health Act, for allowing the campus to be a breeding ground for mosquitoes and posing a public health issue

Teams from the Pangappara health centre have been at work on the campus since November 10 but the district vector control team and the Corporation health staff will be joining them now. Fogging will be done to kill adult mosquitoes and indoor space spraying inside the hostel room, which will be accompanied by a source reduction campaign, officials said.

The district health administration has identified several pockets of dengue within the city itself, where an abundance of breeding sources and intense vector breeding has been spotted

Health officials point out that several large government properties with vast, ill-maintained grounds are also turning out to be hotspots for dengue in the city.

“The Cliff House compound and the sprawling official bungalows around it are all major breeding grounds for mosquitoes. In the Cliff House, seven police personnel there on guard duty were down with dengue, following which a district health team had visited the location. In some of the bungalows where renovation works are going on, building materials and discarded parts of equipment are all thrown about carelessly, leading to rain water stagnation and mosquito breeding,” a health official said.

Health officials said that without public participation, source reduction and mosquito control cannot be taken up successfully.

Kollam district too has reported a significant number of dengue cases over the last 10 days.

In November so far, the State has recorded 739 confirmed cases and 2,056 probable cases of dengue and three probable dengue deaths.

World.title: ASEAN Summit LIVE updates: PM Modi at ASEAN-India Summit; Quad meeting likely after President Trump arrives
World.content:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi participated in the 23rd ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations)-India summit and the 21st East Asia summit on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) in Manila. Philippines is hosting the summits in its capacity as the current chair of the 11-nation ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations). In a pre-departure statement, PM Modi said India’s relationship with the ASEAN region is at the “heart of India’s Act East Policy”.

PM Modi is also expected to meet U.S. President Donald Trump, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the first Quad Summit since 2024 in Manila, on the sidelines of ASEAN summits today (November 17, 2026), sources in New Delhi had confirmed to The Hindu. The meeting would probably take place after Mr. Trump lands in Manila. The confirmation of the Quad Summit in Manila is significant for the Indo-Pacific grouping, and plans to chart out their next course.

Also read | The challenge of holding the Quad together

World.title: CDF Munir underscores importance of sustained engagement, mutual trust in meeting with Iran’s Araghchi
World.content:
Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir underscored the importance of sustained engagement, mutual trust and close coordination between the two countries to promote regional peace and stability during a meeting with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, the military’s media wing said on Tuesday.

According to a statement issued by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), matters of mutual interest, regional security dynamics and evolving geopolitical developments were also discussed between the two.

Both sides also exchanged views on exploring avenues to address common security challenges, it added.

Araghchi appreciated Pakistan’s “constructive role in promoting regional peace and stability and expressed his country’s desire to further strengthen bilateral relations”, ISPR said.

Pakistan has been mediating between Washington and Tehran, making efforts for an end to a war that began with US attacks on Iran on February 28.

Months of diplomacy has failed to resolve the war, while CDF Munir has been playing a key role in Pakistan’s mediation efforts.

His latest meeting with Araghchi took place in Rawalpindi on Monday, when the Iranian foreign minister was in Pakistan, primarily to attend the 30th meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organisation (ECO) Council of Foreign Ministers.

During his visit, the Iranian foreign minister expressed confidence in Pakistan’s role in the mediation and said Tehran trusted Islamabad as a “good friend”.

Islamabad is doing its job and Iran is satisfied with its engagement, he said.

Prior to Monday’s meeting, CDF Munir’s most significant engagement with the Iranians took place last month in Tehran. He was in the Iranian capital along with other officials from member countries of the Makkah defence pact — an tripartite agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye.

The discussions had taken place against a backdrop of heightened concern over the escalating conflict between Yemen’s Ansar Allah rebels against Saudi Arabia, the security of the Strait of Hormuz and the prospect of renewed US and Israeli military action against Iran.

It was decided during the meeting that all participating sides would “continue their dialogue to bolster cooperation among the four regional nations, including in the areas of regional peace and security.”

Officials from Pakistan, including the CDF, have undertaken multiple visits to Iran after the war began. The defence forces chief visited Iran on Oct 21 as well. During that visit, Iranian leaders conveyed to him that the US must take the first steps to rebuild trust and that the acceptance by Washington of Tehran’s seven-point proposal for working towards peace could provide a starting point for renewed negotiations.

He earlier travelled to Tehran on Aug 24 and met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Araghchi and other senior officials to discuss regional security and efforts to restore stability.

Pakistan’s mediation

Pakistan’s efforts for peace between the two sides began soon after the war.

Less than two months after the war started, Pakistan brokered a ceasefire between the two sides on April 8 and Islamabad hosted direct talks between US and Iran on April 11 and 12.

The mediation efforts also led to the signing of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on June 17 between the US and Iran in Geneva.

The MoU set a framework to move towards a permanent end to the war.

While hostilities later renewed between the two sides, Pakistan remained engaged in mediation efforts.

Currently, however, a stalemate remains in the negotiations between the US and Iran.

But Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on Monday that Islamabad had not given up on its diplomatic efforts for a peaceful resolution to the US-Iran war.

Dar said he had “very candid, very frank, very brotherly, very comprehensive discussions” with Araghchi on the sidelines of the ECO meeting.

Noting that the two discussed the latest regional situation, the deputy premier said Iran had “fast-tracked” its seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to a two-day plan .

“So, the response from the United States is pending. We have not given up hope or efforts. We are still doing our best [so] that the situation gets sorted out,” DPM Dar stated.

He also expressed hope that, now that Washington was no longer busy with its midterm elections, it would respond to the proposal “very soon”.

World.title: Trump is not going to let Iran conflict become a 'forever war', asserts Vance
World.content:
US Vice President JD Vance said on Monday that President Donald Trump will not allow the ongoing war on Iran to turn into a prolonged military commitment, rejecting calls for an extended US presence and insisting that the administration remains committed to avoiding another “forever war”.

In an interview with Fox News, Vance said there was no disagreement between him and Trump over the direction of the conflict, emphasising that the president intends to bring the war to an end rather than allow it to become a long-term engagement.

“My prediction is that whatever the president ultimately decides to do, there are going to be people who demand more, who want the war to go on indefinitely,” he said.

“What I feel quite confident about the president of the United States — and again, there’s no daylight here — is that whatever he ultimately decides to do, however he ultimately decides to bring the conflict to a close, he is not going to let this become a forever war,” he added.

Vance’s comments come as the US and Iran remain locked in a conflict while debate intensifies over it costs and duration.

“We are not going to allow this to become a 10- or 15-year commitment, or frankly, even a two-year commitment,” Vance said.

He accused some critics and foreign policy advocates of wanting the US to remain engaged indefinitely, adding that the administration had made a clear commitment to voters to avoid prolonged overseas wars.

“Despite the fact that a lot of neoconservatives and a lot of other people want us to stay there forever, we’re not going to stay there forever. We promised we wouldn’t,” he said.

Vance also expressed confidence that Trump would ultimately end the war with “great results” for the American people.

‘I’m happy to be a heat shield’ for Trump

During the interview, Vance also addressed criticism surrounding the administration’s handling of the Iran conflict and its potential political consequences for Republicans following the 2026 midterm elections.

Asked whether there were differences between him and Trump over the war, he rejected the suggestion, saying there was no disagreement among senior administration officials.

He acknowledged, however, that the conflict had carried political costs, particularly through higher gasoline and energy prices.

“Politically, yes, and I think the president himself has absolutely said this as well. There was a political cost: the higher gas prices, the higher energy prices,” he said.

The vice president also pushed back against criticism directed at him over a memorandum of understanding related to Iran, suggesting that some critics were using him as a substitute target for attacking Trump.

“I’m happy to be a heat shield for the president of the United States,” Vance said.

World.title: Pakistan's fast bowling masterclass bundles Sri Lanka out for 98 in second Test
World.content:
Pakistan’s fast bowlers produced a devastating display to dismiss Sri Lanka for just 98 in 35.3 overs on the opening day of the second Test at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Tuesday, exploiting the movement on offer to leave the visitors with little chance of building a competitive total.

After winning the toss and opting to field, Pakistan reduced Sri Lanka to 36-5 in the morning session before completing the job shortly after lunch, taking the last four wickets for just 13 runs in 6.3 overs.

Mohammad Abbas, Razaullah and Aamer Jamal claimed three wickets each, while Saqib Khan took one. Abbas was the most economical, finishing with 3-14 in 14 overs, including six maidens. Razaullah returned 3-21 in eight overs, while Jamal took 3-24 in 5.3 overs.

Saqib struck first, removing Pasindu Sooriyabandara for two in the fourth over when the opener edged an outswinger to wicket-keeper Ghazi Ghori.

Abbas then dismissed Dinesh Chandimal for seven, caught at short leg by Azan Awais, before Kamindu Mendis chipped a delivery to Tayyab Arif at short cover for eight.

Razaullah, operating at high pace, added to Sri Lanka’s troubles by removing Lahiru Udara for four, with a delivery clocked at 146kph drawing an edge to Mohammad Taha at first slip.

He then trapped Dhananjaya de Silva lbw for one with a delivery that held its line and stayed low. De Silva reviewed the decision, but ball-tracking confirmed the umpire’s call.

Sri Lanka were 36-5 when captain Kusal Mendis and Sonal Dinusha attempted to rebuild. Kusal counterattacked with 32 off 50 balls, hitting five fours, while Dinusha contributed 21 from 40 deliveries, including four boundaries. Their 49-run sixth-wicket stand was the visitors’ only substantial partnership.

Aamer ended the resistance in the 28th over when Kusal mistimed a pull and sent a top edge towards deep backward square, where Razaullah took the catch.

The fast bowler returned after the interval to remove Dinusha, who pulled a short delivery straight to Razaullah in the deep, and Lahiru Kumara, caught by Salman Ali Agha at second slip for a duck.

In between, Razaullah bowled Milan Rathnayaka for nought, while Abbas dismissed Prabath Jayasuriya for three, taking a return catch after the batter chipped a drive back towards him.

The score was the lowest innings total at Rawalpindi, surpassing England’s 112 there in 2024.

World.title: Pakistan condemns Israeli attacks in Syria, calls for withdrawal from occupied territories
World.content:
WASHINGTON: Pakistan on Tuesday strongly condemned Israel’s continued attacks and incursions into Syrian territory, calling for an immediate end to the violations, withdrawal from occupied areas and full compliance with the 1974 Disengagement Agreement and relevant UN Security Council resolutions.

“The occupied Golan is Syrian territory under international law,” Pakistan’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Syed Haider Shah, told the Security Council.

Speaking at a briefing on the political and humanitarian situation in Syria, Ambassador Shah said Israeli violations undermined Syria’s security and obstructed its recovery. He reaffirmed Pakistan’s support for Syria’s political transition, reconstruction and efforts to restore stability.

“Syria’s transition continues despite considerable challenges and a complex regional environment,” he said, adding that the progress achieved by the Syrian government deserved recognition and sustained support.

Pakistan welcomed the Syrian government’s efforts to advance the political transition, rebuild national institutions and strengthen engagement with regional and international partners.

Ambassador Shah said consolidating the progress would require “patient political engagement, economic opportunities and a secure environment.” He also appreciated the Syrian leadership’s emphasis on diplomacy and engagement in navigating the difficult regional environment.

On the economic front, Pakistan welcomed measures taken by the United States, European Union and United Kingdom to lift or ease economic sanctions on Syria and facilitate its reintegration into the international economy.

“These measures have opened important opportunities for economic investment and reconstruction,” the ambassador said, stressing that sustained international engagement was essential to translate sanctions relief into tangible economic recovery.

Pakistan also welcomed investment and reconstruction initiatives undertaken by Syria and its regional and international partners. Their timely implementation, he said, could help restore essential services and ensure that Syrians experienced meaningful improvements in their daily lives.

Ambassador Shah called for sustained humanitarian assistance, saying the scale of Syria’s needs required predictable support and effective cooperation with the Syrian government.

On the political and security front, Pakistan supported continued implementation of the January 29 agreement to integrate security and administrative structures in north-eastern Syria into national institutions. It also welcomed the roadmap agreed by Syria, Jordan and the United States for Suwaidah, describing it as a viable path forward.

The Pakistani envoy warned that Daesh, other terrorist groups and foreign terrorist fighters continued to pose a threat to Syria.

“The threat posed by Daesh, other terrorist groups and foreign terrorist fighters requires continued vigilance,” he said, calling for coordinated counterterrorism cooperation in accordance with international law and relevant Security Council resolutions.

He also welcomed the joint statement issued by Syria and Jordan on October 28 and their agreement to establish a joint security committee to examine the circumstances surrounding recent incidents and strengthen coordination against terrorist threats.

Pakistan expressed regret over civilian casualties and appreciated the two countries’ commitment to preserving their close relations.

The Security Council briefing also highlighted the continuing humanitarian dangers facing Syrians returning to their homes after years of conflict.

UN Assistant Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs Mohamed Yahya told the council that landmines and other explosive remnants of war had killed at least 30 people, including 19 children, over the past month. More than 80 others, including 35 children, were injured.

Yahya warned that the situation was not improving, with returning families facing growing risks from unexploded weapons. He also highlighted shortages in winter assistance and the financial constraints affecting UN humanitarian operations.

The warning comes as nearly four million Syrians have voluntarily returned home since December 2024. Since October alone, another 60,000 internally displaced people and 18,000 refugees have returned. Yet more than 730,000 people remain in camps.

Yahya said humanitarian partners had cleared more than 700,000 square metres of contaminated land during the first half of this year, but much more needed to be done as families returned. Recent flash floods have also displaced explosive ordnance into areas previously considered safer.

Meanwhile, 2.4 million people are expected to need additional assistance this winter. The UN winter response plan, targeting more than 970,000 of the most vulnerable, is only 40 per cent funded. Nearly 200,000 displaced people and returnees are living in damaged shelters.

“Time is running out,” Yahya warned.

The humanitarian crisis is further compounded by the detection of poliovirus in two children in Deir Ez Zor. With the UN humanitarian appeal only one-third funded, the World Food Programme is halving its food assistance programme, while the UN Population Fund has closed 28 health facilities.

Deputy Special Envoy for Syria Claudio Cordone welcomed the formal submission last week of the draft law on transitional justice, but stressed that justice must not be selective and that accountability must apply to crimes “regardless of the perpetrators or the victims”.

Preparations for a permanent constitution and credible, inclusive elections require clarity on processes and timelines, he said, echoing the view that there is no time to waste.

The World Bank estimates the cost of rebuilding damaged physical assets alone at $216 billion, Mr. Cordone noted, calling for sustained international support.

World.title: Flour gets costlier as imports stay insufficient
World.content:
KARACHI: Amid a persistent shortfall, the arrival of imported wheat has so far failed to bring any relief to consumers, as wheat and wheat flour prices continue to rise.

Retailers jacked up the rates of flour No. 2.5 and fine flour to Rs180 and Rs200 per kg, up by Rs10 per kg, citing an increase in the rates by the millers.

So far, more than 100,000 tonnes of wheat have arrived in the country since the last week of October.

Initially, the rate of wheat had plunged to Rs130 from Rs140 per kg after the arrival of the first ship carrying 51,000 tonnes on Oct 28.

The open market, however, saw grain prices reverting to Rs140 per kg last week, forcing millers to raise prices of different flour varieties.

Cereal Association of Pakistan (CAP) Chairman Muzammil Chappal told Dawn that he had been urging the government since May about a possible shortage of four million tonnes this season and at least allowing the private sector to import 2m tonnes, but the government had not paid any heed.

Stakeholders estimate 3-4 million tonnes shortage of wheat

The country is facing a crisis despite a 4.3pc rise in wheat production to 29.61m tonnes in FY26 from 28.40m tonnes in the preceding year, according to the Economic Survey FY26.

According to Mr Chappal, annual demand for wheat ranges between 31m and 32m tonnes.

He said, irrespective of the official wheat harvest of over 29m tonnes in FY26, the government needs to realise that demand for grain is rising as the population grows by over 3pc every year.

Rauf Ibrahim, a wholesaler and trader, said the country needs at least 3m tonnes of wheat, as the new crop from Sindh and Punjab will enter markets between March and May next year.

He said the federal and provincial governments have not launched any effective campaign against hoarders and stock pilferers since the wheat crop hit the markets in FY26. He urged the government to check commodity stocks, especially wheat, in markets and godowns, as speculators and investors have been active in commodity investing.

Mr Ibrahim said millers raised the price of flour No. 2.5, Maida and Fine Flour to Rs8,100, Rs9,000 and Rs9,150, respectively, from Rs7,800, Rs8 ,400 and Rs8,550 per 50kg bag.

High quality Chakki flour is available at Rs200 per kg in the wholesale market, while retailers are charging Rs215.

Millers had raised the prices of different varieties by Rs20 per kg, but later started reducing rates ahead of the arrival of imported wheat. However, they started giving price shocks to consumers again amid the absence of any vigil by the authorities.

One of the reasons behind rising wheat prices in Karachi, Mr Ibrahim said, is that Sindh has been waiting for imported wheat. Millers are facing a dearth of grain in the open market as the arrival of the commodity from Punjab has stopped.

A miller, who asked not to be named, said the situation was alarming as prices had shot up in Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa as well despite the arrival of imported wheat.

The miller claimed there are no uniform flour rates of the entire mill community as every mill is issuing rates as per its wheat stocks and market situation.

Imported quantity not sufficient

He said imported wheat would prove highly insufficient. For example, he added, only Karachi mills require 80,000 bags of 100kg daily for wheat grinding.

Mr Ibrahim said the federal and provincial governments had yet to wake up over the shortage, which is hurting the low- and middle-income groups hard. “They will shudder at the thought of paying Rs2,000 for a 10kg flour bag.” He urged the government to check the stocks of flour millers as they usually keep one to two months’ stocks of grain.

Tandoor owners are in a fix as they confront two problems — high rates for both flour and LPG.

So far they have kept the prices of Chapati, Naan, Sheermal/Taftaan and Qulcha unchanged at Rs20, Rs30-35, Rs100-110 and Rs90-100, respectively.

Published in Dawn, November 17, 2026

World.title: Unmarried women aged 45 or above included in BISP
World.content:
LAHORE: Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP) Chairperson Senator Rubina Khalid has said the BISP Board has approved the inclusion of unmarried women, aged 45 years or above, in the financial help scheme.

Addressing a press conference here on Monday, she said that out of over 10 million BISP beneficiary families across the country, around five million belonged to Punjab.

These figures, she said, clearly reflect that Benazir Income Support Programme is a national social welfare programme providing support to eligible families across the country, irrespective of their political affiliation.

Speaking about the new digital payment system, Ms Khalid said that digital mobile wallets and an interoperable payment system have been introduced to ensure convenient and transparent payments to the beneficiary women.

“Through 1-LINK, six partner banks have been connected to this system, and the beneficiaries will no longer be restricted to a specific centre to receive the Benazir Income Support Programme amount.”

She said that free SIMs have been provided to the beneficiary women and digital wallet accounts have been activated in their names.

They will receive SMS notifications when funds are credited to their accounts and to withdraw their payments.

Published in Dawn, November 17, 2026

World.title: Referendum has no legal standing for provinces, says Sharjeel
World.content:
KARACHI: Declaring that a referendum has no legal standing under the Constitution with regard to new provinces, Sindh Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon said the provincial assembly had already given its verdict on carving out any new province from Sindh.

“All civilised countries of the world function under their constitutions, and Pakistan’s Constitution also clearly defines the procedure through which new provinces could be created,” he told a press conference here on Monday.

“Under the Constitution, the provincial assembly of the area where a new province is proposed to be carved out must take the decision through a two-thirds majority vote,” he said, adding: “A referendum has no legal standing under the Constitution.”

He said that any party could hold a referendum a hundred times, but the real question was what its constitutional and legal status would be.

To a question regarding statements of various members of the federal cabinet on the issue of new provinces, Mr Memon said that federal ministers should be allowed to say whatever they wanted in accordance with their own choice, as everyone had the right to hold an opinion.

“If the government brings any bill on this matter in the National Assembly, the situation will become clear to everyone,” he said.

The minister warned that some parties were trying to create an atmosphere of hatred and division on ethnic and linguistic grounds, and the provincial government would never allow this to happen.

Responding to another question about planned rallies of certain parties in Karachi later this month, Mr Memon said that any party wishing to hold a public gathering must first obtain permission from the government.

“A party that does not obtain permission will not be allowed to hold a public gathering. The government will decide the venue and date of the gathering and no one will be allowed to forcibly impose their own wishes,” he said.

He said that the government was not against peaceful political activities, but everyone was bound to follow the rules and regulations.

Talking about the housing project for flood-hit people, he said that the provincial government had launched the “world’s largest housing project” for poor and flood-affected families, worth more than $2 billion, under which more than one million houses had been completed, while construction work on another 700,000 houses was underway.

He said Pakistan had earned a place in the Guinness Book of World Records in recognition of Sindh’s housing programme for flood victims.

He said that 42,565 Village Reconstruction Committees had been established for the rehabilitation of flood-affected people and reconstruction of their houses, with 42pc representation of women ensured in these committees.

The senior minister said that 2.51m people in the province had been provided protection against floods, including 1.17m women.

“The reconstruction of 205 kilometres of protective embankments has been completed in the province, while 157,000 hectares of agricultural land had been brought back under cultivation in 12 districts,” he said adding that the 30-kilometre-long protective embankment of Manchhar Lake had also been reconstructed.

Mr Memon said that all 44 gates of Sukkur Barrage had been replaced, while 54 out of 65 gates of Guddu Barrage had so far been replaced. “The government’s target is to shift all barrages in Sindh, including Sukkur and Guddu, to a modern and automated system by 2027,” he added.

Similarly, he said, 4,137 kilometres of canal distributaries had been lined in Sindh, resulting in water savings of 4,137 cusecs.

Published in Dawn, November 17, 2026

World.title: Govt reduces petrol, diesel prices by Rs2 per litre
World.content:
The government on Monday reduced the price of both petrol and high-speed diesel by Rs2 per litre, marking the tenth consecutive decrease in the rates.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs328 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs358 on Nov 17 (Tuesday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra).

The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

Under an arrangement announced on Nov 2, for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end.

On Sept 17, the government rolled out the Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Scheme across the country to ease the public’s burden amid rising fuel prices due to the Middle East situation.

The subsidy scheme applies to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles of up to 800cc.

Rise in fuel prices

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months.

Since July 17 , the government has been revising fuel prices on a near-daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the conflict. The federal government had also announced targeted relief measures in April to provide subsidised fuel.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
