World.title: Ilocos Sur honors Elpidio Quirino on his 136th birth anniversary
World.content:
Ilocos Sur honors its native son, former President Elpidio R. Quirino, on his 136th birth anniversary through a floral offering, 21-gun salute, and commemorative program in Vigan City on Monday, November 16, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Ilocos Sur provincial government)

SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — Honoring the life and legacy of one of the country’s distinguished statesmen, the Ilocos Sur government marked the late President Elpidio R. Quirino’s 136th birth anniversary through a commemorative gathering in Vigan City on Monday.

Born in Vigan on November 16, 1890, Quirino served as the country’s sixth president from 1948 to 1953. Before assuming the presidency, he held various public service positions, including legislator, Cabinet member, and vice president.

His administration played a significant role in the country’s postwar recovery, focusing on economic reconstruction, restoring peace and order, and strengthening government institutions. His leadership and contributions remain an important part of Philippine history.

Article continues after this 

READ: Late president Quirino, ex-mayor remembered at Manila South Cemetery

Gov. Jerry Singson led the provincial commemoration, joined by members of the Quirino family, including Cory Quirino, Eddie Quirino, Connie Quirino-Cuneta, and lawyer Carl Vincent Quitoriano.

The tribute began with a floral offering and a 21-gun salute at the Quirino Monument in Plaza Salcedo, followed by a Eucharistic Mass and commemorative program at the Provincial Farmers Livelihood Development Center.

The municipality of Quirino also paid tribute to the late president through a separate wreath-laying ceremony organized by the local government and the Quirino Municipal Police Station.

Mayor Atty. Jemarose Gomintong led the ceremony in honoring the legacy of the town’s namesake. Kenneth P. Tabin/Contributor/coa

World.title: Alleged ex-NPA commander yields in Caraga; arms cache seized
World.content:
ARMS CACHE. Police personnel recover an M1 Carbine rifle, ammunition, a hand grenade, and detonating cords in Sitio Saypon, Barangay Puting Bato, Cabadbaran City, Agusan del Norte on Monday, Nov. 16, 2026, following a tip from a former NPA commander who surrendered to authorities. Photo courtesy of Police Regional Office 13

BUTUAN CITY, Philippines — An alleged former commander of the New People’s Army (NPA) surrendered to police authorities in Caraga on Monday, leading to the recovery of an arms cache in Cabadbaran City, Agusan del Norte, the Police Regional Office 13 (PRO-13) said on Tuesday.

In a statement, PRO-13 director Brig. Gen. Rolindo Suguilon identified the surrenderer only as alias “Mikey,” 44, a resident of Cabadbaran City.

He said that Mikey was a former commanding officer of the Sandatahang Yunit Pampropaganda–Interyor (SYP-I) under the Headquarters Force of the NPA’s Northeastern Mindanao Regional Committee (NEMRC).

Article continues after this 

READ: Arms cache unearthed in Isabela

Mikey yielded to personnel of the 2nd Agusan del Norte Provincial Mobile Force Company (2nd AND PMFC) at Camp Col. Rafael C. Rodriguez in Barangay Libertad here, turning over a .38-caliber Smith & Wesson revolver.

During a subsequent debriefing, the former rebel revealed the location of a hidden arms cache in the hinterland of Sitio Saypon, Barangay Puting Bato in Cabadbaran City.

Acting on the tip, 2nd ADN PMFC operatives scoured the area and recovered an M1 Carbine semi-automatic rifle, two M1 Carbine magazines loaded with 15 rounds of ammunition, an AK-47 magazine with five rounds of ammunition, a hand grenade, and two detonating cords, PRO-13 reported.

Suguilon described the surrender and the seizure of the weapons as a significant blow to the remaining insurgents in the region.

Article continues after this 

“Although the Caraga Region has already been declared under Stable Internal Peace and Security, PRO-13 continues its efforts to encourage those who were misled by the group’s deceptive ideology to surrender, lay down their arms, and return to the folds of the law,” Suguilon said.

READ: Police recover arms cache in Cagayan forest

Article continues after this 

The confiscated firearms, ammunition, and explosives are now in the custody of the 2nd ADN PMFC for proper disposition./coa

World.title: Yangon Condo Raid Reveals Myanmar’s Cyber Scam Sector Thriving in Commercial Capital
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime says it has arrested 106 suspected online scammers in Yangon, signaling the country’s cyber-fraud epidemic has spread from the lawless borderlands to its largest city.

The regime announced Saturday that its forces raided Golden River Residence Condo in Yangon’s Thaketa Township on November 12, arresting 52 Chinese naionals, eight Vietnamese and 46 Myanmar citizens from multiple apartments.

The arrests come as Naypyitaw and Beijing trumpet crackdowns on cyber-fraud syndicates in notorious border scam hubs.

Those reportedly detained included a high-profile target of China’s Public Security Ministry — the first arrest of a warranted Chinese scammer in Myanmar in months. Also seized from the condo were over 120 computers and laptops and nearly 200 mobile phones.

Authorities said the gang ran online investment fraud schemes targeting Chinese, Japanese, South Korean and Indian citizens, while separate Telegram-based operations targeted victims in Brazil and Colombia through fake e-commerce platforms.

The raid came shortly after Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi pressed Myanmar investment minister Aung Kyaw Hoe to intensify efforts to combat scams and prevent a “resurgence of chaos” in Karen State’s Myawaddy crime hub on the Thai border.

Analysts say the Yangon bust signals a growing shift of Myanmar’s online scam industry from border enclaves to urban centers.

After the 2024 collapse of notorious fraud compounds in northern Shan State’s Laukkai and crackdowns along the Chinese and Thai borders, many scam syndicates dispersed in small, mobile operations through remote eastern and southern Shan, according to regime arrest reports and independent monitors.

However, many that had fled to Myawaddy have since moved deeper into the country under the protection of regime-aligned militias and other armed groups.

In September, 28 foreign and Myanmar nationals were arrested in Mandalay — the country’s second city — over an online gemstone scam involving Chinese, Indonesian and Malaysian suspects. The gang was charged with selling fake jade products via livestream and transferring the profits to accounts in Indonesia and Malaysia.

While the Nov. 12 raid was the first of its kind reported in Yangon, former fraudsters told The Irrawaddy that scam operations have long established a foothold in the commercial capital, targeting overseas victims through operations based in condominiums, housing estates and companies registered as legitimate businesses.

Analysts say enforcement efforts target low-level operators while overlooking the networks and militias behind the multibillion-dollar industry. Among them is the regime-aligned Karen Border Guard Force, whose Western-sanctioned leaders remain untouched even as the regime hails the demolition of scam compounds in Myawaddy.

World.title: ASEAN Seeks ‘Calibrated Engagement’ With Myanmar: Statement
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines—Southeast Asian leaders agreed Sunday on pursuing a “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar’s post-coup government, according to a joint statement, as the regional bloc seeks a path towards normalization.

Myanmar is still a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), but it has been frozen out of high-level meetings since a military junta seized power in a coup in 2021.

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize relations with Myanmar since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Bangkok has called for a “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar in an effort to implement ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC) plan aimed at ending the war between the military and a coalition of pro-democracy rebels and ethnic minority armed groups.

ASEAN leaders meeting in Manila adopted that language in calling for the pursuit of “a calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased and progress-based approach, taking into account developments on the ground,” according to the joint statement.

“Subject to sustained and concrete progress in the implementation of the 5PC by Myanmar, ASEAN may consider the gradual restoration of Myanmar’s full political representation,” the statement said.

The five-point plan has yielded little in the half-decade since it was agreed to, with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos conceding at a May summit he had not seen “any progress in Myanmar.”

On Sunday, in opening remarks at an ASEAN leaders’ retreat in Manila, he repeated a question he had posed to the group six months earlier: “What more can we do for Myanmar?”

“I hope our session leads to practical and forward-looking discussions on how we can further advance the implementation of the Five-Point Consensus, make our efforts more responsive to the realities on the ground, and support a peaceful, inclusive, Myanmar-owned and Myanmar-led process,” he said.

The ASEAN bloc’s rotating chair will pass at the end of this year from the Philippines to Singapore, a city-state analysts say opposes normalizing ties with Myanmar.

In 2028, it will be the turn of Thailand, which shares a long border with Myanmar and is leading the charge for closer relations.

“We believe it’s crucial to have someone at the table who can really talk on policy issues because engagement requires that they have someone who can really convey to us the position of Myanmar,” Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told AFP in Singapore on November 5.

“This is not about… recognizing… upgrading their position. But I think in reality, what is important is that we need someone at the table who can speak on behalf of Myanmar.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Seeks Closer Ties With Russian-Led Economic Bloc
World.content:
A delegation from the Eurasian Economic Commission (EEC) visited Naypyitaw this week, as Myanmar’s heavily sanctioned military regime intensifies its geopolitical pivot toward Russian-led multilateral blocs.

During the delegation’s visit—its third to the Myanmar capital—EEC Minister in charge of Integration and Macroeconomics Daniyar Imanaliev held talks with junta Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe on Wednesday.

According to regime media, discussions centered on securing observer status for Myanmar within the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Myanmar’s participation in Eurasian integration forums and exhibitions jointly held by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the EEC.

The EEC minister also held talks with the regime’s commerce and investment ministers, focusing on boosting bilateral cooperation across various sectors including manufacturing, agriculture, e-commerce, energy, transport and digital transformation. The Myanmar side discussed boosting exports of Myanmar’s agricultural and fishery products to five post-Soviet states, and invited investment from the countries in the Dawei Special Economic Zone in southern Myanmar.

Simultaneously, an EEC sub-delegation led by Dmitry Fesenko, head of the industrial development monitoring and analysis department, met with Deputy Industry Minister Dr. Aung Zeya to discuss technical cooperation regarding micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and agro-based industries.

The EAEU—comprising Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia—represents a critical bloc of junta allies. Naypyitaw initiated multi-sector dialogue with the EAEU and EEC in 2022, signing memorandums of understanding for closer cooperation in 2023.

Trade between Myanmar and the EAEU member states more than tripled between 2019 and 2024, surpassing US$1.5 billion, according to EAEU data released last year. Myanmar’s primary exports to the bloc include rice, coffee, palm oil and cocoa beans, while it imports EAEU fertilizers, consumer goods, machinery, metals, cement and pharmaceuticals. The official trade figures exclude weapons and military equipment supplied to the regime by Russia and Belarus, both major arms suppliers.

Despite these figures, regional analysts argue the junta’s Eurasian pivot is driven more by diplomatic survival than viable economic strategy.

“Compared to neighbors like China and Thailand, trade and investment from these [EAEU] countries is worlds apart. Even under the previous governments of U Thein Sein and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, how much investment actually came from them?” an analyst pointed out.

“If the regime wants to do business, it has a massive ASEAN market to tap. The regime’s focus on those faraway markets suggests its motivations are far more geopolitical than economic. They desperately want to join the Russian-led geopolitical bloc.”

Regime chief Min Aung Hlaing, who has publicly condemned major powers for utilizing economic sanctions and political pressure as violations of global norms, personally attended the 4th Eurasian Economic Forum in Belarus last year. During the summit, he made an urgent appeal for Myanmar to be granted EAEU observer status—a demand his foreign minister aggressively reiterated during Imanaliev’s visit this week.

Naypyitaw’s push to integrate into Moscow’s economic architecture mirrors the generals’ broader strategy to embed an isolated regime in non-Western multilateral organizations; in May 2023, Myanmar was formally recognized as a dialogue partner of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), led by China, Russia and India.

World.title: Myanmar’s Dwindling Debt to China, Scammers Nabbed in Shan, and More
World.content:
China no longer Myanmar’s biggest creditor

China is no Myanmar’s principal creditor, even though the military regime is bound for life and beyond by the money and favors it owes its protector. On paper at least, Japan is now Myanmar’s largest foreign government lender, while Beijing’s focus has shifted from extending new loans to managing existing debts.

According to the World Bank’s International Debt Statistics, Myanmar’s public and publicly guaranteed external debt stood at US$10.34 billion last year, down from around US$13.5 billion in 2021. Country-to-country debt accounted for $5.68 billion, with Japan holding $3.86 billion. China was owed only around US$1.5 billion, according to the World Bank’s creditor-by-creditor breakdown.

Prior to the political opening in 2011, China was effectively Myanmar’s only major lender, at interest rates as high as 4.5 percent. But after reforms began, Myanmar regained access to financing from institutions and partners including the Asian Development Bank and the Japan International Cooperation Agency on far more favorable terms.

“Myanmar will not borrow money from China any more if interest rates remain high,” then-deputy finance minister Maung Maung Win pledged in June 2020.

An AidData assessment released in May shows that China committed $14.7 billion in development finance to Myanmar between 2000 and 2023 through 505 projects. Nearly 92 percent took the form of loans, mainly from the Export-Import Bank of China and China Development Bank.

But AidData estimates that Myanmar’s outstanding debt to Chinese creditors had fallen to around US$1.7 billion by the end of 2024 or just about 19 percent of its external public debt.

The loans from China simply stopped. AidData found that China Eximbank, historically the largest lender, has not issued a new loan since 2019. While it was the COVID-19 pandemic that initially slowed lending, the trend has continued throughout the post-coup period.

The reason seems to be that the operating environment in Myanmar is deteriorating. Many planned Chinese-backed projects under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) are in conflict areas or regions entirely beyond the putschist regime’s control. Key trade routes, resource projects and infrastructure investments increasingly depend on arrangements with ethnic armed groups rather than Naypyitaw alone.

Bangladesh ties Rohingya crisis to Beijing’s Indian Ocean ambition

Dhaka has confirmed it is holding discussions with the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) that rules most of Myanmar’s Rakhine State as it seeks a solution to the long-running Rohingya refugee crisis—and that could force China’s hand in dealing with the new reality there.

At stake for Bangladesh is the burden of hosting over 1 million Rohingya refugees, most of whom fled the military’s brutal 2017 clearance operations. And since the AA controls entire Bangladeshi border with Myanmar, including Paletwa Township in neighboring Shin State, Dhaka has opened pragmatic dual-track discussions, engaging both the AA and the military regime after Naypyitaw’s repeated failures to facilitate the repatriation.

China, meanwhile, remains focused on its multi-billion-dollar projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC). The key project—a deep-sea port and special economic zone in Kyaukphyu—is designed to solve Beijing’s “Malacca Dilemma” by giving it maritime access to the Indian Ocean. Kyaukphyu also serves as the terminus for the twin oil and gas pipelines currently pumping energy to Yunnan Province. Yet the port project remains stalled, with Kyaukphyu under AA siege.

Dhaka is increasingly looking to China for leverage. During Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to Beijing in June—which closely followed a trip by Myanmar regime chief Min Aung Hlaing—Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed a tripartite China–Myanmar–Bangladesh economic corridor. That would provide Beijing with an alternative overland route to the Indian Ocean while Kyaukphyu remains in limbo.

In July, China’s ambassador to Bangladesh explicitly tied this proposed corridor to resolving the refugee crisis, suggesting it could facilitate Rohingya repatriation.

International scrutiny of the western front is intensifying. UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar Kelley Currie is currently in Bangladesh to assess the armed conflict in Rakhine and the deteriorating situation in the refugee camps. Yet Beijing’s diplomatic shield of the military usurpers in Naypyitaw remains firmly in place. Addressing the UN General Assembly’s Third Committee in late October, China’s representative reiterated that the crisis must be resolved bilaterally between Myanmar and Bangladesh, free from Western interference, a process China insists it is facilitating.

The International Court of Justice will rule next week whether the Myanmar military’s crackdown against the Rohingya people constituted a genocide.

No end to arrests of Chinese scammers in Shan

Some 759 foreigners were arrested between Aug. 1 and Oct. 31 for alleged involvement in scam operations in Shan State, and 502 were Chinese, regime media report.

Another 15 Chinese scammers were arrested on Monday in rural parts of Kyethi Township, southern Shan State. The township lies in an area that is contested by two rival ethnic armed groups: the Restoration Council of Shan State (RCSS) and the Shan State Progress Party (SSPP), whose headquarters are in nearby Wan Hai.

After a Chinese-led crackdown on industrial-scale scam compounds in the Kokang region of northern Shan State in late 2023, operations scattered across at least 17 townships in southern and eastern Shan, including Tangyan, Laihka, Tachileik and Muse. Others famously relocated to Karen State’s Myawaddy Township on the Thai border.

In other words, the syndicates adapted, their units becoming smaller and more nimble across scattered locations and moving further inland from prying eyes on the international border. Now they settle in places like Kyethi, where they can exploit lawlessness and administrative vacuums or collaborate with junta-aligned militias and armed groups.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: ASEAN Should Accept Myanmar Back at Diplomat Level: Bangkok
World.content:
BANGKOK—Myanmar’s foreign minister should be allowed back into meetings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) regional bloc, Thailand’s top diplomat said on Thursday after a visit to the war-torn country.

Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said his meetings with regime leader Min Aung Hlaing and others had revealed “a desire on the part of Myanmar to engage, to return to ASEAN.” But he said there was no talk of specific steps.

Myanmar has been excluded from high-level meetings of the 11-nation ASEAN since a 2021 military coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and triggered an ongoing civil war.

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize ties since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president earlier this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

“For Thailand, we believe that the next step is to have the foreign minister of Myanmar participate in the ASEAN meetings at the level of foreign minister,” Sihasak told reporters.

His comments came ahead of a meeting of ASEAN leaders starting Sunday in the Philippines.

Sihasak said he had also raised the “very urgent problem” of water pollution among tributaries of the Mekong River, which straddles five Southeast Asian countries and China, saying a working group would meet later this month.

Last week, authorities in northern Thailand suspended tap water production after arsenic levels at the waterworks intake was found to be 30 times higher than the safety standard. More than a dozen villages were affected by the suspension.

A subsequent field sample from the nearby Sai River measured arsenic at 25 times the safety standard, the government said.

Thai officials previously pinned the toxic sediment on wastewater from mining activity upstream in Myanmar.

Sihasak said he also raised the issue of a spillover of violence into Thailand.

World.title: Myanmar Faces Year of Blackouts as Regime Admits 30% Power Shortfall
World.content:
Myanmar’s rotating power cuts will remain in place through 2027, with generation expected to meet only 70 percent of national demand, Deputy Energy Minister Aye Kyaw announced Wednesday.

Addressing the regime’s rubber-stamp parliament, he said next summer’s 24-hour electricity demand is forecast at 5,010 MW, while generation capacity is only 3,540 MW.

“That’s why we need to continue the load shedding measures,” he said.

Despite having the poorest electricity access in the region, Myanmar made significant progress in grid connectivity under the National League for Democracy’s 15-year National Electrification Plan in 2015. By 2020, more than half of households had electricity access, and the NLD’s World Bank-backed plan aimed to achieve nationwide electrification by 2030.

However, the plan was scrapped after the 2021 coup, and regime mismanagement has since triggered rolling power outages across the country.

The World Bank says reliable supply has dropped sharply since the military takeover, affecting nearly half of connected households — with 41.6 percent receiving only enough electricity for basic lighting and phone charging, and 9.1 percent getting no electricity at all.

It blames the deepening generation crisis on the suspension of LNG power plants, declining domestic gas production, hydropower stress, infrastructure damage, and stalled investment.

In response, the regime reintroduced nationwide rolling blackouts, leaving residents in even major cities struggling to manage households and livelihoods.

“We have to be ready to fill up the water, cook meals, and iron our clothes the moment the power comes back on,” Ko Thant Zin from Insein Township in the suburbs of Yangon told the Irrawaddy.

He said the electricity supply rotates between four hours on and four hours off.

“Under the civilian government, the roads were bright with lights. Now, I have to open my eyes wide to see the way ahead while driving at night,” he commented.

The deputy energy minister told citizens to install solar panels if they want a reliable supply. However, import curbs and surging prices have put solar options out of reach for most urban residents.

“Forget about solar panels, most people can’t even afford a portable power pack,” a resident of downtown Yangong’s Botahtaung Township told The Irrawaddy. “Prices have been skyrocketing because of import restrictions.”

He added that power cuts would cause major suffering during the El Niño heatwave forecast for November through January.

“I can’t imagine how we will get through next summer,” he said, reacting to the rationing announcement. “It will be especially tough for young children and the elderly.”

Demand driven by outages has seen the price of solar panels surge to a record high. Yangon residents said a household solar power system now costs at least 10 million kyats (around US $4,760), putting it beyond the reach of ordinary families.

Last month, Yangon City authorities mandated that all commercial projects and high-rise buildings must install solar power systems to operate elevators and emergency lighting, as part of a nationwide push for solar amid deepening power blackouts.

The World Bank says chronic power shortages remain one of the main constraints on Myanmar’s economy, limiting its recovery and keeping poverty persistently high.

The deputy energy minister also announced plans to develop two 55 MW small-modular-reactors in cooperation with Russia’s atomic agency, ROSATOM, starting in fiscal 2028-29. The project is slated for completion in fiscal 2035-36 but locations have yet to be announced.

World.title: Three Years After Operation 1027, Hopang Transformed Under Wa Rule
World.content:
Friday marks three years since Hopang in the Wa Self-Administered Zone experienced its first taste of the joint ethnic offensive known as Operation 1027, when drones deployed by the Brotherhood Alliance bombed a monastery sheltering retreating Myanmar military personnel from nearby Kunlong base.

For the Myanmar military, which had controlled Hopang for decades, the drone strike was an early warning that its grip on the town was nearing an end. For the United Wa State Army (UWSA), it presented an opportunity to gain one of the most important towns in Wa territory without firing a shot.

Less than two months after the Nov. 13 drone attack, forces of the Brotherhood Alliance—which grouped the Arakan Army, Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA)—and allied groups entered Hopang with little resistance. Rather than holding the town themselves, they quickly handed it over to their ally, the UWSA.

Operation 1027, which inflicted one of the most devastating military setbacks in the Myanmar military’s history, had begun on Oct. 27, 2023, in Chinshwehaw, a border town just 8 km from Hopang. Just 19 km away, Kunlong, a key town on a China-Myanmar trade route, also fell after sustained drone attacks by alliance forces.

As Kunlong collapsed, its commander, officers and wounded soldiers fled to Hopang.

“A battalion commander and a soldier entered the monastery building and pleaded for shelter,” recalled a witness who was in the compound. “They told the abbot they had been under drone attacks for four days, and had only managed to retreat after receiving supporting fire.”

That same night, drones struck the monastery.

For Hopang residents, who had watched the fighting around Kunlong from hilltop pagodas, the attack on the monastery signaled that war was coming closer. By the next morning, many were fleeing the town, leaving their homes and shops behind.

Some local drivers found themselves ferrying displaced families back and forth, while others stayed behind to guard their properties. Residents feared not only a potential urban battle similar to the fighting in Kunlong, but also the prospect of Myanmar military airstrikes.

One restaurant owner recalled watching looters load crates of beer from his shop onto vehicles through CCTV cameras while he was fleeing.

Among those who fled were a monk who was injured in the November 13 drone attack, as well as health workers from a public hospital in Hopang.

Hopang was home to a military battalion and a police station, but all the surrounding towns including Kunlong and Chinshwehaw were controlled by the Brotherhood Alliance. At this point, Hopang was effectively isolated.

When MNDAA troops entered Hopang in early January 2024, the remaining military and police units reportedly surrendered with little resistance. Under a prior arrangement between the MNDAA and the UWSA, control of the town was then transferred to the Wa army.

Unlike Lashio, Laukkai, Chinshwehaw or Kunlong, Hopang largely escaped major battle damage. Yet residents say the town has since undergone a different kind of transformation, one increasingly shaped by Chinese capital and Wa administration.

The ethnically diverse town, home to Shan, Wa, Bamar, Kachin, Ta’ang and other communities, was once known for its Buddhist, Christian and traditional ethnic festivals. Today, residents say casinos, bars, hotels, massage parlors and prostitution-related businesses funded by Chinese investors have proliferated.

Some residents also complain of heavy taxation and a justice system that includes public executions, practices rarely seen under previous administrations.

The yuan now dominates much of the local economy, with residents increasingly pricing goods in the Chinese currency rather than kyats. In the healthcare arena, expensive Chinese-run private hospitals have emerged alongside the only public hospital.

Over the past three years, rumors have repeatedly surfaced that the UWSA will return Hopang to the regime. Residents say they see no sign that this is imminent, however.

The town, which participated in the 2010, 2015 and 2020 elections, did not take part in the regime-organized 2025 poll and is absent from the list of constituencies scheduled to be put to a vote in additional elections scheduled for April 2027.

Recently, regime Defense Minister and peace negotiator Lieutenant General Yar Pyae visited Panghsang, the UWSA headquarters. There was no indication that Hopang’s status was discussed during his meetings with Wa leaders, however.

While the UWSA remained officially neutral during Operation 1027, it emerged among the campaign’s biggest beneficiaries. Without openly joining the offensive, it gained full control of Hopang and Panlong, while also securing partial control along with the Myanmar military over Tangyan, a strategically important town on the route to Lashio, the largest town in northern Shan.

Three years after the first drone bombs fell on Hopang, the town has changed beyond recognition for longtime residents.

During Operation 1027, the MNDAA and TNLA went on to seize almost the whole of northern Shan State including the capital Lashio and all vital trade routes with China.

However, under strong Chinese pressure, in 2025 the ethnic armies were forced to halt fighting the Myanmar military and hand back several liberated towns to the regime.

World.title: Myanmar’s Coup President Barred From Upcoming 49th ASEAN Summit
World.content:
The Philippines announced Wednesday that Myanmar regime leaders remain barred from joining the 49th ASEAN summit and high-level meetings in Manila from November 15 to 17, upholding a ban imposed after the 2021 military coup.

Myanmar will instead be represented by the Director-General of its ASEAN affairs department, according to a statement issued by Manila’s Department of Foreign Affairs.

“We welcome this official confirmation that there is no place [at the summit] for junta leader Min Aung Hlaing,” Khin Ohmar, a prominent Myanmar democracy activist and founder of the Progressive Voice human rights foundation, told The Irrawaddy.

“ASEAN made the right decision in line with its principles. We have been demanding that no junta member be permitted to join the summit.”

She added that ASEAN would have sacrificed its credibility and responsibility to the people of Myanmar by inviting the junta leader, who faces a genocide ruling at the international court later this month.

Confirmation that the ban remains in place came after domestic and international rights groups warned the regional bloc against legitimizing a regime that is intensifying violence against civilians.

On Monday, the Special Advisory Council for Myanmar (SAC-M) and ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights urged regional leaders “to immediately confirm” that Min Aung Hlaing and his junta cohorts would be excluded from the summit.

It also called on ASEAN leaders to adopt “measurable benchmarks for compliance” with the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC), along with “a series of escalating punitive steps” if the junta continues to defy the peace plan.

Regime leaders were barred from regional summits for failing to implement the April 2021 consensus, including an immediate end to violence and constructive dialogue with the opposition.

The regime largely ignored the 5PC before formally rejecting it in a July 2026 vote by its rubber-stamp parliament. However, it continues to pay lip service to the plan.

During his latest talks with ASEAN special envoy Theresa Lazaro in Naypyitaw in October, Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe claimed the regime was implementing the 5PC “without compromising its national interests and sovereignty in accordance with its own roadmaps and objectives.”

The UN reports that at least 8,384 civilians have been killed by regime forces since the coup, in an escalating military campaign that has also left over 4 million displaced. Meanwhile, nearly 23,000 political prisoners remain in detention, including deposed democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

However, ASEAN members began bilateral engagement with the regime after it rebranded in civilian clothing in April following elections widely condemned as a sham. Since then, coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing has been invited on official visits to bloc members Laos, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Malaysia.

Both Malaysia—once a vocal critic of the regime—and Thailand drew widespread condemnation from rights groups for hosting the junta leader.

Both nations defended the visits as pragmatic re-engagement in search of solutions to challenges they face, such as refugee repatriation for Malaysia and transborder issues for Thailand.

Critics have warned that bi-lateral engagement may sway a collective ASEAN decision to reintegrate the regime.

However, the move to uphold the summit ban marks a major setback for a junta desperate for legitimacy on the international stage.

“This is a huge blow to the junta. I am sure it has not expected this kind of decision,” Khin Ohmar commented. “It also signals that the junta’s election farce failed to confer legitimacy, since even those advocating its return to the international stage want to avoid being seen as complicit in its violence.”

World.title: IMF: Kazakhstan’s Construction Push Must Balance Growth Needs With Inflation Risks
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s planned large-scale construction and infrastructure investment program could sustain economic growth but also add to inflationary pressures, particularly if productivity gains do not match increased public spending, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

At a press briefing on Nov. 17, Amina Lahreche, chief of the IMF mission to Kazakhstan, presented preliminary findings from the fund’s Article IV consultation, projecting economic growth of 4.6% in 2026 and 4.8% in 2027. The IMF expects inflation to remain elevated despite recent progress. It declined to 9.2% in October, but the fund projects it will reach 9.6% by the end of 2026 and 8.4% by the end of 2027, gradually converging toward the National Bank of Kazakhstan’s 5% target by 2029.

Lahreche attributed persistent price pressures to strong domestic demand, increases in regulated prices and elevated inflation expectations. She said a tighter and better-coordinated policy mix would be necessary to bring inflation down while supporting sustainable growth.

Construction spending could fuel inflation

The IMF’s projections account for the government’s planned withdrawal of approximately 6.5 trillion tenge ($14.3 billion) from the National Fund through 2029 to finance infrastructure and construction projects. The government has also proposed declaring 2027 the Year of Nationwide Large-Scale Construction as part of a broader push to modernize infrastructure and stimulate economic activity. Asked how the planned spending could affect inflation, Lahreche said withdrawals from the National Fund would inject additional financing into the economy and sustain demand.

“Demand pressures are largely coming from the public sector spending this coming year. And withdrawals from the National Fund are going to push additional financing into the economy,” she said.

However, the IMF does not question Kazakhstan’s need for large-scale public investment, given its infrastructure needs and development ambitions. The key, Lahreche said, is ensuring that spending is efficient and translates into tangible economic gains.

“Public investment is necessary in Kazakhstan. This is a growing country. It has needs, but it’s important to spend efficiently so that you support the economy, support growth and productivity, but avoid spending too fast and having losses because productivity is not efficient,” she said.

She emphasized the importance of careful project selection, sound planning, reliable information and accountability mechanisms, including audits, to assess how public funds are spent and identify areas for improvement.

The challenge is ensuring that increased investment supports productivity rather than simply adding to domestic demand. Without corresponding productivity gains, higher spending could complicate efforts to bring inflation under control and erode household purchasing power.

“With productivity gains, there’s more income that can be distributed in the economy without necessitating an increasing price,” Lahreche said.

The IMF also called for closer adherence to expenditure and National Fund transfer rules, stronger non-oil revenue and better coordination of state-owned enterprises’ activities with the government budget to prevent excessive demand pressures and crowding out private investment. It noted that well-selected infrastructure and digital investments could also lift growth through stronger productivity gains.

CPC disruptions weigh on oil outlook

The IMF expects Kazakhstan’s oil sector to remain a limited contributor to economic growth in 2027, partly reflecting disruptions to oil production and exports in 2026. Asked whether the fund had considered further attacks on the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC), a key export route for Kazakh oil, Lahreche said the projections already incorporated the impact of existing disruptions.

“We know that these disruptions will have implications also for 2027, which is why we see that the oil sector will not be a major engine of growth in 2027,” she said.

However, further disruptions remain part of the IMF’s risk assessment rather than its baseline forecast. The fund identified possible additional interruptions to oil production and exports, lower hydrocarbon prices and weaker growth among Kazakhstan’s major trading partners as external risks to its economic outlook.

Lahreche said the IMF could not predict whether further disruptions would occur, but acknowledged that additional shocks could affect the economy.

With oil output expected to remain broadly unchanged, the fund sees non-oil activity, supported by public spending, as the main driver of growth next year.

Private sector development remains key to diversification

The IMF reiterated that structural reforms to strengthen the private sector remain essential to Kazakhstan’s long-term economic diversification. Lahreche said productivity improvements and sustainable growth would depend on creating conditions for private companies to expand and compete. Among the priorities, she identified privatization, improvements to the business environment, stronger competition and deeper capital markets to provide businesses with better access to financing.

“We think that’s very important, because as we look to the growth over the long term, it is really the private sector that is a source of productivity enhancement and long-term sustainable growth,” she said.

The IMF also recommended maintaining a sufficiently restrictive monetary policy until inflation approaches its target, while preserving financial stability safeguards as mortgage lending expands. The banking sector remains well-capitalized, liquid and profitable, according to the fund. However, it advised continued monitoring of faster-growing lending segments and the use of state-backed credit guarantees.

Overall, the IMF said Kazakhstan needs a more disciplined public sector spending approach, coordinated monetary and fiscal policies, and structural reforms to support private sector-led growth. The IMF’s final assessment will be presented in its staff report, expected to be published in January 2027

World.title: Kazakhstan Discusses $50 Million Logistics Hub and Digital Middle Corridor Pilot with Belgian Companies
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is discussing a $50 million investment in a transport and logistics hub in the Zhetysu Region and a 90-day pilot project to digitize freight operations along the Middle Corridor, as the country seeks to expand its transit capacity and improve cargo movement between China and Europe.

The initiatives were discussed during meetings between Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi and senior executives of three Belgian companies – Sarens Group, Ahlers Logistics and BIM e-Solutions – during his working visit to Belgium on Nov. 16, according to the ministry.

During talks with Hendrik Sarens, Senior Advisor to Sarens Group, and Matthias Sarens, Construction Director of the Transport and Logistics Center (TLC) at the Khorgos Customs and Logistics Platform, the parties reviewed plans for a $50 million investment project to establish a transport and logistics hub in Kazakhstan’s Zhetysu Region.

The project envisages building a 2.1-kilometer bypass road, temporary storage facilities and specialized infrastructure for handling heavy cargo. Once operational, the hub is expected to increase capacity at the Nur Zholy border crossing, ease freight congestion and strengthen Kazakhstan’s role as a transit link between China and Europe.

Separate meetings with Dave van den Bos, CEO of Ahlers Logistics, and Michael Barrie, Head of BIM e-Solutions, focused on expanding logistics operations and introducing digital technologies along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor.

One proposal under consideration is a 90-day Digital Middle Corridor pilot project. It aims to introduce digital freight tracking, facilitate customs data exchange, reduce border delays and improve transparency in cross-border transport operations.

The discussions reflect Kazakhstan’s efforts to combine infrastructure investment with digital solutions to improve the Middle Corridor’s capacity, efficiency and competitiveness as a major Eurasian transit route.

World.title: Kazakhstan Turns to Strategic Mining to Boost Crypto Reserves
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is introducing a new model of cryptocurrency mining that links access to electricity with the accumulation of a national strategic crypto reserve. The rules governing strategic digital mining, approved by the government on July 18, took effect on July 28, allowing large-scale miners to secure electricity quotas at regulated prices in exchange for transferring part of their mined digital assets to the state reserve.

The framework introduces an alternative to the general mining regime, allowing eligible operators to sign long-term electricity supply agreements with power generation companies. The government has allocated a 300-megawatt electricity quota for the program, provided through the Ekibastuz GRES-1 power plant.

The initiative is part of Kazakhstan’s broader effort to formalize its digital asset industry, attract investment in computing infrastructure and strengthen its position in the regional digital economy.

How the new mining regime works

Under the general framework, digital miners purchase electricity under standard market conditions in accordance with Kazakhstan’s law on electricity, according to a legal analysis published by KPMG Law Kazakhstan.

The strategic mining regime, however, provides access to electricity quotas at prices not exceeding the applicable ceiling tariff of the power generation company. In 2026, these tariffs range from 1.46 to 56.63 tenge per kilowatt-hour, depending on the power producer’s category. In return, miners must transfer part of their mined digital assets to the National Strategic Crypto Reserve.

The Kazakh Energy Ministry establishes ceiling tariffs for power generation companies every seven years.

The key distinction is the electricity supply arrangement. Strategic miners can receive an allocated electricity quota and enter into long-term direct agreements with power generation companies, while a portion of their digital assets contributes to the national reserve.

In a comment to The Astana Times, the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development outlined the main requirements for obtaining strategic miner status.

According to the ministry, participation in the program is voluntary, and the regulations do not establish a minimum investment threshold in monetary terms. However, applicants must have data centers and computing equipment that meet specific infrastructure and technical requirements, which entails investment in establishing or acquiring the necessary facilities.

“The main requirement is ownership of a digital mining data center with a capacity of at least 150 megawatts. The data center must be located at a single address. Combining the capacities of several data centers located at different addresses to meet this requirement is not permitted,” the ministry said.

Applicants must also have technical specifications for connecting to electricity grids through transformer substations with a voltage of 35 kilovolts or higher and an authorized capacity of at least one megawatt. Each unit of computing equipment must have a processing capacity of at least 150 terahashes per second (TH/s).

Therefore, the investment required to participate is determined by the data center’s capacity and the specifications of its installed equipment rather than by a fixed financial threshold.

The regulations also establish additional eligibility criteria. Applicants must have no outstanding debts on mandatory payments or encumbrances on their property. They must also have at least two agreements with telecommunications operators, a service center located on the premises and qualified personnel.

Electricity allocation and state oversight

The ministry said the strategic mining mechanism provides electricity within an approved allocation.

“Under the regulations, a quota of 300 megawatts has been allocated for these purposes by the Bulat Nurzhanov Ekibastuz GRES-1 power plant. The ministry has approved the composition and regulations of the commission responsible for strategic digital mining. The commission includes representatives of the Ministry of Energy and KEGOC, ensuring that electricity allocation issues are reviewed with the participation of the authorized energy regulator and the national grid operator,” the ministry said.

When reviewing each application, the commission checks whether sufficient electricity capacity remains available within the allocated quota. Signing a 10-year electricity supply agreement does not automatically grant miners the right to increase their consumption without limits.

Any increase in the allocated capacity requires a separate review by the commission. Applicants must submit documentation confirming the relevant technical connection specifications, the availability of an automated commercial electricity metering system, specialized automatic load-disconnection equipment and a telecommunications system compatible with those used by the system operator and electricity transmission company.

The regulations also require separate accounting of electricity consumption and monitoring of compliance with allocated quotas. Electricity supply can be restricted or suspended in cases provided for by law and the relevant agreements.

In practical terms, electricity demand is managed through quotas, technical connection requirements, consumption monitoring and load restriction mechanisms.

A regulated industry

The new mechanism builds on Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to formalize digital mining.

The digital assets law, adopted in early 2023, introduced the legal definitions of digital mining and mining pools, as well as a licensing framework for the first time.

Since 2024, the Committee for Digital Assets and Breakthrough Technologies under the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development has served as the licensing authority. The industry has since come under an expanding system of registries and regulations. By mid-2026, the rules governing mining pool accreditation had been revised a second time, bringing the market closer to regulated-industry standards.

Today, a legally operating mining company must obtain a license, register every piece of equipment in the state registry and conduct its operations exclusively through an accredited Kazakh mining pool.

According to the ministry’s latest figures, 70 digital mining entities currently operate in Kazakhstan. The number of industry participants fluctuates throughout the year. At certain points in 2025, the figure exceeded 70 before declining to its current level. The country also has five accredited mining pools, while more than 470,000 units of digital mining equipment have been registered.

Cybersecurity challenges

Yevgeny Pitolin, founder of Heartland technology consultancy, said the development of strategic digital mining and large-scale computing centers represents a promising direction for Kazakhstan.

“This creates new opportunities for the digital economy, investment attraction and the development of technological infrastructure. However, as these projects expand, the approach to security must evolve as well,” Pitolin told The Astana Times.

He emphasized that cybersecurity is no longer an optional addition but an essential requirement for developing any large-scale digital infrastructure. Security measures must be incorporated into projects from the outset and treated as equally important as technological and economic considerations.

“The more data is concentrated in one place, the greater the interest from malicious actors. Common risks include ransomware attacks, data and computing resource theft, industrial espionage, as well as infiltration of systems through contractors and software providers,” Pitolin said.

The threat extends beyond data security. A computing center is a complex technological system that includes electricity supply, cooling and network infrastructure. A malfunction or cyberattack targeting any of these components could disrupt the operation of the entire facility.

“Kazakhstan has a certain foundation for countering these threats, including specialized professionals, information security companies and experience in responding to cyber incidents. However, the emergence of large-scale computing centers will require further development of these capabilities and stricter requirements for infrastructure operators,” he said.

Among the immediate priorities, Pitolin identified continuous monitoring, access controls, regular vulnerability assessments, backup systems for critical components and the ability to respond quickly to cyberattacks.

“I believe the country’s digital development must go hand in hand with stronger cybersecurity. This will largely determine how secure and resilient Kazakhstan’s digital infrastructure will be in the long term,” Pitolin said.

World.title: Kazakhstan, EU Discuss Strengthening Interregional Connectivity and Transport Cooperation
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and the European Union have discussed ways to strengthen transport, logistics and energy cooperation, with a focus on improving connectivity between Europe and Asia and advancing the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor.

The discussions took place at the Second Ministerial Meeting on Interregional Connectivity between the European Union, the Black Sea region, the South Caucasus and Central Asia in Brussels on Nov. 16. The meeting brought together foreign ministers from EU member states and partner countries, as well as European Commission representatives.

Speaking at the meeting, Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi highlighted the development of the country’s transit and transport potential and infrastructure modernization as strategic priorities outlined by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, the ministry reported.

He emphasized the importance of developing the Middle Corridor as a key link in strengthening trade and transport connections between Europe and Asia, reaffirming Kazakhstan’s commitment to closer cooperation with European and regional partners.

Particular attention was given to cooperation with the European Union under its Global Gateway initiative, which offers opportunities to attract investment, modernize transport infrastructure and implement mutually beneficial joint projects.

Tileuberdi stressed the need to simplify logistics procedures and develop an efficient, resilient and sustainable transport network connecting the two regions.

The meeting also addressed prospects for closer energy cooperation, including cross-border renewable energy projects and measures to strengthen regional energy security.

World.title: Almaty Open Named ATP 250 Tournament of Year for First Time
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Almaty Open has been named the ATP 250 Tournament of the Year for the first time at the ATP Awards 2026, earning recognition as the best among 29 tournaments in the category.

The tournament outperformed two long-established Swedish competitions, the Nordea Open in Bastad and the Bybit Stockholm Open, reported the Kazakhstan Tennis Federation’s press service.

The award was decided through a vote by professional tennis players, who assessed the quality of tournament organization and the conditions provided for competitors. The recognition reflects Kazakhstan’s growing presence on the international tennis scene and strengthens the country’s position as a host of major sporting events.

The tournament’s history in Kazakhstan dates back to 2020, when an ATP 250 event was first held in Astana under the name Astana Open. In 2022, it was temporarily upgraded to ATP 500 status, attracting some of the world’s leading players. Since 2024, the competition has been held in Almaty as the Almaty Open.

In 2026, Almaty hosted the tournament for the third time, with Almaty Arena serving as its main venue. Organizers have focused on developing infrastructure, improving service quality and providing comfortable conditions for players and their teams.

Players praised the practice courts, relaxation and recovery areas, accommodation at a wellness complex overlooking the mountains, and a culinary program led by chef Fabien Ferré, who holds three Michelin stars.

Yuri Polsky, general director of the Almaty Open and vice president of the Kazakhstan Tennis Federation, said the award was a great honour for the tournament team and recognition of the joint efforts of organisers, partners and sponsors.

“It is a great honour for us that Almaty Open has been recognised as the ATP Tournament of the Year following an independent assessment by players. We are deeply grateful to the players for their trust, especially those who return to Almaty year after year. (…) We would also like to express our gratitude to the Almaty city administration for its assistance in holding the competition and for helping create the conditions needed to host an international sporting event of this level,” he said.

According to him, this recognition will provide additional motivation for the entire team to continue developing the tournament with even greater dedication.

The ATP Awards 2026 also recognised the Rolex Shanghai Masters in the ATP Masters 1000 category and the Qatar ExxonMobil Open in Doha in the ATP 500 category as Tournaments of the Year.

Seven other tournaments received the Standards of Excellence award following the players’ vote for their high level of organization and compliance with ATP standards.

World.title: Who Is Designing Kazakhstan’s Future?
World.content:
A country may have abundant natural resources, ambitious strategies and individual technological achievements. But sustainable development begins with the capacity to turn scientific thought into working industries, new sectors, modern infrastructure and a decent quality of life. This work cannot be done without the engineering community.

When the future of Kazakhstan’s economy is discussed, the usual topics are growth rates, investment, government programs and new enterprises. Far less often do we ask who determines the country’s technological future. Which industries must we build today so that, twenty years from now, we do not depend on other countries’ technological solutions? What engineering competencies must emerge in the regions so that they become not merely sites for hosting factories, but centers for developing and deploying new technologies?

These questions are especially relevant in light of the tasks set by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev: diversifying the economy and developing manufacturing, artificial intelligence, infrastructure and human capital. The outcome depends not only on investment volume, but also on the country’s ability to turn scientific knowledge into its own technologies and competitive products.

Kazakhstan marks 35 years of independence. The National Academy of Engineering of Kazakhstan (NAE RK) also celebrates its 35th anniversary. The coincidence of these dates is symbolic: the emergence of domestic engineering science is inseparable from the formation of the economic and technological sovereignty.

The historical highlights

The academy’s history began in November 1991, when scientist Umirbek Dzholdasbekov initiated the establishment of the Kazakh Branch of the Engineering Academy of the USSR; it was later transformed into the National Academy of Engineering.

For almost three decades, NAE RK President Academician Bakytzhan Zhumagulov has strengthened its scientific and public standing. Under his leadership, the academy has become a sustainable engineering community that brings together leading scientists and representatives of universities, industry and regional scientific schools and can serve as a platform for professional discussion of the country’s strategic development tasks.

Knowledge into industrial value

The effectiveness of engineering science cannot be measured solely by the number of publications, patents or conferences held. Its true value is revealed when a development moves from the laboratory to the industrial site, creates jobs, reduces production costs and generates new added value.

We have statistics on industrial output, investment, employment and infrastructure. But these indicators do not fully capture a territory’s ability to master new technologies independently, create innovative products and sustain complex production processes. A large deposit does not mean a region is ready for deep processing of raw materials. That requires accessible energy, water resources, transport infrastructure, modern technology, skilled specialists and scientific support.

Without a comprehensive engineering assessment, even substantial investment can entrench a raw-materials specialization without creating new sources of economic growth. It therefore seems worthwhile to develop a National Engineering Readiness Index of the regions – the Engineering Readiness Index (ERI) – which would assess not only existing industrial potential, but also regions’ capacity to adopt advanced technologies, create new products, develop engineering competencies, improve resource efficiency and modernize enterprises.

The next step could be a National Engineering Map of Kazakhstan’s Future – a tool for long-term technological forecasting that brings together the regions’ strategic missions, promising industries, technology readiness levels, infrastructure constraints, investment needs and a forecast of demand for engineering personnel. If the index shows how ready a region is for technological development, the engineering map should identify the solutions needed to realize its potential. This shifts the focus from the traditional question, “where should investment be directed?” to a more meaningful one: “what kind of economy do we want to build in this territory twenty years from now, and what must be done today to achieve it?”

Engineering the green transition

This approach is particularly important in implementing Kazakhstan’s Carbon Neutrality Strategy to 2060. It should be seen not only as fulfilling climate commitments, but also as an opportunity to renew the economy’s technological base thoroughly. Kazakhstan can mainly purchase foreign technologies and pay for their installation and maintenance, or it can use the environmental transition as an incentive to develop its own engineering schools, applied research and equipment manufacturing.

New requirements for industry are also taking shape internationally. The Paris Agreement aims to hold the increase in global temperature well below 2 degrees Celsius and continue efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees Celsius. For Kazakhstan, these goals mean reducing emissions, modernizing energy-intensive sectors and improving the competitiveness of export products. Kazakhstan’s updated Nationally Determined Contribution for the period to 2035 provides for a 17% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions from the 1990 level, and up to 25% subject to international support.

These tasks take on particular urgency at COP31 in Antalya this November. Kazakhstan has presented initiatives on developing climate finance, renewable energy, methane emission reduction, digitalization of energy infrastructure and international cooperation on carbon markets. In particular, a national climate investment platform is under discussion, intended to help prepare and attract financing for environmentally significant projects.

At the same time, the practical effectiveness of climate policy depends largely on the economic instruments in place. Kazakhstan has operated a greenhouse gas emissions trading system since 2013. According to the Zhasyl Damu, it covers 145 enterprises and 234 allowance-bearing installations. The carbon budget parameters call for a reduction from 163.6 million tonnes of CO2 in 2026 to 148.1 million tonnes by 2030. These figures reflect the scale of the transformation ahead and the need to give industry access to technological solutions.

Against the backdrop of the new climate commitments, the shift from carbon regulation as a tool for accounting for emissions to real technological modernization of industry takes on particular importance. This requires combining the potential of the emissions trading system, the adoption of best available techniques, engineering expertise and investment mechanisms. The scientific and engineering community can offer concrete solutions to direct financial resources toward the technological renewal of enterprises, with measurable environmental and economic results. The National Academy of Engineering could play an important role in shaping such solutions by providing independent assessments of technologies, their industrial applicability and investment effectiveness.

External economic challenges must also be considered. The European Union’s introduction of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) heightens the importance of reliable data on product carbon intensity and the efficiency of production technologies. For Kazakh exporters, this is not only an additional reporting requirement but also an incentive to reduce specific emissions, improve energy efficiency and modernize technology. Without its own engineering and research base, adapting to the new conditions will increase dependence on external technological solutions.

Strengthening the academy’s strategic role

The National Academy of Engineering has an opportunity to strengthen its role as an independent scientific and technological partner of the state. This is not about replacing the functions of government bodies or existing expert organizations. Instead, what is needed is an additional professional mechanism to assess the long-term technological consequences of major investment decisions, the prospects for adopting domestic developments, the risks of technological dependence, and industry’s need for new competencies.

One of the initiatives can be an annual national report, Kazakhstan’s Technological Readiness: Regions, Industry, Engineering Personnel. A report could combine an assessment of regions’ engineering readiness, the maturity of promising technologies, the state of engineering education, the results of commercializing scientific research, the possibilities for implementing best available techniques (BAT), and a forecast of the economy’s need for specialists. It would be not only an analytical document but also the basis for a permanent professional dialogue among the state, industry, universities and the scientific community.

However, no technological forecast will be realized without people able to bring it to life. Today, the workforce training system is largely oriented toward the needs of the existing economic structure, whereas new production areas require competencies that are only now taking shape. Artificial intelligence, robotics, new materials, hydrogen technologies, digital production management and environmental modernization are changing the content of engineering work. Therefore, it is necessary to forecast not only the number of specialists but also the future structure of engineering competencies, develop joint programs between universities and enterprises, and expand opportunities for retraining current specialists and for practical training at industrial sites.

Over 35 years, the National Academy of Engineering has moved from preserving the scientific and technical potential of a young independent state to helping resolve complex issues of industrial, innovative and environmental development. Today a new historic task arises before it: to help shape Kazakhstan’s technological future by bringing together knowledge, experience, universities’ capabilities, and the needs of real production.

A state’s competitiveness is determined not by the number of strategies developed or even the volume of investment attracted, but by its ability to turn knowledge into new technologies, enterprises and production opportunities. Kazakhstan needs an economy in which regions not only extract resources but also create knowledge-intensive products; universities not only train specialists but also help develop technologies; and engineering organizations not only support decisions already made but also help define the country’s development directions.

Whereas engineers were once more often asked how to build what had already been planned, today they must help decide what needs to be built, why that in particular, and what result future generations will receive.

This is a new historic mission of the National Academy of Engineering.

Because a state’s wealth is determined not only by what lies beneath its soil, but by what the knowledge, talent and engineering minds of its citizens can create.

The author is Doctor of Economic Sciences Gulbazar Mediyeva, the Vice President of the National Academy of Engineering, and Scientific Adviser to the International Center for Green Technologies and Investment Projects.
