World.title: Tokayev Meets Central Election Commission Chairman Ahead of Nov. 29 Maslikhat Elections
World.content:
ASTANA — President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with Chairman of the Central Election Commission Nurlan Abdirov to discuss preparations for early elections of deputies to maslikhats at all levels, scheduled for Nov. 29, according to the presidential press service.

Abdirov briefed Tokayev on the work of election authorities ahead of the vote. Tokayev stressed the importance of conducting the elections in line with the constitutional principle of Law and Order and ensuring equal conditions for all candidates and political parties.

He also noted that the upcoming renewal of the deputy corps would significantly strengthen the work of local representative bodies.

Earlier, while inspecting polling stations across the country’s regions, Abdirov also said Kazakhstan has 228 maslikhats at various levels, with more than 9,000 candidates competing for 3,447 seats.

He highlighted efforts to prepare members of district election commissions, including training seminars and two rounds of testing designed to assess both the quality of training organised by territorial election commissions and the effectiveness of the seminars themselves.

“I instructed territorial election commissions to continue training election commission members in the remaining time before the elections. This is important to ensure that the electoral campaign is conducted in strict compliance with the law, with openness and transparency,” Abdirov said.

He added that the Central Election Commission was paying particular attention to organizing training seminars during visits to the regions.

World.title: Kazakhstan Seeks to Develop Middle Corridor as Green Trade Route Between Asia and Europe
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to strengthen the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor, as a key trade link between Asia and Europe, focusing on increasing freight volumes, digitalizing logistics and introducing environmental standards.

These priorities were discussed at a Nov. 16 special session organized by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Trade and Integration and QazTrade during the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Türkiye.

The Middle Corridor is becoming an increasingly important route for international trade. Stretching nearly 7,000 kilometers, it passes through Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea and the countries of the South Caucasus, providing access to European markets. Cargo delivery along the route takes an average of 15 to 20 days, making it a competitive alternative to traditional maritime shipping.

Freight volumes have increased significantly in recent years. In 2020, the route carried 800,000 tons of cargo, compared with 4.5 million tons in 2024, representing more than a fivefold increase.

Container traffic has also continued to grow. In 2025, approximately 77,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) were transported along the route, a 36% increase compared with the previous year. During the first eight months of 2026, container traffic reached 44,200 TEUs. Meanwhile, 419 container trains departed from China, an 84% increase compared with the same period in 2025.

However, the route’s development is no longer measured solely by delivery times and freight volumes. As environmental requirements in international trade become more stringent, the sustainability of transport and logistics operations is gaining importance.

Speaking at the session, Vice Minister of Trade and Integration Zhanel Kushukova said Kazakhstan’s export competitiveness depended not only on the environmental characteristics of its products but also on the efficiency of international logistics.

“The competitiveness of our exports depends not only on how environmentally friendly the production process is. It is also determined by how efficiently, quickly and sustainably we can deliver goods to international markets,” Kushukova said.

According to Kushukova, Kazakhstan views the Trans-Caspian route not merely as an alternative transport direction, but as an emerging green corridor that should meet the evolving requirements of international trade.

One example is the Port of Kuryk on Kazakhstan’s Caspian coast. The port has received EcoPorts certification, confirming the implementation of European approaches to environmental management in port operations. It has also been certified under the international ISO 14001 environmental management standard.

For Kazakh exporters, the development of such infrastructure has practical implications. Environmental standards are increasingly taken into account when organizing international supply chains, making it important for transport routes to combine reliability and efficiency with environmental responsibility.

Digitalization is another priority for the Middle Corridor. Efforts include aligning procedures among participating countries, improving transport transparency and establishing a unified digital environment. These measures are expected to help businesses track cargo movements, plan delivery times and reduce administrative obstacles at border crossings.

Participants in the session also discussed increasing the route’s capacity, introducing environmentally friendly solutions and strengthening cooperation between transport and trade organisations. Kushukova emphasised that further development of the TITR would require coordinated efforts from all countries involved in transportation along the route.

World.title: “Relations with Russia cannot be restored”: Georgian prime minister on the country’s foreign policy
World.content:
Kobakhidze on Georgia-Russia relations

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze spoke at National Business Association conference on 16 November, commenting on relations with Russia and the European Union, prospects for political stability in the country and economic development.

Kobakhidze confirmed that dialogue with Moscow would continue. A first meeting is planned shortly between Georgia’s new special representative for relations with Russia, Giorgi Zurabashvili, and Russia’s deputy foreign minister Mikhail Galuzin. Various issues are expected to be discussed.

However, Kobakhidze stressed that two main obstacles prevent full restoration of relations with Russia: its occupation of Georgian territories – Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia), and its recognition of them as “independent”.

“Georgia’s leadership will not reverse its decision on this issue. It cannot be reversed,” the prime minister said.

Speaking about Georgia’s relations with the European Union, Irakli Kobakhidze criticised European bureaucracy, saying it was failing to take Europe’s real interests into account.

He argued that closer relations with Georgia should be one of Europe’s top priorities.

“Against the backdrop of isolation from Russia and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, Georgia remains Europe’s only land gateway to the east.

When you artificially create a problem at a time like this, when you obstruct open and transparent dialogue, it shows that European bureaucracy is once again acting against Europe’s objective interests,” Kobakhidze said.

Irakli Kobakhidze also spoke about the importance of political stability in the country.

He said the government had managed to protect Georgia from attempts at destabilisation funded by foreign forces.

He described the adoption of a law restricting foreign funding for NGOs and media as one of the important steps in this process.

Context: The law has been strongly criticised by the EU and international organisations, which warn that it threatens civil society, restricts media freedom and undermines democratic standards in Georgia.

“Recently, we have managed to ensure political stability, which was not easy. We had to take very bold and decisive steps to protect our country, including from external threats, and to safeguard our sovereignty and independence,” he said.

According to Kobakhidze, stability is a necessary condition for the consistent development of the economy and business.

He also stressed that Georgia’s economic growth was underpinned by an effective economic framework, legislation and a strong government team.

He singled out Minister of Economy and Sustainable Development Mariam Kvrivishvili for special praise.

News in Georgia

World.title: Verbal clash, insults and fistfight live on Armenia’s Public TV channel
World.content:
Fight on Armenia’s Public TV channel

People in Armenia are discussing a heated exchange on Armenia’s Public Television. During the programme Big Debate, political analyst Harutyun Mkrtchyan and journalist Boris Murazi traded insults and swore at each other before getting into a fight live on air. They kicked each other. The presenters had to call security staff into the studio, but even they could not calm the angry guests down.

Presenter Tatev Danielyan reminded the participants that thousands of people were watching the programme. “This is a sign of disrespect — not only towards each other, but also towards the viewers,” she said. Presenter Petros Ghazaryan added that the broadcaster would not cut the footage from the recorded programme and would show it on air.

However, the Television and Radio Commission criticised the decision to broadcast the footage unedited.

The commission members expressed “concern” over the programme makers’ position and editorial policy.

“Open displays of violence and insults cannot be justified by the participants in the discussion, the heated nature of the debate, an attempt to boost ratings or even formal compliance with the principle of impartiality,” they said.

The commission also expressed “bewilderment” that the programme had not aired live but had been recorded in advance, yet the broadcaster had chosen not to remove the scenes of violence.

Vasak Darbinyan, chairman of the Public Broadcaster’s Council, disagreed with the Television and Radio Commission. He asked what the commission expected the broadcaster to do when programme guests behaved in an “unrestrained and vulgar” manner.

“I think it was perfectly normal for the Public Broadcaster to show all of this on air. What, should they have hidden the truth and portrayed these public figures as ‘sweet and innocent’? Should they have said: ‘You know, they are actually very nice people, even though they may swear or kick each other on air’? Did you expect a ‘sanitised’ version? Why should people not know what they are really like?” Darbinyan said.

What led to the on-air fight

During a debate on opposition consolidation, political analyst Harutyun Mkrtchyan said:

“Mr Murazi, if I’m not mistaken, the press has reported that you provided sexual services to former Armenian President Serzh Sargsyan.”

Journalist Boris Murazi called it disgraceful to publish such allegations:

“I could provide similar services to the adult female relatives of those making such claims, their mothers, for example.”

Tensions escalated when Murazi urged Mkrtchyan to behave himself, calling him “ara”. This is an informal and contemptuous way of addressing a man. In Armenia, the term is considered rude and derogatory.

A verbal altercation followed, with both men using obscene language. A standard censoring tone drowned out the swearing on air.

After the exchange, the programme guests resorted to violence. They punched and kicked each other.

Television and Radio Commission statement on the “legitimisation of violence on air”

The Television and Radio Commission says that the Public Broadcaster, which should set an example for other TV companies, has a duty in such situations to:

comply with legal requirements;

avoid stirring up emotions among viewers;

prevent the legitimisation of violence on air.

Amendments to the Law on Audiovisual Media prohibit the distribution of information that promotes violence and cruelty in audiovisual programmes.

The commission members said that, beyond legal requirements, broadcasters must also follow ethical and professional standards. These should take priority when covering any events involving scenes of violence:

“After all, there are professional techniques that can neutralise provocations by participants in a discussion, defuse tensions, prevent violence and steer the debate in a constructive direction — especially when the programme is not live but recorded in advance.”

The Television and Radio Commission regulates the Public Television broadcaster. The commission members therefore called on the broadcaster to comply with the established standards on scenes of violence, hate speech and insults.

Social media reactions

Opinions on social media were divided. Most users condemned both the incident and the decision to broadcast it. However, some supported one side or the other in the dispute.

Here are some of the comments posted on social media:

“Shame on everyone who agrees to appear as a guest on Public TV after this.”

“Whatever you say, things were not as bad on Public TV as they are in parliament. That’s a whole different level… You should be ashamed of yourselves. You have turned our country into a laughing stock in the eyes of the whole world.”

“Another show, another talentless performance. When will people learn to ignore these characters and stop falling for their provocations?”

“Everything was right. Murazi put up with it for long enough. He should have put that ill-mannered representative of the Civil Contract party [a reference to a supporter of the ruling party] in his place much earlier.”

“Shame on them. We all spit on the National Television and Radio Commission and everyone holding a senior public office in Armenia. Or perhaps they will mistake our spit for raindrops?”

“It is unclear why these politicians hate each other so much. They should get down to work instead!”

“The Civil Contract party will give Harutyun Mkrtchyan a pat on the back. As for Boris Murazi’s behaviour, they will say: ‘See what a lesson the opposition has taught this pro-government propagandist?’ In the end, matters of national importance will sink to the level of Murazi and Mkrtchyan. And all of us will watch our own country’s decline over a glass of bitter wine.”

Fight on Armenia’s Public TV channel

World.title: Moscow and Tbilisi prepare to resume dialogue
World.content:
The Kremlin has established contact with Giorgi Zurabashvili, the Georgian prime minister’s new special representative for relations with Russia. His Russian counterpart will be Mikhail Galuzin, a deputy foreign minister responsible for Russia’s policy towards the South Caucasus. The Russian Foreign Ministry told the Izvestia newspaper.

“Russia has consistently advocated building pragmatic and mutually beneficial relations with Georgia,” the ministry said.

According to Moscow, the main topics for talks between the two sides will include increasing trade and tourism, expanding transport links and promoting cultural exchanges between the two countries.

The Russian Foreign Ministry has also given the new format broader political significance, saying it is effectively linked to the resumption of Russian-Georgian dialogue, which began in 2012 and continued for almost a decade.

Giorgi Zurabashvili, Georgia’s first deputy foreign minister, was appointed the prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia in late October 2026. He has retained his post at the ministry. However, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze has clarified that Zurabashvili will represent Georgia in relations with Russia specifically in his capacity as a special representative.

Giorgi Zurabashvili

Tbilisi has therefore given its informal dialogue with Moscow a higher political status and a clear mandate.

At the same time, Irakli Kobakhidze says Georgia’s position on restoring diplomatic relations with Russia remains unchanged. The government has no plans to reconsider its decision on this matter.

Reaction in Georgia

Georgian opposition politician Zurab Japaridze criticised the decision, saying the authorities were moving step by step towards restoring relations with Russia. He said the ultimate goal could be the reopening of a Russian embassy in Tbilisi.

He also criticised bilateral talks with Russia without the participation of international partners. In his view, Georgia should not be left alone at the negotiating table with Moscow.

Speaking to journalists, Irakli Kobakhidze said that Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories and its recognition of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) as independent states remained the main obstacles to restoring diplomatic relations.

However, he said that despite Georgia’s firm and unchanged position on restoring diplomatic ties, the dialogue between the special representatives would continue actively. The two sides would discuss all issues covered by the format.

The date and venue of the first meeting between Galuzin and Zurabashvili remain unknown. Kobakhidze said the meeting would probably take place soon, but not necessarily in Tbilisi or Moscow. It could be held in a third location.

How dialogue between Tbilisi and Moscow resumed after the 2008 war

Diplomatic relations between Georgia and Russia were severed after the August 2008 war. Immediately after the war ended, Moscow recognised the independence of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region. Tbilisi responded by cutting diplomatic ties, which have never been officially restored.

However, after a change of government in Georgia in 2012, Tbilisi made an attempt to normalise relations with Moscow. The new ruling Georgian Dream party said that a constant state of confrontation with Russia was not in the country’s interests and that cooperation on practical issues was possible without changing Georgia’s position on territorial integrity or its foreign policy course.

As part of this policy, in November 2012, then Georgian Prime Minister Bidzina Ivanishvili appointed Zurab Abashidze as his special representative for relations with Russia. His Russian counterpart was Grigory Karasin, a deputy foreign minister.

Zurab Abashidze and Grigory Karasin

Their first meeting took place on 14 December 2012 in Switzerland. It was the first direct round of talks between Georgian and Russian representatives since 2008. The two sides agreed to continue the dialogue on a regular basis, focusing mainly on trade and economic relations, humanitarian issues and cultural exchanges.

The format later became known as the Karasin–Abashidze talks. Meetings were held mostly in Prague, and their agenda was deliberately limited. The sides could discuss trade, transport links, tourism and humanitarian issues, but not Georgia’s territorial integrity or security.

Talks on the latter issues continued within the framework of the Geneva International Discussions, established after the 2008 war with the mediation of the EU, the UN and the OSCE. Tbilisi stressed that the Karasin–Abashidze format should not replace or undermine the Geneva talks.

The launch of the dialogue also brought practical results. After Russia imposed an embargo in 2006, its market reopened to Georgian wine and mineral water in 2013. Some freight transport links resumed, trade between the two countries expanded, and exports of Georgian products to Russia increased. Regular flights and transport links later became part of the agenda as well.

However, improved economic relations did not break the political deadlock. Moscow continued to maintain military and political control over Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region and did not reverse its decision to recognise them as independent states. Meanwhile, the Georgian authorities maintained that the country’s territorial integrity and its right to determine its own foreign policy were not up for negotiation.

In 2023, Russia lifted visa requirements for Georgian citizens and ended its ban on direct flights to Georgia. Tbilisi described these decisions as unilateral steps, but economic and transport links between the two countries expanded further.

Dialogue between Moscow and Tbilisi

World.title: Former Abkhaz MP opens fire on opposition leader’s son with assault rifle
World.content:
The son of Abkhazia’s opposition leader and MP Kan Kvarchia has been seriously wounded in the region’s capital.

Former MP Nodik Kvitsinia, who shot him with an assault rifle, voluntarily surrendered to the police.

The incident took place on the afternoon of 15 November at a private house in Sukhum, where the families of Kan Kvarchia and Nodik Kvitsinia were discussing a property-related dispute.

According to available information, Kvitsinia at one point left the house and walked towards his car, which was parked near the gate. He returned carrying a Kalashnikov assault rifle and opened fire on Efrem Kvarchia, Kan Kvarchia’s son.

Six bullets hit the young man. He remains in critical condition in the intensive care unit at Sukhum Republican Hospital.

After the shooting, Nodik Kvitsinia got into his car and drove to the city police department to surrender.

The Aiaashara Telegram channel, citing its sources, reports that Kvitsinia told investigators that his main target had been Kan Kvarchia himself, not his son.

Nodik Kvitsinia

The latest incident is not Nodik Kvitsinia’s first crime. In 2016, while serving as a member of parliament, he was sentenced to 16 years in prison for organising the kidnapping and murder of a Russian businessman and his female companion.

Despite the seriousness of the crime, Kvitsinia did not serve his full sentence. In 2023, authorities granted him amnesty to mark the 30th anniversary of the Abkhaz victory in the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war. He qualified for the amnesty as a war veteran.

Nodik Kvitsinia is not the only MP with a murder conviction in the history of the Abkhaz parliament.

In December 2024, a heated argument broke out between MPs Adgur Kharazia and Kan Kvarchia during a parliamentary committee meeting. In the heat of the dispute, Kharazia pulled out a pistol and opened fire at Kvarchia in the meeting room, seriously wounding him. A stray bullet killed another MP, Vakhtang Golandzia.

The trial in this case is still ongoing, and Kharazia, who has been stripped of his parliamentary immunity, remains in pre-trial detention.

Given this alarming pattern and the fact that Abkhazia is due to hold its next parliamentary elections in March 2027, social media users are suggesting, perhaps jokingly but perhaps seriously, that every parliamentary candidate should undergo a medical assessment to determine their mental fitness.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: IMF: Deteriorating relations between Georgia and EU could dampen investor confidence
World.content:
According to an assessment by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), rising domestic political tensions in Georgia and deteriorating relations with the European Union could undermine investor confidence.

The fund also points to economic risks stemming from the escalation of the war in the Middle East. It says considerable uncertainty continues to surround Georgia’s economic outlook.

The IMF’s overall assessment is that Georgia’s economy is growing and its banking system remains stable for now, but this growth masks a number of significant problems and risks.

The IMF’s key messages

1. Political tensions are also hurting the economy

The IMF explicitly warns that rising domestic political tensions in Georgia and deteriorating relations with the EU could undermine investor confidence.

When the political situation in a country becomes unpredictable and relations with the European Union grow strained, investors tend to become more cautious. They may postpone plans to open a new factory, hotel, company or other business.

As a result, less money flows into the country, fewer jobs are created and economic growth may slow. In other words, a political crisis is not just a problem for politicians: it can also affect people’s jobs and incomes.

2. Economic growth may depend to some extent on external factors

The IMF believes that the end of the war in Ukraine could bring both positive and potentially challenging changes for Georgia. An end to the war would contribute to regional stability and boost trade.

But there is another side to this: increased migration and financial flows have supported economic activity in Georgia in recent years. Put simply, after the war, Georgia could lose some of the people and money that have brought additional revenue into its economy in recent years.

This does not mean that an end to the war would necessarily be bad for Georgia’s economy. The IMF is simply warning the government that it needs to prepare for this change.

International Monetary Fund (IMF) delegation meets with the Ministry of Finance

3. Public debt is falling, but investment is stalling

The IMF forecasts that Georgia’s budget deficit will reach 1.5% of GDP in 2026, while public debt will fall to around 33%. At first glance, these figures look positive. The budget deficit shows how much government spending exceeds its revenue. Public debt is the total amount a country has borrowed and will have to repay in the future.

However, the IMF highlights one important factor: the budget deficit came in lower than planned not only because of higher revenues, but also because capital spending was delayed. What does this mean? The government planned to spend a certain amount on infrastructure, construction and other investment projects, but progress on these projects stalled.

This means that a low budget deficit does not always indicate that the government is meeting all its economic commitments more effectively. Sometimes it also means that planned projects are not being completed on time.

4. Despite economic growth, a significant share of the population remains out of work

This is one of the IMF’s most important messages for Georgia.

The fund notes that the country’s economy has grown in recent years and the labour market has also shown some improvement. However, employment remains low compared with countries at a similar stage of development.

Moreover, many people who do have jobs work in sectors with low productivity and relatively low wages. In other words, someone may be employed, but their salary and working conditions may not allow them to significantly improve their standard of living.

The IMF sees better vocational education, training for in-demand professions and the creation of higher-quality jobs as key to addressing this problem. In other words, economic growth alone is not enough — it is important to ensure that the population benefits from it.

5. Banks are stable, but rising dollar-denominated lending remains a concern

The IMF considers Georgia’s banking sector to be in good health. Banks have sufficient capital, remain profitable and report low levels of non-performing loans. However, the fund singles out dollarisation as a particular concern.

Dollarisation means that a significant share of loans and financial obligations in a country are denominated in foreign currencies, mainly US dollars. Why is this dangerous? Imagine someone takes out a mortgage in dollars but earns their salary in Georgian lari. If the lari weakens against the dollar, they will have to pay more in lari to service the loan, even though their monthly payment in dollars has not changed.

This risk is particularly relevant for households whose income is in lari but whose financial obligations are denominated in foreign currency. The IMF therefore considers the growth in foreign currency lending, including mortgages, a trend that requires close attention.

6. Why does the 2027 budget matter?

According to the IMF, Georgia’s draft budget for 2027 envisages a deficit of 2.5% of GDP. At the same time, the government plans to increase social spending, public sector salaries and capital investment.

This means the government intends to spend more on both social programmes and infrastructure and other investment projects.

The key question is how effectively the government will use these funds and how much the additional spending will improve people’s quality of life.

The IMF on Georgia’s economy

World.title: New Social Democratic Party formed in Georgia
World.content:
Social Democratic Party in Georgia

Georgia’s political movement For Social Democracy held a congress on 15 November at which it formally established the Social Democratic Party.

The founders linked the creation of the party to the country’s political and social crisis.

They argued that political and economic inequality, the collapse of democratic institutions and Georgia’s isolation from the European Union were contributing to growing authoritarianism.

The party says its aim is to build a politically and economically just state.

The new political force brings together representatives of various sectors, campaigners for social justice, workers’ rights and environmental protection, students and Georgian citizens living abroad.

At the congress, a 16-member governing body was elected to oversee the party’s activities for the next year. The party’s charter was also approved, and members of its audit commission were elected.

The founding congress of Georgia’s Social Democratic Party

“Overcoming despair and nihilism”: Party’s key priorities

The new party says its aim is to “overcome the despair and nihilism that have spread across the country, bring citizens who have been excluded from politics back into political life and place society’s real problems at the centre of the political agenda”.

“Georgia has managed to bring repressive rule to an end in the past. But it has yet to change the political and economic system that repeatedly plunges the country back into authoritarianism,” Sofo Verdzeuli, one of the leaders of the For Social Democracy movement, said at the founding congress.

She identified the protection of human dignity, citizens’ rights and the country’s sovereignty as the party’s main priorities.

“This is a response to policies that seek to control citizens through fear. The party will oppose the use of people as political instruments,” she said.

The party’s priorities include fair wages, affordable healthcare and education, social protection and environmental protection.

Its programme calls for the democratic transformation of the political and economic system, a fair justice system, stronger local democracy and decent working conditions.

Verdzeuli said Georgian society was living under Russian occupation and understood the value of peace. However, she stressed that peace meant not only the absence of war but also social justice.

“We believe democracy cannot have a future without social justice, but neither can justice exist without a democratic political system,” Verdzeuli said.овать без демократической политической системы», – сказала Вердзеули.

The new political force aims to represent the interests of 99% of the country’s population.

This was stated by Gota Chanturia, a participant in the founding congress.

“Society is constantly being told that the main threat to the country comes from various minorities, who must therefore be restricted or excluded. In reality, the threat comes from financial corporations and the business elite, which have been damaging the country’s resources and future for decades,” Chanturia said.

He called for cooperation with teachers, students, cultural workers and people from a range of professions, including metro drivers, couriers, taxi drivers, doctors and nannies.

Chanturia placed particular emphasis on environmental and animal rights activists. He said the party aimed to bring together various social and environmental movements under a single political programme.

“This is a demand to live in a country where there is justice for people, animals and the entire environment,” he said.

Chanturia stressed that uniting these groups could create a force capable not only of resisting but also of transforming the country.

History of the Social Democratic Party’s formation

The new political project, For Social Democracy, dates back to 17 February 2025, when people from various professional backgrounds gathered at a monument to writer Egnate Ninoshvili in Tbilisi on his birthday to announce the creation of a new left-wing political movement.

According to its founders, the movement emerged from growing cooperation between left-wing groups in the periods before and after the October 2024 parliamentary elections.

The alliance initially brought together more than 100 people. According to information published in November 2026, its membership has since grown to more than 200.

The movement’s founders include constitutional law expert Vakhushti Menabde, political scientist and left-wing activist Levan Lortkipanidze, Tatia Dvali, Elene Pasuri and others. Its members also include Sofo Verdzeuli, Gota Chanturia, Giga Bekauri, Nikoloz Tsikaridze, Maia Barkaia and Ia Eradze.

The party’s core membership consists of people from a wide range of professional and civic backgrounds, some of whom have spent years working on human rights, labour rights, social justice and environmental protection.

More about the party’s prominent founders

One of the most prominent founders of the Social Democratic Party is Vakhushti Menabde, an expert in political law and associate professor at Ilia State University’s Faculty of Law.

Vakhushti Menabde

Vakhushti Menabde has worked for many years in the fields of human rights and democratic institutions, including at the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA), the Public Defender’s Office and the Human Rights Education and Monitoring Centre.

Menabde also participated in the constitutional reform process and represented citizens before the Constitutional Court for many years.

Another prominent figure in the movement is Levan Lortkipanidze, a political scientist, researcher of political parties and left-wing activist.

Levan Lortkipanidze

Levan Lortkipanidze was involved in founding and running several socialist and green youth movements in Georgia in the 2010s. His academic and civic work has focused on left-wing political ideas, socialist heritage and green politics.

Lortkipanidze has worked at the Caucasian House and contributed to the publication of Georgian-language left-wing political literature.

Sofo Verdzeuli, one of the movement’s leaders who spoke at the new party’s founding congress, works in the field of legal policy.

Sofo Verdzeuli

Sofo Verdzeuli is a co-founder of the online publication Commentary, alongside Vakhushti Menabde, and editor of its legal policy section.

Her work focuses on the analysis of legal and political issues.

Gota Chanturia, who delivered a speech at the founding congress on the social foundations of the new political alliance, is known for his civic activism.

Gota Chanturia

Gota Chanturia’s public statements and activism have focused on civic resistance and criticism of government policies.

The timing and context of the establishment of the For Social Democracy movement in Georgia are important to understanding its political identity.

In February 2025, when the movement was founded, Georgia was experiencing a peak in large-scale pro-European protests.

The founders said their aim was to give the protests a socio-economic dimension, rather than simply demand a change of government.

Their criticism was not limited to the current government. In its founding statement in 2025, the movement criticised the policies of both the ruling Georgian Dream party and the previous government led by former President Mikheil Saakashvili, which was in power from 2003 to 2012.

The founders of the For Social Democracy movement argued that under both administrations, political and economic power had been concentrated in the hands of a small number of groups, ultimately contributing to growing authoritarianism.

On 12 November 2026, the movement published a 48-page policy document.

It sets out specific proposals on progressive taxation, minimum wages, the right to strike in solidarity with other workers, the democratisation of the economy and expanded social protection.

The document draws on the social-democratic legacy of the First Georgian Republic.

Social Democrats oppose ruling party’s bid to ban five opposition parties

Vakhushti Menabde and Levan Lortkipanidze have repeatedly spoken out against a lawsuit filed by the ruling Georgian Dream party with the Constitutional Court seeking to ban five opposition parties.

Background: The lawsuit was signed by 88 MPs from the ruling party and targets five opposition groups: Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists. Georgian Dream argues that the parties violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits political parties whose aim is to overthrow or forcibly change the country’s constitutional order. One of the arguments cited is the parties’ refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the current authorities. The lawsuit also accuses them of organising attempts to overthrow the government. The United National Movement faces an additional accusation of undermining the country’s independence and violating its territorial integrity. This is based on allegations that the party, which was in power at the time, was responsible for the August 2008 war with Russia over South Ossetia. All five parties deny the allegations. The court is expected to issue its final ruling by 24 June 2027. A simple majority is required to uphold the lawsuit, meaning the votes of four of the seven judges would be sufficient.

Speaking on Palitra News’ Political Space programme on 20 October, Menabde said banning a political party was one of the most consequential decisions in a democracy.

He argued that political parties represented sections of the electorate and that banning them deprived some citizens of the opportunity to participate in the political process. According to Menabde, a ban would require evidence that a party posed a genuine and persistent threat to democracy and the rule of law.

He also said that systematic human rights violations committed during the United National Movement’s time in power could not serve as grounds for banning the party today.

Lortkipanidze said the process of banning political parties was contributing to rising political tensions and confrontation within society. In his view, the situation created favourable conditions for manipulation by what he described as an oligarchic government.

World.title: 48th pro-European Saturday march in Tbilisi, protesters’ stories. Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
Pro-European protests in Georgia, video

The 48th consecutive Saturday march took place in Tbilisi on 14 November. Thousands of people continue to demand that Georgia return to the path of European integration, as protests have now continued for more than two years.

November is a particularly painful month in this context. On 28 November, it will be two years since Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Georgia, then an EU candidate country, was suspending its EU integration process.

In recent weeks, the Saturday march has been held under the same main slogan: “Georgia against Ivanishvili”, referring to billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder and honorary chairman of ruling Georgian Dream party.

A large-scale march is planned for 28 November. Organisers are urging people across the country to take part and show their support for Georgia’s European integration.

“Mzisa Gabeshia – thank you for your fight,” reads the banner held by a Saturday march participant in the photo below.

On 14 November, 75-year-old Mzisa Gabeshia was buried in the town of Martvili. For months, she had held solo protests in support of Georgia’s European integration and the demonstrations in Tbilisi.

News of her health problems emerged recently. She had been battling a serious illness. Activists from Tbilisi travelled to Martvili to attend her funeral and pay their respects.



“Mzisa Gabeshia – thank you for your fight,” reads a banner held by one of the march participants

The photo below shows Teona Tamazashvili, mother of young programmer Tamar Bachaliashvili, who was found dead in her car in May 2023 under suspicious circumstances. Investigators classified her death as suicide, but her family rejects this conclusion.

Tamazashvili regularly joins the Saturday marches, calling for the investigation to be reopened. She urges fellow citizens to support her weekly protest outside the prosecutor’s office every Monday.

“The mother of a murdered child is calling you,” reads the banner she is holding.



Young singer Sofo Batilashvili, pictured below, is a regular participant in pro-European protests in Tbilisi. Last week, a court fined her 3,000 lari (about $1,150) for posting a video on social media of herself performing “Ole Ola”, a song containing profanities directed at the ruling party.

“Vakho Sanaia, all the way!” reads a banner held by a participant in the Saturday march (pictured below).

In October, prominent TV presenter and Formula journalist Vakho Sanaia was sentenced to 30 days of administrative detention over Facebook posts and videos that a court deemed insulting to parliament speaker Shalva Papuashvili and other members of the ruling party.

Context

The “Saturday marches” are part of an ongoing protest movement that has continued in Georgia for more than two years.

Protesters are demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration and that all political prisoners be released. They are also calling for the repeal of all anti-democratic laws passed by the ruling Georgian Dream party over the past two years.

Protesters and opposition parties point out that part of Georgian society still does not recognise the results of the parliamentary election held in autumn 2024. They are calling for early parliamentary elections.

Over the course of nearly two years of protests, dozens of people have been arrested. Many have been charged with criminal offences and sentenced to prison.

For the first time in independent Georgia’s history, the country has around 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the independent media outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. She was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer.

The protests continue despite an intensifying crackdown on civil society and the media.

News in Georgia

World.title: Georgia’s former prisons chief and ex-prison director accused of helping organise beating of inmate
World.content:
The beating of crime boss Peikrishvili

The Georgian Prosecutor’s Office has charged seven people over the October beating of a crime boss in a prison cell, Davit Peikrishvili. The accused include Giorgi Pataridze, former head of the Special Penitentiary Service, Ramaz Pirtskhalava, former director of Prison No. 8, where the incident took place, and five inmates.

Deputy Prosecutor General Amiran Guluashvili said inmates beat Davit Peikrishvili at Penitentiary Institution No. 8 over four days, from 16 to 20 October.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, the alleged attackers were inmates Avtandil Bilanishvili, Vato Kipiani, Shota Kipiani, David Kacharava and Pavel Gotsiridze. Prosecutors charged them with intentionally causing less serious bodily harm as part of a group. The offence carries a prison sentence of four to six years.

On 14 November, a court ordered their pre-trial detention as part of the investigation.

The authorities released Giorgi Pataridze, former head of the Special Penitentiary Service, and Ramaz Pirtskhalava, former prison director, on bail of 10,000 lari each (around $3,000). Prosecutors charged Pataridze with exceeding his official powers and Pirtskhalava with abusing his official powers.

Both offences carry prison sentences of up to three years.

The beating forms part of a long-running feud between members of Georgia’s criminal underworld. The dispute began outside prison and continued after some of those involved ended up in the same facility.

Georgian media and social networks have long discussed the alleged links between people involved in the case and the country’s elite circles. Their arrests have therefore attracted considerable attention.

In particular, media outlets often describe crime boss Avtandil Bilanishvili as a friend of Bera Ivanishvili, the son of billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili. The latter founded the ruling Georgian Dream party and is widely regarded as the country’s de facto ruler.

The prosecution’s version of events

According to investigators, decisions by the prison service leadership made the violence possible.

The Prosecutor’s Office says that on 16 October 2026, four inmates were transferred to Davit Peikrishvili’s cell at the request of Vato Kipiani. The transfer followed instructions from then head of the Penitentiary Service Giorgi Pataridze and a decision by the director of Prison No. 8. The four inmates were Ramaz Pirtskhalava, Vato and Shota Kipiani, and Avtandil Bilanishvili.

David Kacharava and Pavel Gotsiridze were already in the same cell.

The Prosecutor’s Office says this arrangement alone violated the requirements of the Penitentiary Code and the prison’s internal regulations.

According to the prosecution, five inmates began beating Peikrishvili that same day and continued the attacks regularly until 20 October.

He suffered multiple injuries to various parts of his body, including four broken ribs, fractures to the transverse processes of his vertebrae and a concussion.

The Prosecutor’s Office classifies the injuries as less serious bodily harm that caused a prolonged health disorder.

The Prosecutor’s Office said it would submit a motion to the court within the timeframe set by law, seeking pre-trial measures against the accused. The investigation remains ongoing.

Former head of the Special Penitentiary Service Giorgi Pataridze

What Davit Peikrishvili told the court

On 12 November, Davit Peikrishvili addressed a court hearing and said that his attackers beat him because he refused to give them access to his phone. He claimed that prison officials and senior penitentiary service officials were involved.

Peikrishvili also stressed that the prosecutor bore responsibility for failing to keep the location of his phone secret.

“They showed me my phones in the cell. By then, they had already beaten and tortured me. […] The prosecutor’s responsibility is obvious. […] They then took me to Vivamedi clinic and sent me back. Gotsiridze and Shota Kipiani, together with prison staff, watched me to make sure I did not tell anyone what had happened. They kept me in isolation. My only hope was to survive until Monday, when a lawyer could come to see me.

“Before that, I had a lawyer whom I had been friends with for 11 years. I am also the godfather of his son. But he told me he could no longer represent me because he did not trust the prosecutor,” Peikrishvili said.

Background

Paata Gogiashvili, Peikrishvili’s lawyer, first raised concerns about a possible beating on 20 October.

On the same day, Peikrishvili was transferred to Vivamedi clinic. The clinic’s director confirmed to Tabula that medical staff had admitted him with injuries to his hands.

At the time, the Penitentiary Service denied that Peikrishvili’s cellmates had assaulted him. In its initial statement, the agency said that Peikrishvili had unexpectedly left the room during a meeting with his lawyer, smashed a window in the corridor and threatened to hurt himself with a shard of glass.

The statement referred to a threat of self-harm, not an actual injury inflicted by the prisoner.

The Justice Ministry’s General Inspectorate initially investigated the incident. On 25 October, it transferred the case to the Prosecutor General’s Office to ensure an objective investigation.

The following day, the Prosecutor’s Office asked the Justice Ministry to suspend Giorgi Pataridze, head of the Special Penitentiary Service. Pataridze left his post that same day.

Peikrishvili’s family later reported another possible case of violence.

On 25 October, the brothers’ mother said that inmates had also beaten Davit’s brother, Giorgi, in his cell. The Penitentiary Service again denied that any assault had taken place. According to the Public Defender’s Office, Giorgi Peikrishvili had not raised any concerns about his safety at the time.

The Prosecutor’s Office opened criminal proceedings against Davit and Giorgi Peikrishvili on 2 October. It accuses the brothers of laundering money on an especially large scale. The charge carries a prison sentence of up to 12 years.

On 23 September, Tbilisi City Court ordered the pre-trial detention of Davit and Giorgi Peikrishvili and their personal bodyguard, Aleksandre Chapodze.

Who are the Peikrishvili twin brothers?

The Peikrishvili brothers, Davit and Giorgi

The names of brothers Giorgi and Davit Peikrishvili have been linked to Georgia’s criminal underworld in the media for many years.

The brothers became particularly “well known” in 2010 through the so-called illegal bookmakers case, which also involved former footballer Giorgi Demetradze.

Their names later surfaced in a case involving an attack on a cryptocurrency exchange and in a case concerning an alleged plot to assassinate them in Ukraine.

The relationship between the Peikrishvili brothers and crime boss Vato Kipiani dates back at least to 2010.

At the time, Davit Peikrishvili won around $140,000 betting on the FIFA World Cup but could not collect his winnings. According to investigators, Giorgi Demetradze and Vato Kipiani helped him resolve the issue.

In 2011, a court sentenced Giorgi Demetradze to six years in prison. Davit Peikrishvili reached a plea agreement and served a two-year prison sentence.

Vato Kipiani was acquitted in the case.

Peikrishvili’s name also surfaced in a case linked to a high-profile murder in Tbilisi in 2016. Crime boss Soso Jokhadze was shot dead in his own car.

Badri Natobadze, a friend of the Peikrishvili brothers, was convicted of the murder.

In the following years, media outlets reported a theory that Jokhadze’s murder could trigger a new wave of revenge attacks and clashes. In this context, they also mentioned Vato Kipiani, who had links to Jokhadze’s circle.

In January 2020, the security services of Georgia and Ukraine carried out a joint operation and foiled an alleged plot to kill the Peikrishvili brothers. Authorities arrested six people in Georgia and one in Ukraine.

According to a statement by the Prosecutor’s Office at the time, Vato Kipiani had commissioned the explosive device intended to kill Peikrishvili. Ukrainian authorities later deported Kipiani to Georgia, where police arrested him in 2021.

Local media cited the feud that followed Soso Jokhadze’s murder as one possible motive for the alleged plot. However, investigators never established the exact motive.

Vato Kipiani

In October 2023, an attack took place at a cryptocurrency exchange in Tbilisi. The attackers stole around $740,000.

Media reports identified Davit Peikrishvili as the alleged organiser of the attack. Prosecutors charged the brothers in connection with the case. A court of first instance sentenced them to 11 years in prison, but an appeals court later acquitted them.

On 22 September 2026, law enforcement officers arrested Davit and Giorgi Peikrishvili during a special operation in Tbilisi. They also arrested Davit Peikrishvili’s personal bodyguard.

Initially, the Interior Ministry charged the brothers with group violence and extortion. Their lawyer said they denied the charges.

On 2 October, the Prosecutor’s Office brought an additional charge against the brothers: laundering money on an especially large scale.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, between 2020 and 2026, the brothers split up funds of illegal origin and used other people’s bank accounts to move the money. They then consolidated the funds in their own accounts through multiple bank transfers.

The agency said the brothers accumulated the equivalent of around 10 million lari (approximately $3.7 million) in various currencies in their accounts. Investigators allege that they used the money to repay bank loans and purchase movable and immovable property.

The charge carries a prison sentence of up to 12 years.

The beating of crime boss Peikrishvili

World.title: Russia, Central Asia discuss joint plan amid push for Eurasian connectivity
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 17. Russia and Central Asian countries have discussed the implementation of the Joint Action Plan for 2025-2027, focusing on political, trade, economic, transport, and humanitarian cooperation, the Russian Foreign Ministry reported.

According to the report, the discussions took place during a video conference held on November 16 between Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin and senior representatives of the foreign ministries of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.

The participants reviewed progress in implementing the Joint Action Plan adopted following the second Central Asia-Russia summit, held in Dushanbe on October 9, 2025. They also discussed prospects for further cooperation and the schedule of upcoming events in the Central Asia-Russia format, the ministry said.

Separately, Tajikistan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs noted in its press release that the talks addressed prospects for cooperation in the political, trade and economic, transport, and humanitarian spheres.

The Joint Action Plan for 2025-2027 was adopted at the second Central Asia-Russia Summit, with the participation of the presidents of Russia, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. The document was approved alongside the summit's final communiqué and is intended to translate the leaders' political agreements into practical cooperation among the six countries.

The plan covers a broad range of areas, including trade and investment, industrial cooperation, transport and logistics, energy, healthcare, environmental protection, regional security, migration, education, culture and tourism. Particular emphasis is placed on removing trade barriers, attracting mutual investment, developing production and supply chains, increasing the use of national currencies in mutual settlements, and strengthening transport corridors across Eurasia. The countries also intend to deepen cooperation in digital technologies, artificial intelligence and renewable energy.

Transport connectivity is one of the plan's key economic priorities. The summit participants agreed to continue developing international transport corridors across Eurasia, with particular attention to increasing the capacity of the North-South International Transport Corridor. They also highlighted the importance of improving logistics infrastructure, facilitating cross-border trade and expanding interregional economic ties.

Implementation of the plan is coordinated through the foreign ministries of the six participating countries, with sector-specific cooperation involving relevant government agencies. Progress is reviewed through regular ministerial meetings, while the results of the plan's implementation are expected to be presented at the third Central Asia-Russia Summit in 2027.

The wider regional context also includes Turkmenistan's 2026 chairmanship of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), during which the country has prioritized the development of international transport corridors and stronger connectivity among CIS countries.

The chairmanship concept identifies the development of the North-South and East-West transport corridors, expansion of trade and investment, and stronger economic links between member states as key areas of cooperation. It also envisages improvements to transport infrastructure, logistics and regional connectivity.

Several CIS-level meetings held in Turkmenistan during the year have provided a platform for advancing this agenda. At the May 2026 meeting of the CIS Council of Heads of Government in Ashgabat, Turkmenistan emphasized the integration of the Turkmenbashi International Seaport with railway routes in Central Asia and the Caspian region, as well as the development of multimodal transport links. The discussions also addressed expanding mutual trade, investment and business activity among CIS countries.

Transport cooperation was also a key topic at the 111th meeting of the CIS Economic Council, held in Ashgabat in September. Participants discussed the 2026-2030 Action Plan for implementing the CIS Strategy for Ensuring Transport Security in International Transport Operations and confirmed their readiness to make greater use of the North-South International Transport Corridor.

Turkmenistan also proposed declaring 2029 the Year of CIS Transport Connectivity. The initiative was subsequently approved at the October meeting of the CIS Council of Heads of State in Awaza.

Practical progress in digital transport connectivity has also been recorded along the Middle Corridor. In July 2026, the first eTIR operations across the Caspian Sea included a route linking Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan through a single digital transit procedure. The development marked an important step toward reducing paperwork and facilitating cross-border freight movements along the route.

In an exclusive interview with Trend, International Road Transport Union (IRU) TIR and Transit System Director Tatiana Rey-Bellet said the ambition for 2026 was to extend eTIR operations to Kazakhstan, Georgia and Türkiye. She also noted that Southeast Asian countries were already considering the TIR system to establish intermodal connections with Europe via the Middle Corridor as an alternative to purely maritime routes.

The growing interest in the Middle Corridor is also reflected in the assessment of the International Transport Forum (ITF). In a separate interview with Trend, the organization noted that the route would retain its strategic value as a diversified Asia-Europe connection, even if changing geopolitical conditions made alternative routes through Iran more attractive for certain cargo flows.

World.title: Uzbekistan signs deal with Oman’s Voltamp Energy for $350M solar plant
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 17. Uzbekistan has signed a joint development agreement with Oman's Voltamp Energy and Uzbek company UET Construction in Oman on Tuesday, November 17, to develop a 500-megawatt solar power plant in the Fergana region, with the project expected to attract $350 million in direct investment.

According to Uzbekistan's Ministry of Energy, the agreement was also signed by the Ministry of Investments, Industry and Trade and outlines joint efforts to develop the project and prepare it for implementation.

Once operational, the solar facility is expected to generate approximately 1 billion kilowatt-hours of renewable electricity annually and save around 250 million cubic meters of natural gas.

Voltamp Energy specialists are currently assessing the proposed project site and developing its financial model. The company plans to complete this work and submit a commercial proposal in the near term.

In a separate development, the parties also reached agreements on establishing production of specialized transformer conductors through cooperation between Voltamp Energy and Uzbekistan's Texnokabel Group.

Another project involves constructing a new high-voltage transformer manufacturing plant in the Akhangaran district of the Tashkent region in cooperation with Nura Group.

The initiatives are expected to support the expansion of renewable energy generation in Uzbekistan, increase local production of electrical equipment, facilitate technology transfer and create new jobs.

World.title: Azerbaijan prosecutor general attends IAP meeting in Argentina (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 17. A delegation led by Azerbaijan's Prosecutor General Kamran Aliyev participated in the 62nd meeting of the Executive Committee of the International Association of Prosecutors (IAP), held in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on November 14–15, according to the Prosecutor General's Office of Azerbaijan.

The meeting brought together heads of prosecution authorities and representatives of the association to discuss its activities, governing bodies, international cooperation, and organizational and financial matters. Participants also considered changes to the Executive Committee's composition, amendments to the association's statutes and internal procedures, prosecutor training, the work of specialized networks, and preparations for upcoming international events.

Following his appointment as Argentina's Minister of Justice, IAP President Juan Bautista Mahiques stepped down from his position. Presidential duties were temporarily assigned to Executive Committee member Mohamed Hassana pending the election of a new IAP president.

The committee also considered candidates for key positions within the association. Ingrid Maschl-Clausen was nominated for the post of Secretary General, while Andrew Richardson was nominated for General Counsel. Both candidates were confirmed for their respective positions at the IAP General Meeting, held in a hybrid format on November 16.

At the meeting, IAP General Counsel Tarika Jayaratne presented a report on the association's activities. She also praised the training session titled "Criminal Prosecution of Digital Evidence and Cybercrimes," held at Azerbaijan's National Aviation Academy in June 2026, describing it as an example of best practice.

Speaking at the meetings, Aliyev, who serves as an IAP vice president, highlighted Azerbaijan's active involvement in the association's work and the importance the country attaches to its further development. He also outlined measures implemented to modernize Azerbaijan's prosecution authorities, expand international legal cooperation, and strengthen efforts to combat traditional and emerging forms of crime as part of reforms led by President Ilham Aliyev.

Aliyev also emphasized Azerbaijan's contribution to the association, including the successful organization of the 29th IAP Annual Conference in Baku in 2024 and the country's representation in the IAP's governing bodies. Participants exchanged views on strengthening international cooperation, combating transnational crime, and developing professional ties between prosecution authorities.

During the visit, the Azerbaijani delegation also held meetings with foreign counterparts. Aliyev visited the Embassy of Azerbaijan in Argentina, where he met with embassy staff to discuss ways to strengthen bilateral relations and cooperation.

He also met with Argentina's Federal Prosecutor General Eduardo Casal, Prosecutor General of the Autonomous City of Buenos Aires Martín López Zavaleta, and Minister of Justice Juan Bautista Mahiques. Azerbaijan's Ambassador to Argentina, Ramzi Teymurov, also took part in the meetings.

World.title: KazTransOil's Batumi Oil Terminal increases cargo throughput 2.5% in January-October 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 17. Batumi Oil Terminal LLC (BOT), a Georgian asset of Kazakhstan's KazTransOil JSC, handled 1.572 million tons of oil cargo in January-October 2026, up by 38,500 tons, or 2.5%, compared to the same period last year, the company reported.

The increase was driven by the resumption of crude oil and aviation fuel handling, as well as higher gasoline throughput.

During the first 10 months of 2026, the terminal handled 262,700 tons of Kazakh crude oil, compared to no shipments in the same period of 2025. Gasoline throughput reached 316,500 tons, up by 75,400 tons, or 31.3%, year-on-year.

Aviation fuel handling also increased. Throughput of aviation kerosene totaled 53,500 tons, exceeding the figure for January-October 2025 by 50,700 tons, or more than 19 times.

Located on the Black Sea coast, Batumi Oil Terminal LLC (BOT) provides transshipment services for oil and oil products originating from Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan, Georgia, and other countries.

KazTransOil JSC, a subsidiary of Kazakhstan's national oil and gas company KazMunayGas JSC, has owned BOT since February 2008. BOT, in turn, holds exclusive management rights over 100% of the shares in Batumi Sea Port LLC.

Meanwhile, Batumi Sea Port handled 6.9 million tons of cargo in January-October 2026, up 13% compared to the same period last year.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Oman agree to develop joint copper and mining projects
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 17. Uzbekistan and Oman agreed to pursue joint mining projects, including the exploration and development of copper deposits in Uzbekistan, following a series of meetings held in Oman on November 16.

According to Uzbekistan's Ministry of Mining Industry and Geology, the discussions took place with representatives of major Omani companies during Uzbekistan's state visit to Oman.

The Uzbek delegation met with Mineral Development Oman (MDO), Al Tasnim Group, MB Holding and Al Kalbani Group to discuss investment opportunities and potential joint projects in the mining and geological sectors.

In particular, Uzbekistan and MDO agreed to jointly develop promising copper-bearing areas in Uzbekistan.

The Uzbek side also signed a cooperation agreement with Al Tasnim Group covering critical minerals used in industrial production.

Meanwhile, talks with MB Holding and Al Kalbani Group focused on establishing investment cooperation in the mining and geological sectors and implementing potential joint projects.

The agreements and discussions are expected to help attract foreign investment into Uzbekistan's mining industry, advance new projects and expand economic cooperation between the two countries.

Uzbekistan and Oman have been strengthening their economic partnership, with mining, energy, transport, logistics and industrial development emerging as key areas for expanding bilateral trade and investment ties.

World.title: Uzbekneftegaz, Canada explore new oil and gas investment opportunities
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 17. Uzbekistan's state-owned oil and gas company Uzbekneftegaz and Canada have discussed expanding cooperation in the energy sector, including attracting Canadian investment and introducing advanced technologies into the country's oil and gas industry at a meeting on November 16.

According to Uzbekneftegaz, the issues were discussed at a meeting between Sukhrob Khamroyev, First Deputy Chairman of the company's Management Board, and the Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Canada to Uzbekistan, Christopher Duggan.

The talks focused on opportunities for Canadian investors, potential joint projects and ongoing reforms aimed at improving the investment environment in Uzbekistan's oil and gas sector.

Khamroyev briefed the Canadian ambassador on the business environment for foreign investors and efforts to expand cooperation with international energy companies.

Particular attention was given to the activities of Canada's Condor Energies, which has been working since 2024 to increase gas production at eight fields in the Gazli region operated by Uzbekneftegaz.

The project has already generated $184.1 million in investment, while natural gas production is ongoing. The company expects to increase the relevant production indicators by the end of 2026, according to Uzbekneftegaz.

The project focuses on well repairs, improving well productivity and drilling new wells to increase output.

Additionally, the parties discussed opportunities to build on this experience by expanding cooperation with other Canadian companies, attracting additional investment and introducing advanced technologies.

The meeting concluded with both sides expressing their readiness to continue dialogue and jointly explore promising areas for further cooperation.

World.title: Alleged fugitive fires rifle in fight and crashes stolen car with passengers
World.content:
A 24-year-old alleged fugitive armed with a rifle has been arrested in an extensive operation involving tactical police officers in the remote Northern Territory.

Police alleged the man had been involved in a dangerous driving incident earlier this month in the remote West Daly community of Peppimenarti, about 320km south-west of Darwin.

"Police will allege the offender attended a residence, challenged an occupant to a fight and produced a rifle before firing three shots into the air," police said in a statement.

The man allegedly fired a rifle during a fight in Peppimenarti before driving away in a dangerous manner. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

"He then drove away at speed in a dangerous manner while three adult passengers were travelling unsecured in the tray of the vehicle.

"A short time later, the three passengers were thrown from the vehicle, suffering injuries.

"One woman suffered fractured ribs and a collapsed lung, requiring medical treatment."

NT Police said the man had been on the run since his bail was revoked earlier this year.

"As part of an extensive investigation, an arrest plan was developed and led by detectives … supported by local and specialist police resources," police said.

Before dawn on November 13, members of the Territory Response Group arrested the man in Peppimenarti.

He's since been charged with three counts of recklessly endangering life, and multiple stolen vehicle and dangerous driving charges, and been remanded in custody.

Unrest continues in Wadeye

Separately, another West Daly community has also been stricken with further unrest.

Up to 100 people armed with axes, spears and crossbows were involved in the latest outbreak of violence in the troubled remote NT community of Wadeye.

In yesterday's incident, Northern Territory Police were notified of the fighting at the intersection of Bunduck and Mollinjin streets just before 3pm.

Up to 100 armed people were involved in the most recent bout of unrest in Wadeye. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

They said a victim in their 20s was allegedly struck in the abdomen with a metal bar, while others reported being threatened and having arrows fired in their direction.

Police said they had identified five males aged between 18 and 37 as the main culprits allegedly involved, and investigations were continuing.

The unrest comes after an incident last week where two people allegedly fired arrows at a teenage girl and police officers in the community.

Police said they were called to a home about 10pm on Friday after receiving reports a 21-year-old man had threatened his 18-year-old partner with a bow.

Police officers were allegedly fired at with a bow in the remote community. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

When police arrived and were speaking with the 18-year-old, two arrows were allegedly fired in the direction of her and the officers.

Police took shelter, and when the man fled the scene, they took the victim to a safe location before calling in other officers to help the search for the alleged offender.

Officers then arrested a 21-year-old man and a 14-year-old boy and seized a bow and several arrows.

Wadeye elders desperately try to end feud Leaders in the remote NT community of Wadeye say they fear it is only a matter of time before someone is killed amid ongoing clan violence.

Wadeye, the NT's second largest Indigenous community, has been at the centre of violent unrest for some months now.

Over the space of several weeks in September, groups of up to 150 people armed with crossbows, machetes and spears were fighting in community, attacking homes and police, burning cars and seriously injuring one man.

That violence was part of a decades-old feud between some of Wadeye's 24 clans, and elders told the ABC they feared it was only a matter of time before someone was killed.

World.title: Nine-month wait leaves Australia in a Cricket World Cup conundrum
World.content:
Australia's bid to lock in a revamped batting line-up ahead of next year's ODI World Cup defence is set to face a nine-month stumbling block, with a dearth of 50-over cricket on the horizon.

This month's three-match series against England has become something of a sideshow in Australia, given the Sandpapergate saga and debate over the Test squad make up.

But there will be serious consequences ahead of Wednesday's decider in Hobart.

Australia's heavy run of Test series and the IPL in April and May means the side's next ODI is not until next August, where they will face New Zealand in a top-end series.

The team is then likely to play three warm-up matches in Zimbabwe, before their World Cup opener against India in Cape Town on October 7.

Almost every other country is scheduled to play ODI matches in the coming nine months, but the Test team's busiest year threatens to leave Australia at a disadvantage.

Australia crashes to record ODI loss to England Australia's top order has collapsed dramatically to hand England its biggest ODI win on Australian shores, a 135-run triumph in Adelaide.

Since Australia's 2023 triumph win in India, David Warner, Steve Smith, Glenn Maxwell and Marcus Stoinis have all retired from the format.

Marnus Labuschagne is also no longer in the team, with only the bowlers missing from Australia's first-choice squad in the current matches against England.

Australia at least appear set on Travis Head and Mitch Marsh as openers, while Matt Renshaw, Cameron Green and Josh Inglis look solid in the middle order.

The number three role remains one of interest.

Cooper Connolly made two half-centuries against Zimbabwe on being moved there in September, but has since had a top score of 38 in six innings.

"It's obviously nice to get some consistency in one role," Connolly said on Tuesday.

"I like to pride myself on being versatile and being able to sort of bat anywhere.

"But I'm enjoying that role at number three, especially behind Heady and Bison (Marsh). They get us off to a flyer.

"Any chance you get to lock down a position in the Australian side, you're looking to do that. Whether that's at the top or in the middle, I'm happy with either."

Selectors may be able to use an Australia A tour of England that runs alongside next year's Ashes to experiment somewhat, but Test players will naturally be unavailable.

Australia have been able to play with a largely settled top and middle order in recent ODIs, with reasonable success.

But chief selector George Bailey conceded last week some roles were still yet to be settled on, including finding a finisher to replace the likes of Maxwell and Stoinis.

"Maxi and Stoins's ability to navigate through certain situations and then finish with real strong power is a pretty niche role," Bailey said.

Bailey pointed to Ollie Peake as one option, while long-time T20 specialist Tim David is also now back playing domestic one-day cricket and could be another.

A back-up spinner and another pace-bowling all-rounder option outside of Cameron Green were other roles of importance suggested by Bailey.

Meanwhile Mahli Beardman is expected to return for Wednesday's decider, after he was rested in Adelaide following his 6-24 on debut in Perth.
