World.title: Teenage boy fighting for life after being hit by car in Toowoomba
World.content:
Police say a teenage boy has suffered life-threatening injuries after being hit by a car on a suburban street in Toowoomba.

Paramedics say they were called to McGregor Street in Wilsonton at 3:15pm, following reports that a pedestrian had been struck by a car.

Crews remain at the scene just off Taylor Street, and drivers are being urged to seek alternative routes.

World.title: Queensland YouTuber brothers granted bail after police drug bust
World.content:
Two Queensland brothers, whose YouTube channel about drift cars has nearly 40,000 followers, have been granted bail after being charged over alleged drug trafficking.

Andrew Young, 39, and Stuart Douglas Blair Young, 36, were arrested in October following a three-month investigation into alleged drug trafficking across Toowoomba.

The two men were driving a 2022 Toyota HiAce along the Gore Highway south of the city on October 10 when police intercepted the vehicle.

Police allege a search of the vehicle the Young brothers were travelling in uncovered cocaine and MDMA, more than $9,000 in cash and seven mobile phones. (Supplied: Queensland Police)

Police will allege officers searched the vehicle and found quantities of cocaine and MDMA, more than $9,000 in cash and seven mobile phones.

The pair were charged with a string of offences and were on remand until today when they successfully applied for bail in the Supreme Court in Toowoomba.

The court was told that, during the police investigation into the brothers' alleged offending, an undercover law enforcement participant (LEP) had been communicating with Andrew Young about buying drugs from him.

The bail application was heard in the Toowoomba Supreme Court on Tuesday. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

Barrister Scott Lynch for Andrew Young, who faces 32 offences, including 23 counts of supplying dangerous drugs and one count of trafficking, told the court his client's case was a "bit peculiar".

"On the material disclosed so far, it seems it's a very low-level trafficking where the purchasers have been asking for some drugs and then, of course, the LEP becomes involved and the quantities become … significant," Mr Lynch told the court.

When Mr Lynch said he was yet to see the transcripts of those interactions his client had with the LEP, Justice Catherine Muir interjected to add the transcripts would show "if he's being encouraged" by the officer he was allegedly unknowingly supplying drugs to.

Stuart Douglas Blair Young is charged with 12 offences, including two counts each of supplying dangerous drugs and one count of trafficking. (Supplied: Street Race Solutions)

Defence lawyer Nathan Bouchier said his client, Stuart Young, who is charged with 12 offences, including two counts each of supplying dangerous drugs and one count of trafficking, was facing "quite a different" case to his brother.

Mr Bouchier said the "only evidence" about his clients' alleged involvement in the case was that he was with his brother at times when his brother was supplying the drugs to the undercover officer.

Crown prosecutor Abby Kong told the court she did not oppose both applications for bail, if strict conditions were ordered.

She said she also did not object to the brothers communicating with each other because they operated a business together.

Justice Muir granted both men bail with strict conditions, including a strict curfew, surrendering their passports, and undergoing mandatory drug testing.

They are also prohibited from leaving Queensland.

The matter will return to Toowoomba Magistrates' Court at a later date for a mention hearing.

Police have also charged four other men during the investigation codenamed Operation Starcourt with a string of supply drug charges, including a 23-year-old Toowoomba City man, a 40-year-old Westbrook man, a 31-year-old Cotswold Hills man and a 45-year-old Coral Cove man.

Their matters also remain before Toowoomba Magistrates' Court.

World.title: Buses rerouted, stops closed during Story Bridge closure
World.content:
Buses will be rerouted and five bus stops closed during the three-week closure of the landmark Story Bridge in Brisbane over summer.

The bridge will close to general traffic from 1am Sunday, December 27, to 5am Monday, January 18, for the northern and southern approaches to be resurfaced, and structural maintenance and waterproofing to be completed.

A council spokeswoman said the works on the bridge will cost $14 million, with funds to come out of the Operation Smooth resurfacing budget and the Story Bridge Renewal Project budget.

LNP Transport chair Andrew Wines told Brisbane City Council chambers all buses that use the bridge will be rerouted and five stops closed.

Councillor Wines said there would be alternative stops nearby the closed ones for passengers to use, including two temporary bus stops.

Transport chair Andrew Wines has told Brisbane City Council about the changes to bus routes and stops over the Christmas holidays. (ABC Radio Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

"While the bridge will be closed during these works Brisbane will remain very much open," he said.

"Those services that would ordinarily cross the bridge will be diverted through the inner south busway and across Victoria Bridge."

As Labor opposition councillors called out, Cr Wines continued:

"Some of my councillor colleagues didn't understand, so I'll say it again," he said.

"If your bus ordinarily crosses the Story Bridge, what will happen to it while the works are on, it will come through the inner south busway and cross Victoria Bridge.

"You'll just use a different bridge, that's really all I'm saying. It really isn't that hard an idea."

He said there would be a shuttle service for parts of Kangaroo Point that would take passengers to Woolloongabba Station.

Three-week bridge closure 'unprecedented'

Labor Opposition Leader Jared Cassidy told the meeting that never in its history had the bridge closed for three weeks.

He told the meeting that the council administration should have added more public transport services during the closure to compensate drivers.

"Their only alternative route is through a toll road, or they can spend hours and hours and hours stuck in CBD gridlock," he said.

"The LNP's lack of a public transport plan during the Story Bridge closure over Christmas is going to be a public transport disaster for our city, let alone the congestion disaster we will see, and the hip-pocket disaster we will see by forcing people (to use toll roads)."

Brisbane City Council Opposition Leader Jared Cassidy says more services should have been put on during the Story Bridge closure. (ABC Radio Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

The administration chose to close the bridge during the quieter summer holidays to reduce the impact on drivers and passengers.

Cr Wines urged people to look up the changes on Translink's Journey Planner and plan ahead.

The routes will be available on the website from November 30.

Temporary bus route changes:

Routes 227, 228, 231, 232 and 236: Services will divert via Wellington Road and Latrobe Street, with temporary stops 350 to 400 metres from affected Shafston Avenue stops.

Services will divert via Wellington Road and Latrobe Street, with temporary stops 350 to 400 metres from affected Shafston Avenue stops. Routes 227, 232 and 234: The Main Street stop at Story Bridge East will close, with an alternative stop at Thornton Street, approximately 200 metres away.

The Main Street stop at Story Bridge East will close, with an alternative stop at Thornton Street, approximately 200 metres away. Routes 216, 221, 227, 228, 231, 232 and 236: Services will divert around Shafston Avenue at Connor Street, with alternative stops 250 to 500 metres away.

Services will divert around Shafston Avenue at Connor Street, with alternative stops 250 to 500 metres away. Route N154: Five Main Street stops will no longer be serviced by this route. Passengers can use Route N226 to Wellington Street, with safe drop-offs available along the route.

World.title: New vice-chancellor appointed to lead embattled NT university CDU
World.content:
The Northern Territory's embattled Charles Darwin University (CDU) has appointed a new vice-chancellor and president, as the institution looks to recover from a string of controversies.

CDU announced Fiona Coulson's appointment to the leadership positions this week, after she spent the past nine months filling in the role following former vice-chancellor Scott Bowman's resignation in February.

Professor Bowman stepped down after an accreditation bungle impacting hundreds of CDU TAFE students, which saw them graduate without completing essential units.

Scott Bowman resigned from the vice-chancellor position earlier this year. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Later that same week, CDU walked away from its $1.9 million decision to establish a campus in London, saying the project was no longer financially viable.

And In June, the Fair Work Ombudsman ordered the university to backpay 823 staff more than $4 million in wages.

Professor Coulson told the ABC regaining the community's trust in CDU was of paramount importance in the wake of a difficult period.

NT's sole university to be forced to meet KPIs After a series of scandals, the NT's only university will soon be forced to prove its taxpayer funding is having positive outcomes for students.

"It is regularly that we're reminded of those mistakes, and it's going to take some time to rebuild that trust," she said.

" I think you've got to be open about these things — you own up to it, you take accountability for it, you put the systems and processes in place to ensure they don't happen again. "

She said, however, the decision to establish a London campus was "the right decision at the time," and would have gone ahead were it not for CDU's financial situation.

"Changes to international student numbers changed the project's viability," she said.

CDU has been rocked by a string of bungles over 2026. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

CDU data shows as of 2025, 35 per cent of non-TAFE students at the university were international students, with international student enrolments having almost tripled over the past five years.

Professor Coulson said CDU's reliance on international students was justified.

She flagged she would be advocating for changes to the Commonwealth's student caps, saying the policy had taken a financial toll on the university.

Fiona Coulson has been at CDU since 2022. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"It is a very difficult proposition to run a university in a small population across the vast distances we do," she said.

"The reality is international students support what we do here.

" I refute that we're a visa factory. "

Job redundancies flagged amid restructure

CDU has confirmed two administrative staff have been made redundant, and another eight are being given the option to move to different roles or elect for redundancy, following an ongoing internal restructure at the university.

The ABC understands the restructure was announced to staff on October 30 and will take effect in early December.

A restructure will see some administrative roles at the university made redundant. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Professor Coulson confirmed several roles in the organisation were being "reclassified", but insisted the university was trying to find savings in vacant positions where possible.

"There are some staff that have been negatively affected by this," she said.

"We've gone through a process, and we've really tried to limit those."

Professor Coulson attributed the restructure to the downturn in international student enrolments, reiterating the financial impact of the federal government's international student caps on CDU.

World.title: Twins' death after freebirth could have been avoided, inquest hears
World.content:
Twins delivered via freebirth in northern NSW would probably have survived if their mother had sought antenatal care, an inquest has heard.

WARNING: This story contains details of babies dying at birth that may be distressing to some readers.

The inquest is underway, examining the deaths of four babies, three born by freebirth in northern NSW and one after a homebirth in the Hunter Valley.

The NSW Coroners Court heard evidence in Lismore today about the death of Baby D, who died shortly after his twin was delivered stillborn in northern New South Wales in February 2024.

The baby and his family cannot be named for legal reasons.

Midwifery expert Hannah Dahlen told the court that with medical intervention, the babies would "both probably have survived, but not without risk".

Professor Dahlen's report, and that of fellow midwife Dr Alison Teate, said antenatal care would have detected two babies sharing a placenta, a "very high-risk" pregnancy.

No antenatal care

The court heard Baby D's mother had not engaged antenatal care through the medical system because of a past traumatic birth experience.

In a video played to the court, the woman and her partner told police her first pregnancy was a homebirth overseen by a midwife in northern New South Wales.

After a long labour, the woman was taken to a birth centre.

She said what followed was a "snowball effect of intervention that didn't need to happen", including an epidural, and she was given little information about her treatment.

She said it was not in keeping with the holistic, spiritual birth she had imagined.

The couple said they felt threatened because of their birthing decisions, and were told by nursery staff, "we were going to kill our baby" if medical advice was not followed.

With her second pregnancy, the woman wanted a "sovereign" or freebirth and engaged the services of a doula whom she trusted and who had delivered more than 100 babies over 23 years.

The doula was paid a fee of $4,100 for attending the birth and three additional consultations.

With no ultrasounds or midwife care, Baby D's mother did not know she was having twins who shared a placenta.

The court heard this meant a homebirth would not have been recommended.

In a statement read in court, the doula said she would have suggested the mother seek medical care if she had known the mother was expecting twins, as she was not medically qualified, and had not delivered twins before.

Hannah Dahlen and Alison Teate gave evidence at the inquiry. (ABC North Coast: Cathy Adams)

Professor Dahlen's report said if "managed properly", the risks would have been picked up.

Cord was cut but not clamped

Baby D was born in February 2024, and his mother said he "looked healthy".

That she was pregnant with two babies only came to light when the second baby began to crown.

The baby was born pale, limp, and showing no signs of life. The baby was stillborn, having died in the womb.

The inquest has no jurisdiction to examine how Baby D's brother died.

The court heard that what caused Baby D to decline was unclear, but his mother had said it began after the delivery of his brother.

Counsel assisting the Coroner, Ragni Mather SC, said medical experts suggested twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome may have contributed to the deaths.

The condition can cause an uneven blood flow to babies sharing a placenta and affects around 15 per cent of babies sharing a placenta.

Baby D's mother said in her police statement that the larger size of the stillborn baby supported this theory.

However, the doula's decision to cut Baby D's umbilical cord and not clamp it could have also contributed, the court heard.

The doula claimed the cord had already separated from the placenta when she cut it, and was not bleeding.

But as the baby was placed back into a birth pool that was bloody from the deliveries, it could not be known if the baby had lost blood through the unclamped cord.

The inquest heard that it was a woman's legal right to choose how she gave birth.

Professor Dahlen acknowledged in her report a mother's legal right to reject care once informed.

But she said the mother's previous negative birth experience did not exclude the need to seek medical care when needed.

In a video played to the court, their tearful mother told police she would not change her decisions, despite the outcome.

"I don't regret anything with my prenatal care," she said.

"I believe nothing could be done to help them that wasn't already done.

"They were born with love, and got to leave with love."

World.title: Aboriginal protester guilty of trespass despite 'cultural responsibility' to forests
World.content:
An Aboriginal woman has been found guilty of trespass after a magistrate rejected her claim that she was innocent because she had a "cultural obligation" to protect forests from logging.

Tasmanian-born Yorta Yorta/Dja Dja Wurrung woman Ruth Langford, also known as Tipruthanna, pleaded not guilty in the Hobart Magistrates' Court to one count of trespass.

It related to an incident in January 2025, when she and other activists protested at a logging coupe at Snow Hill in state's northern midlands.

Ms Langford was accused of refusing police orders to leave the site, which was managed by the state-owned forestry company, Sustainable Timbers Tasmania (STT).

During hearings earlier this year, Ms Langford argued that STT had failed to comply with their legal obligations to identify and protect Aboriginal cultural heritage.

She told the court that she held cultural responsibilities within the Palawa Aboriginal community that required her to "protect lands that are being slaughtered".

Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna spoke to the media and her supporters outside court. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Ms Langford said she had permission to be on the site from Palawa/Pakana elder Uncle Jim Everett, whom she described as the rightful owner of the cultural landscape.

In a written decision handed down on Tuesday, Chief Magistrate Catherine Geason agreed that Ms Langford had cultural obligations.

"Ms Langford was entitled to engage in cultural practices and prevent the logging contractors from commencing their work," Ms Geason stated.

However, she said that once Ms Langford was asked to leave, that entitlement ended.

Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna was charged with trespassing at an anti-logging protest at Snow Hill. (ABC News: Paul Yeomans)

Ms Geason said that while it was accepted Uncle Jim was a senior elder, he did not hold the authority to grant lawful permission for Ms Langford to remain at the coupe.

"I acknowledge and recognise Ms Langford's deeply held, genuine and spiritual obligations to protect cultural heritage and to protect old-growth trees, which she regards as kin," Ms Geason said.

"I also acknowledge the evidence of Ms Langford and her witnesses regarding the profound grief and responsibility experienced by Aboriginal people when old-growth forests are cleared.

"However, the court is bound to apply the law as enacted by parliament."

Ms Geason said, on the balance of probabilities, Ms Langford had not established that her cultural obligations amounted to a "reasonable or lawful excuse" to remain on the land.

"As such, the charge of trespass is proved."

Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna at the anti-logging protest in January last year. (Supplied: Bob Brown Foundation)

'I am not a criminal'

Ms Langford told the court she was "exceptionally disappointed".

Outside court, Ms Langford addressed the media and her supporters.

"I am not a criminal," she said.

"And regardless of what the colonial court may determine, we know that our law, our obligation, is in country and country has spoken.

" We all must rise up to protect the very things that give us life. "

Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna says she is pleased with some parts of the chief magistrate's decision. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Despite the verdict, she said she was pleased with some parts of the written decision.

"In my hands is the written reasons why this court denied my internationally recognised rights as an Aboriginal person," she said.

"I am delighted to see that she has clearly recognised that as an Aboriginal woman, I have an obligation to protect country.

"That those old trees hold our law, that that law exists, and that in the finding, the magistrate has recognised that that is true."

Ms Langford said she would continue to practice her cultural obligations.

"We will assert that our law is in country and we are the law holders," she said.

The matter has been adjourned until December 18 for sentencing submissions.

In Tasmania, trespassing on land can incur a maximum penalty of six months jail, or a $5,325 fine.

World.title: What it took to bring live music and late-night crowds back to St Kilda’s famous strip
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life What it took to bring live music and late-night crowds back to St Kilda’s famous strip Cara Waters November 17, 2026 — 7:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Grant Smillie is standing in the middle of the Prince Hotel’s revamped rooftop deck, right where the swimming pool used to be. Now, there’s a piano room covered in leopard-print carpet and a large expanse of decking looking out over Fitzroy Street, where Smillie will be serving up retro-inspired takes on illusion shakers and fruit tingles. The Prince reopens on Thursday, except for the terrace, which opens on November 27. Grant Smillie at The Prince Hotel in St Kilda, which reopens on Thursday. Jason South Downstairs, the front bar has had a spruce-up as well and has new tables and chairs, but Smillie wants to keep it as a locals’ hangout with $2 pots – though only on the first Monday of the month, and only a single keg. The Prince’s new look is a vote of confidence in Fitzroy Street, which has battled vacant shopfronts for years but is now being transformed by a rush of openings and developments.



Vacancy rates on the strip still sit at 10.1 per cent, but down the street the $15 million Novotel hotel opened in September, the Fortis apartments are nearing completion, the Snakepit bar is reopening underneath the George Hotel, and across the road the Saint is set to reopen its multi-level space. Related Article Fitzroy Street's decline a tale of old and new St Kilda They will join wine bar Bar Adri and cafe Where’s Lucy, which both opened on the strip last month. Smillie says it’s a happy coincidence for Fitzroy Street that so many places are set to open at the same time. “It wasn’t like everyone hit the phones and said, ‘Hey, we’re doing this,’” he says. “I don’t think we all knew it was coming. However, if you want to talk about that cultural collision or whatever it is, that alchemy that makes the suburb potentially change, I think that it’s the joinery of all these wonderful projects coming together at one time – strangely, all on top of each other.”



Port Phillip Mayor Libby Buckingham says Fitzroy Street has had its challenges, so it’s exciting to see businesses opening, significant investment taking place and fresh interest in the street. “This resurgence is being driven by growing business confidence, private investment and Fitzroy Street’s enviable location close to the foreshore and Melbourne CBD,” she says. “Our council and traders are also working together to make the street a vibrant, welcoming destination for locals and visitors.” Smillie looks out over Fitzroy Street from The Prince Hotel’s renovated deck. Jason South Ricky Jeffs, chief executive of Erdi Group, which manages Novotel St Kilda and has owned the property since 2018, says Fitzroy Street’s resurgence has followed the gentrification of the strip. “We saw it at its highest, we saw it at its lowest, and now its coming back up,” he says. “It’s been a long time in the making, and we’ve been there across the whole journey.”



Jeffs says the closure of rooming house the Gatwick Hotel, which was turned into luxury apartments for television show The Block, and the opening of the Pride Centre have been catalysts for change. Outreach workers have raised concerns about the impact of the closure of the Gatwick and other rooming houses on those needing emergency accommodation, but Jeffs says it has helped clean up the street. “There’s about $300 million of money being invested in Fitzroy Street, and I think that helps,” he says. “The whole street is now going back to hospitality and residential, which, 20 years ago, that’s what it was like. It’s been a tough period of time between now and then.” Liam Ganley, of the Ganley Group, operates sprawling Irish bar The Fifth Province and is about to reopen the Snakepit, the bar underneath the George Hotel. Ganley says the area has reached a critical mass and is reclaiming its live music roots.



“The big, big problem with St Kilda was the live music scene just got destroyed,” he says. “Look at the George, where you had Nick Cave and all these amazing artists that played there over the years, and then we had this huge issue with regulations.” Ganley says onerous noise restrictions killed the live music scene in St Kilda as venues struggled to exist alongside residents. The Snakepit bar has reopened in the basement of the George Hotel with a music stage. He is optimistic that St Kilda’s designation as a live music precinct means it will be easier to operate a music venue and says that last week the Fifth Province, which holds 1000, was packed and on Saturday night the street was as busy as he had seen it. “When you get a few good operators coming, all of a sudden, the tide runs really, really fast,” he says. “It’s flavour of the month.”



It’s a sentiment Smillie agrees with as he turns up the volume on the newly installed DJ decks at the Prince so a wave of sound hits the room. Related Article City life How St Kilda remains St Kilda against all odds “St Kilda’s always had a bit of a grungy edge,” he says. “Now the street’s clean, it’s much better – it’s vibrant.” What hasn’t changed, says Smillie, is the locals who have been getting behind the street’s resurgence. “They’ve been waiting for this,” he says. “They’ve been here all along.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: A violent bikie’s failed recall can’t erase the evidence of a Big Build turned bent
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsVictoriaBuilding Bad A violent bikie’s failed recall can’t erase the evidence of a Big Build turned bent Adam Carey November 17, 2026 — 7:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

From the moment Joel Leavitt strode through the doors of the royal commission building, sporting garish gold-rimmed Versace sunglasses and a dirty look for the press pack, it was obvious Tuesday’s hearing would be different. For one, the day never even got to what happened at Gap Road, Sunbury, in June 2022, the very subject of this two-week block of hearings. Bandido and ex-CFMEU health and safety representative Joel Leavitt arrives to give evidence on Tuesday. Wayne Taylor Instead, it roamed from Hallam to Hurstbridge to Glenroy, trying to pin an evasive Leavitt down on how an outlaw motorcycle gang member with a violent criminal record was ushered onto these government projects by the construction union, and engaged to enforce its will on who worked and who didn’t. It may be that the hearing never got to Gap Road because the day’s only witness was also the least co-operative so far.



The patched Bandido barely concealed his contempt for the inquiry he was summoned to, stubbornly deflecting question after question from the bar table during five hours of sustained, forensic and sometimes frustrated examination. Related Article Building Bad ‘Bend the knee’: Rail alliance told make peace with union or never work in Melbourne again Sniffing loudly into the microphone, swivelling and shuffling compulsively in the witness chair, he uttered the phrase “I can’t recall” well over 200 times, in the same gravelly voice that pleaded memory failure but in truth implied: “You’re getting nothing out of me.” Counsel assisting the commissioner Chris Carr, SC, was made to dig hard to get even the most basic admissions from Leavitt regarding his activities as a CFMEU health and safety representative on Victorian rail projects between 2021 and 2023. Leavitt grudgingly admitted to having a birthday, which he shared with the commission. “If you say so” and “so it would seem” both got a liberal airing, but in a dismissive tone that conceded nothing more than the fact that Carr had asked him a question.



Many of Carr’s questions were met with questions, a transparent stonewalling tactic that led the visibly frustrated barrister to state not once, but twice: “The way this works is I ask you questions and you answer them, not the other way around.” Leavitt was running down the clock, in the manner of an insubordinate student in detention, muttering monosyllabically into his hand as Carr took on the role of the reprimanding teacher. The claimed lack of recall became so repetitive that Commissioner Chris Kourakis eventually asked Leavitt if he had ever seen a doctor about cognitive decline, given he could recall nothing about what he was doing in 2021 and 2022. “The last few years are pretty blanky in my mind, commissioner,” Leavitt said. He blamed heavy drug use at the time he worked on the Big Build for his terminal failure of recall.



Leavitt’s shadowy role on Victoria’s infrastructure agenda was more widely exposed after he notoriously drove himself to hospital after he was shot in the clubhouse of the Rebels outlaw motorcycle gang in May 2023, in a vehicle issued to him by the government for his CFMEU health and safety role. His role as a CFMEU representative ended soon afterwards. The royal commission spent the entire day grappling with just why the CFMEU had pushed so hard to help an infamous bikie with a violent criminal rap sheet gain employment on the Big Build in the first place. It certainly wasn’t because he was seen as a diligent employee who would work tirelessly to get things done. Sometimes when he was paid, he wasn’t even there.



Text exchanges read out as evidence revealed Leavitt asking a superintendent who oversaw a Big Build site to fill in his time sheets on days he didn’t go to work. Another exchange exposed his delight in arranging a union stunt in which members set up a table and had their “smoko” in the middle of a level crossing in Glenroy, holding up trains and cars in the process. Matt Golding “Cost nearly half a million … Bah Ha ha ha! F--- me, that’s grouse,” the text exchange went. Subsequent exchanges also detailed the muscular Leavitt being directed to throw his considerable weight around about which contractors could and could not work on the $530 million Hurstbridge rail line upgrade.



As Carr probed Leavitt about a text exchange with CFMEU organiser Jerry McQuaid in 2021 about “walloping” construction contractor Laing O’Rourke as a way to get Leavitt onto a level crossing removal project, he claimed to be unsure what the word wallop even meant. But in the same exchange, he argued that a reference to a superintendent as a “c---” – another word that was uttered frequently in evidence – might have been a term of endearment. “C--- can also mean a good c--- in Aussie slang,” he said. At this point, just before lunch, Leavitt had almost succeeded in turning the commission’s inquiries into a farce. It was all so brazen, and so cosy for a man who knew he had the blessing of the CFMEU’s main man on the Big Build.



Leavitt was close with Joe Myles, the CFMEU’s senior leader on civil infrastructure projects in Victoria, the two even going so far as to profess their love for each other. Text exchanges also exposed how he used this camaraderie to get other bikie associates onto Big Build sites. Leavitt’s first day in the witness chair ended in characteristically vulgar fashion when Leavitt asked to be excused so that he could “chuck a piss”. It was an exit in keeping with a man who had spent his entire time on the Big Build taking the proverbial. World.title: John’s parents asked him a daily question. It helped him win a Nobel Prize
World.content:
NationalNSWScience John’s parents asked him a daily question. It helped him win a Nobel Prize Angus Dalton November 17, 2026 — 7:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

John Martinis’ parents – his father a fireman and his mother a homemaker – never asked him what he’d done each day at school. “I was very fortunate that my parents, around the dinner table, would ask instead: ‘Did you ask any questions today?’” the professor of physics at the University of California says. It was a ritual that spurred him into a life of curiosity, endless inquiry and, as of last year, a Nobel Prize. Professor John Martinis, with quantum equipment at the University of Sydney. Steven Siewert Los Angeles-born Martinis shared the 2025 Nobel Prize for Physics for an experiment he ran for his thesis in the mid-1980s which helped transform the magical, mind-bending, immensely powerful realm of quantum physics into something humans could wield for ourselves. The experiment he sweated over in his mid-20s laid the groundwork for today’s superconducting quantum computers, part of a multibillion-dollar industry that could fundamentally change our lives.



Here’s what he did – and what he says about the next stage of the quantum era. A quantum crash course Quantum mechanics describes how matter and energy behave on the tiny scale of atomic particles, such as protons and electrons. In this realm, physics works very differently to what we’re used to. It gets freaky. Picture a tennis ball. In “classical” physics, the ball is always in one place at any one time, even when it’s being belted around a court. In quantum physics, a ball, or a particle, can exist in multiple places or “states” at any one time. This concept is what makes quantum computing so potent. A standard computer “bit” switches between 0 and 1 for calculations. A quantum bit, or qubit, can exist in a state of both 0 and 1 simultaneously, making for vastly faster and more powerful calculations.



In another example, if you throw a tennis ball at a brick wall it will always bounce back. But in the quantum world, a particle has a chance of passing through a barrier it shouldn’t be able to cross – as if the tennis ball ghosted through the wall – in a phenomenon known as quantum tunnelling. Most objects bounce off a barrier. Quantum objects can sometimes pass through a barrier. This is called “tunnelling”. Johan Jarnestad/Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences Martinis and his colleagues were able to replicate quantum tunnelling in a macroscopic, human-made system. “Our quantum system is not made of protons and electrons like normal quantum mechanics,” he tells me at the University of Sydney, where he’s delivering a public lecture jointly hosted by industry body Quantum Australia.



Related Article Explainer

Quantum Computing Chandeliers, ‘qubits’ and Schrödinger’s cat: Inside the bizarre world of quantum computing “It’s constructed from an electrical circuit that you can see. It’s about a centimetre across, so it’s quite big.” That sounds simple. But it was an act of scientific nous that dragged the mystical qualities of quantum physics from the atomic scale to something that could be crafted and controlled by human hands. The experiment Martinis worked with two colleagues – his PhD adviser John Clarke and postdoctoral researcher Michel Devoret, with whom he shared the Nobel Prize – to create an electrical circuit involving a special component called a Josephson junction, made of two superconducting wires separated by an ultra-thin insulating barrier.



They cooled this circuit to almost absolute zero (-273 degrees Celsius, the coldest possible temperature). That triggered billions of electrons within the circuit to form “Cooper pairs” and begin behaving as a synchronised whole, rather than individual particles. 1. Single electrons jostle together in a normal conductor. 2. In a superconducting state, the electrons form pairs, and the current can flow without resistance. But an insulating gap may stop the current. 3. A large number electrons may sometimes behave like a single particle. This enables a current to tunnel across the insulating gap. Johan Jarnestad/The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences This created a system that could exist in one of two states: a zero-voltage state, or a state that produced voltage. The barrier separating these states could be leapt over if the electrons picked up heat energy. But when the system reached a particularly low temperature, suppressing heat, the scientists could still detect spikes of voltage. That meant the unified electrons were crossing straight through the barrier without needing thermal energy. The scientists had achieved quantum tunnelling.



Further, when they irradiated the circuit with microwaves, it absorbed energy at specific “quantised” levels, just like an atom. Put simply, Martinis and his colleagues had built something with the physics of an artificial atom. The elegant “exoskeleton” of an IBM quantum computer, supporting the chip within. IBM, digitally tinted Unlocking a new ‘physics playground’ Martinis says they didn’t set out to invent something new, much less help kick off a new industry that could change the world.



“It was just answering the very simple question,” he says. “Quantum mechanics is known to be the physics of the small – how atoms work, how molecules work. We wanted to show that it’s a more general phenomenon, so you can have current and voltages in a wire, and you can see quantum mechanics. “It means we had this new physics playground where we could make these new atomic systems out of the circuits.” Professor John Martinis, left, accepting the Nobel Prize for Physics in Sweden last year. Nobel Prize Outreach/Clément Morin The experiment laid the foundation for superconducting qubits. Martinis led the team at Google that, in 2019, claimed in Nature that they had achieved “quantum supremacy” with a processor made from 53 of these qubits, meaning they had solved a calculation with a quantum computer beyond the practical limits of any classical computer.



The quantum processor, they claimed, solved a calculation in 200 seconds that would take a supercomputer 10,000 years. That claim has since been subject to rebuttal and debate, with IBM claiming the calculation could be done on a classic system in two-and-a-half days, but the paper nevertheless marked an important moment in the advancement of quantum computing. When will quantum computing change our lives? “For years I would avoid this question,” Martinis says when asked when we might see a useful quantum computer. “But there has been enough progress and enough serious efforts that [now] I say five to 10 years.” Achieving large-scale, error-corrected quantum computing will wreak enormous effects. Standard security encryption we rely on to undergird the internet could be ruled obsolete. And what happens when quantum computing meets AI (QAI) is an open question.



Related Article Exclusive

Quantum Computing ‘It will be us’: Former Australian of the Year is building her answer to OpenAI On the other hand, scientists such as Martinis hope we’ll be able to model the inscrutable complexities of chemical reactions in unprecedented detail to unlock new materials and medicines. Martinis’ experiment was a “complete disaster” when they first tried it, he recalls. Solving it involved a visit to the university’s astronomy department to pick their brains about microwaves. Even since that ritual at the dining table from his childhood, he’s never stopped asking questions or worried about sounding stupid – which allowed him to bottle one of nature’s most remarkable, surreal qualities and fundamentally expand what humans are capable of. “I just find this fun,” he says of pursuing questions about how nature works on the atomic level. “It’s how I’m creative in physics, in the end. It’s the way I think.” The Examine newsletter explains and analyses science with a rigorous focus on the evidence. Sign up to get it each week.

World.title: Paid without turning up, then came a $165,000 pay day: Bikie Joel Leavitt’s Big Build bounty under microscope
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaBig Build royal commission Paid without turning up, then came a $165,000 pay day: Bikie Joel Leavitt’s Big Build bounty under microscope Clay Lucas November 17, 2026 — 7:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A labour hire firm at the centre of claims former premier Jacinta Allan’s office interfered on major projects to favour the CFMEU paid $165,000 to a violent bikie whom the union muscled onto Big Build sites. Senior Bandido Joel Leavitt also claimed wages for shifts on Big Build projects, the royal commission into the Victorian construction industry heard on Tuesday, while he was, in fact, visiting Melbourne gyms, and halted work for a protest that he boasted had cost the publicly funded level crossing removal project half a million dollars. Loading In an extraordinary day in the witness box, Leavitt uttered the phrase “I can’t recall” more than 200 times, blamed heavy drug use and his involvement in a shooting for memory loss, and conceded he could not rule out having billed for hours he never worked. In the final exhibit of the day, counsel assisting the inquiry Chris Carr, SC, tendered an invoice from Leavitt’s company JVL Consulting sent to BK Labour Hire requesting $165,000 for services provided in July last year.



Leavitt told the inquiry he was unable to recall preparing the invoice. When pressed by royal commissioner Chris Kourakis on what consulting services he had performed to justify the sum, Leavitt said his business provided “tips on safety work”. Asked by Kourakis to recall the nature of any purported safety advice he gave, Leavitt replied: “I can’t recall at this time.” During a day of remarkable admissions, Leavitt told the hearing he could not rule out having claimed wages for shifts he never worked, and confirmed he was an active member of the Bandidos outlaw motorcycle gang. Leavitt, a former CFMEU health and safety representative with convictions for rioting, assault and assaulting police, was installed onto major projects after union organisers campaigned for months for the company Laing O’Rourke to hire him in late 2020 and early 2021.



Messages from CFMEU organiser Gerry McQuaid showed the union pushing a Laing O’Rourke site superintendent to put Leavitt on rail projects in Cranbourne and Hallam via BK Labour Hire. As the contractor delayed, McQuaid texted Leavitt that he and a fellow organiser, Paul Tzimas, had been “walloping them all week”, and wrote: “C---s crying want 2 more shoppies [shop stewards] I’ve said no shoppies until Joel starts.” Carr suggested the union went to such lengths to force Laing O’Rourke to employ Leavitt because he was an intimidating bikie. “One possibility might be that the CFMEU wanted to go to such lengths to get you on this job site because you’re an intimidating bikie,” Carr said.



“You’d have to ask them,” Leavitt replied, having told the inquiry earlier that the union backed him because “I’m a good bloke”. Once installed on the $530 million Hurstbridge rail line upgrade, Leavitt exercised authority far beyond a standard workplace safety delegate. Loading The royal commission heard how Leavitt and others purged subcontractors that the CFMEU did not like from taxpayer-funded sites. Carr tendered a message from a CFMEU organiser named Costa instructing Leavitt to remove an earthmoving company from the job: “Anyone with Dundrum, wallop them and f--- them off.”



Costa told Leavitt to raise the issue with the Hurstbridge project superintendent. “So this seems to be a direction from Costa to you to get rid of a particular contractor on the job, and make sure they don’t get back onto the job in future?” Carr asked. “I don’t disagree,” Leavitt said, agreeing it was a possibility Costa believed he held the power to dictate which subcontractors worked on the project. Joal Leavitt appearing at the royal commission on Tuesday. Kourakis intervened to ask: “You don’t see anything odd about you as a health and safety representative (HSR) telling a superintendent on a site that they’re not to have a subcontractor back again?” Leavitt conceded it was a possibility.



Asked by Carr whether the succession of texts showed the CFMEU exercised control over who secured work on Victoria’s $109 billion Big Build program, Leavitt replied: “That’s a possible way of looking at that.” Other messages from March 2023 showed the Hurstbridge rail project superintendent checking with Leavitt over payroll, writing that he had received two pay dockets for a worker named Cheyenne whom he thought had left the site and whom the night supervisor had never seen. Leavitt said he could not explain why a project manager would consult a safety delegate over wages. Carr also cross-examined Leavitt over timesheets submitted on the Hurstbridge project in April 2023, accusing him of engaging in “a bit of petty fraud” by claiming 12-hour shifts starting at 5.30am while mobile phone records showed he was elsewhere. A Big Build timesheet for Leavitt tendered in the royal commission. Phone location data showed that on April 10, 2023, Leavitt did not leave his Roxburgh Park home until 6.20am – 50 minutes after his claimed shifts began – before visiting a gym in Richmond, and returning home for the afternoon.



On April 11, records placed him at home until 8.51am and at a gym in Braybrook, while on April 13 he stayed home until nearly 9am – despite claiming a full 12-hour day. Leavitt suggested he might have been working “on the phone” during the missed shifts before conceding to Kourakis that his job required him to be on-site. Leavitt blamed substance abuse when asked why his handwriting varied across timesheets, telling the inquiry: “Like I said, a lot of drugs. I was in different hazy states.” At one point in the day’s hearing, Leavitt was instructed to write “HSR” (health and safety representative) six times on a piece of paper so it could be compared to the HSR written on the timesheets. Former CFMEU Big Build boss Joe Myles (left) and Leavitt. Carr also tendered messages showing Leavitt worked with former CFMEU Big Build boss Joe Myles to secure construction jobs for other bikies, including Rebels gang member Jahmahl Pearson, who was jailed last year for torching a tobacco shop.



A photo was shown to the commission of Pearson sitting on a seat while he was meant to be working as a traffic controller at a Big Build site. It prompted Leavitt to message CFMEU organiser Joel Shackleton: “That’s where he sits all nights.” Asked how close he was to Myles, who the inquiry heard last week touted a “direct line” to Jacinta Allan’s office, Leavitt replied: “We were reasonably close.” Asked whether the pair told each other they loved each other, Leavitt said: “It’s definitely a possibility over the years.” Further texts revealed Leavitt boasting about disrupting rail and road traffic during a September 2021 protest over COVID-19 health orders closing construction tearooms. Leavitt sent an associate a video showing workers setting up a mock tearoom on the train tracks at the Glenroy Road level crossing in Glenroy, writing: “Can’t have smoko in the sheds. Set up on the train tracks.” The video shows dozens of cars lined up waiting to get across the rail crossing. After the recipient replied, “F--- me that’s grouse,” Leavitt messaged: “Held up trains and traffic and cost nearly half a million.”



Leavitt’s repeated claims that 2021 and 2022 were “pretty blank” in his memory led Kourakis to ask whether he had seen a doctor for cognitive decline, which Leavitt denied. Editor's pick Building Bad ‘Bend the knee’: Rail alliance told make peace with union or never work in Melbourne again The inquiry is examining how outlaw motorcycle gang members were embedded across state infrastructure projects under former CFMEU state secretary John Setka, who was expelled from the union last week by its administration. Last week, former Rail Projects Victoria chief operating officer Peter Wilkinson told the inquiry that Allan’s ministerial office passed on a warning during a 2022 stand-off in Sunbury that contractors “can’t have any more work in Victoria” unless they resolved industrial disputes with the CFMEU, before builders capitulated and installed BK Labour Hire on site. Leavitt’s role first emerged in The Age’s Building Bad investigation in 2024, which revealed he used a vehicle supplied for his Hurstbridge project duties to drive himself to Footscray Hospital after being shot at a Rebels bikie clubhouse in 2023.



Subsequent reporting by The Age and a review by barrister Geoffrey Watson, SC, detailed how rival bikie gangs fought for territorial control on the Hurstbridge upgrade because its 1000-strong workforce made it a lucrative hub for drug distribution as well as high-paid union jobs. The hearings continue. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The Sydney schools where only a fraction of students take religion classes
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation The Sydney schools where only a fraction of students take religion classes Christopher Harris November 17, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Enrolments in special religious education classes have dipped below 10 per cent at some public high schools leaving hundreds of students barred from doing classroom work if they do not opt in to scripture lessons. A snapshot of enrolment data, obtained under freedom of information laws, shows numbers in special religious education classes have mostly declined between 2019 and 2025 across 10 high schools. Inner west public primary student Layla has previously asked Education Minister Prue Car to review the current religious education rules. Peter Rae The data shows only 6 per cent of students at Willoughby Girls High School opted for religious classes last year. In year 9, there were six students enrolled in special religious education and 184 in alternative meaningful activities. Selective schools North Sydney Boys High School and Northern Beaches College Manly Campus have also seen substantial drops over that time period.



Student attendance is not compulsory in religious classes, but as parents at Newtown High School of the Performing Arts discovered this month, the current policy can upend the timetable and consign other students to spending 80 minutes under teacher supervision doing other meaningful activities. Current rules state actual school work cannot be taught while religious classes are in session. Special religious education participation data is not released by the department, but figures obtained under freedom of information laws by the Atheist Foundation and provided to the Herald show enrolments have mostly declined over the past six years. Enrolments increased slightly at Burwood Girls over the period, as well as at Georges River College in Peakhurst and The Ponds High.



However, primary schools are also seeing a drop in religion class enrolments, with Burwood, Ropes Crossing and Cherrybrook falling 20 percentage points or more. Year 6 student Layla, who asked not to use her surname and attends an inner west public school, said she had experienced the weekly frustration of colouring in or watching children’s movies when she could have been learning. “Those students who don’t subscribe to the religions on offer can do ethics, if a parent volunteer is available, but these classes have limited spaces,” she said. She said that in Australia’s multicultural society, public school students should study all religions from an impartial source. “By educating ourselves about various belief systems, we build important life skills including greater respect for cultures other than our own and increased cultural sensitivity,” she said.



Related Article Opinion

Education I’m a Newtown High School parent and my WhatsApp group won’t stop pinging Helen Paterson Contributor Atheist Foundation of Australia communications manager Steve Marton questioned why the state was facilitating religious instruction when a minority of students enrolled at some schools. “Why can’t they do it at the weekend?” he said. The NSW Secondary Principals’ Council, the NSW Primary Principals’ Council and the state’s P&C Federation in 2023 called for an urgent review of religious education, citing the fact that thousands of students were missing out on crucial learning time. A 2015 review of special religious instruction recommended procedures be revised for secondary schools to allow students not participating in religious education to continue their regular classwork. It was not supported by the previous coalition government.



Among the Australian population, the number of people with no religion increased to 38 per cent of the population in the 2021 census. Greens MP for Newtown Jenny Leong wants to abolish special religious education class in public schools. Steven Siewert Greens member for Newtown Jenny Leong has launched a petition calling on Education Minister Prue Car to abolish special religious education class in public schools. She said it was not about being pro or anti religion. “This is about rejecting an approach that takes public school students out of class for an hour every week, segregating them based on religion, to be instructed by unqualified religious volunteers outside the accountability of the school and curriculum,” she said.



“Our public schools should be a place where students can learn openly about the diverse religious faiths in our community, taught by professional teachers.” A Teachers Federation spokesperson said any education, religious or otherwise, should be delivered in line with an approved curriculum and by a qualified teacher. “Setting time aside for scripture detracts from teaching time, professional learning and extracurricular activities from an already crowded curriculum and school day,” he said. Car last week expressed support for special religious education saying it had been part of the state’s public education system since its inception. Opposition education spokesman Mark Speakman said he also supports it.



“Having ‘non-sectarian’ public education does not mean shutting the door on faith,” he said. “It means not preferring one faith over another. This instruction helps to develop well-rounded, confident students, who should not be disadvantaged by being enrolled in these classes.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Holes in the net and 14 spectators: Life on tour for Australian tennis’ ‘glamour’ couple
World.content:
SportTennisAustralian Open Holes in the net and 14 spectators: Life on tour for Australian tennis’ ‘glamour’ couple Adrian Proszenko November 17, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. By the time Jason Kubler completed a three-set victory over fellow Australian Matthew Dellavedova, on court five of the Sydney Tennis Centre, fianceé Maddison Inglis was no longer watching. She was one of 14 spectators – which included your correspondent and photographer – present for the start of the biggest match of this year’s NSW Open so far. Inglis caught only fleeting glimpses of the deciding set, which Kubler won 6-2, before she was required to practice on an adjoining court. Tennis player Maddison Inglis with her fiancé Jason Kubler at the NSW Open. Louise Kennerley Court five is a short stroll from Ken Rosewall Arena, which was reserved for an ITF fixture on Tuesday morning. It’s another world away altogether from Melbourne Park, where Kubler and Inglis captured the imagination of the public at the Australian Open earlier this year as Australian tennis’ latest love match. Inglis progressed all the way to the fourth round, a career best grand slam finish for which she pocketed $480,000 in prizemoney. It prompted a rare moment of self-indulgence: the purchase of a SMEG toaster.



The spoils are significantly smaller at Homebush Bay this week. The men are competing for a share of $107,000 in prizemoney at the NSW Open, while it’s $75,000 for the women. There are no strawberries and cream here. Dellavedova spent much of his match with Kubler remonstrating with the French umpire, over issues that included, but were not limited to, an apparent hole in the net. By the time Kubler finally prevailed, Inglis was preparing for the start of her own Sydney campaign, which was being staged and played concurrently with the men’s competition. Jason Kubler during his NSW Open win against Matthew Dellavedova. Louise Kennerley For all but the very elite professionals in tennis, this is the reality of tour life. It is spent jostling for rankings points in lower-tier events, trying to eke out enough money to keep alive the dream of the big payday that comes with qualifying for the slams. There were times when it looked to be all over. Like when, a decade ago, Kubler checked his balance to find he was down to his final 14 cents.



“It was tough,” Kubler recalled, as he and Inglis sat down with this masthead after his match. “It’s actually not a bad story, like, not that I need to tell it, but after that I started playing a few sort of lower tournaments, and then doing well. Tennis power couple Maddison Inglis and Jason Kubler. Louise Kennerley “Then from having that 14 cents to maybe four months down the road, I ended up getting a wildcard into the Aussie Open that following year. So it’s crazy how much it can change.” Sitting beside him, Inglis chimed in: “It is crazy you got down to that, though.”



“I’m a battler, I’m a battler!” Kubler grinned. Kubler has had to draw on his fighting spirit to make a career out of tennis. This year, he endured a sixth surgery on his left knee, to go with the two to his right. The 33-year-old is currently ranked 562 in the world after a series of injury lay-offs, including a period where he played almost exclusively on clay to take the strain off his legs. Inglis is ranked 138, but both are hopeful of earning a start in the Australian Open main draw. Maddison Inglis (centre) watches fiancé Jason Kubler in action. Louise Kennerley “It would be cool if we could do the same as this year,” Inglis said. The NSW Open is one of the few tournaments for which they are in the same place at the same time. There are periods of the year when they are at different far-flung destinations, trying to make ends meet.



“I remember when I was in my early 20s, then it was a slog, you know?” Kubler said. “You were grinding for, maybe if you won the tournament, you got $7,000. Related Article Novak Djokovic Fresh off beating Djokovic, Rinky Hijikata will take on world’s best at home “Whereas I was checking, and now it’s like $17,000 [US, to win the NSW Open]. I was like, ‘That’s actually not that bad.’ And then the slightly bigger tournaments – say the 100s and the 125s – I think the 125s was like $US33,000 or something. So I was like, ‘Mate, it’s actually pretty good now, you know?’” The pay cheques can be healthy or challenging, depending on the results. However, it’s the love of the game that has them coming back. “There are tough weeks on the road, but the days where you’re just striking it so well – for me, that’s so addictive,” Kubler said.



Inglis interjects: “He loves it! Like, we’ll have a day off and you’re like, ‘Do you want to go have a hit?’ I’m like, ‘No, I really don’t.’” The couple, who live together on the Gold Coast, got engaged on Rottnest Island just weeks before their Australian Open heroics. As for a wedding date? “Don’t bring this conversation up!” Kubler said. “No, we’re hoping for end of next year.” Inglis added: “I’m not too fussed. I want something really small. We will get there, no rush. Tennis is the focus at the moment.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

PropertyNewsLuxury property Kyle Sandilands updates price guide for his glamorous weekender Elizabeth Redman November 17, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Does Kyle Sandilands know something about the property market that others don’t? The radio presenter set a $4.9 million price guide in May on his luxurious weekender located in Sydney’s north-western outskirts. And yet, the guide has been updated to a range between $4.9 million to $5.1m, despite property prices falling. The property is a grand six-bedroom estate, with a swimming pool and outdoor dining area, a jewel-toned home office, chandelier and fireplace. The Georgian-inspired home features a circular driveway with fountain and porte-cochère, a games room, high ceilings and a contemporary kitchen.



A sale at that level could still offer value to a buyer, given the home on almost a hectare in Glenorie was first listed in February with a price guide of $5.7 million to $5.9 million. In May, the guide was changed to $4.9 million ahead of its scheduled auction, but the listing remains available. Sandilands bought the home for $3 million in 2022 and renovated last year. The weekender has room to host and entertain. Belle Property Dural selling agent Carolyn Wheatley was contacted, as was Sandilands’ manager. The former host of The Kyle and Jackie O Show on KIIS, now hosting Kyle Sandilands Live on his own paywalled platform, is based in Sydney’s eastern suburbs.



Earlier this year, when Sandilands challenged KIIS owner ARN over the termination of his contract, he said he wanted to return to work and has “mortgages to pay like everyone else”. Related Article CBD From Vaucluse to Copacabana: Kyle Sandilands has four mortgages to pay Property records show the Glenorie home has a mortgage to NAB and another to Mortgage Holdings Group Pty Ltd, while his Vaucluse home - bought for $14 million in 2023 - also has a mortgage to NAB and another to Mortgage Holdings Group Pty Ltd. ARN and Sandilands settled the litigation and he was delivered a $12 million payout and more than $1 million worth of advertising for his new show on the company’s channels. There were not enough property sales in Glenorie in the past year to calculate a median house price, but the median in nearby Dural is $2,255,000 on Domain data.



Sydney’s median house price is $1.66 million, down 7.9 per cent from its peak, after it fell at the steepest quarterly pace in four years in the September quarter. Property alerts are now available in the SMH app. Turn them on to receive the latest market news and trends.

World.title: Bowen has drawn battlelines with his climate proposals. Now comes the hard part
World.content:
EnvironmentClimate changeParis Agreement Bowen has drawn battlelines with his climate proposals. Now comes the hard part Nick O'Malley November 17, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australia and the Republic of Korea have signed a memorandum of understanding on the sidelines of international climate talks in Turkey which aims to accelerate both nations’ decarbonisation efforts, strengthen clean energy supply chains and unlock trade and investment opportunities. Signed by Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen and his South Korean counterpart, Kim Sungwhan, on the sidelines of the United Nations’ climate summit, COP31, the agreement will give Australia access to the $US1 trillion the South Korean government has pledged to spend decarbonising its economy in the years to 2035. Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen will lead talks as negotiators begin to tussle over key issues. Getty Images “Korea’s clean energy transformation is a major economic opportunity for Australia, particularly for the regional communities that power our economy and produce the resources the world needs,” said Bowen, who is leading global negotiations at the summit. “This is our leadership at COP31: delivering for Australians, stronger industries, greater energy security and more opportunities for new, lasting jobs.” South Korea is Australia’s fourth-largest two-way trading partner, with bilateral trade reaching $67.4 billion in 2025.



Energy analyst Tim Buckley, director of the pro-renewables think tank Climate Energy Finance, said the deal was a crucial step in developing the sort of massive infrastructure that would be needed for Australia to clean up export industries such as green iron ore for the South Korean market. “Australia is only going to be really successful in building zero-emissions export industries of the future through bilateral agreements,” he said, noting that the massive North West Shelf gas project was created by agreements between state, federal and international governments along with the private sector. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese with Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen greeting iron ore magnate and climate advocate Andrew “Twiggy” Forrest at COP31. AAP He said South Korea’s spending commitment was the largest in the world outside China and that Australia was well placed to seek to benefit from it. Matt Kean, chair of Australia’s Climate Change Authority, said the memorandum presented huge opportunities for both nations.



“Korea needs lower-emissions materials to decarbonise its industries and remain internationally competitive,” he said. “Australia has the resources, renewable energy potential and industrial capability to produce them. Both countries stand to benefit.” Related Article Good Weekend ‘I was hooked for life’: The moment as a teenager Chris Bowen will never forget South Korea plans to develop a green steel industry, which would demand green iron ore, which Australia could only provide if massive shared renewable energy projects and export infrastructure were developed. Industry and Innovation Minister Tim Ayres emphasised the strategic industrial gains: “Working more closely with Korea will help Australia move further up the value chain, expand Australia’s industrial capability and make more of the clean energy technologies and materials the world increasingly needs.” Earlier on Tuesday, Bowen, serving as president of negotiations at the COP talks, released a draft text of the agreement that negotiators are working on. The 18-page document has been described as a “Christmas list” of proposals, many of which are not expected to survive the negotiations.



The draft contains reference to ramping up electrification of the global economy, a key goal of Bowen and COP hosts Turkey, and acknowledges that the world will overshoot the Paris target of holding warming to 1.5 degrees. It also includes language calling on developed nations to “take the lead” on emission reductions by reaching net zero emissions by 2030 and net negative emissions by 2040. A “presidency note” attached to the document explained that it was designed to “reflect the breadth of views expressed by parties” and prompt further negotiation, rather than to reflect consensus views. Now that the draft has been released, delegations will continue negotiating towards a document that might win consensus support by the end of the week. “The strategy is to put it out, let people provide their views, to take things out that don’t receive consensus support,” said Bowen in a press conference. “If elements in here don’t get consensus support, they won’t be in the final.” The draft text also contains calls for both a “phase out” and a “transition away from” fossil fuels – language likely to receive forceful pushback from Gulf states and Russia which object to direct references to any sectors or energy sources.



Earlier in the week, Russia signalled a hard stance against calls for a phase-out of fossil fuels. “In the current conditions of excessive pressure on the energy market due to the well-known strait [issue] and other factors, it is absolutely inappropriate to talk about an accelerated phase-out of hydrocarbons, because it will additionally affect the price,” Russian Presidential Special Representative for Climate and Water Resources Ruslan Edelgeriyev told the Interfax news agency. Related Article Climate policy Albanese defends Australia as climate leader after being pushed on world stage to do more Bowen said negotiations so far were constructive. “The general tenor and tone has been very constructive. Parties have come to me with strong views about various things, as you’d expect, and I welcome that. Because there’s no point being unclear about things that parties have strong views on.” In the lead-up to the talks both COP hosts, Turkey and Bowen signalled support for including a target to reach 35 per cent electrification by 2035 both in the outcome of formal negotiations, and in the “action agenda” aspect of the talks. By Saturday, only 30 nations had agreed to the target, though more are expected to sign. “It’s pretty clear in the draft text that we are interested in getting a strong statement on electrification into the final decision,” said Bowen in the press conference.



“That’s something that Australia supports and will continue to support. But we’ll need to work with parties on what is acceptable,” said Bowen. He argued for ambition as the negotiations continued. “Frankly, if we only talk about what we all agree on, if we only put things in the broader statement that got everyone’s support at this point, so early in the process, it’ll be a pretty short document.” Cosima Cassel, who heads the climate diplomacy program for the international climate think tank E3G, said that while it was good the document included all key issues, at 144 paragraphs the text was very long. “The approach looks to be putting it all in and letting parties fight for the trade-offs,” she said.



“The test will be whether the final decision keeps the core elements once that process plays out: ambition on overshoot, defence of the science, clean electrification and forward progress on adaptation finance.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.
