World.title: Enforce the rules for signs of the time
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Enforce the rules for signs of the time November 17, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. VOTING ETIQUETTE The state election is nearly with us, and already we’re seeing the usual confrontations about election signage start up again.

The Australian Electoral Commission and the Victorian Electoral Commission should make, and enforce, very clear rules about where, and how many, election signs can be displayed. This is especially needed near polling places, but also other public locations, such as shopping centres and train stations.

Last election, one ‘early bird’ candidate would attempt to completely fill the available space with their signs. The next candidate would arrive, and find almost nowhere to put their signs up, other than in front of the existing signs. Subsequent candidates would arrive and find the situation even worse.

Simply restricting each candidate to a set number of signs, or perhaps a quota of no more than 10 per cent of the available space, would remove a lot of confrontation. Any breach could be penalised by a ban of the offending candidate’s signs at that location for 48 hours.

Geoffrey McNaughton, Glen Huntly Avoiding the rat run of pamphleteers

Isn’t it time we banned ‘how-to-vote’ cards – especially at polling booths, both on-the-day and pre-polling?

I and many others find the rat run of party workers handing them out at booths intensely annoying and likely to elicit brusque or even rude comments.

Why cannot parties treat voters like intelligent adults and encourage us to make up our own minds?

We have an amazingly democratic electoral system, an example to the rest of the world, but this is the one feature that really makes me angry.

Mick Webster, Chiltern



Living in the Hawthorn bubble

If it were not for a smattering of corflutes from two candidates and three pamphlets between them thrust in our letter box, we in the Hawthorn electorate would not know there was an election under way. We have no idea who the other candidates are.

We feel treated with disdain by two of the parties vying for government. It is inexplicable they are uninterested in a winnable lower house seat, much less garnering upper house votes.

Graham Devries, Camberwell More to voters’ concerns than potholes

Your correspondent is spot on (Letters 17/11): voter surveys cover very limited ground. They effectively push-poll by omitting important topics such as nature. They waste a golden opportunity to tap into voters’ values.

Are we OK with the destruction of old-growth forests that protect native animals facing extinction? Are we concerned about the wounded waterbirds left by duck shooters? Do we feel safe in national parks where deer hunters operate? Do we support the routine bashing of kangaroo joeys when commercial shooters kill the mother? Should we have tighter controls on gun ownership?

Of course, we worry about bills, jobs, crime and potholes. But most of us can walk and chew gum.

Joan Reilly, Surrey Hills Who is premier if Wilson loses seat?

Your correspondent (15/11) ponders the consequences if the Liberals win the election and Jess Wilson loses her seat, then who would be premier?

Considering the Liberals are outpolling Labor, with the opposition leader on a net approval rating of plus 24 and Ben Carroll on minus 19, there is a higher probability of the premier losing his seat of Niddrie than the alternative scenario. Let’s remember, the opposition does not win elections, the government loses them.

Christo Krousoratis, Templestowe THE FORUM What does my vote buy?

A political party should be compelled to release its policy costings at least by the time pre-poll voting is available to electors. Major parties are waiting until the last minute despite releasing the main thrust and some of the content of their policies.

This election, the costings are more important as the parties are trying to prove themselves to be the best economic managers. Are we supposed to just trust them? The State Parliamentary Budget Office hasn’t received any details yet, and so it can’t publish anything.

One Nation has said it won’t even publish costings before the election.

The political parties are trying to sell us something, and we are supposed to buy it with our vote. We don’t yet know what we are buying or what it costs. I’ve already got too much unusable snake oil from the last federal election.

Greg Tuck, Warragul



AFL has enough funding

Pay for your own facilities, AFL. You get enough money from the population via gambling. Taxpayers shouldn’t be funding you. Budget like everyone else does for things you want -- like stadiums in Tasmania (″⁣Carroll kicks in $55m for AFL clubs″⁣, 16/11).

Belinda Burke, Hawthorn How to alienate voters

Adam Carey’s article (“Labor’s fast-track planning scheme gives tick to all but one proposal”, 17/11) exemplifies how the corporatisation of political parties in Australia has replaced community consultation with centralised control.

Labor’s barge-through and build-big attitude has alienated many previous supporters. There is little evidence that the Coalition will be much better.

It’s time to hunt around for candidates who are not captured by vested interests or party control and can independently represent their communities.

Allan Dowsett, Preston Kennett’s shadow

As a resident of another community whose train station was shut down by Jeff Kennett in the 1990s, I sympathise with the Mildurans who want their passenger rail services back (″⁣Can trains stop Hanson ‘Beatlemania’ in its tracks? Jess Wilson hopes so″⁣, 16/11).

Kennett’s campaign closures of services from technical high schools to regional railway stations destroyed jobs and devastated local communities.

In recent years, both major parties have repeatedly promised to bring back many of the stations that Kennett shut down, but are always unable to do so due to the high costs involved, demonstrating that reversing Kennett’s legacy is easier said than done.

The conservative philosopher Roger Scruton once remarked that ″⁣good things are easily destroyed but not easily created″⁣. This maxim has clearly been vindicated by Kennett’s premiership and its aftermath.

Nikhil Dhanabal, Clyde North Electricity transformation

Reading ″⁣Jess we can – but campaign launch serves a reminder the Liberals haven’t yet″⁣, (15/11) provides a handy look at many of the reasons a Liberal Victorian government might be anything but the best thing for the state.

Showcasing the most recent four leaders in the past four years with Matthew Guy, Brad Battin, John Pesutto, and now Jess Wilson reminds us of the recent disunity and in-fighting.

Mention of Ted Baillieu and Denis Napthine sends shivers of the damaging approach to restructuring the energy system they presided over.

And yet, the underwhelming Ben Carroll does not seem to realise the solid gold he sits on following the great work of Lily D’Ambrosio in setting up a vast renewable energy transformation that has given Victoria’s power the lowest wholesale electricity prices in the country (according to the Australian Energy Market Operator).

Not once have we heard reference to this. Of equal concern is the lack of parliamentary depth that looms with an influx of inexperienced One Nation and Liberal candidates.

Robert Brown, Camberwell Contain measles threat

Re ″⁣US anti-vax rhetoric sparks fears over measles″⁣, 17/11. I am a former registered nurse and among the thousands of patients I cared for over many years, one memory remains vivid – the tragic death of a 14-year-old girl from pan encephalitis, a rare, but well recognised, complication of the measles virus. There are also other non life-threatening complications such as ear infections which can lead to permanent hearing impairment.

Robert F Kennedy Jr is profoundly uninformed, and sadly, Americans are now paying the price of the folly of his selection as health secretary.

The public need to be educated on science-based facts, and dangerous so-called “wellness influencers” shut down where possible.

Travellers to Australia from infected areas of America, and elsewhere, should be required to have a current vaccination certificate for entry here.

It is time for immediate responsible action.

Christine Harris, Mordialloc



Puberty blockers

Federal Health Minister Mark Butler’s challenge to state and territory governments to align with the National Health and Medical Research Council’s interim advice (″⁣Butler challenges states to allow puberty blockers″⁣, 16/11) is a welcome and necessary intervention against politically motivated healthcare bans.

Medical decisions for vulnerable adolescents must be guided by clinical expertise and scientific evidence, not populist political interference.

Denying access to puberty blockers does not stop young people from experiencing gender dysphoria; it simply forces them into a harmful ″⁣wait and see″⁣ approach that withholds essential care and causes preventable psychological distress during an already difficult stage of life.

Puberty blockers offer vital breathing room, safely pausing unwanted and irreversible physiological changes that conflict with a young person’s identity. Decades of clinical use and research show that timely, supportive, gender-affirming care drastically improves mental health and wellbeing among transgender teenagers.

State governments must listen to medical consensus.

Tim Singleton Norton, Reservoir Flinders St patina

Reading restaurateur Chris Lucas’ vision for the demolition of all but the facade of Flinders Street Station, one can only wonder if he has spent much time overseas? If he has, how could he fail to grasp that it’s the old buildings, tiled and plastered with character and history, which attract millions of people to Europe year after year, feeding our collective soul.

The thought of rampaging through Flinders Street Station to make way for more new hotels, more new restaurants and yet more shopping is abhorrent. As one who has attended many exhibitions in the beautiful rooms above the station, I see it as a truly magical space, offering huge potential to anyone clever enough to be inventive while fully embracing the character and patina already on offer.

Laurie Chartres, Hawksburn No pride in selling rocks

Being a quarry for the world didn’t make Donald Horne proud. (“That’s the difference Australian mining makes”, 17/11).

He saw us not as a country to be proud of, but a lucky one, run by second-rate people who share its luck. Much of his assessment is still true.

I might take more pride in Australia if we owned up to the fact that, including exports, our small nation is responsible for 4.5 per cent of global emissions.

I would also be proud if we stopped exporting LNG to the several countries that are undermining decarbonising by creating new gas markets and that on-sell our gas.

Taxing those gas exports more appropriately would show we valued our people’s futures and would make me proud.

There are many ways I want to be proud of my country. Selling rocks isn’t one of them.

Helen Bowman, Preston Mapping the world

I am struck by the letters in The Age worrying about the cuts to immigration and effects on care. One aged care facility I have been told of has a map of the world on display. Pins indicate all the places the workers in the facility come from, such as Nepal, India and the Philippines.

This reportedly encourages all sorts of positive conversations about migration and immigrant workers. A good idea to foster understanding?

Maila Stivens, St Kilda Pat Cummins’ delivery

I found the description of Pat Cummins’ performance in his press conference as statesman-like by some commentators disappointing.

He was well-prepared and stood for 68 minutes taking questions. There is more to statesmanship than that.

There was little substance to many of his answers which essentially defended his previous response, and that of his employer. He was scant on detail, had selective memory, did not address issues of institutional accountability and dismissed Usman Khawaja’s accounts as ″⁣nonsense″⁣.

He accuses Khawaja of being ″⁣casual″⁣. Calling for collective responsibility and challenging a convenient narrative is not casual in my opinion.

Dismissing someone’s lived experience strikes me as someone speaking from a position of privilege with little understanding of how systemic bias, unconscious prejudice and exclusion occur.

Pat Cummins wants to draw a line under Sandpaper-gate.

That means confronting uncomfortable truths not defending a flawed investigation and system by saying ″⁣nothing else to see here″⁣.

Dhiren Singh, Malvern



AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding State election

They’ve all got plans, but who’s got the money?

Wendy Baker, Lilydale Your correspondent (Letters, 17/11) equates informal voting with wasting a vote. This is not quite right – to leave a poorly stocked shop without buying anything is still to vote with your feet.

Peter Drum, Coburg If three AFL clubs are promised $55 million, then what about the arts? How about a measly $1 million or so to put an organ in Hamer Hall to complete its recent upgrade?

Rod Watson, East Brighton



I’m waiting for One Nation to offer every Victorian $5000 if we vote for them.

Peter Sherry, Maidstone Great to see Ben Carroll is currently reading anti-corruption crusader Robert F. Kennedy’s book, The Last Campaign (CBD 17/11). Maybe he could next start on Dale Carnegie’s book, How to Win Friends and Influence People.

Robin Jensen, Castlemaine Furthermore

Prime Minister – don’t embarrass Australia by standing in the same photo as Putin.

Graham Fetherstonhaugh, North Fitzroy Re US measles outbreak. If you go with medieval medicine, you get medieval outcomes

Nina Wellington Iser, Hawthorn Cricket

Were the field umpires asleep when ball tampering was occurring? Surely, the umpires must also bear some of the responsibility for the sandpaper saga.

Martin Newington, Aspendale



Re the sandpapergate issue, I haven’t lost any respect for the Australian cricket team; women’s that is. In fact, I am still very proud of them.

Jill Kennare, Henley Beach SA We had sandpapergate, now we have sandpapergategate.

David Priest, Cabarita Finally

When is the AFL going to introduce being able to handball a goal?

Richard Sykes, Bell Park The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: What it took to bring live music and late-night crowds back to St Kilda’s famous strip
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life What it took to bring live music and late-night crowds back to St Kilda’s famous strip Cara Waters November 17, 2026 — 7:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Grant Smillie is standing in the middle of the Prince Hotel’s revamped rooftop deck, right where the swimming pool used to be. Now, there’s a piano room covered in leopard-print carpet and a large expanse of decking looking out over Fitzroy Street, where Smillie will be serving up retro-inspired takes on illusion shakers and fruit tingles. The Prince reopens on Thursday, except for the terrace, which opens on November 27. Grant Smillie at The Prince Hotel in St Kilda, which reopens on Thursday. Jason South Downstairs, the front bar has had a spruce-up as well and has new tables and chairs, but Smillie wants to keep it as a locals’ hangout with $2 pots – though only on the first Monday of the month, and only a single keg. The Prince’s new look is a vote of confidence in Fitzroy Street, which has battled vacant shopfronts for years but is now being transformed by a rush of openings and developments.



Vacancy rates on the strip still sit at 10.1 per cent, but down the street the $15 million Novotel hotel opened in September, the Fortis apartments are nearing completion, the Snakepit bar is reopening underneath the George Hotel, and across the road the Saint is set to reopen its multi-level space. Related Article Fitzroy Street's decline a tale of old and new St Kilda They will join wine bar Bar Adri and cafe Where’s Lucy, which both opened on the strip last month. Smillie says it’s a happy coincidence for Fitzroy Street that so many places are set to open at the same time. “It wasn’t like everyone hit the phones and said, ‘Hey, we’re doing this,’” he says. “I don’t think we all knew it was coming. However, if you want to talk about that cultural collision or whatever it is, that alchemy that makes the suburb potentially change, I think that it’s the joinery of all these wonderful projects coming together at one time – strangely, all on top of each other.”



Port Phillip Mayor Libby Buckingham says Fitzroy Street has had its challenges, so it’s exciting to see businesses opening, significant investment taking place and fresh interest in the street. “This resurgence is being driven by growing business confidence, private investment and Fitzroy Street’s enviable location close to the foreshore and Melbourne CBD,” she says. “Our council and traders are also working together to make the street a vibrant, welcoming destination for locals and visitors.” Smillie looks out over Fitzroy Street from The Prince Hotel’s renovated deck. Jason South Ricky Jeffs, chief executive of Erdi Group, which manages Novotel St Kilda and has owned the property since 2018, says Fitzroy Street’s resurgence has followed the gentrification of the strip. “We saw it at its highest, we saw it at its lowest, and now its coming back up,” he says. “It’s been a long time in the making, and we’ve been there across the whole journey.”



Jeffs says the closure of rooming house the Gatwick Hotel, which was turned into luxury apartments for television show The Block, and the opening of the Pride Centre have been catalysts for change. Outreach workers have raised concerns about the impact of the closure of the Gatwick and other rooming houses on those needing emergency accommodation, but Jeffs says it has helped clean up the street. “There’s about $300 million of money being invested in Fitzroy Street, and I think that helps,” he says. “The whole street is now going back to hospitality and residential, which, 20 years ago, that’s what it was like. It’s been a tough period of time between now and then.” Liam Ganley, of the Ganley Group, operates sprawling Irish bar The Fifth Province and is about to reopen the Snakepit, the bar underneath the George Hotel. Ganley says the area has reached a critical mass and is reclaiming its live music roots.



“The big, big problem with St Kilda was the live music scene just got destroyed,” he says. “Look at the George, where you had Nick Cave and all these amazing artists that played there over the years, and then we had this huge issue with regulations.” Ganley says onerous noise restrictions killed the live music scene in St Kilda as venues struggled to exist alongside residents. The Snakepit bar has reopened in the basement of the George Hotel with a music stage. He is optimistic that St Kilda’s designation as a live music precinct means it will be easier to operate a music venue and says that last week the Fifth Province, which holds 1000, was packed and on Saturday night the street was as busy as he had seen it. “When you get a few good operators coming, all of a sudden, the tide runs really, really fast,” he says. “It’s flavour of the month.”



It’s a sentiment Smillie agrees with as he turns up the volume on the newly installed DJ decks at the Prince so a wave of sound hits the room. Related Article City life How St Kilda remains St Kilda against all odds “St Kilda’s always had a bit of a grungy edge,” he says. “Now the street’s clean, it’s much better – it’s vibrant.” What hasn’t changed, says Smillie, is the locals who have been getting behind the street’s resurgence. “They’ve been waiting for this,” he says. “They’ve been here all along.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: A violent bikie’s failed recall can’t erase the evidence of a Big Build turned bent
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsVictoriaBuilding Bad A violent bikie’s failed recall can’t erase the evidence of a Big Build turned bent Adam Carey November 17, 2026 — 7:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

From the moment Joel Leavitt strode through the doors of the royal commission building, sporting garish gold-rimmed Versace sunglasses and a dirty look for the press pack, it was obvious Tuesday’s hearing would be different. For one, the day never even got to what happened at Gap Road, Sunbury, in June 2022, the very subject of this two-week block of hearings. Bandido and ex-CFMEU health and safety representative Joel Leavitt arrives to give evidence on Tuesday. Wayne Taylor Instead, it roamed from Hallam to Hurstbridge to Glenroy, trying to pin an evasive Leavitt down on how an outlaw motorcycle gang member with a violent criminal record was ushered onto these government projects by the construction union, and engaged to enforce its will on who worked and who didn’t. It may be that the hearing never got to Gap Road because the day’s only witness was also the least co-operative so far.



The patched Bandido barely concealed his contempt for the inquiry he was summoned to, stubbornly deflecting question after question from the bar table during five hours of sustained, forensic and sometimes frustrated examination. Related Article Building Bad ‘Bend the knee’: Rail alliance told make peace with union or never work in Melbourne again Sniffing loudly into the microphone, swivelling and shuffling compulsively in the witness chair, he uttered the phrase “I can’t recall” well over 200 times, in the same gravelly voice that pleaded memory failure but in truth implied: “You’re getting nothing out of me.” Counsel assisting the commissioner Chris Carr, SC, was made to dig hard to get even the most basic admissions from Leavitt regarding his activities as a CFMEU health and safety representative on Victorian rail projects between 2021 and 2023. Leavitt grudgingly admitted to having a birthday, which he shared with the commission. “If you say so” and “so it would seem” both got a liberal airing, but in a dismissive tone that conceded nothing more than the fact that Carr had asked him a question.



Many of Carr’s questions were met with questions, a transparent stonewalling tactic that led the visibly frustrated barrister to state not once, but twice: “The way this works is I ask you questions and you answer them, not the other way around.” Leavitt was running down the clock, in the manner of an insubordinate student in detention, muttering monosyllabically into his hand as Carr took on the role of the reprimanding teacher. The claimed lack of recall became so repetitive that Commissioner Chris Kourakis eventually asked Leavitt if he had ever seen a doctor about cognitive decline, given he could recall nothing about what he was doing in 2021 and 2022. “The last few years are pretty blanky in my mind, commissioner,” Leavitt said. He blamed heavy drug use at the time he worked on the Big Build for his terminal failure of recall.



Leavitt’s shadowy role on Victoria’s infrastructure agenda was more widely exposed after he notoriously drove himself to hospital after he was shot in the clubhouse of the Rebels outlaw motorcycle gang in May 2023, in a vehicle issued to him by the government for his CFMEU health and safety role. His role as a CFMEU representative ended soon afterwards. The royal commission spent the entire day grappling with just why the CFMEU had pushed so hard to help an infamous bikie with a violent criminal rap sheet gain employment on the Big Build in the first place. It certainly wasn’t because he was seen as a diligent employee who would work tirelessly to get things done. Sometimes when he was paid, he wasn’t even there.



Text exchanges read out as evidence revealed Leavitt asking a superintendent who oversaw a Big Build site to fill in his time sheets on days he didn’t go to work. Another exchange exposed his delight in arranging a union stunt in which members set up a table and had their “smoko” in the middle of a level crossing in Glenroy, holding up trains and cars in the process. Matt Golding “Cost nearly half a million … Bah Ha ha ha! F--- me, that’s grouse,” the text exchange went. Subsequent exchanges also detailed the muscular Leavitt being directed to throw his considerable weight around about which contractors could and could not work on the $530 million Hurstbridge rail line upgrade.



As Carr probed Leavitt about a text exchange with CFMEU organiser Jerry McQuaid in 2021 about “walloping” construction contractor Laing O’Rourke as a way to get Leavitt onto a level crossing removal project, he claimed to be unsure what the word wallop even meant. But in the same exchange, he argued that a reference to a superintendent as a “c---” – another word that was uttered frequently in evidence – might have been a term of endearment. “C--- can also mean a good c--- in Aussie slang,” he said. At this point, just before lunch, Leavitt had almost succeeded in turning the commission’s inquiries into a farce. It was all so brazen, and so cosy for a man who knew he had the blessing of the CFMEU’s main man on the Big Build.



Leavitt was close with Joe Myles, the CFMEU’s senior leader on civil infrastructure projects in Victoria, the two even going so far as to profess their love for each other. Text exchanges also exposed how he used this camaraderie to get other bikie associates onto Big Build sites. Leavitt’s first day in the witness chair ended in characteristically vulgar fashion when Leavitt asked to be excused so that he could “chuck a piss”. It was an exit in keeping with a man who had spent his entire time on the Big Build taking the proverbial. World.title: John’s parents asked him a daily question. It helped him win a Nobel Prize
World.content:
NationalNSWScience John’s parents asked him a daily question. It helped him win a Nobel Prize Angus Dalton November 17, 2026 — 7:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

John Martinis’ parents – his father a fireman and his mother a homemaker – never asked him what he’d done each day at school. “I was very fortunate that my parents, around the dinner table, would ask instead: ‘Did you ask any questions today?’” the professor of physics at the University of California says. It was a ritual that spurred him into a life of curiosity, endless inquiry and, as of last year, a Nobel Prize. Professor John Martinis, with quantum equipment at the University of Sydney. Steven Siewert Los Angeles-born Martinis shared the 2025 Nobel Prize for Physics for an experiment he ran for his thesis in the mid-1980s which helped transform the magical, mind-bending, immensely powerful realm of quantum physics into something humans could wield for ourselves. The experiment he sweated over in his mid-20s laid the groundwork for today’s superconducting quantum computers, part of a multibillion-dollar industry that could fundamentally change our lives.



Here’s what he did – and what he says about the next stage of the quantum era. A quantum crash course Quantum mechanics describes how matter and energy behave on the tiny scale of atomic particles, such as protons and electrons. In this realm, physics works very differently to what we’re used to. It gets freaky. Picture a tennis ball. In “classical” physics, the ball is always in one place at any one time, even when it’s being belted around a court. In quantum physics, a ball, or a particle, can exist in multiple places or “states” at any one time. This concept is what makes quantum computing so potent. A standard computer “bit” switches between 0 and 1 for calculations. A quantum bit, or qubit, can exist in a state of both 0 and 1 simultaneously, making for vastly faster and more powerful calculations.



In another example, if you throw a tennis ball at a brick wall it will always bounce back. But in the quantum world, a particle has a chance of passing through a barrier it shouldn’t be able to cross – as if the tennis ball ghosted through the wall – in a phenomenon known as quantum tunnelling. Most objects bounce off a barrier. Quantum objects can sometimes pass through a barrier. This is called “tunnelling”. Johan Jarnestad/Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences Martinis and his colleagues were able to replicate quantum tunnelling in a macroscopic, human-made system. “Our quantum system is not made of protons and electrons like normal quantum mechanics,” he tells me at the University of Sydney, where he’s delivering a public lecture jointly hosted by industry body Quantum Australia.



Related Article Explainer

Quantum Computing Chandeliers, ‘qubits’ and Schrödinger’s cat: Inside the bizarre world of quantum computing “It’s constructed from an electrical circuit that you can see. It’s about a centimetre across, so it’s quite big.” That sounds simple. But it was an act of scientific nous that dragged the mystical qualities of quantum physics from the atomic scale to something that could be crafted and controlled by human hands. The experiment Martinis worked with two colleagues – his PhD adviser John Clarke and postdoctoral researcher Michel Devoret, with whom he shared the Nobel Prize – to create an electrical circuit involving a special component called a Josephson junction, made of two superconducting wires separated by an ultra-thin insulating barrier.



They cooled this circuit to almost absolute zero (-273 degrees Celsius, the coldest possible temperature). That triggered billions of electrons within the circuit to form “Cooper pairs” and begin behaving as a synchronised whole, rather than individual particles. 1. Single electrons jostle together in a normal conductor. 2. In a superconducting state, the electrons form pairs, and the current can flow without resistance. But an insulating gap may stop the current. 3. A large number electrons may sometimes behave like a single particle. This enables a current to tunnel across the insulating gap. Johan Jarnestad/The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences This created a system that could exist in one of two states: a zero-voltage state, or a state that produced voltage. The barrier separating these states could be leapt over if the electrons picked up heat energy. But when the system reached a particularly low temperature, suppressing heat, the scientists could still detect spikes of voltage. That meant the unified electrons were crossing straight through the barrier without needing thermal energy. The scientists had achieved quantum tunnelling.



Further, when they irradiated the circuit with microwaves, it absorbed energy at specific “quantised” levels, just like an atom. Put simply, Martinis and his colleagues had built something with the physics of an artificial atom. The elegant “exoskeleton” of an IBM quantum computer, supporting the chip within. IBM, digitally tinted Unlocking a new ‘physics playground’ Martinis says they didn’t set out to invent something new, much less help kick off a new industry that could change the world.



“It was just answering the very simple question,” he says. “Quantum mechanics is known to be the physics of the small – how atoms work, how molecules work. We wanted to show that it’s a more general phenomenon, so you can have current and voltages in a wire, and you can see quantum mechanics. “It means we had this new physics playground where we could make these new atomic systems out of the circuits.” Professor John Martinis, left, accepting the Nobel Prize for Physics in Sweden last year. Nobel Prize Outreach/Clément Morin The experiment laid the foundation for superconducting qubits. Martinis led the team at Google that, in 2019, claimed in Nature that they had achieved “quantum supremacy” with a processor made from 53 of these qubits, meaning they had solved a calculation with a quantum computer beyond the practical limits of any classical computer.



The quantum processor, they claimed, solved a calculation in 200 seconds that would take a supercomputer 10,000 years. That claim has since been subject to rebuttal and debate, with IBM claiming the calculation could be done on a classic system in two-and-a-half days, but the paper nevertheless marked an important moment in the advancement of quantum computing. When will quantum computing change our lives? “For years I would avoid this question,” Martinis says when asked when we might see a useful quantum computer. “But there has been enough progress and enough serious efforts that [now] I say five to 10 years.” Achieving large-scale, error-corrected quantum computing will wreak enormous effects. Standard security encryption we rely on to undergird the internet could be ruled obsolete. And what happens when quantum computing meets AI (QAI) is an open question.



Related Article Exclusive

Quantum Computing ‘It will be us’: Former Australian of the Year is building her answer to OpenAI On the other hand, scientists such as Martinis hope we’ll be able to model the inscrutable complexities of chemical reactions in unprecedented detail to unlock new materials and medicines. Martinis’ experiment was a “complete disaster” when they first tried it, he recalls. Solving it involved a visit to the university’s astronomy department to pick their brains about microwaves. Even since that ritual at the dining table from his childhood, he’s never stopped asking questions or worried about sounding stupid – which allowed him to bottle one of nature’s most remarkable, surreal qualities and fundamentally expand what humans are capable of. “I just find this fun,” he says of pursuing questions about how nature works on the atomic level. “It’s how I’m creative in physics, in the end. It’s the way I think.” The Examine newsletter explains and analyses science with a rigorous focus on the evidence. Sign up to get it each week.

World.title: Paid without turning up, then came a $165,000 pay day: Bikie Joel Leavitt’s Big Build bounty under microscope
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaBig Build royal commission Paid without turning up, then came a $165,000 pay day: Bikie Joel Leavitt’s Big Build bounty under microscope Clay Lucas November 17, 2026 — 7:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A labour hire firm at the centre of claims former premier Jacinta Allan’s office interfered on major projects to favour the CFMEU paid $165,000 to a violent bikie whom the union muscled onto Big Build sites. Senior Bandido Joel Leavitt also claimed wages for shifts on Big Build projects, the royal commission into the Victorian construction industry heard on Tuesday, while he was, in fact, visiting Melbourne gyms, and halted work for a protest that he boasted had cost the publicly funded level crossing removal project half a million dollars. Loading In an extraordinary day in the witness box, Leavitt uttered the phrase “I can’t recall” more than 200 times, blamed heavy drug use and his involvement in a shooting for memory loss, and conceded he could not rule out having billed for hours he never worked. In the final exhibit of the day, counsel assisting the inquiry Chris Carr, SC, tendered an invoice from Leavitt’s company JVL Consulting sent to BK Labour Hire requesting $165,000 for services provided in July last year.



Leavitt told the inquiry he was unable to recall preparing the invoice. When pressed by royal commissioner Chris Kourakis on what consulting services he had performed to justify the sum, Leavitt said his business provided “tips on safety work”. Asked by Kourakis to recall the nature of any purported safety advice he gave, Leavitt replied: “I can’t recall at this time.” During a day of remarkable admissions, Leavitt told the hearing he could not rule out having claimed wages for shifts he never worked, and confirmed he was an active member of the Bandidos outlaw motorcycle gang. Leavitt, a former CFMEU health and safety representative with convictions for rioting, assault and assaulting police, was installed onto major projects after union organisers campaigned for months for the company Laing O’Rourke to hire him in late 2020 and early 2021.



Messages from CFMEU organiser Gerry McQuaid showed the union pushing a Laing O’Rourke site superintendent to put Leavitt on rail projects in Cranbourne and Hallam via BK Labour Hire. As the contractor delayed, McQuaid texted Leavitt that he and a fellow organiser, Paul Tzimas, had been “walloping them all week”, and wrote: “C---s crying want 2 more shoppies [shop stewards] I’ve said no shoppies until Joel starts.” Carr suggested the union went to such lengths to force Laing O’Rourke to employ Leavitt because he was an intimidating bikie. “One possibility might be that the CFMEU wanted to go to such lengths to get you on this job site because you’re an intimidating bikie,” Carr said.



“You’d have to ask them,” Leavitt replied, having told the inquiry earlier that the union backed him because “I’m a good bloke”. Once installed on the $530 million Hurstbridge rail line upgrade, Leavitt exercised authority far beyond a standard workplace safety delegate. Loading The royal commission heard how Leavitt and others purged subcontractors that the CFMEU did not like from taxpayer-funded sites. Carr tendered a message from a CFMEU organiser named Costa instructing Leavitt to remove an earthmoving company from the job: “Anyone with Dundrum, wallop them and f--- them off.”



Costa told Leavitt to raise the issue with the Hurstbridge project superintendent. “So this seems to be a direction from Costa to you to get rid of a particular contractor on the job, and make sure they don’t get back onto the job in future?” Carr asked. “I don’t disagree,” Leavitt said, agreeing it was a possibility Costa believed he held the power to dictate which subcontractors worked on the project. Joal Leavitt appearing at the royal commission on Tuesday. Kourakis intervened to ask: “You don’t see anything odd about you as a health and safety representative (HSR) telling a superintendent on a site that they’re not to have a subcontractor back again?” Leavitt conceded it was a possibility.



Asked by Carr whether the succession of texts showed the CFMEU exercised control over who secured work on Victoria’s $109 billion Big Build program, Leavitt replied: “That’s a possible way of looking at that.” Other messages from March 2023 showed the Hurstbridge rail project superintendent checking with Leavitt over payroll, writing that he had received two pay dockets for a worker named Cheyenne whom he thought had left the site and whom the night supervisor had never seen. Leavitt said he could not explain why a project manager would consult a safety delegate over wages. Carr also cross-examined Leavitt over timesheets submitted on the Hurstbridge project in April 2023, accusing him of engaging in “a bit of petty fraud” by claiming 12-hour shifts starting at 5.30am while mobile phone records showed he was elsewhere. A Big Build timesheet for Leavitt tendered in the royal commission. Phone location data showed that on April 10, 2023, Leavitt did not leave his Roxburgh Park home until 6.20am – 50 minutes after his claimed shifts began – before visiting a gym in Richmond, and returning home for the afternoon.



On April 11, records placed him at home until 8.51am and at a gym in Braybrook, while on April 13 he stayed home until nearly 9am – despite claiming a full 12-hour day. Leavitt suggested he might have been working “on the phone” during the missed shifts before conceding to Kourakis that his job required him to be on-site. Leavitt blamed substance abuse when asked why his handwriting varied across timesheets, telling the inquiry: “Like I said, a lot of drugs. I was in different hazy states.” At one point in the day’s hearing, Leavitt was instructed to write “HSR” (health and safety representative) six times on a piece of paper so it could be compared to the HSR written on the timesheets. Former CFMEU Big Build boss Joe Myles (left) and Leavitt. Carr also tendered messages showing Leavitt worked with former CFMEU Big Build boss Joe Myles to secure construction jobs for other bikies, including Rebels gang member Jahmahl Pearson, who was jailed last year for torching a tobacco shop.



A photo was shown to the commission of Pearson sitting on a seat while he was meant to be working as a traffic controller at a Big Build site. It prompted Leavitt to message CFMEU organiser Joel Shackleton: “That’s where he sits all nights.” Asked how close he was to Myles, who the inquiry heard last week touted a “direct line” to Jacinta Allan’s office, Leavitt replied: “We were reasonably close.” Asked whether the pair told each other they loved each other, Leavitt said: “It’s definitely a possibility over the years.” Further texts revealed Leavitt boasting about disrupting rail and road traffic during a September 2021 protest over COVID-19 health orders closing construction tearooms. Leavitt sent an associate a video showing workers setting up a mock tearoom on the train tracks at the Glenroy Road level crossing in Glenroy, writing: “Can’t have smoko in the sheds. Set up on the train tracks.” The video shows dozens of cars lined up waiting to get across the rail crossing. After the recipient replied, “F--- me that’s grouse,” Leavitt messaged: “Held up trains and traffic and cost nearly half a million.”



Leavitt’s repeated claims that 2021 and 2022 were “pretty blank” in his memory led Kourakis to ask whether he had seen a doctor for cognitive decline, which Leavitt denied. Editor's pick Building Bad ‘Bend the knee’: Rail alliance told make peace with union or never work in Melbourne again The inquiry is examining how outlaw motorcycle gang members were embedded across state infrastructure projects under former CFMEU state secretary John Setka, who was expelled from the union last week by its administration. Last week, former Rail Projects Victoria chief operating officer Peter Wilkinson told the inquiry that Allan’s ministerial office passed on a warning during a 2022 stand-off in Sunbury that contractors “can’t have any more work in Victoria” unless they resolved industrial disputes with the CFMEU, before builders capitulated and installed BK Labour Hire on site. Leavitt’s role first emerged in The Age’s Building Bad investigation in 2024, which revealed he used a vehicle supplied for his Hurstbridge project duties to drive himself to Footscray Hospital after being shot at a Rebels bikie clubhouse in 2023.



Subsequent reporting by The Age and a review by barrister Geoffrey Watson, SC, detailed how rival bikie gangs fought for territorial control on the Hurstbridge upgrade because its 1000-strong workforce made it a lucrative hub for drug distribution as well as high-paid union jobs. The hearings continue. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The Sydney schools where only a fraction of students take religion classes
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation The Sydney schools where only a fraction of students take religion classes Christopher Harris November 17, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Enrolments in special religious education classes have dipped below 10 per cent at some public high schools leaving hundreds of students barred from doing classroom work if they do not opt in to scripture lessons. A snapshot of enrolment data, obtained under freedom of information laws, shows numbers in special religious education classes have mostly declined between 2019 and 2025 across 10 high schools. Inner west public primary student Layla has previously asked Education Minister Prue Car to review the current religious education rules. Peter Rae The data shows only 6 per cent of students at Willoughby Girls High School opted for religious classes last year. In year 9, there were six students enrolled in special religious education and 184 in alternative meaningful activities. Selective schools North Sydney Boys High School and Northern Beaches College Manly Campus have also seen substantial drops over that time period.



Student attendance is not compulsory in religious classes, but as parents at Newtown High School of the Performing Arts discovered this month, the current policy can upend the timetable and consign other students to spending 80 minutes under teacher supervision doing other meaningful activities. Current rules state actual school work cannot be taught while religious classes are in session. Special religious education participation data is not released by the department, but figures obtained under freedom of information laws by the Atheist Foundation and provided to the Herald show enrolments have mostly declined over the past six years. Enrolments increased slightly at Burwood Girls over the period, as well as at Georges River College in Peakhurst and The Ponds High.



However, primary schools are also seeing a drop in religion class enrolments, with Burwood, Ropes Crossing and Cherrybrook falling 20 percentage points or more. Year 6 student Layla, who asked not to use her surname and attends an inner west public school, said she had experienced the weekly frustration of colouring in or watching children’s movies when she could have been learning. “Those students who don’t subscribe to the religions on offer can do ethics, if a parent volunteer is available, but these classes have limited spaces,” she said. She said that in Australia’s multicultural society, public school students should study all religions from an impartial source. “By educating ourselves about various belief systems, we build important life skills including greater respect for cultures other than our own and increased cultural sensitivity,” she said.



Related Article Opinion

Education I’m a Newtown High School parent and my WhatsApp group won’t stop pinging Helen Paterson Contributor Atheist Foundation of Australia communications manager Steve Marton questioned why the state was facilitating religious instruction when a minority of students enrolled at some schools. “Why can’t they do it at the weekend?” he said. The NSW Secondary Principals’ Council, the NSW Primary Principals’ Council and the state’s P&C Federation in 2023 called for an urgent review of religious education, citing the fact that thousands of students were missing out on crucial learning time. A 2015 review of special religious instruction recommended procedures be revised for secondary schools to allow students not participating in religious education to continue their regular classwork. It was not supported by the previous coalition government.



Among the Australian population, the number of people with no religion increased to 38 per cent of the population in the 2021 census. Greens MP for Newtown Jenny Leong wants to abolish special religious education class in public schools. Steven Siewert Greens member for Newtown Jenny Leong has launched a petition calling on Education Minister Prue Car to abolish special religious education class in public schools. She said it was not about being pro or anti religion. “This is about rejecting an approach that takes public school students out of class for an hour every week, segregating them based on religion, to be instructed by unqualified religious volunteers outside the accountability of the school and curriculum,” she said.



“Our public schools should be a place where students can learn openly about the diverse religious faiths in our community, taught by professional teachers.” A Teachers Federation spokesperson said any education, religious or otherwise, should be delivered in line with an approved curriculum and by a qualified teacher. “Setting time aside for scripture detracts from teaching time, professional learning and extracurricular activities from an already crowded curriculum and school day,” he said. Car last week expressed support for special religious education saying it had been part of the state’s public education system since its inception. Opposition education spokesman Mark Speakman said he also supports it.



“Having ‘non-sectarian’ public education does not mean shutting the door on faith,” he said. “It means not preferring one faith over another. This instruction helps to develop well-rounded, confident students, who should not be disadvantaged by being enrolled in these classes.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Holes in the net and 14 spectators: Life on tour for Australian tennis’ ‘glamour’ couple
World.content:
SportTennisAustralian Open Holes in the net and 14 spectators: Life on tour for Australian tennis’ ‘glamour’ couple Adrian Proszenko November 17, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

By the time Jason Kubler completed a three-set victory over fellow Australian Matthew Dellavedova, on court five of the Sydney Tennis Centre, fianceé Maddison Inglis was no longer watching. She was one of 14 spectators – which included your correspondent and photographer – present for the start of the biggest match of this year’s NSW Open so far. Inglis caught only fleeting glimpses of the deciding set, which Kubler won 6-2, before she was required to practice on an adjoining court. Tennis player Maddison Inglis with her fiancé Jason Kubler at the NSW Open. Louise Kennerley Court five is a short stroll from Ken Rosewall Arena, which was reserved for an ITF fixture on Tuesday morning. It’s another world away altogether from Melbourne Park, where Kubler and Inglis captured the imagination of the public at the Australian Open earlier this year as Australian tennis’ latest love match. Inglis progressed all the way to the fourth round, a career best grand slam finish for which she pocketed $480,000 in prizemoney. It prompted a rare moment of self-indulgence: the purchase of a SMEG toaster.



The spoils are significantly smaller at Homebush Bay this week. The men are competing for a share of $107,000 in prizemoney at the NSW Open, while it’s $75,000 for the women. There are no strawberries and cream here. Dellavedova spent much of his match with Kubler remonstrating with the French umpire, over issues that included, but were not limited to, an apparent hole in the net. By the time Kubler finally prevailed, Inglis was preparing for the start of her own Sydney campaign, which was being staged and played concurrently with the men’s competition. Jason Kubler during his NSW Open win against Matthew Dellavedova. Louise Kennerley For all but the very elite professionals in tennis, this is the reality of tour life. It is spent jostling for rankings points in lower-tier events, trying to eke out enough money to keep alive the dream of the big payday that comes with qualifying for the slams. There were times when it looked to be all over. Like when, a decade ago, Kubler checked his balance to find he was down to his final 14 cents.



“It was tough,” Kubler recalled, as he and Inglis sat down with this masthead after his match. “It’s actually not a bad story, like, not that I need to tell it, but after that I started playing a few sort of lower tournaments, and then doing well. Tennis power couple Maddison Inglis and Jason Kubler. Louise Kennerley “Then from having that 14 cents to maybe four months down the road, I ended up getting a wildcard into the Aussie Open that following year. So it’s crazy how much it can change.” Sitting beside him, Inglis chimed in: “It is crazy you got down to that, though.”



“I’m a battler, I’m a battler!” Kubler grinned. Kubler has had to draw on his fighting spirit to make a career out of tennis. This year, he endured a sixth surgery on his left knee, to go with the two to his right. The 33-year-old is currently ranked 562 in the world after a series of injury lay-offs, including a period where he played almost exclusively on clay to take the strain off his legs. Inglis is ranked 138, but both are hopeful of earning a start in the Australian Open main draw. Maddison Inglis (centre) watches fiancé Jason Kubler in action. Louise Kennerley “It would be cool if we could do the same as this year,” Inglis said. The NSW Open is one of the few tournaments for which they are in the same place at the same time. There are periods of the year when they are at different far-flung destinations, trying to make ends meet.



“I remember when I was in my early 20s, then it was a slog, you know?” Kubler said. “You were grinding for, maybe if you won the tournament, you got $7,000. Related Article Novak Djokovic Fresh off beating Djokovic, Rinky Hijikata will take on world’s best at home “Whereas I was checking, and now it’s like $17,000 [US, to win the NSW Open]. I was like, ‘That’s actually not that bad.’ And then the slightly bigger tournaments – say the 100s and the 125s – I think the 125s was like $US33,000 or something. So I was like, ‘Mate, it’s actually pretty good now, you know?’” The pay cheques can be healthy or challenging, depending on the results. However, it’s the love of the game that has them coming back. “There are tough weeks on the road, but the days where you’re just striking it so well – for me, that’s so addictive,” Kubler said.



Inglis interjects: “He loves it! Like, we’ll have a day off and you’re like, ‘Do you want to go have a hit?’ I’m like, ‘No, I really don’t.’” The couple, who live together on the Gold Coast, got engaged on Rottnest Island just weeks before their Australian Open heroics. As for a wedding date? “Don’t bring this conversation up!” Kubler said. “No, we’re hoping for end of next year.” Inglis added: “I’m not too fussed. I want something really small. We will get there, no rush. Tennis is the focus at the moment.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Kyle Sandilands updates price guide for his glamorous weekender
World.content:
PropertyNewsLuxury property Kyle Sandilands updates price guide for his glamorous weekender Elizabeth Redman November 17, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

Does Kyle Sandilands know something about the property market that others don’t? The radio presenter set a $4.9 million price guide in May on his luxurious weekender located in Sydney’s north-western outskirts. And yet, the guide has been updated to a range between $4.9 million to $5.1m, despite property prices falling. The property is a grand six-bedroom estate, with a swimming pool and outdoor dining area, a jewel-toned home office, chandelier and fireplace. The Georgian-inspired home features a circular driveway with fountain and porte-cochère, a games room, high ceilings and a contemporary kitchen.



A sale at that level could still offer value to a buyer, given the home on almost a hectare in Glenorie was first listed in February with a price guide of $5.7 million to $5.9 million. In May, the guide was changed to $4.9 million ahead of its scheduled auction, but the listing remains available. Sandilands bought the home for $3 million in 2022 and renovated last year. The weekender has room to host and entertain. Belle Property Dural selling agent Carolyn Wheatley was contacted, as was Sandilands’ manager. The former host of The Kyle and Jackie O Show on KIIS, now hosting Kyle Sandilands Live on his own paywalled platform, is based in Sydney’s eastern suburbs.



Earlier this year, when Sandilands challenged KIIS owner ARN over the termination of his contract, he said he wanted to return to work and has “mortgages to pay like everyone else”. Related Article CBD From Vaucluse to Copacabana: Kyle Sandilands has four mortgages to pay Property records show the Glenorie home has a mortgage to NAB and another to Mortgage Holdings Group Pty Ltd, while his Vaucluse home - bought for $14 million in 2023 - also has a mortgage to NAB and another to Mortgage Holdings Group Pty Ltd. ARN and Sandilands settled the litigation and he was delivered a $12 million payout and more than $1 million worth of advertising for his new show on the company’s channels. There were not enough property sales in Glenorie in the past year to calculate a median house price, but the median in nearby Dural is $2,255,000 on Domain data.



Sydney’s median house price is $1.66 million, down 7.9 per cent from its peak, after it fell at the steepest quarterly pace in four years in the September quarter. Property alerts are now available in the SMH app. Turn them on to receive the latest market news and trends.

World.title: RNZ confirms staff will be told from this week which jobs will go
World.content:
This story has been updated to clarify staff will be told from this week which jobs will be part of the 58 redundancies.

RNZ has confirmed that staff will be told from this week which jobs will go as part of the proposed 58 redundancies.

The public broadcaster last week revealed a shock $12 million budget blow-out, which is more than 25 times the $470,000 it had expected to lose over the year to June.

RNZ staff spent their lunch breaks on Tuesday protesting job cuts outside the broadcaster's Auckland and Wellington offices, with a rotating cast of journalists, producers, operators and other union members waving signs and flags during the hour-long protest.

But in an email sent to staff later that afternoon, acting chief executive Mark Stevens said change proposals will be shared with affected teams and individuals from later this week.

Stevens said affected staff members will progressively leave between December and 31 March, and any proposals will be guided by the Charter, audience needs and strategy.

"It is for RNZ to determine following consultation with potentially impacted staff and unions which positions may need to be disestablished."

The restructuring is expected to cost $2.5m, contributing to an expected deficit of $7.8m for 2026/27 this year.

Stevens said the proposals would be across all levels and all parts of the business.

"We cannot achieve the level of staffing reduction required to sufficiently reduce our expenditure in line with the approved budget by proposing to protect any specific parts of RNZ."

Stevens said the immediate challenge was that RNZ was currently costing more to run than it was funded for and "this needs to be addressed".

"We recognise that the changes being proposed, and the uncertainty around them, will be difficult."

In a statement, E tū and the Public Service Association (PSA) said the move was "rushed and irresponsible, with no business case shared, the independent review not yet under way, and no new Government in place".

E tū national secretary Rachel Mackintosh said RNZ's leadership was making the wrong call, and making it far too fast.

"More than 200 people stood outside RNZ today and asked for one thing: show us the alternatives. A few hours later, staff got an email saying the proposals are coming anyway. That's not listening.

"We've asked for the business case behind the 58 again and again. We still haven't seen it. RNZ is planning to spend $2.5 million on restructuring to make these cuts, but it can't show workers how it got to that number."

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons said it was a "leadership-made crisis", and it was "irresponsible to make decisions this big under a caretaker Government".

"Final election results are 10 days away, and RNZ will have a new Media Minister whoever forms the Government. Funding for RNZ is a decision for that Government. RNZ's own figures show its funding has been cut by 9 percent over the past two years. Workers deserve to know whether that's going to continue before they're asked to give up their jobs."

Fitzsimons confirmed the unions were seeking legal advice, and they were advising staff not to attend meetings about any proposed changes on Wednesday.

World.title: East Cape resident says talk of managed retreat 'extremely upsetting' and 'shocking'
World.content:
Members of a small Tairāwhiti community are reeling over the prospect of having to leave their land, after a report from the Gisborne District Council (GDC) identified "managed retreat" or "retreat" as the long-term option for them.

The report - 5F Storm Independent Review - is the result of a review commissioned by the Gisborne District Council into several neighbouring areas devastated by a storm at the end of January. It was carried out by engineering firm Tonkin + Taylor, and released to affected residents last month.

The three "catchments" examined were Wharekahika or Hicks Bay, Onepoto Bay and Punaruku, which includes the settlement of Te Araroa. According to the report, the most recent census data showed 270 people lived in the areas.

For all three areas, the report ruled out "structural protection measures" because they were deemed either infeasible or ineffective.

It noted the "extreme rainfall" during the 21-22 January storm caused widespread landsliding and flooding in the area. It also stated that climate change was expected to increase the frequency of extreme rainfall events like the January storm.

As a result "managed retreat from the most at-risk properties is an option in all catchments, especially Punaruku where there was an acute risk to life". The report also identified that for some areas at risk, the main long-term option is managed retreat.

Audio player for " Tairawhiti community reeling over prospect of having to leave land " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/regions/2643066%2Feast-cape-resident-says-talk-of-managed-retreat-extremely-upsetting-and-shocking

Tairawhiti community reeling over prospect of having to leave land Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Several residents have rejected the GDC review, and have said the process lacked transparency and consultation.

Nina McClutchie runs food caravan 35 Eat street at Te Araroa Holiday Park, and said she and holiday park owner Bill Martin were blindsided by the review report.

"We knew that there was one being put together, but… it just landed on us. We had no specific date or idea that it was going to be as quick as what it was.

"[We're] extremely upset, especially around the relocation topic because…a small group of us have been working hard to get the camp cleaned up and to get open, hopefully again for Christmas.

"So for this relocation topic to come up is quite disturbing because none of us want to go.

McClutchie criticised the lack of communication from GDC over the entire process, and the absence of timeframes in the report over potential options.

"We've asked what does a managed retreat look like, and they weren't able to answer at this stage, and they haven't even given us a guideline of how long it's going to take them to answer us so I'm out on the wind there.

"I think it's shocking. You really can't come to us and say that without being really transparent right across the board with how this is going to work."

Flood damage at Te Araroa Holiday Park. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Sean Deery is an advocate for several affected parties, including McClutchie, and Pikitanga marae in Te Araroa.

He believed the GDC-commissioned report needed to be independently reviewed and a more inclusive process where affected residents and whānau were properly involved needed to be implemented. Deery is a project manager and has whakapapa links to the area through his grandmother.

"They should all be there at the table at the beginning of the process, so everyone understands what is going to happen, how it is going to happen, and there's buy-in from all the stakeholders

"If you don't get the buy-in, people don't understand; they get the wrong idea.

"And this is why I'm saying that the council - in my view - has rushed things... and they've left out the community."

Deery also said he was still waiting on information about the review process he asked GDC for five months ago.

GDC principal scientist Murray Cave disagreed with comments the review process lacked consultation.

"We bent over backwards to make sure that we talked to everyone that we needed to talk to.

"Since the review's come out, we've actually spoken to some of those parties multiple times, where they've sought further clarification, and that process will be ongoing."

A peer review into the Tonkin + Taylor report had also been confirmed.

Cave also said all scenarios would've been discussed during the review process. He couldn't recall if the words "retreat" or "managed retreat" were used specifically, but said any shock around the scenarios was news to him.

"Where we have those areas that were raised about managed retreat - which is in some instances relating to specific properties- you've got to realise that a lot of those properties... already had red placards on them, so it would not have been a surprise."

Cave also confirmed to Checkpoint that the GDC would not be offering buyout payments, and said any money would need to come from central government.

"If it was being made available to us from the Crown, we'd clearly consider that as an option. But that is something for the government to consider," he said.

World.title: Why sea lions are breaking into a Dunedin plant  nursery
World.content:
Audio player for " Dunedin plant nursery being overrun by sea lions " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/community/2643296%2Fwhy-sea-lions-are-breaking-into-a-dunedin-plant-nursery

Dunedin plant nursery being overrun by sea lions Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

A Dunedin beachside plant nursery is having to fortify its perimeter against determined and surprisingly nimble sea lions.

The marine mammals have been storming the barricades at Tomahawk Smaills BeachCareTrust Nursery during breeding season.

Rabbits were now also able to get through the nursery's compromised pest fence to feast on natives.

Smaills BeachCare Trust Nursery manager, Nicole Bezemer, told Checkpoint the female sea lions were looking for more secretive locations to give birth to their pups.

Sea lion Tektite feeding her newborn pup by the volunteer shelter. Supplied / Nicole Bezemer

"They're moving away from the ocean, away from the beaches, up through the dunes, and they're looking for spots where they can hide away from male sea lions who are on patrol," she said.

"Basically, they're looking to be first in line to fire next season's pups, and so, what we're finding is that our nursery, which is situated right at Smaills Beach, has become a bit of a destination maternity ward for pregnant sea lions."

Bezemer said the local sea lions weren't bursting through the fence, and were extremely discreet when pregnant.

Tektite and pup inside nursery, blocking access to the toilet facilities. Supplied / Nicole Bezemer

It took her at least an hour for her to notice that a sea lion named Tektite - who was about to give birth that morning - was tucked away behind a volunteer shelter, she said.

"What we see with our sea lions around the Otago Region is that they're large animals, but they're amazingly nimble when it comes to a regular stock fence," Bezemer said.

"For instance, a regular fence you might see around a sheep paddock is around 1.2 metres high. Even with barbed wire along the top, we'll still get sea lions able to navigate themselves over those fences.

"So, what we're looking at is an extremely sturdy treated timber fence of around 1.6 metres high that we've likened it to creating something similar to a Texan bull yard at Smaills Beach."

Pup poking through the makeshift barricade of pallets. Supplied / Nicole Bezemer

She said the sea lions' resourcefulness had taken a few people by surprise.

World.title: A wound that won't heal: Family desperate for answers after death in police custody
World.content:
Audio player for " Family of man who died in police custody desperate for answers " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/crime-and-justice/2641816%2Fa-wound-that-won-t-heal-family-desperate-for-answers-after-death-in-police-custody

Family of man who died in police custody desperate for answers Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

The family of a man who died in police custody say they're desperate for answers, more than 17 months on.

"All we can say is he was alive when he was arrested and he was dead within 24 hours of that," his sister said.

Bradley McLeod had been in prison in Australia for 11 years serving time for rape, before being deported to New Zealand in May 2025.

A month later, on 16 June, he was arrested. Police won't say why, nor will they tell RNZ what charges McLeod faced.

According to McLeod's family, he was arrested about 3.30am. Sometime while in police custody he told officers he was injured and needed medical attention, and at 8.22pm on the same day, McLeod died, they said.

Now, his family have been left with questions, after getting little to no answers from authorities.

501 deportee

Speaking to RNZ, McLeod's mother and sister made no secret of his criminal history.

He had early convictions for drug offending and assaulting a police officer.

For more than a decade, he had been in Australia's Wolston prison.

McLeod's mother, Kim Williamson, said her son knew he had done wrong.

"He knew it was going to be a struggle for him coming back [to New Zealand] but he had the support systems in place," she said.

McLeod was working at a fresh start. He achieved his Bachelor's in Christian Ministry, completing a qualification in six years.

He had planned to plant a farm as his mission and wanted to go to Colombia to support the homeless and work with children.

His sister said her brother wanted to use his hard-learned lessons to help others.

"He was really focused on particularly wanting to help those who had found themselves on a similar path around drugs and alcohol," she said.

McLeod returned to New Zealand in May 2025 as a 501 deportee.

He had moved around, staying with a few different people before ending up in New Plymouth.

His sister Alecia Williamson said it was a challenge for him.

"He definitely struggled to come back and re-adjust, it's a big change," she said.

"He was institutionalised for 11 years, so he knew he was going to face struggles when he got out."

Williamson said McLeod had been on a waitlist for mental health support from the moment he returned.

McLeod's arrest

His family said police had told them McLeod had been arrested for attempted breaking and entering.

One of the few reasons police had given for his death was a delay in receiving medical care, Williamson said.

His family said McLeod had suffered serious injuries before he died.

But how he received those injuries remained unclear.

McLeod's sister said not knowing what happened was like a "constant wound that does not get to scab over".

"We can't say either way what happened to him," she said.

"All we can say is he was alive when he was arrested and he was dead within 24 hours from that."

Williamson said the family wasn't able to process their loss until they had answers.

"You can't move on and heal from something when you don't know what you're healing from."

Family toll

His mother Kim said the lengthy delays in getting answers had taken a toll on her and her family's mental health.

"How would they feel in our position if it was one of their children or family members?" She asked.

"It makes me feel like they already painted a picture of Bradley, and it makes me feel like it doesn't matter to them because he was a nothing, he was a piece of s*** basically is what they've tried to portray him as."

Both she and Alecia pointed to high-profile cases from the Independent Police Conduct Authority that concluded in less time.

Findings in the Jevon McSkimming and Tom Phillips cases here returned in 16 and 11 months respectively.

"Get it so that families are not sitting in this, so that they can move on, Alicia Williamson said.

She said it should not be up to families to put pressure on authorities to get a decision.

"I emailed the Commissioner and Minister of Police, it then got passed down to somebody else. It shouldn't take us following up all the time for the appropriate eyes to get on the case, for it to get a kick in the pants," she said.

Williamson and her mother weren't alone in waiting.

Another report from the Independent Police Conduct Authority (IPCA) into the death of Taranaki Fuimaono in police custody took more than three years to be released.

Police response

RNZ asked police if there had been CCTV footage of how McLeod received his injuries, if staff had faced disciplinary action or been stood down, and if they thought the 17-month wait for McLeod's family was acceptable.

Detective superintendent Ross McKay said McLeod's death was subject to a coronial investigation.

Police were also conducting an internal investigation, he said.

As such, McKay said they could not comment further.

The IPCA was also investigating. A spokesperson told RNZ they had completed their investigation but couldn't say when it would be released.

They too wouldn't answer specific questions.

World.title: NZ banks make more money on loans than Australian counterparts
World.content:
Audio player for " What's the biggest risk to our economy right now? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2636079%2Fnz-banks-make-more-money-on-loans-than-australian-counterparts

New Zealand banks are making more money out of their loans than their counterparts in Australia, the Reserve Bank says - and what home loan borrowers pay is set to rise.

It has released its latest financial stability report, which notes that while the global economic environment is uncertain, local financial institutions are well placed to withstand financial market turbulence and support the economy.

As part of the report, it has looked at banks' net interest margins, or NIMs, which represent the difference between the cost of their funding and what they make from lending.

For the past 20 years, they have generally hovered between 2 percent and 2.5 percent, and have been higher when interest rates were higher. Increased competition helped reduce NIMs more recently.

"NIMs have generally been higher in New Zealand than in Australia over the past decade. Differences in competitive conditions appear to have contributed to this gap, although lending composition and equity funding also help to explain it. The analysis does not identify how much of the gap is explained by each factor," the Reserve Bank noted.

It said customers having money in products that paid no interest, such as transaction accounts, had helped the banks' margins but the Reserve Bank said this explained little of the trans-Tasman gap.

RNZ / Amrita Marks / Supplied

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub (pictured) said OECD data had shown New Zealand bank margins being among the highest and there was little indication that would change.

He said people left money in accounts that were not earning interest largely because of inertia, but also because often they needed the money to be accessible.

"What's been interesting is you look at KiwiSaver and other fund managers and they do have a lot of cash and other pie funds so they are trying to compete but they haven't been successful yet.

"People are not very active in the way they look after their savings… and quite often the savings might be small amounts spread across many people."

The Reserve Bank said competitive pressure could reduce NIMs, such as from open banking, payment modernisation and new digital financial services.

"Financial stability does not depend on any particular level of NIM. Lower margins resulting from stronger competition or greater efficiency would not, in themselves, be a financial stability concern. What matters is that banks remain sufficiently profitable and resilient. Current levels of profitability and strong capital positions provide banks with capacity to absorb lower margins.

The effect of lower margins would also depend on whether banks can adapt through efficiency gains, balance-sheet growth, other income, or changes in their business models."

The Reserve Bank noted that the housing market had further softened over the past six months and sales were low compared to available listings.

But lower mortgage rates had supported an improvement in borrower stress metrics.

"The share of mortgage lending that is non-performing has fallen from 0.64 percent in early 2025 to 0.5 percent in September. Lending in default remains higher among high-LVR borrowers, although stress has eased within this group. Mortgagee sales and realised mortgage losses are low.

"While early-stage arrears have declined this year as well, recent increases in mortgage rates and rising unemployment could slow or reverse this improvement. We expect the average mortgage rate paid by borrowers to increase from around 4.8 percent to 5.4 percent over the next year, based on current mortgage rates and market pricing for future interest rates. Even so, this remains well below the late-2024 peak of 6.4 percent."

Some borrowers who bought in Auckland or Wellington near the 2021 house price peak with limited equity remained particularly vulnerable, the bank said.
