"Even if they continue to meet their loan repayments, lower house prices have reduced equity for some borrowers, making it harder for them to refinance or move home."

It said it had heard demand for new townhouses was becoming saturated and pockets of unsold townhouse stock were emerging.

While it was not concerned about the impact of the softening housing market on financial stability, Eaqub said it might be underestimating the extent of the downturn. He pointed to recent Real Estate Institute data that showed a sharp drop in house sales in October.

"The drop in house sales was extraordinary. The worst part of it was it was synchronised across every region in New Zealand. I don't understand why people are not more concerned by this because I look at what's going on in terms of house sales they give us a very strong signal that interest rates are already so high that people are behaving very strangely.

"The current level of sales is more what I would expect from 6.5 percent mortgage rates, not 5.5 percent. And can we really have an investment-led recovery next year if people aren't borrowing money?"

World.title: Education Minister deeply disappointed after disruption to level 1 English exam
World.content:
Education Minister Erica Stanford says it is deeply disappointing that there has been another problem with NCEA exams.

The Qualifications Authority has apologised for the disruption to today's online level 1 English exam and says it will undertake a full independent review.

"Any disruption during an exam is simply not good enough," it said.

Stanford said the disruption was much smaller than last week's in English Level 2 but it is still disappointing after repeated assurances from NZQA and its IT provider.

She told NZQA to make sure there are paper back ups for all remaining exams, regardless of the size.

Chief executive, Christian Hawkesby, said in a statement it was a very different situation to the problem that affected last week's level 2 English exam.

"What happened today was a slowdown in the system that lasted approximately 20 minutes. The system then returned to full operation, and students were able to log back in and continue their exams online," he said.

"We spent the entire weekend extensively testing the system in preparation for today's exam, which was the largest of the year. We also received assurances from our technology provider that the system was ready, so we are extremely disappointed with today's performance."

Hawkesby said there were similar problems in 2023, but the system performed well through 2024 and 2025.

"The Minister has been seeking assurances over the past two years that those problems would not recur. Today's performance has fallen short of those expectations," he said.

"We will be undertaking a full independent review, including a thorough examination of our provider's performance. We are taking this extremely seriously and will be raising our concerns directly with the provider."

Hawkesby said there were no further exams near the size of the English exams.

"Our largest remaining exam has around 15,000 students, and the system has handled exams of that scale successfully. We are not anticipating further issues, but we are taking absolutely nothing for granted," he said.

"Out of an abundance of caution, we will have paper backups available for every remaining exam, regardless of the number of students sitting it. We want students, families and schools to have confidence that we are prepared."

Audio player for " Teachers report further issues with online NCEA exams " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/education/2641683%2Feducation-minister-deeply-disappointed-after-disruption-to-level-1-english-exam

Teachers report further issues with online NCEA exams Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

English teachers association president Pip Tinning told Checkpoint that after years of problems she was beginning to feel the English exams were jinxed.

She said today's problems were sufficiently widespread to cause major concern among teachers.

"It seems like it might be a capacity issue with the exams and with the number of students who are sitting exams at once," she said.

"If that's the case then it's a real issue having that digital-first philosophy."

Tinning said it had reached the point that students needed to prepare for exam failures.

"What we're looking at is making sure that we're telling our students two things. Make sure you're getting your handwriting stamina up really well but also those derived grades are going to be increasingly important if this is going to continue to be an issue and it is year after year now," she said.

Tinning said young people were resilient and many would take the setback in their stride.

"But there will be some really upset kids," she said.

"If it's something that you experience more than once, sitting exams digitally is problably something that you are going to start avoiding."

Tinning said the ongoing problems suggested the system was not ready for the government's plan to make exams compulsory when it introduces a new qualification to replace NCEA in 2029 and 2030.

Meanwhile a student told RNZ everyone at their school ran into problems with Monday's level 3 History exam.

"Students were repeatedly kicked out and/or faced a particular error message: 'Something's not quite right... Please wait 3 seconds and click retry'," said the student who asked not be named.

"We were offered the opportunity to switch to paper after already being halfway through the standards... Making that switch would ultimately have eaten into even more time that was already running short."

The student said the problem meant they only completed one of the two papers they had planned to tackle.

World.title: 'Not the time': Fire and Emergency axes restructure plans
World.content:
Fire and Emergency NZ's board has announced it will not go ahead with a planned restructure.

Last November, FENZ proposed axing about 140 jobs and changing about 700 other roles among its 3000 staff. Controversy over changes to the likes of wildfire response roles followed.

The plans had been in limbo after a court found FENZ did not consult staff properly.

On Tuesday afternoon the New Zealand Professional Firefighters Union said its national committee met the FENZ board and had withdrawn plans for two 10-hour strikes on November 27 and December 2.

Fire and Emergency New Zealand board chair Raveen Jaduram said the restructure had been designed more than a year ago, before the findings of a recent Parliamentary Select Committee inquiry into the organisation's fleet and the resignation of chief executive Kerry Gregory.

"The board has reached that conclusion, yes," Jaduram told RNZ when asked whether the restructure was the right path for Fire and Emergency.

"The proposal was to save money. I mean, we need to make sure we spend money wisely. And my view, and the board supports me in this, is that there are many other ways in which we can achieve the same outcome," he said.

Jaduram said the organisation also needed to rebuild trust with its workforce and unions.

FENZ board chairman Raveen Jaduram. RNZ / Dan Cook

He acknowledged trust had broken down between Fire and Emergency and the New Zealand Professional Firefighters Union (NZPFU), which had been opposing the proposed changes.

"Trust has been broken. It's taken a long time. I wasn't there. I'm here now, and I'm resetting the relationship, rebuilding the trust," he said.

He said the board had also agreed to change the organisation's culture and way of operating.

"And the culture that I, as chair, want the organisation to have is very different from the culture that I have walked into."

Jaduram also said remaining senior leaders could stay if they supported the changes, but those who did not agree with the organisation's new direction could choose to leave.

NZPFU national secretary Wattie Watson said members welcomed the decision to dump the planned restructure.

She said the Public Service Association (PSA) and NZPFU wrote to the FENZ board a couple of weeks ago calling for a stop to the restructure.

"Given the crisis in FENZ, including the leadership crisis, public statements of no trust and confidence in the people who put up this proposal. This was Kerry Gregory's vision. It just wasn't founded in purpose or evidence. It was going to be a disaster so the board has done the right thing and put a stop to it," Watson said.

Watson said she was encouraged by the tone of the board's statement.

"The indication from the statement is that they want to refocus the organisation both in funding and intent back to what the purpose of the organisation is, which is to protect and preserve life and property," she said.

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons said the move was an important victory for staff and the public but should never have taken so long.

"We had to resort to litigation. The Employment Relations Authority telling FENZ it was unlawful and then we were going to have go back and require a compliance order when they didn't listen to the authority. Finally common sense has prevailed," she said.

Fitzsimons said the decision was a relief for PSA members who had spent a year living with the threat of losing their jobs.

"Today's decision is a tribute to the courage and determination of our members who stood up, challenged these decisions and won. Now FENZ needs to give its people real stability. That means filling vacancies and giving those on temporary and fixed-term contracts certainty, not leaving them in limbo until mid-2027," she said.

World.title: Schools cutting back on sports, field trips as cost of relief teachers soars
World.content:
Audio player for " Schools having to cut back as cost of hiring relief teachers soars - PPTA " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/education/2642489%2Fschools-cutting-back-on-sports-field-trips-as-cost-of-relief-teachers-soars

Schools having to cut back as cost of hiring relief teachers soars - PPTA Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Schools are cutting back on sports and field trips as well as professional development as the cost of hiring relief teachers soars.

More than $208.5 million was allocated by the Ministry of Education last year specifically for relief teachers, up 7.5 percent on the previous year.

The ministry said they cannot confirm how much of that money has actually been spent.

However, the Post Primary Teachers Association said the relievers fund was nowhere near enough and that means schools were having to trim elsewhere.

PPTA president, Chris Abercrombie told Checkpoint the ministry was "washing its hands" of the issue, and that the funding allocated wasn't covering what was needed by schools.

"[Schools are] making decisions. It could be that the Year 13 class doesn't have a reliever if the teacher's away, that you don't get to have that field trip because we can't find relief, we can't pay for it.

"Or that other teachers are having to give up their non-contact time to cover classes because we can't just can't get relievers."

Abercrombie said while schools were telling him different things, the struggle to provide relief was consistent across the board.

In urban areas, competition to secure a reliever was difficult, with some booked up weeks or even months in advance, while smaller communities were struggling to find any cover at all.

Abercrombie said he had heard of some schools using teacher aides or support staff to cover classes by getting them a limited authority to teach.

"That's just a stopgap solution, it's not actually a long-term plan to support the workforce."

Abercrombie said the root of the issue was schools not being given enough funding in the first place.

"Schools are just not given enough money for their day-to-day running. They're about 12 percent below inflation over the last four years, five years. So they're running on empty basically."

Teacher shortages were also an issue, with relievers being used to plug gaps where full-time staff couldn't be found.

"You need to cover for a month because the teacher we're bringing in from overseas can't get in yet, or we actually haven't found anyone for this position. So that takes them away from that relief pool, that day-to-day relief pool, and that puts again more pressure on the system in general ... we just don't have enough teachers."

Abercrombie said a lack of workforce planning from the government made it impossible to say how many teachers would be needed in the future, putting pressure on the whole system.

Without overseas teachers plugging some of the gaps, Abercrombie said the system "would have collapsed".

With competition for relievers so tight some schools had stopped offering teachers annual leave, Abercrombie said.

"Schools say we will only cover if you're sick or have illness in the home and so that does, again, put pressure on teachers. The burnout is real, especially as you're covering for other teachers."

Other schools had opted to hire a permanent reliever, something Abercrombie said was an expensive and unsustainable solution.

He said if the issue was going to be solved, operations costs needed to be increased.

"It needs to be immediate 12 percent [increase] to just keep up with inflation.

World.title: Power player banned for six AFL matches for betting on games
World.content:
Port Adelaide footballer Josh Sinn has been suspended for six AFL matches for betting on league games, one of which involved his own club.

The AFL said Sinn placed bets totalling $195 on four matches, including one involving the Power.

But Sinn, who missed the season due to injury, did not play in the game.

The four bets were uncovered by an AFL Integrity Unit investigation and were placed between April 25 and May 2.

All were unsuccessful, according to the league, which said Sinn was "not found to have used any inside information in placing the bets".

Sinn has been banned from the opening six rounds of next year's AFL season, but will be allowed to play in practice and pre-season matches, as well as SANFL games that coincide with the AFL's rounds five and six.

Alcohol and gambling ads 'deeply embedded' in AFL Every NRL and AFL club has an alcohol sponsor this season while every NRL and five AFL clubs are sponsored by gambling companies, a new report has found.

The league said Sinn had admitted to the breach and apologised to both it and the Power.

AFL chief operating officer Tom Harley said that, in determining the penalty, the league had "taken into account that [Sinn] did not play in any of the matches involved and was not found to have used inside information".

"Josh has admitted the conduct, accepted responsibility and expressed remorse," Harley said in a statement.

"Players know they cannot bet on AFL matches. Betting on a match involving your own club and teammates is particularly serious and, in this case, materially increased the sanction."

At a media conference this afternoon, Power CEO Matthew Richardson said the club was "extremely disappointed in Josh".

He said the club was first informed of the matter halfway through the year.

"We were first advised late in June, and that investigation was completed late last week," Richardson said.

"Josh is a young man who has made a very poor decision. Josh appreciates that, he's owning that.

"Our focus will be absolutely on supporting Josh as he now undertakes further education around gambling, and we'll support him in rebuilding his trust with our playing group, with our football club and with the community more broadly."

The league said Sinn would be required to undergo additional education to the gambling harm training that players received.

Richardson said the AFL had conducted a "really detailed investigation" into the breaches, which he described as "disappointing" and "stupid".

"What I do know is that the AFL have got really sophisticated tracking mechanisms," he said.

"The integrity of our game is paramount, but people make mistakes, and that's what's happened here. It's a serious mistake, hence the penalty."

World.title: The longer-term thinking driving Swimming Australia's newest event
World.content:
Swim GP's Melbourne debut ticked plenty of boxes at the weekend.

A whole bevvy of happy swimmers and cheery coaches who were clearly fully invested in the contest, competing in front of packed stands, with plenty viewing at home too.

But Swimming Australia chief executive Rob Woodhouse says this is only the start.

"Overall, [we're] really pleased," Woodhouse told ABC Sport, post the inaugural event.

"The two most pleasing aspects were the reaction and the buy-in from the athletes and coaches themselves … and the crowds.

Cheering fans were fully invested in the teams during the inaugural Swim GP. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"It's pretty rare that we can encourage and get young fans of swimming … getting them in the stands so they can watch the races and they can cheer and they can have their favourite team and favourite colours and things like that.

How Swim GP may have given a glimpse of the future of para-sport Swim GP's all-action, high-octane racing is designed to provide a boost for Australia's swimmers in the lead-up to LA28 and Brisbane 2032, and puts para-swimming front and centre.

"The reaction in the actual venue of the crowd, and a really good young crowd, was terrific. That's what we're aiming to do."

More than 3,500 supporters enjoyed the inaugural event live at the Melbourne Sports and Aquatics Centre in Albert Park, with Saturday night's session a complete sellout.

The made-for-TV event was also a boost for Channel Nine, who helped to develop the event, with Swimming Australia saying it achieved a peak reach of 1.13 million people, and an average audience of 237,000 for Friday night's offering.

In the currency of the modern media landscape, almost 3 million social media views sealed the deal for what was a productive evening all round.

It certainly went some way to help cement the current crop of Dolphins as celebrities in their own right, ahead of a huge six years of sport that culminates with the Brisbane 2032 Olympics.

A ready-made fan base

The fans embraced the swimmers in Melbourne. ( Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Swimming Australia made no secret of its aim to targeting a younger age group, between five and 15 years of age, to build its athletes' brand — and it has a ready-made fan base that already exists in plain sight.

Three of the four teams: Kingtide, Wahoo and Kraken were partnered with swim-school providers Carlile, Rackley and GoSwim/Belgravia respectively, who have around 200 learn-to-swim schools around the country.

Woodhouse confirmed that integrating the estimated 600,000 families and 1 million kids who are involved in learn-to-swim programs with the Dolphins was a key part of the organisation's wider strategy leading into Brisbane 2032.

Swimming Australia wants its learn-to-swim participants to learn to love the sport. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"The wider message is about the industry and us and our athletes, Paralympic and Olympic athletes, engaging all the way down to learn-to-swim level," Woodhouse explained.

"If you get kids picking up a ball at four or five years of age then they're probably going to get hooked and join [a football team].

"In swimming we should be in the retention game, not the recruitment game.

"These providers like Rackley and Carlisle and Belgravia, getting them involved with this event they'll start, through those respective teams, to build a far greater awareness of Swim GP, of the teams and of the athletes, which brings in the younger fans.

"If we can build all of that fandom in the lead up to Brisbane '32, then we're going to be in a lot better position in five or six years."

Swim GP shone a spotlight on Australia's Dolphins. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Then there's the question of keeping athletes in the sport for as long as possible to spread important water safety messages.

"Certainly we have a long-term vision of Swimming Australia to be able to have athletes on contract where we're able to pay them to be ambassadors for, not just for the sport and swimming for Australia at Paralympics and at Olympics, but to actually be the custodians of those really important messages of drowning prevention and swimming safe," Woodhouse said.

"If we start doing that and keep kids in the sport longer, not about racing or anything like that, but just that fun element, then we're going to get the natural flow of all kids joining clubs and then going potentially into that pathway of competitive swimming and building up into higher performance pathways.

"It's a big flow-on effect, but it's a system-wide integration … being able to engage with everyone in the industry for the benefit of everyone, particularly for the kids."

Learnings from the ISL and ahead to LA28

Swimming Australia wants its swimmers exposed to big crowds in the lead up to LA. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Swim GP is not a new concept, with Woodhouse leaning on his experiences with the International Swimming League (ISL), where he was chief executive of the London Roar franchise.

Woodhouse said there were discussions to get an Australia-based franchise into the league before it ran into a litany of problems, headlined by COVID.

That was enough to suggest Australia was ready for its own version of the competition, that and the prospect that Australia will become the centre of the swimming world in the coming years.

"I'm very confident, and our team are very confident, that Australia will become the centralised location for elite swimming between 2028 and 2032," Woodhouse said.

"Just as we want our athletes to go and get experience in California and race in LA, as they've done this year and last year ahead of the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games, a lot of the other athletes from around the world are going to want to come to Australia to compete, to acclimatise, to train and things like that.

Australia is primed to be the centre of the swimming world in the coming years. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"So we've got two or three years to build the models from Swim GP, but I actually believe we've got enough talent and big names here in Australia to build it without any international athletes.

"Then, if internationals do want to come after the '28 Olympics and Paralympics and compete with us, then obviously they'd be welcomed.

"But we've got a strong enough base of athletes here to make it a big success."

Part of that involves moving the competition around to different cities, perhaps by having a series of two or three meetings take place around the country.

And although this was "pressure-free" competition, with no emphasis on times of making squads, there is also a high performance element at play.

Although Swim GP was fun, coaches want to up the pressure. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"Both our head coaches, [Paralympic head coach] Mel Tantrum and [Olympic head coach] Rowan Taylor [said] they absolutely want a packed stadium for our trials," Woodhouse said.

"The [LA28] Olympic team, they're competing at SoFi Stadium, 40,000 screaming Americans, while the Paralympic team will be down at Long Beach with 4,000 or 5,000 fans.

"Particularly for the Para-athletes, some of those athletes do have sensory issues, so for them to have some experience coming out to all of that noise and those bright flashing lights and all those sorts of things is really, really important.

"[The crowd in LA] will make a hell of a lot of noise and it's very intimidating," Woodhouse, who has experience to lean on as a bronze medallist in the 400m IM at the last LA Games in 1984, continued.

"There are different pressures, of course; this was all about fun and entertainment. But there are those really important experiential benefits for them as well."

World.title: Melbourne Cup runner So You Are found in Sydney skip bin
World.content:
Melbourne Cup runner So You Are has been found in a Sydney skip after it died from a severe bout of colic.

Sydney man Gregg Jowett released a video on social media on Monday after he discovered a horse in a skip at Lucas Heights. The horse appeared to share the markings of So You Are, which finished eighth in this year's Melbourne Cup.

On Tuesday REC Equine Specialists confirmed the horse in Mr Jowett's video was So You Are, who died on Monday.

Trainer Bjorn Baker said he expected a full explanation from REC Equine Specialists about how and why the horse's remains ended up in a skip bin.

"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said.

"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserves to be treated with respect and dignity after his death.

"I understand the specialist hospital facility REC Equine Specialists are investigating the circumstances, and I expect a full explanation of what occurred.

"My thoughts remain with the Ramsey family [owners], and with all my staff, for whom this has compounded an already devastating loss."

Video of So You Are in a skip bin, filmed by Sydney resident Gregg Jowett, has rocked the racing industry. (Facebook: Gregg Jowett)

REC Equine Specialists released a statement extending its deepest sympathy to the owners, trainer, and connections of So You Are, unreservedly apologising for the distress the video caused.

"On Monday 16 November, So You Are was brought into our hospital for emergency treatment of severe colic," REC Equine Specialists said in a statement.

"Despite the best efforts of our veterinary team, he could not be saved and was humanely euthanased under anaesthesia.

"After his death, So You Are was collected by our contracted service provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried," it said.

"What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone else who cared for him. We are deeply sorry."

REC said it was not responsible for the burial of So You Are, but said it should have known how the horse was handled after leaving its care.

"So You Are was in our care. We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that," it said.

"We should have known exactly how horses were handled after leaving our hospital, and we did not. That process is not good enough, and it must change.

"We have spoken with So You Are's owners and trainer to apologise personally. We are working with our service provider and the facility operators, together with Racing NSW, to establish how this happened and to put in processes to ensure it never happens again."

So You Are died from colic 13 days after running in the 2026 Melbourne Cup. (Getty Images: Racing Photos/George Sal)

So You Are had a successful spring, winning four times including a trio of Group 3 races at Rosehill, Randwick and the Bendigo Cup.

The five-year-old finished eighth in the Melbourne Cup, won by Point Of Law.

REC said it would no longer use the service provider and was reviewing how service providers it contracted cared for horses after death, from collection to final burial.

It said it would share the findings with Racing NSW.

Waste management company Cleanaway, which runs the Lucas Heights landfill, said So You Are's body had been moved to a skip bin in a permitted area of the site.

"Cleanaway's Lucas Heights landfill is licensed to accept and dispose of animal carcasses," a spokesperson said.

"The horse carcass delivered to the facility arrived in a small tipper truck, which is not permitted on the landfill tipping face for safety reasons.

"In accordance with established procedures, the carcass was transferred into a skip bin to enable its safe disposal at the landfill."

'Distressing and completely unacceptable'

The fallout from the distressing footage of deceased Melbourne Cup runner So You Are in a skip bin has been immediate.

ABC Sport understands that interim Racing NSW boss Graeme Hinton is working to create new industry standards to ensure animals are provided with dignity and respect after their death.

It is understood the new standards will be released at the end of the month.

Racehorse So You Are dies of colic Trainer Bjorn Baker says the five-year-old horse, which finished eighth in the Melbourne Cup, was rushed to hospital but died following a severe bout of colic.

Racing NSW released a statement saying So You Are was awaiting burial when the video was recorded, and that it would conduct an investigation.

"The way in which So You Are's body was left is distressing and completely unacceptable. So You Are deserved to be treated with dignity and respect," the statement said.

"Under NSW Department of Primary Industries guidelines, a licensed landfill is the preferred option for animals who have died via euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process.

"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner.

"If through the course of our ongoing investigation any wrongdoing is found, Racing NSW will not hesitate to take appropriate action."

Animal Justice Party NSW Upper House MP Emma Hurst held a press conference in Sydney following the treatment of So You Are.

She said the news was "absolutely heartbreaking", but not surprising.

"This horse has been treated as though he is nothing more than a piece of rubbish," she said.

"To be completely honest, I'm not entirely surprised. We've had complaints about the racing industry for the entire eight years that I have been in parliament," she said.

"There are serious questions around the entire racing industry, and this most recent incident just raises more questions."

She called for greater transparency and accountability within the racing industry and called on the state government for further action.

World.title: Wallabies in danger of missing 'big three' target
World.content:
Coach Les Kiss is determined to ensure Australia finishes among the top three Southern Hemisphere teams in the Nations Championship after a rare weekend blowout for the Wallabies, All Blacks and Springboks.

For only the second time in rugby history, all of the "big three" were turned over on the same weekend by Northern Hemisphere opposition as South Africa lost 21-19 in France, New Zealand were sensationally beaten 35-28 in Wales and Australia lost narrowly 15-12 to Scotland at Murrayfield.

That had only previously occurred in July 2022, when all three suffered home defeats: New Zealand losing 23-12 to Ireland in Dunedin, South Africa going down 13-12 to Wales in Bloemfontein and Australia falling 25-17 to England in Brisbane.

Now, Australia has fallen to fourth in the Southern Hemisphere table of the Nations Championship, leapfrogged by Argentina, and should the Wallabies succumb to a fifth-straight Test defeat against Wales on Saturday, it will finish in that position.

Should Argentina upset France, even a Wallabies win would not be enough to claw them back to that third spot.

Wallabies attacking woes The Wallabies once again show precious little in an attacking sense, as Scotland edge a "turgid" encounter at Murrayfield.

But Kiss made it clear this would represent failure for a team that had come on its British sojourn seeking a top-three finish.

"We were aiming for the top-three when we came here, New Zealand and South Africa already being up there and going to be hard to reel in," Kiss said.

"So we were aiming for the top-three for sure, and that's what we'll measure ourselves on."

It is still only halfway through the tour, but the grim scenario of a second-straight European wipe-out looms following defeats in England, Italy, Ireland and France last year, the first time in 67 years that such a whitewash had occurred.

Les Kiss has watched his Wallabies side lose four Tests on the trot. (Getty Images: Stu Forster)

Asked if the Wallabies had lost their confidence, Kiss mused: "Yeah, you do want a team with a bit of swagger. There's been losses throughout the last few years that have seemed to hang on, that's for sure.

"I wouldn't say it's confidence, I wouldn't say it's just belief. I think it's a mixture of those things coming together and it's just down to them believing that they can now win those big moments."

He referred to that last-second burst down the right touchline on Sunday, when Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Max Jorgensen and Tom Wright could not quite turn the break into a match-winning moment.

"The losses obviously takes its toll but, mate, they're hardy and they're going to continue to work hard," Kiss said.

It all gives Saturday's Test against a Welsh side currently residing on cloud nine even more of a "must-win" feel.

Wales beat All Blacks Wales has pulled off one of the greatest wins in its recent history, beating the All Blacks for the first time in 73 years in a Nations Championship boilover.

Captain Harry Wilson counters: "Every Test match is must-win. We're going to go into the Wales game with the same attitude we do every time. We need a win. We're going to do everything in our power to make sure we can."

But Kiss admitted the incredible Welsh win over the All Blacks, their first in 73 years, had "changed everyone's minds" about Steve Tandy's reinvented team.

"Honestly, it was compelling. It was phenomenal what they did. So we're going to need to be good to go there on a short turnaround."

But could Australia be facing a side with energy levels zapped from their legs after throwing themselves into a record-breaking 346 tackles against New Zealand? Kiss just smiled: "Nah, they'll be energised. That's inspiring what they did, isn't it?

"We've just got to make sure we've got our reason to be up for it too, which is that it's a bloody important Test match to win."

AAP

World.title: Khawaja avoids sandpaper questions on first TV appearance since 7.30
World.content:
Usman Khawaja has avoided being asked about Sandpapergate in his first television appearance since last week's refusal to fully answer questions on the ABC.

After cancelling some interviews with mainstream media outlets last week during his tour to promote his autobiography Sabr, Khawaja appeared on Channel 10's Sam Pang Tonight on Monday.

The Gold Logie-winning host asked the former opener about everything from his relationship with David Warner to how he proposed to wife, Rachel.

Khawaja opens up on racism, mental health Usman Khawaja speaks about the racist stereotyping he faced and his early mental health struggles coping with cricket failures.

But conspicuously absent were any questions about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, Khawaja's claims the entire team knew of the plot, or Pat Cummins's denial and 70-minute response last Friday.

Instead, the closest the conversation veered towards ball tampering came when Pang flashed the first page of the sandpaper book chapter, then asked about Will Smith references in it.

Other topics covered included growing up in Pakistan, perfecting the pull shot, and Khawaja feeling Adam Zampa's behind during the national anthem in 2016.

On the topic of his friendship with Warner, Khawaja said the pair were "yin and yang".

"Me and Davey are very different people," Khawaja said. "But when it comes to a lot of things like family, values and how we look after everyone …

"People don't see that side of him, and that's the side that connects us."

Khawaja spoke about his friendship with David Warner. (Getty Image: Alex Davidson, ICC)

Khawaja has previously stated that his Sandpapergate revelations came as a result of promising Warner he would tell the full story of the 2018 saga, which Cricket Australia initially deemed only Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft knew about.

Monday night's interview was in contrast to Khawaja's 12-minute grilling from Sarah Ferguson on ABC's 7:30 last Tuesday, when the opener dodged questions on the matter.

Pang and guest co-host Dave Lawson joked later in Monday's show that he "probably should have gone harder on the whole sandpaper gag thing".

Khawaja is still yet to fully respond to Cummins's denials, but did admit on a podcast recorded last Wednesday and released on Monday that he had to weigh up the damage his claims may cause to ex-teammates.

"I have stood up for three guys I feel like were treated unfairly," Khawaja said on the They Used To Be podcast, referring to Warner, Smith and Bancroft's 2018 suspensions.

"But there are other guys that are still playing in the team right now that there might be some sort of cost. I have tried my best to balance that out."

Khawaja is due to go on The Grade Cricketer podcast on Thursday, before an awkward reunion looms with former coach Darren Lehmann at the Gold Clash celebrity cricket match in Cairns on Sunday.

Lehmann last week rejected any suggestion he or his entire team knew about the use of sandpaper and suggested Khawaja was "trying to sell a book".

Usman Khawaja during his interview on 7.30. (ABC News)

The issue also appears unlikely to fade away quickly, with Bancroft considering speaking publicly in the coming days for the first time since Khawaja's revelations.

Khawaja spoke to Bancroft before the release of his book, which contains claims a coach told Bancroft to ramp up his ball management before Khawaja saw Bancroft place sandpaper in his pocket.

Warner has labelled Khawaja's claims about the scandal "100 per cent accurate". Paceman Mitchell Starc is aligned with Cummins's version of events.

Meanwhile, Steve Smith is now no longer expected to speak on the matter before Sunday's return from a neck injury in the Sheffield Shield, ahead of next month's first Test against New Zealand.

AAP

World.title: Popovic admits Socceroos future uncertain after Asian Cup postponement
World.content:
Tony Popovic has suggested his time in charge of the Socceroos is not over, saying he would be hard pressed to find a job that gives him as much satisfaction as coaching Australia.

Popovic's future has been a topic of hot debate since the delay of January's Asian Cup by 11 months due to the conflict in host nation Saudi Arabia.

The 53-year-old is without a contract beyond Wednesday's (AEDT) friendly with Jordan, which was relocated to Doha after Socceroos players raised security concerns.

"I don't expect it to be the last game, but you never know," Popovic said.

"As it stands, it is, with the Asian Cup postponement."

Popovic turned down a new four-year deal with Football Australia (FA) on the eve of the World Cup this year.

He instead committed to a short-term deal that ran until the end of the Asian Cup. But the tournament's delay has prompted a stand-off over which way the federation goes next.

Tony Popovic is yet to discuss a new contract with FA. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

The initial signs according to FA sources are that the governing body wants Popovic to stay, despite fellow coaches Kevin Muscat being off contract and John Aloisi being out of a job following his sacking by Chinese Super League side Chengdu Rongcheng.

FA chief executive Martin Kuegeler has been in the Middle East in the past week but has yet to sit down with Popovic and go through further details.

Socceroos crush Qatar The Socceroos have enjoyed an emphatic victory in the stronghold of the Asian champions, defeating Qatar 3-0 in Doha.

"We never had any plans to discuss my future during this period," Popovic said.

"So the Asian Cup postponement doesn't change that and I'm sure that'll all happen in the next couple of months."

Popovic, who boasts a record of 12 wins, six draws and seven losses in charge of Australia, had never coached a national team before succeeding Graham Arnold in 2024.

"I don't think I could ever have a job that would be as good as the one I have now," he said.

"I'm in such a privileged position, I don't take it for granted and I'm very grateful.

"I'm coaching my country, the Socceroos, and it doesn't get better than this, so I don't think I'll ever have something that feels as special as this.

"But I also know football things change, whether you have a contract or not."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Arrest over Melbourne Cup theft but trophies still missing
World.content:
A man has been arrested over the theft of three Melbourne Cup trophies won by racehorse Makybe Diva, but the trophies remain missing.

The three cups were stolen from a cabinet at Flemington Racecourse about 6:30am yesterday.

It is believed two men dressed in high-vis broke into the racecourse and stole the trophies from a cabinet where they were displayed.

Victoria Police said a 36-year-old man from Malvern East was arrested after police raided a property at Mount Waverley last night.

The man has been interviewed and released pending summons.

The trophies are yet to be recovered and the investigation is ongoing.

The three Melbourne Cup trophies are valued at $1 million each.

The trophies were stolen from a cabinet at Flemington Racecourse. (ABC News)

Yesterday, Tony Santic, who owned Makybe Diva, said he was "totally devastated" by the theft.

"They were irreplaceable … I just want them back in one piece," Santic said.

" Please just give the cups back. Put them somewhere and let the police know where they are and all's forgiven on my part. "

In a statement, Victoria Racing Club said it was "devastated by the incident".

The cups had been on display at the racecourse for the Spring Racing Carnival since September.

Makybe Diva is the only horse to have won the famous race in three consecutive years, each time being ridden by jockey Glen Boss.

The champion racehorse died earlier this year at the age of 27 after a short battle with the gastrointestinal condition colic.

World.title: Tasmania seeks more stadium money amid cost blowout concerns
World.content:
The Tasmanian government has begun the process of canvassing financial partners to help fund its Macquarie Point stadium, as the $1.13 billion project faces a budget crunch.

The ABC understands preliminary discussions have been held with a number of parties, including the AFL, regarding the prospect of an increased financial contribution towards the stadium, as the government prepares to sign a potential billion-dollar building contract with BESIX Watpac.

The stadium's construction was a condition of Tasmania being granted entry to the AFL. (Supplied: Cox Architecture)

Early informal conversations have also been held between Premier Jeremy Rockliff and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, while private money is also being discussed.

The premier is also aware of cricket's potential role in bringing private money to the project.

But just how much money, if any, the government may be able to secure from the private sector, the AFL and the federal government remains unclear.

The pursuit comes as the stadium project stares down a funding gap, with state funding capped at $875 million, and the project's $1.13 billion cost seemingly in jeopardy.

Anne Beach and Jeremy Rockliff at the stadium construction site in July. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

BESIX Watpac delivered its final fixed-price lump sum number to the Macquarie Point Development Corporation (MPDC) on Friday last week.

But any hope that the stadium project might be completed within its $1.13 billion budget received a blow when development corporation head Anne Beach told a parliamentary committee this month that she was preparing to make a submission to cabinet regarding the project's parameters, which included delivery timelines and overall cost.

The ABC understands the government has been preparing for a cost blowout since at least August, following the submission of tenders by prospective builders.

The OneNZ Stadium at Te Kaha, a project by successful Hobart stadium tenderers, BESIX Watpac. (Supplied: onenewzealandstadium.co.nz)

Approaches to AFL

The ABC can reveal that on August 28 Tasmanian Treasurer and Macquarie Point Urban Renewal Minister Eric Abetz met with the AFL's executive general manager of infrastructure, clubs and finance, Matthew Chun.

The meeting took place two weeks after tenders from the two stadium bidders were received, and in the midst of a technical, commercial and governance assessment of the project.

It was a departure from other progress meetings between the government and the AFL, and the first time the treasurer had met one-on-one with the league's finance boss to discuss the stadium.

It was also particularly timely.

According to the "stadium spending cap" section of the government's stadium "safeguarding commitments" document, which was updated in September, August was earmarked as a "key checkpoint on any threshold budget issues".

Hobart stadium facing 'cost pressures' With an updated price tag for Hobart's AFL stadium expected to be released by the end of the year, the Tasmanian premier has skirted around questions on whether he would limit Tasmania's contribution.

In response to specific questions regarding whether a greater financial contribution had been sought from the AFL, a government spokesperson did not respond directly.

The spokesperson said the meeting between Mr Abetz and Mr Chun "provided an opportunity to provide an update on the project and hear the AFL's perspective on progress".

Mr Chun is also the AFL's representative on the Macquarie Point stadium steering committee.

Eric Abetz (left) has met with the AFL about the stadium project. (ABC News: Mackenzie Archer)

Three other meetings between the government and AFL have taken place this year — in March, April and July.

All involved Mr Rockliff, with one an introductory meeting between the premier and incoming AFL chairman Craig Drummond.

Those meetings focused on the progress of the Tasmania Devils Football Club, rather than specifically about the stadium.

The AFL is already contributing $15 million towards the Macquarie Point stadium, and a further $10 million to the Tasmania Devils Training and Administration facility in Kingborough.

The ABC asked the AFL whether the government had sought extra funds from it, and whether the league was considering providing it with extra financial assistance.

An AFL spokesperson said: "The Tasmania Devils Football Club and Macquarie Point stadium continue to make great progress ahead of the Devils' inaugural AFL season in 2028."

It is understood Jeremy Rockliff informally raised the prospect with Anthony Albanese of more federal money for the project. (ABC News: Jessica Moran)

Rockliff sounds out Commonwealth

The hunt for more stadium money ramped up in September, when the premier flew to Canberra to meet with Mr Albanese and Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles, where the new AFL team and stadium were on the agenda.

The trip coincided with the launch of the Parliamentary Friends of the Tasmania Devils group, which saw Devils bosses Brendon Gale, Grant O'Brien and Kath McCann also travel to Canberra for a meet-and-greet with a number of Tasmanian federal politicians, as well as a meeting with the deputy prime minister, where the stadium was discussed.

It is understood Mr Rockliff informally raised the prospect with Mr Albanese of the federal government contributing more money to the Macquarie Point project over and above the $240 million it has already committed, as part of a meeting about general Tasmanian matters.

An artist's impression of the planned playing surface at the Macquarie Point roofed stadium. (Supplied: MPDC)

Publicly, the federal government has insisted its contribution is capped, but it is understood that privately, the idea of contributing further funds towards broader precinct costs at Macquarie Point has not been completely dismissed.

However, it is understood no formal request or commitment has been made.

In a statement, a Tasmanian government spokesperson said it "continues to engage with its funding partners on the Macquarie Point Multipurpose Stadium and the broader precinct".

Stadium could get private funding

Private money is also on the table, with cricket looming as a dark horse in the search for extra funds to help pay for the stadium.

At least one prospective buyer of the Hobart Hurricanes Big Bash team, which could be partially sold via Cricket Australia's Big Bash League (BBL) privatisation process, is attracted by the prospect of investing in the project, the ABC understands.

Prior to the Canberra trip, Mr Rockliff discussed the prospect of private money for Macquarie Point in a meeting with Cricket Tasmania boss Dominic Baker and chair Tim Scott.

The meeting took place on September 8, the same day Cricket Australia publicly announced it would invite private investment into the BBL.

The seating at OneNZ Stadium, a project by Macquarie Point tender winner, BESIX Watpac. (Supplied: onenewzealandstadium.co.nz)

Any potential stadium cost blowouts would need a creative solution, as the state government previously agreed to a state funding cap for the project in order to secure enough votes for it to pass parliament.

The cap was a condition of upper house independent MLC Bec Thomas, ahead of last year's crucial parliamentary vote.

As part of that agreement, the government was to seek any additional funds required from external partners, namely the AFL, federal government and Cricket Australia if it was in danger of breaching the cap.

With state parliament adjourning next week, a number of crossbench MPs have written to the premier and the Labor opposition leader calling for an extension of sitting days this year so the stadium's final cost can be scrutinised.

Tech.title: Hacker behind 2022 GTA VI leaks pleads guilty
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

GTA VI: all the news on Rockstar’s next entry in the Grand Theft Auto series

Arion Kurtaj, a member of the Lapsus$ cybercrime group who leaked 90 videos of Grand Theft Auto VI in 2022 and hacked other big companies, pleaded guilty on Monday, according to the UK’s Crown Prosecution Service (CPS).

Kurtaj, who is now 21, hacked BT/EE sometime between August and November 2021, and starting in early November of that year, the company “noted a marked increase in unauthorised SIM swaps of their customers mobile phones.” He was charged for those offenses and moved to a hotel for his “own protection” in September 2022, but “breached his bail conditions to carry out further hacks on major companies using a mobile phone, the hotel TV’s Wi-Fi and a firestick,” including hacks on Rockstar Games, Uber, and Revolut, the CPS says.

He was sentenced to life in a secure hospital in December 2023 because of his autism, but in January, Kurtaj was deemed fit for trial and moved to prison, the BBC reports.

Kurtaj is set to be sentenced on November 23rd. GTA VI will be released on November 19th.

Tech.title: Tech leaders are convinced that Jensen Huang’s exit was a plot against him
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation from Nvidia after more than 33 years has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry. Now prominent figures are calling for Huang’s reinstatement, and many are also hopping on board with a theory spreading throughout Silicon Valley: that the scandal is the result of a plot against the former CEO.

David Sacks, a venture capitalist and former White House AI crypto advisor, has made it clear that he’s skeptical about The New York Times’ reporting. In a post on X, Sacks points to an article from CNN, which says US officials still can’t confirm that Alice Huang was a spy. “The spy narrative is collapsing already,” Sacks writes. He continued to question the spy allegations during Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event on Monday, saying: “The reason why Jensen lost his job is because of this lurid Chinese spy allegation. So if no one’s willing to back that up now, then again, I question why this entire chain of events happened.”

Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney similarly expressed concern about how Huang’s resignation played out. In a reply to Sacks’ post about the CNN article, Sweeney said, “What?! So journalists with sketchy motives portrayed rumors from god-knows-who (lobbyists?) as facts sourced from intelligence officials and gaslit the NVIDIA board to push out the founder, CEO, and once-in-generation visionary?” Amjad Masad, the CEO of the AI app and website builder Replit, called the timing of Huang’s resignation “suspicious,” adding that “if Jensen, the premier champion of open models, is taken out then anyone who wants AI closed, centralized, and controlled might benefit.”

SemiAnalysis, a research and consulting firm for the semiconductor and AI industry, posted a “conspiracy theory take on the situation,” speculating that Huang’s removal is a way to “remove opposition to an extremely hawkish China export control bill,” referring to the Remote Access Security Act (RASA). The bill, which Huang opposed, would extend AI export controls to cloud servers that allow companies in restricted countries to rent access to Nvidia’s AI chips. The Department of Commerce released an interim final rule on Monday in an attempt to address this loophole.

More than 185,000 people, including Sweeney, Masad, Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, have signed a “Stand with Jensen” letter, calling for his reinstatement as CEO. The letter similarly calls for a closer look into the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy,” the letter says. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership. The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed.”

Tech.title: United Airlines system outage disrupts departures just days after the big ground stop
Tech.content:
is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Less than a week after an issue with air traffic control communications and radar caused the FAA to halt takeoffs nationwide, United Airlines departing flights are being disrupted by an outage. At 6:13PM ET, United said the problem has been fixed:

Earlier today we experienced a technology-related issue that impacted some departing flights. The issue has been resolved. Please check the latest status of your flight at united.com or the United app.

The outage is also coming after last week’s global Microsoft Outlook shutdown, and the great-bank-outage-that-wasn’t earlier Monday afternoon. According to posts on social media, a number of people onboard the planes have heard from their pilots that a systemwide IT outage for United has caused problems with a weight and balance calculator that has stopped them from getting clearance to take off.

United tweeted earlier that “We are troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights. There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights.”

Update, November 16th: Added note that United says the problem has been resolved.

Tech.title: In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
Tech.content:
Before Clavicular and other manosphere streamers were introducing young guys to the concept of breaking their facial bones to become more attractive, there was an older generation of creators building massive followings with content focused on chemical biohacking. Were it not for steroid-obsessed influencers like Anthony “Tony Huge” Hughes launching YouTube channels over a decade ago, looksmaxxing might not have become such a prominent part of the digital media landscape in 2026. These creators became internet famous by presenting themselves as peak male specimens. But their larger-than-life online personas often concealed the truth about how sinister and toxic this kind of influencing can really be.

Hughes is the gravitational center of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death — Hulu’s new three-part docuseries from director Stacey Lee. The series is both a deep dive into Hughes’ strange life and a fascinating exploration of how perilous the creator economy can be in the age of manosphere and looksmaxxing influencers. Through Hughes’ ever-expanding orbit of creators, Lee is able to highlight how lonely, impressionable men are all too easily radicalized by what they see and post online. And it makes clear that all these men are trapped in a deadly psychological prison of their own making.

Get Huge takes some time to touch on Hughes’ former life as a bankruptcy lawyer and supplement salesman who was investigated by the FDA for hawking unapproved performance-enhancing drugs. But most of the series takes place in Pattaya, Thailand, where Hughes spends his days producing content showcasing his extravagant life of nonstop partying and injecting substances that swell his muscles to huge proportions. Hughes takes pride in his image as a man with access to a harem of women, and the fact that his money gives him power over many of the people around him. He presents himself as the ruler of a small kingdom — and his entire brand is built on the idea that he can show people how to become more like him.

The men caught in Hughes’ aspirational fantasy aren’t just stateside fans who’ll never reach his muscle-y heights. He is also marketing himself to other established bodybuilding influencers who might be interested in joining his inner circle by following him to Thailand. These include a menagerie of biohacking / manosphere influencers who became vital parts of Hughes’ operation over the years. Leo Longevity (legal name Laith Abdallah Algaz), Elon Muscular (his legal name isn’t revealed), and Connor Murphy all built sizable social media presences of their own. But they were each compelled to move to Pattaya and join Hughes’ entourage by a powerful desire to feel connected to something larger and more fulfilling than their individual followings.

As Get Huge features clips of Hughes’ videos — the bulk of which are now only featured on Rumble and X following multiple account bans on YouTube and TikTok — you can see that he’s trying to sell his audience on his highly specific way of life. Hughes’ own videos make it seem like he’s living his dream surrounded by people who revere him. But with each interview, Get Huge makes it clear that for all of his posturing, Hughes has been living in something of a nightmare — one where many of his disciples have died under mysterious circumstances.

As these men explain why they were drawn to Hughes, you get the sense that looksmaxxing culture is a direct response to the widespread disaffection that followed the last decade of interconnected societal shifts, from the #MeToo movement to Donald Trump’s presidencies. Hughes seems very much like an entrepreneur profiting from men’s loneliness by convincing them that their lives would be better if they were part of his community. As Get Huge first maps out Hughes’ friendships, they all appear to be anchored by an odd, sometimes envious, but genuine kind of intimacy. But as the documentary digs deeper into its subjects’ lives, it becomes hard to see them as anything but emotionally stunted men who perform cartoonish masculinity for one another in ways that are psychologically unhealthy and, at times, physically dangerous.

Image: Hulu

Part of what makes Get Huge such an unsettling watch is how relatively calm and collected Hughes and the other interviewees are as they begin to discuss how many people in their circle have died in recent years. Hughes and Murphy grow closer as friends following Algaz’s death in 2023, but they seem to bond by making Algaz the butt of the joke in content produced after his death. Simply by letting these men speak frankly about their social dynamics, Get Huge reveals the manosphere as a space in which connections built on mogging and the objectification of women can quickly deteriorate into infighting and petty jealousy. Elon Muscular readily speculates that Murphy might have had something to do with Algaz’s death because Murphy openly jokes about it. And the entire situation becomes that much stranger and more grim when Get Huge reveals that Murphy drowned shortly after the series initially wrapped filming.

Though the deaths in Hughes’ circle bring a dark whodunit energy to Get Huge, the documentary emphasizes how much peril comes as a part of existing in the looksmaxxing space. Rather than trying to solve the mystery of how Algaz died, the docuseries presents his story as a cautionary tale. He’s an object lesson in how this lifestyle can warp a person’s perception of reality in a way that ultimately cuts them off from the kind of help they really need.

What might be most disturbing about Get Huge is the way it ends. The series follows Hughes to a youth bodybuilding event where he talks up his less-than-legal products to a new group of boys — some as young as 13. To keep his momentum going, Hughes has to appeal to a new, younger audience that doesn’t understand how everything about looksmaxxing is a performance. Though the docuseries gives you the distinct impression that people like Murphy and Algaz felt a true belonging with Hughes, its closing shots call into question how genuine any of his connections with other bodybuilders really are. By juxtaposing the deaths of Hughes’ adult acolytes with his focus on turning children into fans, Get Huge paints a clear picture of how the manosphere’s promise of emotional connection often ends in a twisted kind of exploitation. And that extractive energy feels foundational to a culture that runs on people turning every aspect of their lives into content.

All three episodes of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death are now streaming on Hulu and Disney Plus.

Tech.title: California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday, Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a “dangerous product without proper oversight,” as reported earlier by Reuters.

The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.” It alleges that OpenAI recently told the attorney general’s office that it “lost control” of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing.

“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.”

OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms. It’s also giving safety evaluators at Apollo Research access to its AI systems as part of a pilot program that monitors models for misalignment.

“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

Tech.title: Sam Altman says he wants everyone ‘to have a lot of RAM’
Tech.content: “The world did not build out that much, and now we have seen DRAM prices — I don’t know exactly, but maybe they went up 5x, 7x, something like that. I think it would be much better if the world just had a lot of memory. That comment, which I think got misinterpreted, but there is a true part of it, which I will stand by is that, if we’re going to be in this memory supply shortage, then in some sense — whether or not we’ll decide to do it, because I think there are other tradeoffs like people having their own at-home inference — the optimal thing would be, can we share this memory and have it working 100 percent of the time rather than sometimes off in someone’s edge device? Again, optimal use of this limited supply. Maybe it’s not the reason to make the decision but that’s what I was trying to say.”
